name: Ambient
desc: Emphasizes texture and tone over traditional musical structure, aimed at evoking a particular atmosphere or mood.

subgenres.name: Ambient Americana
subgenres.desc: Made using traditional Americana and Country instrumentation, typically to evoke a pastoral atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Dark Ambient
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes an ominous, gloomy, and dissonant atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Black Ambient
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements such as guitars, synthesizers, harsh or whispered vocals, raw production, or other elements associated with Black Metal and Dungeon Synth.

subgenres.name: Ritual Ambient
subgenres.desc: Dark, disturbing, ritualistic, and occult atmosphere, often taking inspiration from various existing ritual practices around the world.

subgenres.name: Space Ambient
subgenres.desc: Flowing and relaxing synthesizer-based music derived from Progressive Electronic, often oriented around imagery of outer space.

subgenres.name: Tribal Ambient
subgenres.desc: Combines the theory and atmosphere of Ambient with traditional instruments and sounds from around the globe.

name: Blues
desc: Originated toward the end of the 19th century in African American communities in the United States, particularly the Deep South; drew on traditional Spirituals and Work Song; highly influential to the whole of Western popular music.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed out of Work Song and Spiritual to become the most prominent early form of Blues.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Chicago Blues
subgenres.desc: Unplugged Blues made in the Chicago region, primarily during the 1930s and 1940s.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Jug Band
subgenres.desc: Usually features a jug as the bass instrument as well as other homemade (or easily affordable) instruments, such as kazoos and washboards.

subgenres.name: Piedmont Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.

subgenres.name: Boogie Woogie
subgenres.desc: Early, uptempo Blues featuring the piano as the main instrument, with soloing and improvisation played over the top of a repetitive eight note bassline.

subgenres.name: Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Various styles of Blues originating in the rural US South, typically relying on expressive vocal delivery and featuring simple, usually acoustic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Delta Blues
subgenres.desc: One of the earliest forms of Blues, named for the Mississippi Delta region of the United States where it developed, with a highly rhythmic style and a typical 12-bar structure.

subgenres.name: Bentonia School
subgenres.desc: Brooding, hypnotic minor-key open-tuning guitar style with a looser structure, often featuring high, "haunting" vocals.

subgenres.name: Hill Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a steady hypnotic groove, sparse percussive and highly energetic guitar riffs, and often features meandering structures with unconventional and usually fewer chord changes compared to Delta Blues.

subgenres.name: Piedmont Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.

subgenres.name: Electric Blues
subgenres.desc: Major development in sound and reach of Blues when it became possible to amplify the instruments of small combos.

subgenres.name: British Blues
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by the burgeoning United States Blues scene, particularly Chicago Blues.

subgenres.name: Chicago Blues
subgenres.desc: Heavily inspired by old-time rural blues, transferring it into a small band setup, while maintaining the rough and gritty edges of its ancestry.

subgenres.name: Electric Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Originating in (but not limited to) Texas; includes Jazz influences like Swing rhythms and sometimes the addition of a horn section.

subgenres.name: Swamp Blues
subgenres.desc: Originated in Baton Rouge, Louisiana in the 1950s, with a laid-back and relaxed sound that takes influence from Zydeco and Cajun Music.

subgenres.name: Fife and Drum Blues
subgenres.desc: Rooted in martial Fife and Drum Corps music, originated among Afro-American communities in Mississippi.

subgenres.name: Jump Blues
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1930s with influence from Jazz styles such as Swing and Big Band, featuring fast tempos and raucous performances.

subgenres.name: Piano Blues
subgenres.desc: Features the piano as a lead instrument performed solo or with a small ensemble, ranging from mid-tempo ballads to fast-paced dance styles.

subgenres.name: Soul Blues
subgenres.desc: Shares similarities with Soul and incorporates the eponymous soulful inflections of Gospel, Jump Blues and soul into the vocals.

subgenres.name: Vaudeville Blues
subgenres.desc: Vaudeville incorporating heavy Blues elements.

name: Classical Music
desc: Part of a broad generalization about the structure and function of music throughout history across the globe, describing traditions distinct from Traditional Folk Music and popular music.

subgenres.name: Buganda Royal Court Music
subgenres.desc: Highest traditional and refined musical forms of Buganda, reserved for the Kabaka (the king of Buganda).

subgenres.name: East Asian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Covers all the forms of pan-East Asian Classical Music sharing origins in Chinese Classical Music.

subgenres.name: Chinese Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Classical Music of China, encompassing royal court music.

subgenres.name: Baisha xiyue
subgenres.desc: Mainly performed for funeral ceremonies of the Naxi ethnic group in the Yunnan province in China.

subgenres.name: Chinese Literati Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Chinese literati; primarily played on the guqin and invoking emotional restraint, self-cultivation, and introspection.

subgenres.name: Dongjing
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Chinese Taoist Ritual Music from the Nakhi (Naxi) people, historically performed around Yunnan and Sichuan.

subgenres.name: Yayue
subgenres.desc: Incorporates folk and religious traditions of Chinese Music; literally translated as 'elegant music'.

subgenres.name: Japanese Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Classical music of Japan.

subgenres.name: Gagaku
subgenres.desc: One of the oldest forms of Japanese Classical Music, based on the pentatonic Yo scale, characterized by an elegant sound that is typically solemn, slow-paced, and resonant.

subgenres.name: Heikyoku
subgenres.desc: Semi-classical bardic tradition in Japan analogous to the troubadour music of medieval Europe.

subgenres.name: Honkyoku
subgenres.desc: Japanese Classical Music performed solo on a bamboo flute shakuhachi.

subgenres.name: Jiuta
subgenres.desc: Originally created by solo performers singing and playing shamisen, but since the late 18th century increasingly often performed by sankyoku ensembles (shamisen, koto and shakuhachi or kokyu).

subgenres.name: Jōruri
subgenres.desc: Consists of a singing narrator (tayū) with shamisen accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Meiji shinkyoku
subgenres.desc: Meiji-era compositions, using a distinctive, brighter scale, usually performed with two kotos.

subgenres.name: Nagauta
subgenres.desc: Japanese Classical Music used in Kabuki, a form of theatre oriented to dance-drama.

subgenres.name: Noh
subgenres.desc: Played by an hayashi ensemble, consisting of a fue (flute), a kotsuzumi (shoulder drum), a ōtsuzumi (hip drum), and a taiko (stick drum).

subgenres.name: Shōmyō
subgenres.desc: Japanese Buddhist chant that utilizes the yō scale.

subgenres.name: Sōkyoku
subgenres.desc: Gained popularity during the Edo period, played with a koto or a guzheng and sometimes accompanied by shamisen and/or shakuhachi.

subgenres.name: Danmono
subgenres.desc: Sōkyoku composed for koto, a thirteen-string traditional instrument.

subgenres.name: Kumiuta
subgenres.desc: Typically performed by a single singer playing koto or less often shamisen for accompaniment, often with lyrics adapted from classical poetry.

subgenres.name: Korean Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Classical Music of Korea.

subgenres.name: Aak
subgenres.desc: Korean Classical Music that dates back to the early 12th century.

subgenres.name: Dang-ak
subgenres.desc: Korean Classical Music that dates back to the Later Silla period of 668–935.

subgenres.name: Hyang-ak
subgenres.desc: One of the most common and oldest surviving forms of Korean court music.

subgenres.name: Jeong-ak
subgenres.desc: Also known as proper music; dates back to the Later Silla period of 668–935.

subgenres.name: Gagok
subgenres.desc: Vocal songs derived from Korean Classical Music backed by a small orchestra of Jeong-ak ("aristocratic or proper music").

subgenres.name: Vietnamese Court Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional court music of Vietnam, specifically that of the Nguyễn dynasty.

subgenres.name: Vietnamese Opera
subgenres.desc: Classical musical theatre and its associated form of Vietnamese Court Music, related strongly to Chinese Opera.

subgenres.name: Inkiranya
subgenres.desc: Influential drumming style originating in Burundi carried out by a percussion ensemble.

subgenres.name: Kete
subgenres.desc: Traditional percussive style played at special occasions in the courts of high ranking Asante chieftains.

subgenres.name: Maqāmic Music
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Middle East and founded upon maqāmāt scales, encompassing an extensive and diverse cultural and musical legacy that spans from Morocco to Southeast Asia.

subgenres.name: Arabic Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Arabic Classical Music tradition, whose guidelines for modulation, rhythm, and tuning were set down in treatises in the 8th and 9th centuries, based around Maqāmic Music.

subgenres.name: Andalusian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Arabic Classical Music tradition that had its beginnings in Al-Andalus, the medieval Islamic Iberian peninsula, which later spread and developed in the Maghreb.

subgenres.name: Iraqi Maqam
subgenres.desc: Highly structured but semi-improvised and rhythmically complex compositions built around set structures which consist of specific maqam modes.

subgenres.name: Sawt
subgenres.desc: Poetic vocal form with complex rhythms, emotive singing, and distinctive lute-backed melodies commonly found in the Gulf region and based on a maqam system.

subgenres.name: Azerbaijani Mugham
subgenres.desc: Highly improvisational form of modal music characterized by the singing style and the themes of Azerbaijan’s history.

subgenres.name: Persian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional art music of the Persian civilization.

subgenres.name: Shashmaqam
subgenres.desc: Modal suite that brings together lyrical and instrumental songs, poetry, and dance shared by Tajik Music and Uzbek Music.

subgenres.name: Sufiana kalam
subgenres.desc: Classical music from Kashmir, the northernmost part of the Indian subcontinent.

subgenres.name: Turkish Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Classical music of Turkey, which uses the makam modal system, with the primary emphasis often being on the singers, who are accompanied by small ensembles.

subgenres.name: Turkish Mevlevi Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music performed among Turkish practitioners of the Mevlevi order of Sufism.

subgenres.name: Twelve Muqam
subgenres.desc: Uyghur muqam suite of 12 different muqam performances, originating in Southern Xinjiang.

subgenres.name: Minyue
subgenres.desc: Modernized composition for Chinese instruments on the basis of Chinese Folk Music, incorporating aspects of Western Classical Music.

subgenres.name: Pìobaireachd
subgenres.desc: Art tradition which originated in the Scottish Highlands, usually associated with the Great Highland bagpipes.

subgenres.name: South Asian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre that covers the diverse forms of Classical Music from South Asia.

subgenres.name: Carnatic Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Culture shared by the Dravidian cultures in South India separate from regional folk genres.

subgenres.name: Konnakol
subgenres.desc: Traditional song utilizing solkattu, syllablic patterns to mimic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Hindustani Classical Music
subgenres.desc: North Indian traditional music (including parts of Pakistan, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Bhutan) with roots reaching back to the 12th century CE.

subgenres.name: Dhrupad
subgenres.desc: Ancient style of classical Hindustani vocal and instrumental music.

subgenres.name: Kafi
subgenres.desc: Sufi vocal style popular in Pakistan, differentiated from Qawwali by its small ensemble size and simple arrangements.

subgenres.name: Khayal
subgenres.desc: Predominant vocal style, often with a significant amount of improvisation.

subgenres.name: Klasik
subgenres.desc: Encompassing the various styles of Afghan Classical Music, which diverged from the North Indian styles.

subgenres.name: Qawwali
subgenres.desc: Sufi Music in India and Pakistan using the raga and tala templates of Hindustani Classical Music, with an emphasis on ecstatic performance and devotional lyricism.

subgenres.name: Shabad kirtan
subgenres.desc: Religious Sikh Hymn backed by specially selected ragas and taal.

subgenres.name: Tarana
subgenres.desc: Vocal composition with Persian or Arabic syllables and phonemes.

subgenres.name: Thumri
subgenres.desc: Hindustani classical style based on North Indian folk literature.

subgenres.name: Odissi Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional dance and classical music from the Odisha region of Eastern India.

subgenres.name: Southeast Asian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Formal music developed in Southeast Asian countries (Burma, Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, East Timor, Brunei Darussalam) usually in form of gong-chime orchestras such as gamelan, kulintang and pi phat.

subgenres.name: Burmese Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional court music of Myanmar, developed from Southeast Asian, Hindu and Chinese influences.

subgenres.name: Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Originated in the island of Java; played by an ensemble typically consisting of metallophones and gongs, sometimes augmented with drums, flutes, and human voices.

subgenres.name: Balinese Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Broad classification grouping various forms of Gamelan with native roots in Bali.

subgenres.name: Gamelan angklung
subgenres.desc: Takes its name from the angklung, an instrument made of bamboo tubes.

subgenres.name: Gamelan beleganjur
subgenres.desc: Loud, chaotic, highly percussive, and with heavy tempo changes.

subgenres.name: Gamelan gender wayang
subgenres.desc: Performed with two/four metallophones made out of bronze keys with suspended bamboo tube resonators connected to them.

subgenres.name: Gamelan gong gede
subgenres.desc: Ceremonial style characterized by a simpler and more melodic approach with clearer and more stable progressions compared to other Balinese orchestras.

subgenres.name: Gamelan gong kebyar
subgenres.desc: Free compositional techniques and rapidly changing dynamics.

subgenres.name: Gamelan jegog
subgenres.desc: Played entirely on marimba-like instruments made from bamboo which widely differ in size.

subgenres.name: Gamelan selonding
subgenres.desc: Ensemble consists of four to six musicians playing metallophones made out of iron in a seven-tone scale.

subgenres.name: Gamelan semar pegulingan
subgenres.desc: Originated in the 16th-17th centuries; features a soft, delicate, and ethereal sound.

subgenres.name: Gamelan degung
subgenres.desc: Sundanese Gamelan performed by a small orchestra of bronze gongs and metallophones.

subgenres.name: Javanese Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Broad classification grouping Gamelan genres native to Javanese culture.

subgenres.name: Gamelan sekaten
subgenres.desc: Javanese ceremonial Gamelan played with large instruments, strictly unaccompanied by vocals.

subgenres.name: Solonese Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Style originating from Surakarta; known for its subtle and more delicate sound.

subgenres.name: Malay Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Developments of Gamelan that are performed by Malay native groups, mostly established by the Pahang and Terengganu royal courts of the Malay Peninsula.

subgenres.name: Kacapi suling
subgenres.desc: Sundanese music played by an ensemble consisting of one or two kacapis (zithers), one suling (flute), and occasionally a set of kendangs (drums).

subgenres.name: Kakawin
subgenres.desc: Form of Indonesian poetry written in Kawi, performed melodically using a structured pattern of long and short syllables.

subgenres.name: Kulintang
subgenres.desc: Southeast Asian gong-chime ensemble consisting mainly of gong-chimes of various sizes, with the addition of larger gongs, various drums, and occasionally xylophones and non-percussion instruments.

subgenres.name: Mahori
subgenres.desc: Thai and Khmer traditional orchestra combining xylophones and gong-chimes of Piphat/Pinpeat with strings of Khrueang sai ensemble.

subgenres.name: Malay Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditionally played in the royal courts of the several Malay kingdoms, empires and sultanates that existed throughout history.

subgenres.name: Malay Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Developments of Gamelan that are performed by Malay native groups, mostly established by the Pahang and Terengganu royal courts of the Malay Peninsula.

subgenres.name: Pinpeat
subgenres.desc: Orchestra of wind and percussion instruments having its origins in the Khmer Empire era.

subgenres.name: Saluang klasik
subgenres.desc: Played by a duo or a trio of musicians, including a saluang (a kind of end-blown bamboo flute) player and a traditional singer.

subgenres.name: Talempong
subgenres.desc: Gong-chime ensemble focused around the talempong kettle gong.

subgenres.name: Tembang Sunda Cianjuran
subgenres.desc: Sung free-verse poetry in Sundanese language, usually by a solo vocalist, accompanied by a mellow-sounding Kacapi suling ensemble.

subgenres.name: Thai Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Emerged from the royal courts of Central Thailand around the 13th century, based on a traditional Thai sound-scale of seven tempered notes.

subgenres.name: Fon leb
subgenres.desc: Traditional performance music originating in northern Thailand consist of an ensemble with Piphat instruments and a pair of female choreographers.

subgenres.name: Khrueang sai
subgenres.desc: Thai Classical Music emphasizing string instruments while also incorporating other kinds of instruments to enrich the sound.

subgenres.name: Piphat
subgenres.desc: Led by wind and percussion instruments, with ensembles ranging from 6 to 10 instruments.

subgenres.name: Tibetan Buddhist Chant
subgenres.desc: Ritual vocal music of the Tibetan Buddhist faith characterized by its low pitch, droning repetitiousness, and frequent use of overtone singing.

subgenres.name: Western Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Broad range of art music associated with the aristocracy that originated in Europe around 500 AD.

subgenres.name: Art Song
subgenres.desc: Vocal music with text often set to Poetry, typically for single vocalist with instrumental accompaniment, distinguished by its design for concert recital and high artistic demands requiring classically trained musicians.

subgenres.name: Elizabethan Song
subgenres.desc: Monophonic style developed in Renaissance England that is typically composed in strophic form for one to several vocalists with instrumental accompaniment ranging from solo lute to chamber ensemble.

subgenres.name: Lied
subgenres.desc: Form of song arising from 19th century German Romanticism, usually for solo vocalist & piano with a text derived from poetry.

subgenres.name: Mélodie
subgenres.desc: French form typically with a greater emphasis on emotional restraint, refinement, subtlety, and concision.

subgenres.name: Orchestral Song
subgenres.desc: Classical song for solo voice or voices with orchestral accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Bagatelle
subgenres.desc: Brief composition with an unpretentious, playful sound.

subgenres.name: Ballet
subgenres.desc: Western art music, often Orchestral Music, written to accompany classical dance productions of the same name.

subgenres.name: Ballet de cour
subgenres.desc: Earliest form developed by the French royal court and characterized by its artistic diversity, regimented structure, grand spectacle, and overt political elements.

subgenres.name: Comédie-ballet
subgenres.desc: French form of musical drama from the 17th century that combines operatic singing, classical dance, and theater.

subgenres.name: Opéra-ballet
subgenres.desc: Principally French style of musical drama that combines operatic singing with classical dance, usually with small Orchestral Music accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Baroque Music
subgenres.desc: Constant rhythmic flow, or a steady motion throughout, generally focusing on a single melodic idea and including some form of counterpoint.

subgenres.name: Ballet de cour
subgenres.desc: Earliest form developed by the French royal court and characterized by its artistic diversity, regimented structure, grand spectacle, and overt political elements.

subgenres.name: Comédie-ballet
subgenres.desc: French form of musical drama from the 17th century that combines operatic singing, classical dance, and theater.

subgenres.name: Opéra-ballet
subgenres.desc: Principally French style of musical drama that combines operatic singing with classical dance, usually with small Orchestral Music accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela barroca
subgenres.desc: Earliest form that draws from a broad range of artistic sources, including theater, operatic singing, instrumental music, dance, popular music, poetry, and comedy.

subgenres.name: Baroque Suite
subgenres.desc: Collection of varied dance pieces, usually in the same key, structured on the music of European courtly dances.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Originated in the late 19th century, taking the European music that had been brought to the country by colonists and brought in parts of Brazilian Music.

subgenres.name: Valsa brasileira
subgenres.desc: Brazillian Waltz characterized by its slow rhythms and romantic sound.

subgenres.name: Byzantine Music
subgenres.desc: Music from Byzantine era.

subgenres.name: Byzantine Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical chant of Christian churches following the Orthodox rite.

subgenres.name: Cantata
subgenres.desc: Vocal style for solo singers with instrumental & Choral accompaniment comparable to Oratorio, though often smaller in scale, more songlike, and with less focus on dramatic narrative.

subgenres.name: Canzona
subgenres.desc: Song-like structures and a contrapuntal texture technique known as imitation.

subgenres.name: Capriccio
subgenres.desc: Typically short and loosely structured, characterized by spontaneity, humor, and technicality.

subgenres.name: Chamber Music
subgenres.desc: Western Classical Music performed by a small ensemble, usually only a few performers.

subgenres.name: String Quartet
subgenres.desc: Small scale composition for an ensemble that consists of two violins, one viola, and one cello, with complex interplay and multiple (usually four) movements.

subgenres.name: Character Piece
subgenres.desc: Broad instrumental genre, usually for solo piano, written to evoke an extramusical concept or mood.

subgenres.name: Nocturne
subgenres.desc: Intimate piece meant to evoke associations with the night.

subgenres.name: Choral
subgenres.desc: Choir-sung classical works covering periods from medieval music (an early form being Gregorian Chant) up to present day.

subgenres.name: Choral Concerto
subgenres.desc: Composition for unaccompanied choir, set to sacred texts of Eastern Orthodox tradition.

subgenres.name: Choral Symphony
subgenres.desc: Combines symphonic Orchestral Music forces & structure with vocal parts for choir.

subgenres.name: Cinematic Classical
subgenres.desc: Orchestral compositions generally associated with soundtracks to modern high-budget films, games, and other non-live media.

subgenres.name: Epic Music
subgenres.desc: Often associated with Electronic production, heavy percussion such as taiko drums, Choral vocals, and orchestral instrumentation to create a bombastic style commonly linked to movie trailers.

subgenres.name: Spaghetti Western
subgenres.desc: Epic, cinematic sound evoking imagery of the Wild West, featuring a Surf Rock-inspired guitar tone while taking inspiration from the melodies and harmonies of traditional Mexican Music.

subgenres.name: Classical Period
subgenres.desc: Refers to the phase in Western Classical Music history occurring from roughly 1750 to 1820, characterized by its emphasis on clarity, simplicity, and balance.

subgenres.name: Classic Ragtime
subgenres.desc: Draws on the complexity and formal structures of Western Classical Music, cycling through multiple strains (themes); emerged from Missouri's Sedalia school.

subgenres.name: Concerto
subgenres.desc: Multi-movement classical works for one or more soloists and an ensemble.

subgenres.name: Concerto for Orchestra
subgenres.desc: Mostly modern form in which virtuosic solo passages are alternately played among different portions of the orchestra.

subgenres.name: Concerto grosso
subgenres.desc: Oldest form developed during the Baroque Music era in which the body of the music is alternately shared between a small group of soloists and a larger orchestra.

subgenres.name: Sinfonia concertante
subgenres.desc: Fuses symphonic compositional structure and instrumentation with parts written for concertante soloists.

subgenres.name: Divertissement
subgenres.desc: Straightforward tuneful music historically written to serve as light entertainment for events or as interstitial movements within larger theatrical works.

subgenres.name: English Pastoral School
subgenres.desc: Early 20th-century English classical composers turning to English folk and pastoral influences.

subgenres.name: Étude
subgenres.desc: Composition written to both showcase & sharpen a particular playing or compositional technique, often requiring great skill from its performers.

subgenres.name: Fantasia
subgenres.desc: Free-form, improvisational, and with contrasting sectional writing, sometimes based on preexisting melodies and generally meant to evoke a sense of imaginative exploration.

subgenres.name: Fugue
subgenres.desc: Contrapuntal composition and technique for a fixed numbers of musical voices; following the imitations of one main theme.

subgenres.name: Impromptu
subgenres.desc: Composition written to sound like a spur-of-the-moment improvisation.

subgenres.name: Latin American Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Western Classical Music with influences from Hispanic American Music.

subgenres.name: Light Music
subgenres.desc: Instrumental, typically through-composed style performed by an orchestra or small ensemble, with simpler arrangements and an emphasis on strong melodies.

subgenres.name: Madrigal
subgenres.desc: Secular polyphonic music based around poetry and generally performed by unaccompanied vocal ensembles of two to eight persons.

subgenres.name: Medieval Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Composed during the Medieval period lasted approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries.

subgenres.name: Ars antiqua
subgenres.desc: Mainly sacred European medieval music from the period of 1170 to 1310, featuring the birth of measuring time in music and the use of polyphonies for four voices.

subgenres.name: Ars nova
subgenres.desc: Period (around 1310-1380) that succeeded Ars antiqua, mixing the sacred with the secular.

subgenres.name: Ars subtilior
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the final period of late medieval music (around 1380-1420) and continued to use the technique of isorhythms but with added complexity.

subgenres.name: Contenance angloise
subgenres.desc: Distinct style of Polyphonic Chant developed in fifteenth-century England.

subgenres.name: Medieval Lyric Poetry
subgenres.desc: Lyric poetry from Medieval Europe, roughly from the 11th to the 14th century, most prominently the troubadours of southern France.

subgenres.name: Plainsong
subgenres.desc: Monophonic chanting in the context of Roman Catholic and modern Anglican liturgy.

subgenres.name: Ambrosian Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical chant practiced in parts of Italy and Switzerland, characterized by stepped melodic progression.

subgenres.name: Canto beneventano
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition of Southern Italy characterized by lengthy melodies, extensive use of repetition, and a steady, undulating progression.

subgenres.name: Canto mozárabe
subgenres.desc: Iberian form of plainchant that flourished roughly 550-1085 AD.

subgenres.name: Celtic Chant
subgenres.desc: Extinct tradition of Catholic liturgical chant developed by the Celtic Christians of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany.

subgenres.name: Gallican Chant
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition originating from the region of Gaul (now modern-day France).

subgenres.name: Gregorian Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical, monophonic chant that accompanied Mass and other rituals in Western Christianity.

subgenres.name: Sarum Chant
subgenres.desc: Latin Plainsong tradition of Salisbury, England, characterized by its unadorned simplicity.

subgenres.name: Old Roman Chant
subgenres.desc: Plainchant tradition of Medieval Rome that was closely related to Gregorian Chant, though often more musically ornate.

subgenres.name: Modern Classical
subgenres.desc: Multitude of compositional approaches from turn of the 20th century onward, deviating from previous compositional norms in favor of innovation.

subgenres.name: American Gamelan
subgenres.desc: Mid-20th-century style, influenced by arrangements, instrumentation, rhythms, timbres, and tunings of Indonesian Gamelan.

subgenres.name: Expressionism
subgenres.desc: Originating between the abandonment of tonality at the conclusion of the period of Romanticism and the creation of twelve-tone composition.

subgenres.name: Futurism
subgenres.desc: Radical and militant attitude, rejection of Western Classical Music and traditional criteria of craft, non-conformity, and a fascination with machines.

subgenres.name: Impressionism
subgenres.desc: Originated in late 19th to early 20th century France as a reaction to Romanticism, placing a greater focus on depicting atmosphere and mood rather than fixed concepts.

subgenres.name: Indeterminacy
subgenres.desc: Leaves elements of composition, performance, or both up to chance.

subgenres.name: Microtonal Classical
subgenres.desc: Eschews the traditional twelve-tone scale of Western Classical Music, utilizing intervals outside of its bounds.

subgenres.name: Minimalism
subgenres.desc: Developed in the United States in the 1960s; recognized for its repetitive nature and use of static harmony.

subgenres.name: Holy Minimalism
subgenres.desc: Style informed by Christian Liturgical Music that emphasizes slow sustained rhythmic values, soft dynamics, and silence to produce a contemplative and reverential atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Musique concrète instrumentale
subgenres.desc: Acoustic, through-composed Classical Music that relies heavily on unconventional instrumental techniques.

subgenres.name: Neoromanticism
subgenres.desc: Modern redevelopment of 19th-century idioms using complex structures and polytonality informed by but distinct from Expressionism.

subgenres.name: New Complexity
subgenres.desc: Dense, difficult, and rigorously academic approach to Modern Classical composition which emerged in the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Post-Minimalism
subgenres.desc: Seeks to push Minimalism's linear composition style forward, and takes in influences from genres such as Jazz, Traditional Folk Music, and others.

subgenres.name: Totalism
subgenres.desc: Adds complex rhythmic structures and emphasis on surface energy to Minimalism.

subgenres.name: Process Music
subgenres.desc: Compositions centering musical processes, both audible and inaudible.

subgenres.name: Serialism
subgenres.desc: Compositional method in which pitches are grouped into sets (tone rows) to determine the order and frequency of their use.

subgenres.name: Integral Serialism
subgenres.desc: Application of twelve-tone technique in early Serialism to as many compositional factors as possible (in an attempt to apply total serial control).

subgenres.name: Sonorism
subgenres.desc: Techniques and forms that emphasize texture and timbre.

subgenres.name: Spectralism
subgenres.desc: Compositional practice involving analysis, manipulation, and transformation of sound spectra.

subgenres.name: Stochastic Music
subgenres.desc: Composition featuring guided indeterminism, where the following state is only partially determined by the preceding state.

subgenres.name: Motet
subgenres.desc: Extremely diverse form of vocal music, usually written as a style of Polyphonic Chant for A cappella soloists or choir.

subgenres.name: Neoclassicism
subgenres.desc: Return to the more formal and less expansive structures and forms, beginning shortly after World War I as a reaction to what some composers perceived as excesses of Romanticism.

subgenres.name: Opera
subgenres.desc: European tradition which combines drama and distinctive vocal style in the context of Western Classical Music, usually performed as a theatrical work on stage.

subgenres.name: Ballad Opera
subgenres.desc: English reaction to the Italian Opera styles with a satirical sense of humor and scores borrowing from Traditional Folk Music and popular music.

subgenres.name: Grand opéra
subgenres.desc: French style characterized by its enlarged scope and sense of grandeur, with bigger orchestras and casts, and ornate sceneries and costumes.

subgenres.name: Monodrama
subgenres.desc: Mostly modern style written for a single virtuoso singer with accompaniment, often shorter in length and with a more philosophically introspective or abstract libretto.

subgenres.name: Opéra-ballet
subgenres.desc: Principally French style of musical drama that combines operatic singing with classical dance, usually with small Orchestral Music accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Opera buffa
subgenres.desc: Lighthearted and amusing counterpart to Opera seria; developed in Naples in the first half of the 18th century.

subgenres.name: Opéra-comique
subgenres.desc: French style of Opera characterized by the use of some spoken dialogues to connect major arias and sung parts, as well as a more restrained approach to recitatives.

subgenres.name: Opera semiseria
subgenres.desc: Popular in the early and middle 19th century, containing appeals to emotion of Opera seria as well as some comedy elements present in Opera buffa.

subgenres.name: Opera seria
subgenres.desc: Italian Opera popular among European nobility and royalty throughout most of the 18th century, typified by its exaggerated dramatic flair and interspersed with dry recitative.

subgenres.name: Operetta
subgenres.desc: Light opera interspersed with spoken dialogues, being usually satirical and/or humorous in nature and centered around romantic plots and dancing scenes.

subgenres.name: Kalon'ny fahiny
subgenres.desc: Fusion of music from the highlands of Madagascar and western Operetta.

subgenres.name: Romantische Oper
subgenres.desc: Early 19th century Germanic style of Opera influenced by German Folk Music and legends with a focus on fantasy, emotivity, heroic figures, and nationalism.

subgenres.name: Singspiel
subgenres.desc: German form of Opera distinguished by the prominent usage of spoken dialogues mixed with lyrical or folklore arias/ballads.

subgenres.name: Tragédie en musique
subgenres.desc: French Opera genre developed by Jean-Baptiste Lully and Philippe Quinault in the second half of the 17th century, consisting of alterations made to the coeval Italian format to better fit the French language and please an audience more accustomed to the ballet de cour.

subgenres.name: Verismo
subgenres.desc: Developed in Italy around the turn of the 20th century and favored melodramatic realism, a rejection of bel canto standards, and declamatory singing.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela
subgenres.desc: Spanish dramatic genre where spoken scenes are mixed with passages sung in operatic or popular styles.

subgenres.name: Género chico
subgenres.desc: Light, small-scale musical comedy with mild social commentary, populist themes, and catchy melodies.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela barroca
subgenres.desc: Earliest form that draws from a broad range of artistic sources, including theater, operatic singing, instrumental music, dance, popular music, poetry, and comedy.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela grande
subgenres.desc: Romantic musical comedy akin to Operetta developed during the mid-19th century.

subgenres.name: Zeitoper
subgenres.desc: Short-lived scene in Weimar Germany, often having satirical plots and allusions to popular music.

subgenres.name: Oratorio
subgenres.desc: Composition for vocal soloists, choir, and orchestra, often making use of a comprehensive textbook of contemplative nature.

subgenres.name: Orchestral Music
subgenres.desc: Western Classical Music performed by an orchestra.

subgenres.name: Orchestral Song
subgenres.desc: Classical song for solo voice or voices with orchestral accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Symphonic Mugham
subgenres.desc: Introduces elements of Azerbaijani Mugham into the structure of the composition, played on a full western orchestra.

subgenres.name: Tone Poem
subgenres.desc: Programmatic work, usually in a single movement, that is entirely based on external non-musical themes, ideas, tales, etc.

subgenres.name: Overture
subgenres.desc: Typically single-movement form akin to the Tone Poem written as the prelude to a larger work or in association with a programmatic concept.

subgenres.name: Passion
subgenres.desc: Musical re-enactment of the suffering and crucifixion of Christ, typically based on one of the four canonical Gospels.

subgenres.name: Prelude
subgenres.desc: Brief work with an improvisatory feeling, usually for keyboard, that serves either as a standalone piece or an introduction to a complimentary work of music.

subgenres.name: Renaissance Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses Western Classical Music from the 15th to 16th centuries.

subgenres.name: Contenance angloise
subgenres.desc: Distinct style of Polyphonic Chant developed in fifteenth-century England.

subgenres.name: Elizabethan Song
subgenres.desc: Monophonic style developed in Renaissance England that is typically composed in strophic form for one to several vocalists with instrumental accompaniment ranging from solo lute to chamber ensemble.

subgenres.name: Franco-Flemish School
subgenres.desc: Musical movement centered in the Low Countries, known for its intricate polyphony, emotional expression, and influence on European sacred and secular music from the 1440s to 1550.

subgenres.name: Ricercar
subgenres.desc: Early instrumental genre, usually for solo lute or keyboard, written either as a brief introductory work or imitative contrapuntal piece.

subgenres.name: Roman School
subgenres.desc: Composers of primarily Christian Liturgical Music active in Rome in the 16th and 17th centuries, developing a musically conservative compositional style seen as appropriate for church performance.

subgenres.name: Romanticism
subgenres.desc: Expressive and emotional qualities, especially in terms of melody.

subgenres.name: Grand opéra
subgenres.desc: French style characterized by its enlarged scope and sense of grandeur, with bigger orchestras and casts, and ornate sceneries and costumes.

subgenres.name: New German School
subgenres.desc: Mid-19th-century Romantic movement experimenting in harmonics and form and engaged in social issues.

subgenres.name: Romantische Oper
subgenres.desc: Early 19th century Germanic style of Opera influenced by German Folk Music and legends with a focus on fantasy, emotivity, heroic figures, and nationalism.

subgenres.name: Saint Petersburg School
subgenres.desc: Interrelated circles of 19th century Russian Western Classical Music composers focused on developing a distinctly Russian national style.

subgenres.name: Serenade
subgenres.desc: Light, tuneful, and relatively straightforward music historically associated with outdoor entertainment for evening gatherings.

subgenres.name: Sonata
subgenres.desc: Broad instrumental genre for one to three soloists that has changed significantly throughout its history, now typically a suite of four or fewer contrasting movements, at least one of which is written in sonata form.

subgenres.name: Spanish Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Incorporation of Spanish Music within the context of Western Classical Music, particularly characterized by the use of the classical guitar.

subgenres.name: Canto mozárabe
subgenres.desc: Iberian form of plainchant that flourished roughly 550-1085 AD.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela
subgenres.desc: Spanish dramatic genre where spoken scenes are mixed with passages sung in operatic or popular styles.

subgenres.name: Género chico
subgenres.desc: Light, small-scale musical comedy with mild social commentary, populist themes, and catchy melodies.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela barroca
subgenres.desc: Earliest form that draws from a broad range of artistic sources, including theater, operatic singing, instrumental music, dance, popular music, poetry, and comedy.

subgenres.name: Zarzuela grande
subgenres.desc: Romantic musical comedy akin to Operetta developed during the mid-19th century.

subgenres.name: Symphony
subgenres.desc: Large-scale works, typically Orchestral Music in four movements: 1) allegro, almost always in sonata-allegro form 2) a slow movement 3) scherzo or minuet 4) finale, typically allegro or rondo.

subgenres.name: Choral Symphony
subgenres.desc: Combines symphonic Orchestral Music forces & structure with vocal parts for choir.

subgenres.name: Sinfonia concertante
subgenres.desc: Fuses symphonic compositional structure and instrumentation with parts written for concertante soloists.

subgenres.name: Theme and Variation
subgenres.desc: Main theme followed by a number of variations on the theme.

subgenres.name: Toccata
subgenres.desc: Virtuoso piece, usually for solo keyboard or plucked string instrument, characterized by its free rhythm, rapid fingerwork, and contrasting sectional writing.

name: Country
desc: American genre derived from Southern and Appalachian forms of American Folk Music and later Rock and Pop influences, with a focus on the life and culture of rural America.

subgenres.name: Alt-Country
subgenres.desc: Arose in the 1980s and 1990s, performed by artists with roots in Alternative Rock and Indie Rock who were disconnected from the mainstream Country industry.

subgenres.name: Gothic Country
subgenres.desc: Evokes the Southern Gothic literary genre through morbid lyrical themes and melancholic sounds that emphasize its American Folk Music and Post-Punk influences.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Born in the Appalachian region of the United States during the late 1930s, characterized by fingerpicked banjo along with other traditional instruments.

subgenres.name: Progressive Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Modernization with varied influences including Jazz, Folk, Rock, and other forms of Country.

subgenres.name: Jamgrass
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes instrumental jamming and extended performances with many outside influences.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Contemporary Country
subgenres.desc: Incorporates both heavily Pop-influenced styles, and the more pop-averse movement of Neo-Traditionalist Country.

subgenres.name: Boyfriend Country
subgenres.desc: Soft, sentimental, and acoustic-leaning style featuring romantic lyrics, slick Contemporary R&B stylings, and light percussion.

subgenres.name: Bro-Country
subgenres.desc: 21st century style with an often party-oriented sound and lyrical content, taking strong influence from Hard Rock, Hip Hop and Pop.

subgenres.name: Neo-Traditionalist Country
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1980s as a reaction to the increased dominance of Country Pop, moving instead towards a Honky Tonk-rooted sound that centered the Singer-Songwriter.

subgenres.name: Country & Irish
subgenres.desc: Developed in Ireland; combines North American Country with Irish Folk Music influences, often in the form of traditional Irish songs that have been adapted into country numbers.

subgenres.name: Country Boogie
subgenres.desc: Uptempo style built around the Boogie Woogie rhythm, with strong beats and prominent electric guitar leads, made popular in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Country Folk
subgenres.desc: Emphasises Traditional Country instrumentation as well as influences from contemporary Singer-Songwriter traditions, such as a gentler disposition and prominent lyrical storytelling focus.

subgenres.name: Country Pop
subgenres.desc: Combination of Country with Pop to appeal to a larger audience.

subgenres.name: Boyfriend Country
subgenres.desc: Soft, sentimental, and acoustic-leaning style featuring romantic lyrics, slick Contemporary R&B stylings, and light percussion.

subgenres.name: Bro-Country
subgenres.desc: 21st century style with an often party-oriented sound and lyrical content, taking strong influence from Hard Rock, Hip Hop and Pop.

subgenres.name: Countrypolitan
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Pop-oriented orchestration and songwriting while reducing the role of Country instrumentation and rhythms; often featuring lush string arrangements and group backing vocals.

subgenres.name: Urban Cowboy
subgenres.desc: Melds Country and 1970s L.A. soft Pop, sometimes leaning towards Disco.

subgenres.name: Honky Tonk
subgenres.desc: Upbeat style that retains much of the common instrumentation of Traditional Country, as well as featuring prominent guitars (especially the steel guitar), strong backbeats and lyrics commonly about the working-class life.

subgenres.name: Bakersfield Sound
subgenres.desc: Heavily based on electric instrumentation and a defined backbeat.

subgenres.name: Truck Driving Country
subgenres.desc: Concerns the lifestyle of professional truck drivers, often drawing from Country Rock and Bakersfield Sound musically.

subgenres.name: Nashville Sound
subgenres.desc: Production style characterized by smooth vocals over a relaxed ensemble of guitars and rhythm section, and variously incorporating elements from other styles of Country and Pop.

subgenres.name: Countrypolitan
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Pop-oriented orchestration and songwriting while reducing the role of Country instrumentation and rhythms; often featuring lush string arrangements and group backing vocals.

subgenres.name: Progressive Country
subgenres.desc: Blend of traditionalist Country styles with elements of Rock, Contemporary Folk, and other countercultural genres; characterized by realistic, self-reflective lyrics and non-traditional songwriting and production elements.

subgenres.name: Outlaw Country
subgenres.desc: Rock-influenced reaction to mainstream Country Pop trends, featuring rebellious personas, darker lyrics, and Western-inspired outlaw imagery.

subgenres.name: Traditional Country
subgenres.desc: Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Close Harmony
subgenres.desc: Traditional two-part harmony singing performed mostly by brothers.

subgenres.name: Country Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Western
subgenres.desc: Reflects and portrays the lifestyles of cowboys and other settlers of the Western United States through both Traditional Folk Music and popular song.

subgenres.name: Western Swing
subgenres.desc: Blend of Traditional Country string instrumentation with the driving rhythms of Jazz and regional dance traditions, often prominently featuring fiddle and steel guitar.

name: Dance
desc: Rooted in Disco and developed largely within Electronic Dance Music; emphasizes rhythm and is generally produced for play by DJs at clubs, parties, or festivals.

subgenres.name: Alternative Dance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates rhythms and synthesizers from Electronic Dance Music within the context of Alternative Rock and related styles; predominantly popular in the 1990s.

subgenres.name: Grebo
subgenres.desc: Short-lived English subculture and associated music; raw, futuristic, sample-heavy form of Alternative Dance with a dirty guitar sound.

subgenres.name: New Rave
subgenres.desc: High energy mid-2000s style combining the tight and punchy grooves of Dance-Punk Revival with synths and four-on-the-floor rhythms from genres like Electroclash and Electro House.

subgenres.name: Dance-Pop
subgenres.desc: Simple, catchy melodies and throbbing beats inspired initially by Disco and later various House styles.

subgenres.name: Bubblegum Dance
subgenres.desc: Playful, childlike style with a Bubblegum-like atmosphere that often incorporates high-pitched, light-hearted, and usually female-fronted vocals.

subgenres.name: Disco polo
subgenres.desc: Polish Dance-Pop, originally established from contemporary wedding / feast songs and Italo-Disco.

subgenres.name: Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Electro-influenced; developed in Latino communities in New York and Miami in the 1980s, especially dominated by Latin Freestyle and its Latin influences.

subgenres.name: Latin Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Displays a heavy influence of Hispanic American Music alongside the Disco, Hip Hop, and Electro influences of Freestyle.

subgenres.name: Funk melody
subgenres.desc: Light and melodic take on Funk brasileiro, developed alongside Funk carioca.

subgenres.name: Romanian Popcorn
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the second half of the 2000s in Romania, often featuring brass melodies and "staccato" pluck grooves.

subgenres.name: Tecnorumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.

subgenres.name: Township Bubblegum
subgenres.desc: Synth-heavy Dance-Pop style popular in the South African townships in the 1980s and early 1990s.

subgenres.name: Disco
subgenres.desc: Combines the lush orchestration of Philly Soul and bass grooves of Funk with a four-on-the-floor rhythm.

subgenres.name: Boogie
subgenres.desc: Continuation of the Disco sound with increased influence from Funk, Synth Funk, and R&B and a slower tempo, often featuring drum machines and filter modulated synthesizers.

subgenres.name: Electro-Disco
subgenres.desc: Disco instrumentation is largely - if not entirely - replaced by synthesizers and augmented with futuristic elements such as the vocoder.

subgenres.name: Hi-NRG
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s and quickly became the most popular form of Electronic Dance Music in the LGBT club scenes of San Francisco and New York, characterized by its uptempo, high-energy sound.

subgenres.name: Italo-Disco
subgenres.desc: Produced primarily in Italy and is characterized by the use of synthesizers, drum machines, and sometimes vocoders to create a mechanical, Electronic version of Disco with futuristic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Spacesynth
subgenres.desc: Highly melodic, often instrumental futuristic strain, formed under the heavy influence of Space Disco, Progressive Electronic and, later, early Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: Doskpop
subgenres.desc: Grew out of the Amiga Demoscene in the late 1980s with the imitation of Spacesynth in the context of the restrictions and aesthetics of Demostyle.

subgenres.name: Red Disco
subgenres.desc: Continuum of various eclectic forms, derived mainly from late Euro-Disco, but also Italo-Disco, Hi-NRG and Eurobeat, and developed in the Soviet Union in the mid-to-late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Space Disco
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Europe in the mid-to-late 1970s, characterized by layers of oscillating synth, space-oriented sound effects, and a futuristic sound inspired by contemporary sci-fi media.

subgenres.name: Euro-Disco
subgenres.desc: European style that moved away from the genre's Rhythm & Blues and Soul roots, speeding up the tempo and adding Electronic instruments like synthesizers and drum machines as a backing for more melodic Europop-influenced vocals.

subgenres.name: Latin Disco
subgenres.desc: Disco that incorporates elements from Hispanic American Music styles.

subgenres.name: Mutant Disco
subgenres.desc: Danceable basslines, syncopated grooves, and angular guitar riffs, characterized by a spirit of experimentation and integration of disparate sounds.

subgenres.name: Nu-Disco
subgenres.desc: 21st-century trend mixing modern, polished Electronic production with the aesthetics, structures, and lively, organic beats of 1970s and 1980s Disco.

subgenres.name: Electronic Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Broad category for subgenres mainly derived from Disco, featuring Electronic sounds, synthesizers, drum machines and varying BPM ranges.

subgenres.name: Artcore
subgenres.desc: Combines an eclectic mix of Electronic Dance Music genres with the instrumentation and melodic stylings of genres like Cinematic Classical for a maximalist and emotional sound.

subgenres.name: Balani Show
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s in Mali; peaks at around 170BPM and prominently features looping, cut-up balafon samples.

subgenres.name: Balearic Beat
subgenres.desc: Variety of relaxed, laid-back music that originates from the Balearic Islands off the coast of Spain, and particularly the club scene in Ibiza.

subgenres.name: Bérite Club
subgenres.desc: Originated in the underground club scene of Paris in the mid-to-late 2010s, drawing on a variety of international club styles for its combination of prominent and erratic drum programming with freezing and looping chopped-up samples.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat
subgenres.desc: Syncopated drum patterns (breakbeats), generally driving the groove at 110-160 BPM, emerging in the late 1980s from sampling drum breaks, before forming an umbrella genre separate from Drum and Bass, Downtempo, and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Acid Breaks
subgenres.desc: Incorporates prominent "squelching", resonant low pass filter sounds typical to Acid House, and often other "trippy" effects into intense, syncopated, broken rhythms in the tempos of 110-150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Big Beat
subgenres.desc: Popular in Britain during the late 1990s, driven by edited breakbeats and prominent basslines.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Originated from the combination of sampled breakbeats and energetic rhythms with the "rave" influences set by early-1990s Techno and Acid House, including upbeat "stab" riffing and sample-based production.

subgenres.name: Darkside
subgenres.desc: Dark atmosphere and fast rhythms; served as a forerunner of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Breaks
subgenres.desc: Revival of Breakbeat Hardcore which emerged in the 2000s, bringing in modern influences and production techniques.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Kota
subgenres.desc: Indonesian style that slows down the syncopated rhythms of Funkot to moderate tempos around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Jungle Dutch
subgenres.desc: Combines the high-pitched synth leads of Dutch House with the frantic "tribal" rhythms of Jungle Terror.

subgenres.name: Florida Breaks
subgenres.desc: Developed during the mid-1990s, combining major influences of Hip Hop derivatives such as Miami Bass and Electro along with elements of 1990s Electronic Dance Music genres like House or Techno.

subgenres.name: Funky Breaks
subgenres.desc: Merging popular 1990s breaks styles like Big Beat with major Funk and Soul elements.

subgenres.name: Nu Skool Breaks
subgenres.desc: Developed in the late 1990s and early 2000s; takes elements from Drum and Bass, UK Garage, and Techno.

subgenres.name: Progressive Breaks
subgenres.desc: Derivative of Progressive House that incorporates its lush, melodic synth leads and atmospheres into Breakbeat's syncopated and broken rhythms.

subgenres.name: Psybreaks
subgenres.desc: Uses Psytrance-derived sound design, such as squelchy sounds and psychedelic effects.

subgenres.name: West Coast Breaks
subgenres.desc: Combines the earlier breakbeats of Hip Hop and early Breakbeat or even Miami Bass, with various 1990s Electronic Dance Music genres like Trance and Techno.

subgenres.name: Broken Beat
subgenres.desc: Choppy, syncopated grooves and loose influence from 1970s Jazz-Funk, with eclectic roots spanning Drum and Bass, Deep House, Acid Jazz, and Afrobeat.

subgenres.name: Bubblegum Bass
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s, exaggerating the cutest and most feminine parts of 2000s Pop and combining them with bouncy, plastic synths over rhythms and sounds derived from a variety of contemporary club styles.

subgenres.name: Bubbling
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Netherlands in the late 1980s, fusing sped-up Dancehall with Dutch Antillean music and contemporary Dutch rave.

subgenres.name: Budots
subgenres.desc: Originated from the southern Philippines; notable for its distinct high-pitched synth hooks.

subgenres.name: Coupé-décalé
subgenres.desc: Bass-heavy and minimal style of Ivorian popular dance music, drawing heavily from Zouglou and Congolese rhythms.

subgenres.name: Cruise
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced Nigerian dance music, utilising chopped, often humorous, samples.

subgenres.name: Dariacore
subgenres.desc: SoundCloud-based scene developed in the early 2020s, combining prominent vocal samples and distorted, dense production with influences from a wide range of Electronic Dance Music genres, often incorporating musical and visual references to popular media and internet culture.

subgenres.name: Deconstructed Club
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2010s as the hybridization of diverse Electronic Dance Music genres with an abrasive Post-Industrial sound.

subgenres.name: Dek Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent heavy, sustained bass tones, percussion derived from South Asian Music, and often high-pitched sound effects or samples; commonly played at extreme volumes in DJ/sound system competitions.

subgenres.name: Digital Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Fast, syncopated breakbeat patterns (often sampled or programmed) with prominent basslines, commonly within the 160-180 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Atmospheric Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent in the mid-1990s, uses faster, de-emphasized breakbeats, and places a greater focus on melodic elements such as slow, warm basslines and atmospheric melodies inspired by Ambient and Ambient House.

subgenres.name: Dancefloor Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s as a more accessible and polished style with melodic, prominent synth leads derived from Jump-Up and punchy, often synthesized drums.

subgenres.name: Darkstep
subgenres.desc: Hard, uptempo and uses heavy breakbeats, Post-Industrial-influenced sound design, and horror movie samples to create a sinister, claustrophobic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Crossbreed
subgenres.desc: Harsh and dense mixture of Darkstep with Hardcore [EDM] developed in the late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Skullstep
subgenres.desc: Repetitious, aggressive, off-beat rhythms often programmed using distorted, harsh, and noisy percussion that usually resembles clangy "pots and pans", machine gun-like snares.

subgenres.name: Deep Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Sub-bass-rich, repetitive, minimalist, and rhythm-focused production.

subgenres.name: Drumfunk
subgenres.desc: Focuses on complex drum beats made to emulate live recordings.

subgenres.name: Drumstep
subgenres.desc: Dancefloor-friendly, loud, and heavy combination of the drum programming and tempo of Jump-Up with the half-time rhythm and midrange LFO wobble of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Dubwise Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Implementing Reggae and Dub influences, usually vocal dubs, delay effects, and reggae instrumentation, with the clean production and rhythms of post-2000s styles.

subgenres.name: Footwork Jungle
subgenres.desc: Combining Footwork's archetypal percussion, skittering drum fills, handclaps, and syncopated rhythms, with Drum and Bass drum programming and breakbeats, merging the two into unconventional, frantic drumming and dense, off-kilter rhythms.

subgenres.name: Halftime
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Drum and Bass (mainly Neurofunk) characterized by off-kilter rhythms playing at around 80-85 BPM (half of normal DnB pace), influenced by Dubstep, Wonky, Trap [EDM], and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Hardstep
subgenres.desc: Very compressed and sparse drumming, extensive use of kick drums and gritty, minimalistic production style with emphasis on simple, deep, modulated bass patterns.

subgenres.name: Jazzstep
subgenres.desc: Combines the rhythm and speed of Drum and Bass with the melodies, composition, and instrumentation of Jazz.

subgenres.name: Jump-Up
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s, characterized by loud "wobbling" basslines, simpler drum loops, and a light-hearted and warm sound.

subgenres.name: Jungle
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 1990s from Breakbeat Hardcore, featuring rapid, chaotic-sounding breakbeats and strong basslines; known as the forerunner of most Drum and Bass styles.

subgenres.name: Ragga Jungle
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 1990s in London, combining Jungle breakbeats with heavy influence from Ragga.

subgenres.name: Liquid Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric and melodic genre that developed in the early 2000s; utilizes polished and smooth production, simpler structures, and originally sampled Funk and Soul.

subgenres.name: Sambass
subgenres.desc: Combines Drum and Bass tempos and drum patterns, in addition to its Funk and Soul influences, with various styles of Brazilian Music.

subgenres.name: Minimal Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Minimalist, sparse sound; emerged in two main 2000s strains, one Dubstep-inspired and one IDM-inspired, which crossed paths in the 2010s.

subgenres.name: Autonomic
subgenres.desc: Mechanical, machine-like, "autonomic" rhythms that take primary influence from the cold, minimal sounds of mid-2000s UK Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Microfunk
subgenres.desc: Minimal, glitchy, and "bleep"-y sound inspired by IDM.

subgenres.name: Neurofunk
subgenres.desc: Focuses on technical songwriting with warped, complex bass sounds, distorted and modulated synths (often with repeated stabs over the basslines), and dark but clean production.

subgenres.name: Technoid
subgenres.desc: Influenced by the repetitive and mechanical sound of Techno.

subgenres.name: Techstep
subgenres.desc: Futuristic, dark, and gritty sound; quantized and compressed drum breaks, distorted bass lines, and a focus on a sci-fi atmosphere and sampling sources.

subgenres.name: Trancestep
subgenres.desc: Combination of Trance melodies and structure with the breakbeats, fast tempos, and rolling basslines of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Half-time syncopated and sparse beats set around 140 BPM with heavy sub-basses; emerged in South London in the early 2000s.

subgenres.name: Brostep
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Dubstep which replaces its sub-bass-oriented sound with an emphasis on catchy or aggressive mid-range melodies.

subgenres.name: Briddim
subgenres.desc: Combining the kick-clap rhythms and syncopation of Riddim with Brostep sound design.

subgenres.name: Colour Bass
subgenres.desc: Combines aggressive wobbling basses with the euphoric drops of Melodic Dubstep and Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Deathstep
subgenres.desc: Darker, heavier form of Brostep that uses "machine gun" basses, atonal synths, and elements from genres like Death Metal and Metalcore.

subgenres.name: Minatory
subgenres.desc: Extreme, experimental style of Deathstep, with a harsh sound and sudden BPM changes.

subgenres.name: Drumstep
subgenres.desc: Dancefloor-friendly, loud, and heavy combination of the drum programming and tempo of Jump-Up with the half-time rhythm and midrange LFO wobble of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Tearout [Brostep]
subgenres.desc: Heavy and distorted, closely affiliated with Deathstep and other styles of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Chillstep
subgenres.desc: Relaxed Dubstep influenced by Downtempo and Ambient.

subgenres.name: Dungeon Sound
subgenres.desc: Commonly features dark textures, spatial production, and midrange basses.

subgenres.name: Melodic Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Melodious, tuneful drops, rich, lush synth leads, powerful stretched chords, and light and harmonious sound design.

subgenres.name: Purple Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s out of the Dubstep scene of the time, incorporating synth leads and basslines inspired by 1980s Synth Funk and 1990s G-Funk, and Video Game Music, into a rhythmic palette mostly derived from dubstep and Grime.

subgenres.name: Riddim
subgenres.desc: Repetitive and relatively simplistic style inspired by mid-to-late-2000s UK Dubstep, often using robotic and/or squishy sound design along with bouncy square basses and less prominent buildups.

subgenres.name: Future Riddim
subgenres.desc: Melodic and futuristic style inspired by Future Bass, and to a lesser extent Colour Bass and Melodic Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Liquid Riddim
subgenres.desc: Distinct for its atmospheric production, overpowering ambience, watery synths, and melodic bass patterns.

subgenres.name: Tearout
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s, characterized by a gritty, aggressive sound and closely affiliated with early, deep Dubstep.

subgenres.name: East Coast Club
subgenres.desc: Group of club styles from the US East Coast that combines Miami Bass rhythms with influence from Breakbeat and Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Jersey Club
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Newark in the late 2000s; features fast tempos, hard kicks, and less prominent breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Philly Club
subgenres.desc: Builds on Baltimore Club with a faster tempo and sometimes influences from more modern genres like Trap [EDM].

subgenres.name: EBM
subgenres.desc: Melodic and dancefloor-friendly take on Post-Industrial music that developed in the early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Dark Electro
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1990s in Europe, incorporating the abrasiveness of old school Industrial but with a greater focus on a horror-inspired atmosphere and harsh, distorted vocals.

subgenres.name: Aggrotech
subgenres.desc: Merges aggressive-sounding synths and apocalyptic atmospheres with harsh 4/4 beats and fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Futurepop
subgenres.desc: Derivative of EBM, retaining its apocalyptic worldview but incorporating heavy influence from the melodic style of Synthpop.

subgenres.name: New Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s in Belgium; characterized by dark basslines, hard-hitting grooves and a slow tempo.

subgenres.name: Hard Beat
subgenres.desc: Short-lived, harder, harsh form of New Beat with Industrial, Acid House and EBM-influenced arrangement.

subgenres.name: Electro
subgenres.desc: Syncopated rhythms programmed on the Roland TR-808 drum machine, often resembling Funk breaks, along with simple funky basslines.

subgenres.name: Electroclash
subgenres.desc: Draws from 1980s styles such as Electro, New Wave, and Electro-Disco combined with Techno, resulting in minimal, throbbing beats and basslines, buzzing synthesizer parts, vocoders and often monotone, half-spoken, half-sung vocals.

subgenres.name: Electro-Disco
subgenres.desc: Disco instrumentation is largely - if not entirely - replaced by synthesizers and augmented with futuristic elements such as the vocoder.

subgenres.name: Hi-NRG
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s and quickly became the most popular form of Electronic Dance Music in the LGBT club scenes of San Francisco and New York, characterized by its uptempo, high-energy sound.

subgenres.name: Italo-Disco
subgenres.desc: Produced primarily in Italy and is characterized by the use of synthesizers, drum machines, and sometimes vocoders to create a mechanical, Electronic version of Disco with futuristic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Spacesynth
subgenres.desc: Highly melodic, often instrumental futuristic strain, formed under the heavy influence of Space Disco, Progressive Electronic and, later, early Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: Doskpop
subgenres.desc: Grew out of the Amiga Demoscene in the late 1980s with the imitation of Spacesynth in the context of the restrictions and aesthetics of Demostyle.

subgenres.name: Red Disco
subgenres.desc: Continuum of various eclectic forms, derived mainly from late Euro-Disco, but also Italo-Disco, Hi-NRG and Eurobeat, and developed in the Soviet Union in the mid-to-late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Space Disco
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Europe in the mid-to-late 1970s, characterized by layers of oscillating synth, space-oriented sound effects, and a futuristic sound inspired by contemporary sci-fi media.

subgenres.name: Electro latino
subgenres.desc: Mixes elements of Merengue and Reggaetón with polished production from mainstream House subgenres; often shares traits with Latin Pop, having anthemic melodies and verse-chorus structures.

subgenres.name: Electro Swing
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, energetic style that splices Swing with Electronic Dance Music, looking to recapture the atmosphere of late 1920s to mid-1940s Jazz within a more updated club-friendly medium.

subgenres.name: Eurobeat
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced with roots in Hi-NRG and Italo-Disco; became mainly popular in Japan in the 1990s.

subgenres.name: J-Euro
subgenres.desc: Italian-oriented Japanese scene of Eurobeat, which emerged with Japanese-language covers of Italian songs in the early-to-mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Eurodance
subgenres.desc: Takes elements of Euro-Disco, House, Techno, and Hi-NRG while featuring on-beat kick, hi-hat and snare sounds at around 110 to 150 bpm.

subgenres.name: Bubblegum Dance
subgenres.desc: Playful, childlike style with a Bubblegum-like atmosphere that often incorporates high-pitched, light-hearted, and usually female-fronted vocals.

subgenres.name: Italo Dance
subgenres.desc: Appeared in the 1990s after the decline of Italo-Disco, featuring rhythmic influence from that genre.

subgenres.name: Flex Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Largely instrumental; infused with Electronic Dance Music elements.

subgenres.name: Footwork
subgenres.desc: Extensive use of drum fills, tom drums, handclaps, and snares within fast-paced, highly syncopated beats not bound to a 4/4 kick rhythm.

subgenres.name: Footwork Jungle
subgenres.desc: Combining Footwork's archetypal percussion, skittering drum fills, handclaps, and syncopated rhythms, with Drum and Bass drum programming and breakbeats, merging the two into unconventional, frantic drumming and dense, off-kilter rhythms.

subgenres.name: Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Electro-influenced; developed in Latino communities in New York and Miami in the 1980s, especially dominated by Latin Freestyle and its Latin influences.

subgenres.name: Latin Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Displays a heavy influence of Hispanic American Music alongside the Disco, Hip Hop, and Electro influences of Freestyle.

subgenres.name: Funk mandelão
subgenres.desc: Simple lyricism, raw and minimalistic production, and distinct drops with bursting bass.

subgenres.name: Beat bruxaria
subgenres.desc: São Paulo-originated Funk brasileiro with aggressive, distorted and high-pitched beats featuring minimalistic percussion and diversified sampling.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Phonk
subgenres.desc: Merges Funk automotivo's rhythms, vocals, and energy, with the energetic and nocturnal production typical of the Drift Phonk scene, and Phonk House.

subgenres.name: Funk automotivo
subgenres.desc: Catchy, repetitive synths accompanied by a strong four-on-the-floor kick and loud, reverberated vocals.

subgenres.name: Ritmada
subgenres.desc: Short, repetitive and resonant beats with more danceable, immersive grooves drawn out of Afro-Brazilian instrumentation, a cleaner, more radio-friendly sound and greater focus on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Funkot
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced Indonesian form of Electronic Dance Music that combines Eurodance and Trance synths with the syncopated rhythm from Dangdut koplo.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Kota
subgenres.desc: Indonesian style that slows down the syncopated rhythms of Funkot to moderate tempos around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Jungle Dutch
subgenres.desc: Combines the high-pitched synth leads of Dutch House with the frantic "tribal" rhythms of Jungle Terror.

subgenres.name: Future Bass
subgenres.desc: Woozy, detuned synthesizers, 7th chords, harsh basslines, syncopated percussion with fast-paced hi-hats and a melodic, carefree atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Kawaii Future Bass
subgenres.desc: "Cute" style of Future Bass rooted in anime and video game culture; emerged in Japan in the mid-2010s.

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Future Rave
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2010s by combining the mainstage EDM approach with influences from then-popular forms of Techno and old-school Trance/rave-inspired grooves and atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Ghettotech
subgenres.desc: Fuses the syncopation and synthesized sounds of Electro and Detroit Techno with the cut-up samples of Ghetto House and fast rhythms of Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Glitch Hop [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Tempos around 100-110 BPM, swung, bouncy drum patterns, and a focus on upbeat, danceable drops and buildups.

subgenres.name: Ghetto Funk
subgenres.desc: Rich sampling, drawing from classic Hip Hop as well as from Funk and Soul, and strong midtempo break grooves.

subgenres.name: Neurohop
subgenres.desc: Features the complex bass of Neurofunk and a frantic and mechanical sound design.

subgenres.name: Gqom
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2010s in Durban townships, features highly syncopated, bass-heavy, stripped-down beats and dark, raw atmosphere, often with ominous synth pads and aggressive vocal chants.

subgenres.name: Grime
subgenres.desc: UK Garage-derived production style characterized by dark, fast-paced, often aggressive beats that commonly features fast-paced MCing.

subgenres.name: Neo-Grime
subgenres.desc: Mixes Wave with Grime and other forms of UK Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Weightless
subgenres.desc: Typically instrumental, leftfield Grime style characterized by sparse, "weightless" percussion and spectral, atmospheric production.

subgenres.name: Hardcore [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for a wide variety of fast-paced and energetic Electronic Dance Music styles that have been developed since the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: Acidcore
subgenres.desc: Developed out of the 1990s Acid Techno scene utilizing its prominence of "acid" TB-303 bassline sequences into more intense rhythms derived from earlier Hardcore [EDM], Gabber and Trance music.

subgenres.name: Amigacore
subgenres.desc: Gabber-like forms of Hardcore [EDM] written in first-gen trackers for theAmigalike ProTracker and OctaMED, resulting in a minimalistic raw lo-fi sound.

subgenres.name: Belgian Techno
subgenres.desc: Early form of Hardcore [EDM], resulting from the further evolution of New Beat due to the strong influence of Techno and EBM.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Originated from the combination of sampled breakbeats and energetic rhythms with the "rave" influences set by early-1990s Techno and Acid House, including upbeat "stab" riffing and sample-based production.

subgenres.name: Darkside
subgenres.desc: Dark atmosphere and fast rhythms; served as a forerunner of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Breaks
subgenres.desc: Revival of Breakbeat Hardcore which emerged in the 2000s, bringing in modern influences and production techniques.

subgenres.name: Breakcore
subgenres.desc: Mixes Hardcore [EDM] with cut-up, complex, and frequently noisy breakbeats at very high tempos inspired by Jungle and Drum and Bass, often with heavy use of sampling.

subgenres.name: Lolicore
subgenres.desc: Heavily distorted or high-pitched Anime vocal samples and complex cut-up breakbeats with extreme tempos.

subgenres.name: Mashcore
subgenres.desc: Sampling, particularly from Pop and Electronic Dance Music, as well as playful melodies, hard kicks, and the typical breakcore breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Raggacore
subgenres.desc: Prominently incorporates samples from Ragga and Dancehall, typically through shouted vocal lines and Reggae-influenced instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Crossbreed
subgenres.desc: Harsh and dense mixture of Darkstep with Hardcore [EDM] developed in the late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Darkcore
subgenres.desc: Aggressive, dark, and often midtempo with influences from Doomcore, Industrial Hardcore, and Nu Style Gabber.

subgenres.name: Deathchant Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Took shape in the UK in the late 1990s and early 2000s, characterized by rapid rhythms with Gabber-influenced kicks, frequent use of breakbeats and Hip Hop-inspired sampling.

subgenres.name: Digital Hardcore
subgenres.desc: High-tempo fusion of Hardcore Punk and Electronic, combining harsh vocals and electric guitars of the former with electronic instruments.

subgenres.name: Doomcore
subgenres.desc: Often somber and contemplative in mood, a feature achieved by the common use of long-stretched ambient pads, and sometimes even samples of screaming and other "spooky" sounds.

subgenres.name: Frapcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in France in the mid-2010s, uses French rapping with 4-on-the-floor Hardcore [EDM] and especially Gabber instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Freeform Hardcore
