subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s, combining fast and hard-hitting rhythms with heavy influence from the synthesizers of Trance.

subgenres.name: Frenchcore
subgenres.desc: Off-beat, bouncy rhythmic patterns and tempos around the 200 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Gabber
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced and energetic, often in the 160-220 BPM range, with a hallmark of a distinctive distorted kick sound.

subgenres.name: Nu Style Gabber
subgenres.desc: Emerged near the end of the 1990s; deeper, more harmonic bassdrums with constant use of supersaw melodies, breakdown sections and slower tempos closer to the 150-180 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Happy Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1990s from the UK Breakbeat Hardcore scene; characterized by saccharine vocals, uplifting piano riffs and spacey effects, gradually developing to emphasize extremely fast-paced four-on-the-floor beats.

subgenres.name: Bouncy Techno
subgenres.desc: Average tempo of 160 to 180 BPM, four-on-the-floor beats, melodic and repetitive synth melodies, drums with hard kicks, short breaks, progressive stomping rhythms, and offbeat notes.

subgenres.name: UK Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Powerstomp
subgenres.desc: Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.

subgenres.name: Hardtek
subgenres.desc: Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.

subgenres.name: Raggatek
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.

subgenres.name: Industrial Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Fuses the sonic palettes and aesthetics of Industrial with the intense rhythms of Gabber, Speedcore, Doomcore and other subsequent styles.

subgenres.name: Speedcore
subgenres.desc: Exceedingly fast tempos, frequently above 300 BPM, and often aggressive themes and samples.

subgenres.name: Extratone
subgenres.desc: At and above the threshold of 1000 BPM where sequences of kick drums begin to form a continuous pitch.

subgenres.name: Splittercore
subgenres.desc: Faster version of Speedcore with BPM ranging from around 600 to 1000.

subgenres.name: Terrorcore
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rhythms from earlier Gabber with a faster BPM (usually no more than 300) and darker approach.

subgenres.name: Uptempo Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Utilizes lo-fi production, harsh kicks, and elements borrowed from Rawstyle and other gritty Hardcore [EDM] styles while usually sitting at around 185-220 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hard Dance
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for EDM mainly developed out of Hard Trance and UK Hard House; usually characterized by fast tempos, hard kick drums and a "bouncy" syncopated groove.

subgenres.name: Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Hard, four-on-the-floor kick drums, fast tempo around 150 BPM, reverse bass and harsh, distorted synths.

subgenres.name: Dubstyle
subgenres.desc: Characterized by the incorporation of the half-time rhythms and wobbly basslines of Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Early Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Forerunner subgenre that emerged around the turn of the 2000s from Hard Trance and Gabber, distinguished by the signature reverse bass groove, slower tempo around 140 BPM and straightforward, repetitive sound.

subgenres.name: Euphoric Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Melodic, more lighthearted, and accessible Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Nustyle
subgenres.desc: Developed out of Early Hardstyle from the mid-to-late 2000s, by incorporating distorted, crunchy, pitched kicks, faster tempo around 150 BPM, and detuned supersaw/square synth leads playing stompy, dramatic melodies.

subgenres.name: Psystyle
subgenres.desc: Prominent Psytrance influences, especially the basslines and energy of mainstream psytrance.

subgenres.name: Rawstyle
subgenres.desc: Incorporates earlier Hardstyle and Hardcore [EDM] influences into the sound of 2010s hardstyle, creating a distinctly harsh, simplistic, raw, and dark sound, with fast BPM.

subgenres.name: Rawphoric
subgenres.desc: Combines raw harsh kicks with the uplifting melodies of Euphoric Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Hardtek
subgenres.desc: Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.

subgenres.name: Raggatek
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.

subgenres.name: Hard Trance
subgenres.desc: Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.

subgenres.name: Jumpstyle
subgenres.desc: Features a heavy 909 kick drum, four-on-the-floor beat, and a tempo between 140 and 150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Lento violento
subgenres.desc: Features a "slow and violent" sound between 70-120 BPM with hard kicks inspired by Hardcore [EDM] and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: NRG
subgenres.desc: Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.

subgenres.name: UK Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Powerstomp
subgenres.desc: Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.

subgenres.name: UK Hard House
subgenres.desc: Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.

subgenres.name: Scouse House
subgenres.desc: Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.

subgenres.name: Hardbass
subgenres.desc: Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: Hard Drum
subgenres.desc: Highly percussive, syncopated rhythms, influences from global contemporary genres, and lack of melodic elements, with a tempo lingering around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hardvapour
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Hardcore [EDM] and Techno and made in response to the Vaporwave movement.

subgenres.name: Hardwave
subgenres.desc: Harder, festival-oriented offshoot of Wave, combining its "reese" basses and icy synths with Trap [EDM] drum patterns, build-up-drop structures, and fuller sound influenced by Trance and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: House
subgenres.desc: Generally features a four-on-the-floor beat within 110-140 BPM, a groove built on swing and syncopation, synthesized basslines, repetitive melodic elements, and an upbeat mood.

subgenres.name: Acid House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s, characterised by repetitive basslines created with the distinctive modulated "squelching" sound of the Roland TB-303 synthesiser.

subgenres.name: Afro House
subgenres.desc: Emerged by fusing Deep House with Southern African Music, characterized by hypnotizing drum patterns of shakers and congas, often sampled African vocals or soulful original features, and spiritual, organic, melodic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: 3-Step
subgenres.desc: Distinct three-kick-drum rhythm, blends influences from Amapiano and Broken Beat, resulting in relaxed, freeform, playful, Jazz-like feel.

subgenres.name: Amapiano
subgenres.desc: House from South Africa deriving from previous popular genres including Gqom, Kwaito, and Deep House.

subgenres.name: Afropiano
subgenres.desc: Blends the easy-going, poppy, and melodic Afrobeats sound and rhythms with major Amapiano elements, like lush, jazzy, and laid-back atmospheres often featuring light piano chords.

subgenres.name: Ambient House
subgenres.desc: Primarily British genre developed in the 1990s with beats, synthesizers, and vocals in styles similar to House, treated with effects that are often described as "dream-like" or "chilled out".

subgenres.name: Ballroom
subgenres.desc: Emerging from the predominantly Black and LGBT Harlem ballroom culture, it is characterized by hard-hitting rhythms, generally improvised chanting by MCs known as commentators, and a distinctive crash sample.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Bass House
subgenres.desc: Busy, punchy percussion, prominent basslines and dirty, distorted synths resembling other bass music genres, with influences including Brostep, Fidget House, Bassline, Speed Garage, and Tech House.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: Bassline
subgenres.desc: Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.

subgenres.name: Big Room House
subgenres.desc: Energetic, festival-oriented style characterized by heavy reverb, intense build-ups, strong kicks, minimalistic drop melodies, and sparse, raw breakdowns.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Bass
subgenres.desc: Originated in the 2010s in Brazil, taking influences from Deep House and Tech House, characterized by deep, punchy basslines making use of detuning and filtering effects.

subgenres.name: Mega funk
subgenres.desc: Blends funk vocal performances with production derived from mainstage 2010s House genres like Brazilian Bass and Slap House.

subgenres.name: Slap House
subgenres.desc: Taking influences from Brazilian Bass and Future House, characterized by prominent, "bouncy" bassline and simple, upbeat melodies.

subgenres.name: Bubbling House
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Netherlands in the 2000s, combining the older style of Bubbling with more modern House, especially Dutch House.

subgenres.name: Changa tuki
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Chicago Hard House
subgenres.desc: Originated from Chicago around the mid-1990s as a development of Ghetto House, emphasizing hard-hitting, off-beat drum patterns, fast tempos, and lack of melodies.

subgenres.name: LA Hard House
subgenres.desc: Distorted, minimalistic TR-909 derived rhythms, basic climaxing structures and heavy reliance on high-pitched synthesizer / hoover sounds.

subgenres.name: Chicago House
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for a broad variety of House that originated from Chicago in the (mostly mid-to-late) 1980s and early 90s.

subgenres.name: Deep House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United States during the mid-1980s, featuring a relaxed tempo and influences from Jazz, Funk, and Soul.

subgenres.name: Lo-Fi House
subgenres.desc: Primarily distinguished from earlier styles of outsider house by its stricter reliance on deep house elements, cranky, nocturnal, and nostalgic atmospheres, and a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Diva House
subgenres.desc: Dominant, anthemic female vocals, common use of piano stabs, and energetic, driving four-on-the-floor rhythms.

subgenres.name: Hardbag
subgenres.desc: Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.

subgenres.name: Electro House
subgenres.desc: Warm analog basslines, punchy percussion, crisp high-pitched synthesizer leads, and clipped vocal samples.

subgenres.name: Complextro
subgenres.desc: Features densely-layered sound design, fast-paced cut-up sections, aggressive stabs, and common crossover with Brostep and Fidget House.

subgenres.name: Dutch House
subgenres.desc: High-pitched wonky synth melodies and heavy influence from Fidget House which developed in the Netherlands around 2007-08.

subgenres.name: Noiadance
subgenres.desc: Blends Dutch House production with Funk brasileiro vocals and drumming on top of Moombahton rhythms.

subgenres.name: Fidget House
subgenres.desc: Makes heavy use of Breakbeat Hardcore-esque synth stabs, pitch bending of basslines, and cut-up vocal samples, as well as glitchy, or "choppy", 4/4 rhythms.

subgenres.name: French Electro
subgenres.desc: Mixes Electro House with major elements of genres such as Electroclash, Nu-Disco, Synth Funk, and even Electro-Industrial, resulting in a harsh, punchy, and funky midtempo sound.

subgenres.name: Melbourne Bounce
subgenres.desc: Offbeat basslines giving it a "bouncy" groove, and minimalistic, side-chained melodies often making use of Dutch House-influenced synths, horns or vocal chops, resulting in a flippant, party-oriented atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Eletrofunk
subgenres.desc: Blends Funk brasileiro vocals with production from popular late 2000s and early 2010s House.

subgenres.name: Euro House
subgenres.desc: Vocal-focused style emerging in the late 1980s in Europe, developing in parallel with Eurodance.

subgenres.name: Hardbag
subgenres.desc: Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.

subgenres.name: Festival Progressive House
subgenres.desc: Uplifting, melodic, energetic but clean drops, featuring modern supersaws and pianos, taking influences from Progressive House, Uplifting Trance, but applying them to a form structurally closer to Big Room House and Electro House.

subgenres.name: French House
subgenres.desc: Originated in France in the mid-1990s, characterized by the use of filtered (low-pass, phaser, etc.) samples of Funk and Disco.

subgenres.name: Funky House
subgenres.desc: Funky, warm, catchy basslines on top of looped Funk or Disco samples, resulting in an upbeat, bouncy, and pacy groove.

subgenres.name: Future Funk
subgenres.desc: Sample-based style influenced by French House and Synth Funk that utilizes Vaporwave editing techniques.

subgenres.name: Future House
subgenres.desc: Features distinctive metallic-sounding drops and frequency-modulated basslines at around 120-130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Future Bounce
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Melbourne Bounce and Future House that combines the former's basslines and bouncy, upbeat drops with the latter's metallic, pronounced synth leads.

subgenres.name: Slap House
subgenres.desc: Taking influences from Brazilian Bass and Future House, characterized by prominent, "bouncy" bassline and simple, upbeat melodies.

subgenres.name: Garage House
subgenres.desc: Disco-influenced style of House that developed in the 1980s, incorporating elements of Gospel, Soul, and Dub, before evolving into a more upbeat style that prominently features crisp syncopated hi-hats and synth stabs.

subgenres.name: Gospel House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates heavy Gospel elements and singing borrowed from classic and contemporary gospel, usually in the form of choir vocals and call-and-response chants.

subgenres.name: Jersey Sound
subgenres.desc: Soulful, melodic, Gospel-infused House music developed in Newark, NJ in the late 1980s and early 1990s with an emphasis on songcraft.

subgenres.name: Ghetto House
subgenres.desc: Rough sound based around minimal drum machine-driven tracks and heavy usage of vocal samples.

subgenres.name: Juke
subgenres.desc: Faster than Ghetto House, playing at 160bpm, and makes striking use of unconventional drum patterns which differ wildly from other House styles.

subgenres.name: G-House
subgenres.desc: Deep, dark form of House music that primarily incorporates rap samples or original rapping on top of minimal, bassy beats.

subgenres.name: Hip House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates production elements of early Hip Hop and usually rapping into 1980s House.

subgenres.name: Italo House
subgenres.desc: Originated in Italy during the late 1980s, making use of anthemic pianos, diva vocals, and Dance-Pop song structures.

subgenres.name: Jackin' House
subgenres.desc: Punchy, 'shuffly' percussion, strong grooves, funky basslines, and chopped-up samples.

subgenres.name: Kwaito
subgenres.desc: Emerged from South Africa in the early 1990s, taking influence from Disco and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Bacardi
subgenres.desc: Bacardi is a type of House music from South Africa derived from Kwaito, delivering upbeat, danceable rhythms with lively snares and hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Latin House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Latin music (various Hispanic American Music and Brazilian Music genres), including their melodies, vocals, and instruments, as well as additional Latin percussion.

subgenres.name: Melodic House
subgenres.desc: Arpeggiated synth lines, focus on a chilled and laid-back atmosphere, and influence from genres such as Progressive House and Deep House.

subgenres.name: Microhouse
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down, minimal form of House, originating in the late 90s, which takes influence from Minimal Techno, Glitch and IDM.

subgenres.name: Organic House
subgenres.desc: Subtle drums and grooves, slow tempos, and acoustic, traditional instrumentation, resulting in an organic, warm sound and spiritual atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Outsider House
subgenres.desc: Mostly derived from Deep House; intentional use of rough, lo-fi production, often utilizing a mix of analog/analog-like and digital instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Lo-Fi House
subgenres.desc: Primarily distinguished from earlier styles of outsider house by its stricter reliance on deep house elements, cranky, nocturnal, and nostalgic atmospheres, and a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Phonk House
subgenres.desc: Merges Drift Phonk's nocturnal atmospheres, cowbell melodies, vocal samples, and energetic production, with House rhythms and tempos, characterized by a banging and upbeat sound.

subgenres.name: Progressive House
subgenres.desc: Trance-influenced strain of House that grew to prominence in the early 1990s, using polished production and gradual progressions.

subgenres.name: Romanian Popcorn
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the second half of the 2000s in Romania, often featuring brass melodies and "staccato" pluck grooves.

subgenres.name: Speed Garage
subgenres.desc: Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.

subgenres.name: Stutter House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2020s taking influences from Melodic House, Trance, and Future Garage; features distinctive chopping of vocal samples and pads.

subgenres.name: Tech House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s taking influences from Techno, broadly characterized by minimalistic and repetitive melodies, focus on the bassline, and constant groove recognizable by prominent off-beat hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Deep Tech
subgenres.desc: Incorporates UK Garage rhythms and synths stabs, influences from British rave music, UK Bass and UK Deep House, resulting in an urban, subdued, but danceable sound with deep, muted basslines.

subgenres.name: Rominimal
subgenres.desc: Hypnotic, minimal, and "dubby" loops, featuring subtle and intricate synth pads, cranky, clicky percussion, and bouncy, pulsing basslines.

subgenres.name: Tribal House
subgenres.desc: Prominent, syncopated rhythms of tribal drums such as toms and bongos on top of a House beat, usually resulting in a percussive, energetic sound, while ranging in mood.

subgenres.name: Guaracha [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Originated in Colombia, featuring "fluttering" trumpets, accordion, and tambora drums.

subgenres.name: Tropical House
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Deep House featuring slow tempos around 100-115 BPM, light percussion and acoustic instrumentation, setting out to create a relaxed, summery, beach-like atmosphere.

subgenres.name: UK Hard House
subgenres.desc: Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.

subgenres.name: Scouse House
subgenres.desc: Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.

subgenres.name: Hardbass
subgenres.desc: Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: UK Jackin'
subgenres.desc: Successor to British Bassline, characterized by strong basslines, dark atmospheres, and dominant grooves.

subgenres.name: Vinahouse
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced House popular in Vietnam, remixing Vietnamese melodies.

subgenres.name: Hypertechno
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2020s by mixing fast tempos, prominent basslines, and hard-hitting drums derived from popular Techno with simplistic, catchy melodies and vocals, often influenced by 2000s Hard Dance, Eurodance and Electropop.

subgenres.name: Hyper Techno
subgenres.desc: Exaggerated fast form of Belgian Techno for the Japanese market, focusing mainly on synth sounds and samples typical of 1990s dance music.

subgenres.name: Jungle Terror
subgenres.desc: Emerging mostly from Dutch House and Big Room House, incorporates Tribal House-influenced percussion, hard kicks, and animal sounds resulting in a wild, jungle-resembling atmosphere in a festival EDM-oriented context.

subgenres.name: Krushclub
subgenres.desc: Bitcrushed synths and occasionally bitcrushed vocals, energetic Jersey Club-derived beats, and elements of Sigilkore's dark production style.

subgenres.name: Kuduro
subgenres.desc: Angolan music combining traditional Kilapanga and Semba with Techno and House.

subgenres.name: Batida
subgenres.desc: Initially developed in the late '80s in Luanda, Angola, as a mixture of Soca- and Zouk-based percussion samples.

subgenres.name: Makina
subgenres.desc: Spanish Techno developed in the early 1990s; strongly influenced by New Beat and EBM, but aiming for a lighter sound.

subgenres.name: Manyao
subgenres.desc: Asian Electronic Dance Music that mixes vocals and melodies from Mandopop with fairly hard, melodic EDM.

subgenres.name: Melodic Bass
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of Melodic Dubstep with euphoric sound design taking influences from Future Bass, guitar melodies and pop-driven structures

subgenres.name: Midtempo Bass
subgenres.desc: Harsh synth leads and a usual tempo of around 90-110 BPM.

subgenres.name: Moombahcore
subgenres.desc: High-pitched synth leads, gritty percussion, a kick-snare pattern, aggressive bass drops, and around 110 BPM while often paralleling Complextro or Brostep.

subgenres.name: Moombahton
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Dutch House characterized by tempos in the 100-110 BPM range, Reggaetón-influenced rhythms, bass-heavy kicks and high-pitched synths.

subgenres.name: Nerdcore Techno
subgenres.desc: Stylistically diverse form of underground Japanese Electronic Dance Music utilizing energetic beats built around samples from pop and/or nerd culture.

subgenres.name: Nu-Disco
subgenres.desc: 21st-century trend mixing modern, polished Electronic production with the aesthetics, structures, and lively, organic beats of 1970s and 1980s Disco.

subgenres.name: Ori deck
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Moombahton and Dubstep to create a style characterized by sluggish, kick-heavy dembow rhythms.

subgenres.name: Post-Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Minimalistic, atmospheric sound design and eclectic drum patterns, derived from but not fitting Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Shangaan Electro
subgenres.desc: South African genre with very fast BPM (around 180) featuring MIDI keyboard sounds and marimba.

subgenres.name: Singeli
subgenres.desc: Developed in Tanzania in the mid-2000s; fuses incredibly rapid beats, usually between 180-300BPM, with MCing and musical influences from older Tanzanian genres.

subgenres.name: Skweee
subgenres.desc: Mid-2000s offshoot of the Nordic Electro scene which uses simple, analogue or Chiptune-inspired synthesizer leads and basslines to create stripped-down, midtempo grooves drawing on Synth Funk and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Slimepunk
subgenres.desc: Loud synth leads with a distorted, gritty, and "slimy" sound design, usually laid on top of production inspired by or taken directly from genres such as Halftime, Trap [EDM], Brostep, and other forms of 2010s EDM.

subgenres.name: Techno
subgenres.desc: Highly beat-driven, repetitive, and mechanical, typically featuring minimal chord variation and melodies, focuses on rhythms and timbral variety; generally produced for club environments.

subgenres.name: Acid Techno
subgenres.desc: Incorporates "squelching" synths from Acid House into a mechanical and usually more energetic Techno context.

subgenres.name: Ambient Techno
subgenres.desc: Blends the mechanical, repetitive beats of Techno with atmospheres and textures inspired by Ambient music, resulting in slower tempos and more understated rhythms.

subgenres.name: Belgian Techno
subgenres.desc: Early form of Hardcore [EDM], resulting from the further evolution of New Beat due to the strong influence of Techno and EBM.

subgenres.name: Bleep Techno
subgenres.desc: Established in the late 1980s in the breakdancing and early rave scene of Yorkshire in the North of England, notable for its "bleepy" synth lines and heavy sub-bass.

subgenres.name: Detroit Techno
subgenres.desc: Features a signature mechanical, detached sound that echoed the atmosphere of Detroit's nightlife and incorporated influences from Electro and Chicago House as well as Synthpop and Electro-Disco.

subgenres.name: Freetekno
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 1990s, commonly played at free parties in Europe, and features a repetitive pounding kick drum at tempos of 170 BPM or above.

subgenres.name: Hardgroove Techno
subgenres.desc: Features shuffling grooves with heavy emphasis on layered percussive elements; often includes a mix of samples and drum machines played at a range of 135-140 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hard Techno
subgenres.desc: Typically rave-oriented form characterized by hard, prominent kick drums, pounding rhythms, fast tempos around 140-160 BPM, and aggressive, often distorted sounds.

subgenres.name: Schranz
subgenres.desc: Characterised by fast tempos, aggressive "whooshing" beat patterns, heavy compression and straightforward song structures.

subgenres.name: Industrial Techno
subgenres.desc: Harder, darker style of Techno which draws parallels with factories and the rhythm of machinery.

subgenres.name: Birmingham Sound
subgenres.desc: Cold, mechanical, and hypnotic tracks, typically lacking the harsher and noisier elements of later Industrial Techno.

subgenres.name: Melodic Techno
subgenres.desc: Trance-influenced subgenre that was established in the mid-to-late 2010s, characterized by gradually progressing structure, and hypnotizing, atmospheric sound with arpeggiated, minor melodies, playing at around 120-125 BPM.

subgenres.name: Minimal Techno
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down and sparse, often featuring a dark sound and a slow, steady development through the track.

subgenres.name: Dub Techno
subgenres.desc: Fuses elements of Minimal Techno with characteristics of Dub.

subgenres.name: Peak Time Techno
subgenres.desc: Hard, dynamic, energetic and accessible subgenre featuring strong kicks, massive dirty synths, tempos around 130 BPM, more suspenseful structures with breaks and build-ups, and big, modern, festival-oriented sound; rose to high popularity in the late 2010s.

subgenres.name: Wonky Techno
subgenres.desc: Strays from the standard beat of Techno, opting for a more fractured sound.

subgenres.name: Techno Bass
subgenres.desc: Minimal, stripped-down with an emphasis on low-frequency bass partitions.

subgenres.name: Car Audio Bass
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimalistic extreme form, focused on ultra-low frequency sine wave notes and mainly intended for stress testing subwoofer sound systems.

subgenres.name: Tecnorumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.

subgenres.name: Trance
subgenres.desc: Evolving, tension-building structures with rapid, minor arpeggios on top of a hypnotic, four-on-the-floor drum patterns at fast tempo around 130-150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Acid Trance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates "squelching" acid basslines into Trance's evolving structure.

subgenres.name: Big Room Trance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates production features associated with Big Room House and dirty, distorted leads influenced by Electro House, Dutch House and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Dream Trance
subgenres.desc: Slow tempo (about 130 BPM) with strong roots in Progressive House, using beats typical of Eurodance and Dance-Pop; emphasizes a laid-back, carefree, and dreamlike sound.

subgenres.name: Euro Trance
subgenres.desc: Emerged as a fusion with Eurodance, features fast tempos, more accessible grooves and structures, and simple, catchy melodies with vocals and saw synth leads.

subgenres.name: Hands Up
subgenres.desc: Prominent, melodic supersaw leads, Dance-Pop derived hooks, and a strong reliance on sidechained basslines and hard, powerful drums.

subgenres.name: Buchiage Trance
subgenres.desc: Japanese style that emerged in Shibuya's club scene in the 2000s and was primarily marketed to gyaru, infused with melodic and rhythmic influence from Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: Hard Trance
subgenres.desc: Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.

subgenres.name: Hi-Tech Full-On
subgenres.desc: Largely Japanese genre with an energetic and glitchy sound derived from Full-On Psytrance and Complextro.

subgenres.name: Ibiza Trance
subgenres.desc: Builds on the relaxing island atmosphere of Balearic Beat, though with a slightly faster tempo of around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: NRG
subgenres.desc: Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.

subgenres.name: Progressive Trance
subgenres.desc: Combination of Trance and Progressive House which emerged in Western Europe in the early to mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a psychedelic feel and an energetic sound; based around influences from Goa Trance and Acid Trance.

subgenres.name: Dark Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Uses more complex sound design based on dark atmospheres and fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Hi-Tech Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Glitchy sound design, morphing synth lines, strange sounds typically evoking futuristic or alien-like atmospheres, and faster tempos than most other forms of Psytrance.

subgenres.name: Psycore
subgenres.desc: Pushes the dark atmospheres of Dark Psytrance to the extreme through the usage of exceptionally high tempos and experimental soundscapes influenced by Dark Ambient and Glitch.

subgenres.name: Forest Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Mimicks the ambience of a forest by using swarming and teeming effects as well as natural samples; features straightforward song structures.

subgenres.name: Full-On Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Faster and more intense, usually set around 145-150 BPM and featuring harder rolling basslines, vocal samples and "spacey" effects.

subgenres.name: Goa Trance
subgenres.desc: Forerunner of Psytrance styles that emerged in the early 1990s, distinguished by old-school, organic sound with rapid, oriental-inspired melodies.

subgenres.name: Nitzhonot
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced, featuring rapid melodic lines and usually hard and high-pitched kicks.

subgenres.name: Progressive Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2000s, featuring a slow tempo range and clean production.

subgenres.name: Zenonesque
subgenres.desc: Experimental and leftfield approach to Progressive Psytrance, mixing the atmospheric and clean Psytrance production typical of it with funky and jazzy elements.

subgenres.name: Suomisaundi
subgenres.desc: Finnish-based deviation of Psytrance with an emphasis on free-form experimentation and humor.

subgenres.name: Tech Trance
subgenres.desc: Late 1990s-emerging subgenre characterized by energetic percussion with loud kicks, filtered hi-hats and tribal drums; side-chained, detuned and repetitive leads, as well as other raw, distorted, and complex sounds influenced by Techno, Hard Trance and Electro House.

subgenres.name: Uplifting Trance
subgenres.desc: Euphoric melodies, buildup-breakdown-anthem structures, common usage of supersaws, and a BPM range of usually around 135-142.

subgenres.name: Vocal Trance
subgenres.desc: Melodic, polished, Pop-like, and vocal-focused with around 120-145 BPM and frequent overlap with Progressive Trance, Uplifting Trance, and Euro Trance.

subgenres.name: Trap [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Trap-influenced syncopated percussion with 808 samples and fast-paced hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Festival Trap
subgenres.desc: Massive, sub-bass-heavy drops with simple melodies, synth leads and production influenced by Big Room House; highly popular from 2013 to 2015.

subgenres.name: Hard Trap
subgenres.desc: Often abrasive subgenre of Trap [EDM] with heavy influence from Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Heaven Trap
subgenres.desc: Blends Trap [EDM]’s signature percussion and sub-basses with euphoric, uplifting, melodious drops prominently derived from Festival Progressive House, contrary to the gritty, "dirty" nature of other EDM trap styles.

subgenres.name: Hybrid Trap
subgenres.desc: Blending Trap [EDM]'s typical percussion and sub-basses with major influences from heavy bass music genres, and in particular, metallic, gritty, and off-kilter sound design, originally derived from Brostep.

subgenres.name: Twerk
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced; draws influence from Bounce and Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Tribal Guarachero
subgenres.desc: Features percussion from Cumbia and Mexican Folk Music with upbeat Electro House-derived production and fast, triplet-oriented rhythmic patterns.

subgenres.name: UK Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent bass/sub-basses, a deep, dark, airy, and mechanical sound derived from Dubstep, and eclectic production influenced by UK Funky, Juke/Footwork, Techno, and Breakbeat.

subgenres.name: UK Funky
subgenres.desc: Influenced by UK Garage-related styles and the regional styles of British immigrants, including Soca and West African-inspired Tribal House.

subgenres.name: UK Garage
subgenres.desc: Shuffling rhythms and influences from sources including Contemporary R&B and Hip Hop, as well as many forms of Electronic.

subgenres.name: 2-Step
subgenres.desc: Originating in London and popular in the late 1990s; jittery, shuffling rhythms rarely following a four-on-the-floor pattern.

subgenres.name: Bassline
subgenres.desc: Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.

subgenres.name: Breakstep
subgenres.desc: Hard-hitting Breakbeat rhythms and heavy, rolling basslines.

subgenres.name: Future Garage
subgenres.desc: Combines the rhythms of late 1990s and early 2000s 2-Step with novel moods and production approaches, commonly featuring jittery, broken rhythms, vocal chops, and warm synth pads and plucks.

subgenres.name: Speed Garage
subgenres.desc: Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.

subgenres.name: Wonky
subgenres.desc: Off-kilter fusion of Dubstep and Hip Hop which first developed in the mid-to-late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Aquacrunk
subgenres.desc: Syncopated, half-time rhythms inspired by Dubstep and Grime, funky, sludgy, "aquatic"-sounding synths and sound design.

subgenres.name: Miami Bass
subgenres.desc: Sustained Roland TR-808 kick drums and faster tempos, along with a distinct Electro influence.

subgenres.name: Atlanta Bass
subgenres.desc: Originated in Atlanta, slower tempos and a more melodic approach than Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Tamborzão
subgenres.desc: Adds Afro-Brazilian percussive elements such as the atabaque sound into the Miami Bass kick drums.

subgenres.name: Techno Bass
subgenres.desc: Minimal, stripped-down with an emphasis on low-frequency bass partitions.

subgenres.name: Car Audio Bass
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimalistic extreme form, focused on ultra-low frequency sine wave notes and mainly intended for stress testing subwoofer sound systems.

subgenres.name: Wa Euro
subgenres.desc: Traditional form of J-Pop that emerged in the second half of the 1980s from late Hi-NRG, '80s British Dance-Pop and Italo-Disco/Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: J-Euro
subgenres.desc: Italian-oriented Japanese scene of Eurobeat, which emerged with Japanese-language covers of Italian songs in the early-to-mid-1990s.

name: Easy Listening
desc: Typically instrumental, including lush arrangements and melodies played by orchestras or big bands aiming for light entertainment.

subgenres.name: Cocktail Nation
subgenres.desc: Decidedly ironic take on Lounge that emerged in the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: Exotica
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1950s as the United States developed a fascination with Polynesia and the South Pacific, incorporates traditional instruments and rhythms from these cultures into a Western Pop context.

subgenres.name: Sitarsploitation
subgenres.desc: Variant of Exotica capitalising on the surge of Western interest in Indian music in the late 1960s; featured melodies played on the sitar (or instruments imitating it) atop Easy Listening accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Light Music
subgenres.desc: Instrumental, typically through-composed style performed by an orchestra or small ensemble, with simpler arrangements and an emphasis on strong melodies.

subgenres.name: Lounge
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United States during the 1950s, emphasizing a chilled-out atmosphere with light instrumentation and sometimes vocals indebted to Vocal Jazz.

subgenres.name: Pops Orchestra
subgenres.desc: Orchestra that plays covers of popular songs as well as famous classical compositions.

subgenres.name: Space Age Pop
subgenres.desc: Inspired by the excitement and optimism of the Space Age during the 1950s and 1960s, frequently experimenting with futuristic sounds made possible by contemporary technology.

name: Electronic
desc: Uses non-traditional electronic instrumentation and sound manipulation technology as the primary backbone of a composition.

subgenres.name: Acholitronix
subgenres.desc: Fusion of traditional Acholi rhythms and melodies with Electronic production, originating in the city of Gulu.

subgenres.name: Algorave
subgenres.desc: Generative dancefloor-oriented music produced live via algorithms.

subgenres.name: Binaural Beats
subgenres.desc: Auditory illusions created when two different frequencies are played simultaneously in separate ears.

subgenres.name: Bit Music
subgenres.desc: Created by sound chips, cards, and sequencers found in video game consoles, personal computers, and arcade machines, as well as synthesizers emulating these sounds.

subgenres.name: Chiptune
subgenres.desc: Used primarily in the 1980s within the context of 8-bit Video Game Music, combining simple synthesized waveforms and noise in a compositionally limited but overtly melodic style.

subgenres.name: FM Synthesis
subgenres.desc: Sound synthesis that combines the simple waveforms of Chiptune with modulating oscillators to create a bouncier synthesizer sound that would be used in arcade cabinets and home video game consoles like theSega Mega Drive/Genesisin the late 1980s.

subgenres.name: MIDI Music
subgenres.desc: Intended for real-time sequenced playback via MIDI protocol on MIDI devices and used primarily in 1990s PC Video Game Music, arranger keyboards and karaoke.

subgenres.name: Black MIDI
subgenres.desc: Consists of extremely dense MIDI piano compositions, impossible to play on physical instruments.

subgenres.name: Sequencer & Tracker
subgenres.desc: Composed for early home computer and game consoles from the late 1980s to the late 1990s, primarily for video game soundtracks.

subgenres.name: 16-bit
subgenres.desc: Created using video game consoles with audio hardware using 16-bit audio samples, most notably theSuper Nintendo Entertainment System.

subgenres.name: Tracker Music
subgenres.desc: Vertical text-based step-sequencer software sampler music in the first and second gen module formats like .MOD, .MED, .S3M, .XM and .IT.

subgenres.name: Amigacore
subgenres.desc: Gabber-like forms of Hardcore [EDM] written in first-gen trackers for theAmigalike ProTracker and OctaMED, resulting in a minimalistic raw lo-fi sound.

subgenres.name: Demostyle
subgenres.desc: Traditional eclectic style of the Demoscene with a special emphasis on tracker techniques and samples, and combining numerous elements of completely different genres - from Italo-Disco, Progressive Electronic and Funk to Belgian Techno, Ambient and Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Doskpop
subgenres.desc: Grew out of the Amiga Demoscene in the late 1980s with the imitation of Spacesynth in the context of the restrictions and aesthetics of Demostyle.

subgenres.name: Bitpop
subgenres.desc: Fuses Bit Music with additional synths, beats, guitars and modern production values, emphasizing highly catchy melodies and relatively fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Celtic Electronica
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Celtic Folk Music with various types of Electronic Dance Music.

subgenres.name: Chillout
subgenres.desc: Broad category of many relaxed styles of Electronic music which predominantly draw influence from Electronic Dance Music subgenres and Ambient.

subgenres.name: Ambient Dub
subgenres.desc: Takes cues from Ambient and Dub reggae, featuring the atmosphere of the former and the Jamaican-style basslines, percussion, and psychedelic production techniques of the latter.

subgenres.name: Ambient House
subgenres.desc: Primarily British genre developed in the 1990s with beats, synthesizers, and vocals in styles similar to House, treated with effects that are often described as "dream-like" or "chilled out".

subgenres.name: Ambient Trance
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s mainly in the form of Chillout remixes of Trance tracks; incorporates its arpeggiated synthesizer sound into Downtempo and Ambient contexts.

subgenres.name: Balearic Beat
subgenres.desc: Variety of relaxed, laid-back music that originates from the Balearic Islands off the coast of Spain, and particularly the club scene in Ibiza.

subgenres.name: Barber Beats
subgenres.desc: Borrows elements from Downtempo, Trip Hop, and Instrumental Hip Hop; emulates 1990s and 2000s Chillout music.

subgenres.name: Downtempo
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric and groove-based with relaxed tempos and mellow beats.

subgenres.name: Trip Hop
subgenres.desc: Evokes a surreal, trippy, dreamy, and sometimes dark atmosphere with offbeat turntable scratches, light vocal melodies, and Hip Hop-influenced beats.

subgenres.name: Psybient
subgenres.desc: Heavy influence from Psytrance and Goa Trance incorporated in an atmospheric Ambient context.

subgenres.name: Digital Fusion
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the hardware-limited sounds of Chiptune and other Bit Music into compositions drawing on Jazz, Cinematic Classical, progressive music, and other Electronic styles, sometimes augmented with live instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Drift Phonk
subgenres.desc: Busy, noisy production inspired by lo-fi Memphis Rap; frequently features 808 cowbell melodies and chopped, compressed samples.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Phonk
subgenres.desc: Merges Funk automotivo's rhythms, vocals, and energy, with the energetic and nocturnal production typical of the Drift Phonk scene, and Phonk House.

subgenres.name: Phonk House
subgenres.desc: Merges Drift Phonk's nocturnal atmospheres, cowbell melodies, vocal samples, and energetic production, with House rhythms and tempos, characterized by a banging and upbeat sound.

subgenres.name: Dungeon Synth
subgenres.desc: Focuses on evoking epic and atmospheric soundscapes primarily associated with fantasy and medieval settings through the usage of synthesizers, keyboards, lo-fi production, and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Comfy Synth
subgenres.desc: Calm, peaceful and soothing sounds, as well as nostalgic, sentimental, or childish atmospheres and aesthetics; often incorporates wholesome themes while utilizing lo-fi or hazy recordings and influences from New Age.

subgenres.name: Winter Synth
subgenres.desc: Cold, minimalistic, and repetitive soundscapes, commonly invoking imagery of winter.

subgenres.name: Electroacoustic
subgenres.desc: Manipulation and processing of sound sources to create atmospheric pieces.

subgenres.name: Acousmatic Music
subgenres.desc: Fixed-media Electroacoustic music designed to be reproduced by multiple loudspeakers without the presence of instrumentalists and visual cues.

subgenres.name: EAI
subgenres.desc: Slow paced, physical, textured aesthetic - often created using unconventional instruments processed through a computer.

subgenres.name: Musique concrète
subgenres.desc: Manipulation of recorded sounds, mostly Field Recordings, natural sounds, and real-world noises, as a process of abstracting "concrete" sounds, or "sound objects", from their acoustic origins.

subgenres.name: Electro Hop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid 2000s featuring upbeat rap verses and catchy hooks over four-on-the-floor Electropop and  Electro House-inspired production.

subgenres.name: Electro-Industrial
subgenres.desc: Formed in the late 1980s and early 1990s; grew out of a combination of EBM and Industrial.

subgenres.name: Dark Electro
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1990s in Europe, incorporating the abrasiveness of old school Industrial but with a greater focus on a horror-inspired atmosphere and harsh, distorted vocals.

subgenres.name: Aggrotech
subgenres.desc: Merges aggressive-sounding synths and apocalyptic atmospheres with harsh 4/4 beats and fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Electronic Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Broad category for subgenres mainly derived from Disco, featuring Electronic sounds, synthesizers, drum machines and varying BPM ranges.

subgenres.name: Artcore
subgenres.desc: Combines an eclectic mix of Electronic Dance Music genres with the instrumentation and melodic stylings of genres like Cinematic Classical for a maximalist and emotional sound.

subgenres.name: Balani Show
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s in Mali; peaks at around 170BPM and prominently features looping, cut-up balafon samples.

subgenres.name: Balearic Beat
subgenres.desc: Variety of relaxed, laid-back music that originates from the Balearic Islands off the coast of Spain, and particularly the club scene in Ibiza.

subgenres.name: Bérite Club
subgenres.desc: Originated in the underground club scene of Paris in the mid-to-late 2010s, drawing on a variety of international club styles for its combination of prominent and erratic drum programming with freezing and looping chopped-up samples.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat
subgenres.desc: Syncopated drum patterns (breakbeats), generally driving the groove at 110-160 BPM, emerging in the late 1980s from sampling drum breaks, before forming an umbrella genre separate from Drum and Bass, Downtempo, and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Acid Breaks
subgenres.desc: Incorporates prominent "squelching", resonant low pass filter sounds typical to Acid House, and often other "trippy" effects into intense, syncopated, broken rhythms in the tempos of 110-150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Big Beat
subgenres.desc: Popular in Britain during the late 1990s, driven by edited breakbeats and prominent basslines.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Originated from the combination of sampled breakbeats and energetic rhythms with the "rave" influences set by early-1990s Techno and Acid House, including upbeat "stab" riffing and sample-based production.

subgenres.name: Darkside
subgenres.desc: Dark atmosphere and fast rhythms; served as a forerunner of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Breaks
subgenres.desc: Revival of Breakbeat Hardcore which emerged in the 2000s, bringing in modern influences and production techniques.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Kota
subgenres.desc: Indonesian style that slows down the syncopated rhythms of Funkot to moderate tempos around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Jungle Dutch
subgenres.desc: Combines the high-pitched synth leads of Dutch House with the frantic "tribal" rhythms of Jungle Terror.

subgenres.name: Florida Breaks
subgenres.desc: Developed during the mid-1990s, combining major influences of Hip Hop derivatives such as Miami Bass and Electro along with elements of 1990s Electronic Dance Music genres like House or Techno.

subgenres.name: Funky Breaks
subgenres.desc: Merging popular 1990s breaks styles like Big Beat with major Funk and Soul elements.

subgenres.name: Nu Skool Breaks
subgenres.desc: Developed in the late 1990s and early 2000s; takes elements from Drum and Bass, UK Garage, and Techno.

subgenres.name: Progressive Breaks
subgenres.desc: Derivative of Progressive House that incorporates its lush, melodic synth leads and atmospheres into Breakbeat's syncopated and broken rhythms.

subgenres.name: Psybreaks
subgenres.desc: Uses Psytrance-derived sound design, such as squelchy sounds and psychedelic effects.

subgenres.name: West Coast Breaks
subgenres.desc: Combines the earlier breakbeats of Hip Hop and early Breakbeat or even Miami Bass, with various 1990s Electronic Dance Music genres like Trance and Techno.

subgenres.name: Broken Beat
subgenres.desc: Choppy, syncopated grooves and loose influence from 1970s Jazz-Funk, with eclectic roots spanning Drum and Bass, Deep House, Acid Jazz, and Afrobeat.

subgenres.name: Bubblegum Bass
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s, exaggerating the cutest and most feminine parts of 2000s Pop and combining them with bouncy, plastic synths over rhythms and sounds derived from a variety of contemporary club styles.

subgenres.name: Bubbling
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Netherlands in the late 1980s, fusing sped-up Dancehall with Dutch Antillean music and contemporary Dutch rave.

subgenres.name: Budots
subgenres.desc: Originated from the southern Philippines; notable for its distinct high-pitched synth hooks.

subgenres.name: Coupé-décalé
subgenres.desc: Bass-heavy and minimal style of Ivorian popular dance music, drawing heavily from Zouglou and Congolese rhythms.

subgenres.name: Cruise
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced Nigerian dance music, utilising chopped, often humorous, samples.

subgenres.name: Dariacore
subgenres.desc: SoundCloud-based scene developed in the early 2020s, combining prominent vocal samples and distorted, dense production with influences from a wide range of Electronic Dance Music genres, often incorporating musical and visual references to popular media and internet culture.

subgenres.name: Deconstructed Club
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2010s as the hybridization of diverse Electronic Dance Music genres with an abrasive Post-Industrial sound.

subgenres.name: Dek Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent heavy, sustained bass tones, percussion derived from South Asian Music, and often high-pitched sound effects or samples; commonly played at extreme volumes in DJ/sound system competitions.

subgenres.name: Digital Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Fast, syncopated breakbeat patterns (often sampled or programmed) with prominent basslines, commonly within the 160-180 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Atmospheric Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent in the mid-1990s, uses faster, de-emphasized breakbeats, and places a greater focus on melodic elements such as slow, warm basslines and atmospheric melodies inspired by Ambient and Ambient House.

subgenres.name: Dancefloor Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s as a more accessible and polished style with melodic, prominent synth leads derived from Jump-Up and punchy, often synthesized drums.

subgenres.name: Darkstep
subgenres.desc: Hard, uptempo and uses heavy breakbeats, Post-Industrial-influenced sound design, and horror movie samples to create a sinister, claustrophobic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Crossbreed
subgenres.desc: Harsh and dense mixture of Darkstep with Hardcore [EDM] developed in the late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Skullstep
subgenres.desc: Repetitious, aggressive, off-beat rhythms often programmed using distorted, harsh, and noisy percussion that usually resembles clangy "pots and pans", machine gun-like snares.

subgenres.name: Deep Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Sub-bass-rich, repetitive, minimalist, and rhythm-focused production.

subgenres.name: Drumfunk
subgenres.desc: Focuses on complex drum beats made to emulate live recordings.

subgenres.name: Drumstep
subgenres.desc: Dancefloor-friendly, loud, and heavy combination of the drum programming and tempo of Jump-Up with the half-time rhythm and midrange LFO wobble of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Dubwise Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Implementing Reggae and Dub influences, usually vocal dubs, delay effects, and reggae instrumentation, with the clean production and rhythms of post-2000s styles.

subgenres.name: Footwork Jungle
subgenres.desc: Combining Footwork's archetypal percussion, skittering drum fills, handclaps, and syncopated rhythms, with Drum and Bass drum programming and breakbeats, merging the two into unconventional, frantic drumming and dense, off-kilter rhythms.

subgenres.name: Halftime
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Drum and Bass (mainly Neurofunk) characterized by off-kilter rhythms playing at around 80-85 BPM (half of normal DnB pace), influenced by Dubstep, Wonky, Trap [EDM], and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Hardstep
subgenres.desc: Very compressed and sparse drumming, extensive use of kick drums and gritty, minimalistic production style with emphasis on simple, deep, modulated bass patterns.

subgenres.name: Jazzstep
subgenres.desc: Combines the rhythm and speed of Drum and Bass with the melodies, composition, and instrumentation of Jazz.

subgenres.name: Jump-Up
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s, characterized by loud "wobbling" basslines, simpler drum loops, and a light-hearted and warm sound.

subgenres.name: Jungle
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 1990s from Breakbeat Hardcore, featuring rapid, chaotic-sounding breakbeats and strong basslines; known as the forerunner of most Drum and Bass styles.

subgenres.name: Ragga Jungle
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 1990s in London, combining Jungle breakbeats with heavy influence from Ragga.

subgenres.name: Liquid Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric and melodic genre that developed in the early 2000s; utilizes polished and smooth production, simpler structures, and originally sampled Funk and Soul.

subgenres.name: Sambass
subgenres.desc: Combines Drum and Bass tempos and drum patterns, in addition to its Funk and Soul influences, with various styles of Brazilian Music.

subgenres.name: Minimal Drum and Bass
subgenres.desc: Minimalist, sparse sound; emerged in two main 2000s strains, one Dubstep-inspired and one IDM-inspired, which crossed paths in the 2010s.

subgenres.name: Autonomic
subgenres.desc: Mechanical, machine-like, "autonomic" rhythms that take primary influence from the cold, minimal sounds of mid-2000s UK Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Microfunk
subgenres.desc: Minimal, glitchy, and "bleep"-y sound inspired by IDM.

subgenres.name: Neurofunk
subgenres.desc: Focuses on technical songwriting with warped, complex bass sounds, distorted and modulated synths (often with repeated stabs over the basslines), and dark but clean production.

subgenres.name: Technoid
subgenres.desc: Influenced by the repetitive and mechanical sound of Techno.

subgenres.name: Techstep
subgenres.desc: Futuristic, dark, and gritty sound; quantized and compressed drum breaks, distorted bass lines, and a focus on a sci-fi atmosphere and sampling sources.

subgenres.name: Trancestep
subgenres.desc: Combination of Trance melodies and structure with the breakbeats, fast tempos, and rolling basslines of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Half-time syncopated and sparse beats set around 140 BPM with heavy sub-basses; emerged in South London in the early 2000s.

subgenres.name: Brostep
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Dubstep which replaces its sub-bass-oriented sound with an emphasis on catchy or aggressive mid-range melodies.

subgenres.name: Briddim
subgenres.desc: Combining the kick-clap rhythms and syncopation of Riddim with Brostep sound design.

subgenres.name: Colour Bass
subgenres.desc: Combines aggressive wobbling basses with the euphoric drops of Melodic Dubstep and Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Deathstep
subgenres.desc: Darker, heavier form of Brostep that uses "machine gun" basses, atonal synths, and elements from genres like Death Metal and Metalcore.

subgenres.name: Minatory
subgenres.desc: Extreme, experimental style of Deathstep, with a harsh sound and sudden BPM changes.

subgenres.name: Drumstep
subgenres.desc: Dancefloor-friendly, loud, and heavy combination of the drum programming and tempo of Jump-Up with the half-time rhythm and midrange LFO wobble of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Tearout [Brostep]
subgenres.desc: Heavy and distorted, closely affiliated with Deathstep and other styles of Brostep.

subgenres.name: Chillstep
subgenres.desc: Relaxed Dubstep influenced by Downtempo and Ambient.

subgenres.name: Dungeon Sound
subgenres.desc: Commonly features dark textures, spatial production, and midrange basses.

subgenres.name: Melodic Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Melodious, tuneful drops, rich, lush synth leads, powerful stretched chords, and light and harmonious sound design.

subgenres.name: Purple Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s out of the Dubstep scene of the time, incorporating synth leads and basslines inspired by 1980s Synth Funk and 1990s G-Funk, and Video Game Music, into a rhythmic palette mostly derived from dubstep and Grime.

subgenres.name: Riddim
subgenres.desc: Repetitive and relatively simplistic style inspired by mid-to-late-2000s UK Dubstep, often using robotic and/or squishy sound design along with bouncy square basses and less prominent buildups.

subgenres.name: Future Riddim
subgenres.desc: Melodic and futuristic style inspired by Future Bass, and to a lesser extent Colour Bass and Melodic Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Liquid Riddim
subgenres.desc: Distinct for its atmospheric production, overpowering ambience, watery synths, and melodic bass patterns.

subgenres.name: Tearout
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2000s, characterized by a gritty, aggressive sound and closely affiliated with early, deep Dubstep.

subgenres.name: East Coast Club
subgenres.desc: Group of club styles from the US East Coast that combines Miami Bass rhythms with influence from Breakbeat and Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Jersey Club
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Newark in the late 2000s; features fast tempos, hard kicks, and less prominent breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Philly Club
subgenres.desc: Builds on Baltimore Club with a faster tempo and sometimes influences from more modern genres like Trap [EDM].

subgenres.name: EBM
subgenres.desc: Melodic and dancefloor-friendly take on Post-Industrial music that developed in the early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Dark Electro
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1990s in Europe, incorporating the abrasiveness of old school Industrial but with a greater focus on a horror-inspired atmosphere and harsh, distorted vocals.

subgenres.name: Aggrotech
subgenres.desc: Merges aggressive-sounding synths and apocalyptic atmospheres with harsh 4/4 beats and fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Futurepop
subgenres.desc: Derivative of EBM, retaining its apocalyptic worldview but incorporating heavy influence from the melodic style of Synthpop.

subgenres.name: New Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s in Belgium; characterized by dark basslines, hard-hitting grooves and a slow tempo.

subgenres.name: Hard Beat
subgenres.desc: Short-lived, harder, harsh form of New Beat with Industrial, Acid House and EBM-influenced arrangement.

subgenres.name: Electro
subgenres.desc: Syncopated rhythms programmed on the Roland TR-808 drum machine, often resembling Funk breaks, along with simple funky basslines.

subgenres.name: Electroclash
subgenres.desc: Draws from 1980s styles such as Electro, New Wave, and Electro-Disco combined with Techno, resulting in minimal, throbbing beats and basslines, buzzing synthesizer parts, vocoders and often monotone, half-spoken, half-sung vocals.

subgenres.name: Electro-Disco
subgenres.desc: Disco instrumentation is largely - if not entirely - replaced by synthesizers and augmented with futuristic elements such as the vocoder.

subgenres.name: Hi-NRG
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s and quickly became the most popular form of Electronic Dance Music in the LGBT club scenes of San Francisco and New York, characterized by its uptempo, high-energy sound.

subgenres.name: Italo-Disco
subgenres.desc: Produced primarily in Italy and is characterized by the use of synthesizers, drum machines, and sometimes vocoders to create a mechanical, Electronic version of Disco with futuristic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Spacesynth
subgenres.desc: Highly melodic, often instrumental futuristic strain, formed under the heavy influence of Space Disco, Progressive Electronic and, later, early Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: Doskpop
subgenres.desc: Grew out of the Amiga Demoscene in the late 1980s with the imitation of Spacesynth in the context of the restrictions and aesthetics of Demostyle.

subgenres.name: Red Disco
subgenres.desc: Continuum of various eclectic forms, derived mainly from late Euro-Disco, but also Italo-Disco, Hi-NRG and Eurobeat, and developed in the Soviet Union in the mid-to-late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Space Disco
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Europe in the mid-to-late 1970s, characterized by layers of oscillating synth, space-oriented sound effects, and a futuristic sound inspired by contemporary sci-fi media.

subgenres.name: Electro latino
subgenres.desc: Mixes elements of Merengue and Reggaetón with polished production from mainstream House subgenres; often shares traits with Latin Pop, having anthemic melodies and verse-chorus structures.

subgenres.name: Electro Swing
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, energetic style that splices Swing with Electronic Dance Music, looking to recapture the atmosphere of late 1920s to mid-1940s Jazz within a more updated club-friendly medium.

subgenres.name: Eurobeat
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced with roots in Hi-NRG and Italo-Disco; became mainly popular in Japan in the 1990s.

subgenres.name: J-Euro
subgenres.desc: Italian-oriented Japanese scene of Eurobeat, which emerged with Japanese-language covers of Italian songs in the early-to-mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Eurodance
subgenres.desc: Takes elements of Euro-Disco, House, Techno, and Hi-NRG while featuring on-beat kick, hi-hat and snare sounds at around 110 to 150 bpm.

subgenres.name: Bubblegum Dance
subgenres.desc: Playful, childlike style with a Bubblegum-like atmosphere that often incorporates high-pitched, light-hearted, and usually female-fronted vocals.

subgenres.name: Italo Dance
subgenres.desc: Appeared in the 1990s after the decline of Italo-Disco, featuring rhythmic influence from that genre.

subgenres.name: Flex Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Largely instrumental; infused with Electronic Dance Music elements.

subgenres.name: Footwork
subgenres.desc: Extensive use of drum fills, tom drums, handclaps, and snares within fast-paced, highly syncopated beats not bound to a 4/4 kick rhythm.

subgenres.name: Footwork Jungle
subgenres.desc: Combining Footwork's archetypal percussion, skittering drum fills, handclaps, and syncopated rhythms, with Drum and Bass drum programming and breakbeats, merging the two into unconventional, frantic drumming and dense, off-kilter rhythms.

subgenres.name: Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Electro-influenced; developed in Latino communities in New York and Miami in the 1980s, especially dominated by Latin Freestyle and its Latin influences.

subgenres.name: Latin Freestyle
subgenres.desc: Displays a heavy influence of Hispanic American Music alongside the Disco, Hip Hop, and Electro influences of Freestyle.

subgenres.name: Funk mandelão
subgenres.desc: Simple lyricism, raw and minimalistic production, and distinct drops with bursting bass.

subgenres.name: Beat bruxaria
subgenres.desc: São Paulo-originated Funk brasileiro with aggressive, distorted and high-pitched beats featuring minimalistic percussion and diversified sampling.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Phonk
subgenres.desc: Merges Funk automotivo's rhythms, vocals, and energy, with the energetic and nocturnal production typical of the Drift Phonk scene, and Phonk House.

subgenres.name: Funk automotivo
subgenres.desc: Catchy, repetitive synths accompanied by a strong four-on-the-floor kick and loud, reverberated vocals.

subgenres.name: Ritmada
subgenres.desc: Short, repetitive and resonant beats with more danceable, immersive grooves drawn out of Afro-Brazilian instrumentation, a cleaner, more radio-friendly sound and greater focus on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Funkot
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced Indonesian form of Electronic Dance Music that combines Eurodance and Trance synths with the syncopated rhythm from Dangdut koplo.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Kota
subgenres.desc: Indonesian style that slows down the syncopated rhythms of Funkot to moderate tempos around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Jungle Dutch
subgenres.desc: Combines the high-pitched synth leads of Dutch House with the frantic "tribal" rhythms of Jungle Terror.

subgenres.name: Future Bass
subgenres.desc: Woozy, detuned synthesizers, 7th chords, harsh basslines, syncopated percussion with fast-paced hi-hats and a melodic, carefree atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Kawaii Future Bass
subgenres.desc: "Cute" style of Future Bass rooted in anime and video game culture; emerged in Japan in the mid-2010s.

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Future Rave
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 2010s by combining the mainstage EDM approach with influences from then-popular forms of Techno and old-school Trance/rave-inspired grooves and atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Ghettotech
subgenres.desc: Fuses the syncopation and synthesized sounds of Electro and Detroit Techno with the cut-up samples of Ghetto House and fast rhythms of Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Glitch Hop [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Tempos around 100-110 BPM, swung, bouncy drum patterns, and a focus on upbeat, danceable drops and buildups.

subgenres.name: Ghetto Funk
subgenres.desc: Rich sampling, drawing from classic Hip Hop as well as from Funk and Soul, and strong midtempo break grooves.

subgenres.name: Neurohop
subgenres.desc: Features the complex bass of Neurofunk and a frantic and mechanical sound design.

subgenres.name: Gqom
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2010s in Durban townships, features highly syncopated, bass-heavy, stripped-down beats and dark, raw atmosphere, often with ominous synth pads and aggressive vocal chants.

subgenres.name: Grime
subgenres.desc: UK Garage-derived production style characterized by dark, fast-paced, often aggressive beats that commonly features fast-paced MCing.

subgenres.name: Neo-Grime
subgenres.desc: Mixes Wave with Grime and other forms of UK Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Weightless
subgenres.desc: Typically instrumental, leftfield Grime style characterized by sparse, "weightless" percussion and spectral, atmospheric production.

subgenres.name: Hardcore [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for a wide variety of fast-paced and energetic Electronic Dance Music styles that have been developed since the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: Acidcore
subgenres.desc: Developed out of the 1990s Acid Techno scene utilizing its prominence of "acid" TB-303 bassline sequences into more intense rhythms derived from earlier Hardcore [EDM], Gabber and Trance music.

subgenres.name: Amigacore
subgenres.desc: Gabber-like forms of Hardcore [EDM] written in first-gen trackers for theAmigalike ProTracker and OctaMED, resulting in a minimalistic raw lo-fi sound.

subgenres.name: Belgian Techno
subgenres.desc: Early form of Hardcore [EDM], resulting from the further evolution of New Beat due to the strong influence of Techno and EBM.

subgenres.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Originated from the combination of sampled breakbeats and energetic rhythms with the "rave" influences set by early-1990s Techno and Acid House, including upbeat "stab" riffing and sample-based production.

subgenres.name: Darkside
subgenres.desc: Dark atmosphere and fast rhythms; served as a forerunner of Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Breaks
subgenres.desc: Revival of Breakbeat Hardcore which emerged in the 2000s, bringing in modern influences and production techniques.

subgenres.name: Breakcore
subgenres.desc: Mixes Hardcore [EDM] with cut-up, complex, and frequently noisy breakbeats at very high tempos inspired by Jungle and Drum and Bass, often with heavy use of sampling.

subgenres.name: Lolicore
subgenres.desc: Heavily distorted or high-pitched Anime vocal samples and complex cut-up breakbeats with extreme tempos.

subgenres.name: Mashcore
subgenres.desc: Sampling, particularly from Pop and Electronic Dance Music, as well as playful melodies, hard kicks, and the typical breakcore breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Raggacore
subgenres.desc: Prominently incorporates samples from Ragga and Dancehall, typically through shouted vocal lines and Reggae-influenced instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Crossbreed
subgenres.desc: Harsh and dense mixture of Darkstep with Hardcore [EDM] developed in the late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Darkcore
subgenres.desc: Aggressive, dark, and often midtempo with influences from Doomcore, Industrial Hardcore, and Nu Style Gabber.

subgenres.name: Deathchant Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Took shape in the UK in the late 1990s and early 2000s, characterized by rapid rhythms with Gabber-influenced kicks, frequent use of breakbeats and Hip Hop-inspired sampling.

subgenres.name: Digital Hardcore
subgenres.desc: High-tempo fusion of Hardcore Punk and Electronic, combining harsh vocals and electric guitars of the former with electronic instruments.

subgenres.name: Doomcore
subgenres.desc: Often somber and contemplative in mood, a feature achieved by the common use of long-stretched ambient pads, and sometimes even samples of screaming and other "spooky" sounds.

subgenres.name: Frapcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in France in the mid-2010s, uses French rapping with 4-on-the-floor Hardcore [EDM] and especially Gabber instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Freeform Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s, combining fast and hard-hitting rhythms with heavy influence from the synthesizers of Trance.

subgenres.name: Frenchcore
subgenres.desc: Off-beat, bouncy rhythmic patterns and tempos around the 200 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Gabber
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced and energetic, often in the 160-220 BPM range, with a hallmark of a distinctive distorted kick sound.

subgenres.name: Nu Style Gabber
subgenres.desc: Emerged near the end of the 1990s; deeper, more harmonic bassdrums with constant use of supersaw melodies, breakdown sections and slower tempos closer to the 150-180 BPM range.

subgenres.name: Happy Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1990s from the UK Breakbeat Hardcore scene; characterized by saccharine vocals, uplifting piano riffs and spacey effects, gradually developing to emphasize extremely fast-paced four-on-the-floor beats.

subgenres.name: Bouncy Techno
subgenres.desc: Average tempo of 160 to 180 BPM, four-on-the-floor beats, melodic and repetitive synth melodies, drums with hard kicks, short breaks, progressive stomping rhythms, and offbeat notes.

subgenres.name: UK Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Powerstomp
subgenres.desc: Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.

subgenres.name: Hardtek
subgenres.desc: Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.

subgenres.name: Raggatek
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.

subgenres.name: Industrial Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Fuses the sonic palettes and aesthetics of Industrial with the intense rhythms of Gabber, Speedcore, Doomcore and other subsequent styles.

subgenres.name: Speedcore
subgenres.desc: Exceedingly fast tempos, frequently above 300 BPM, and often aggressive themes and samples.

subgenres.name: Extratone
subgenres.desc: At and above the threshold of 1000 BPM where sequences of kick drums begin to form a continuous pitch.

subgenres.name: Splittercore
subgenres.desc: Faster version of Speedcore with BPM ranging from around 600 to 1000.

subgenres.name: Terrorcore
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rhythms from earlier Gabber with a faster BPM (usually no more than 300) and darker approach.

subgenres.name: Uptempo Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Utilizes lo-fi production, harsh kicks, and elements borrowed from Rawstyle and other gritty Hardcore [EDM] styles while usually sitting at around 185-220 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hard Dance
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for EDM mainly developed out of Hard Trance and UK Hard House; usually characterized by fast tempos, hard kick drums and a "bouncy" syncopated groove.

subgenres.name: Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Hard, four-on-the-floor kick drums, fast tempo around 150 BPM, reverse bass and harsh, distorted synths.

subgenres.name: Dubstyle
subgenres.desc: Characterized by the incorporation of the half-time rhythms and wobbly basslines of Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Early Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Forerunner subgenre that emerged around the turn of the 2000s from Hard Trance and Gabber, distinguished by the signature reverse bass groove, slower tempo around 140 BPM and straightforward, repetitive sound.

subgenres.name: Euphoric Hardstyle
subgenres.desc: Melodic, more lighthearted, and accessible Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Nustyle
subgenres.desc: Developed out of Early Hardstyle from the mid-to-late 2000s, by incorporating distorted, crunchy, pitched kicks, faster tempo around 150 BPM, and detuned supersaw/square synth leads playing stompy, dramatic melodies.

subgenres.name: Psystyle
subgenres.desc: Prominent Psytrance influences, especially the basslines and energy of mainstream psytrance.

subgenres.name: Rawstyle
subgenres.desc: Incorporates earlier Hardstyle and Hardcore [EDM] influences into the sound of 2010s hardstyle, creating a distinctly harsh, simplistic, raw, and dark sound, with fast BPM.

subgenres.name: Rawphoric
subgenres.desc: Combines raw harsh kicks with the uplifting melodies of Euphoric Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Hardtek
subgenres.desc: Modern version of the "tribecore" sound featuring deep alternating basses and festival EDM-influenced drops.

subgenres.name: Raggatek
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Reggae, Ragga and Dancehall, combining half-time instrumental sections with Hardtek's fast four-on-the-floor rhythms, as well as vocal samples, clean basslines and skank rhythms.

subgenres.name: Hard Trance
subgenres.desc: Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.

subgenres.name: Jumpstyle
subgenres.desc: Features a heavy 909 kick drum, four-on-the-floor beat, and a tempo between 140 and 150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Lento violento
subgenres.desc: Features a "slow and violent" sound between 70-120 BPM with hard kicks inspired by Hardcore [EDM] and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: NRG
subgenres.desc: Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.

subgenres.name: UK Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Four-on-the-floor beat around 175 BPM, thick, prominent basslines, and uplifting synth leads, with a cleaner and more accessible sound than other forms of Hardcore [EDM].

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Powerstomp
