subgenres.desc: Prominent, "stomping", and slightly distorted kick, relentless, repetitive reverse basses on the offbeats (borrowed from Hardstyle) that drive the tracks, giving the genre its distinct energetic sound, and cacophonous, noisy riffs and synth leads.

subgenres.name: UK Hard House
subgenres.desc: Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.

subgenres.name: Scouse House
subgenres.desc: Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.

subgenres.name: Hardbass
subgenres.desc: Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: Hard Drum
subgenres.desc: Highly percussive, syncopated rhythms, influences from global contemporary genres, and lack of melodic elements, with a tempo lingering around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hardvapour
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Hardcore [EDM] and Techno and made in response to the Vaporwave movement.

subgenres.name: Hardwave
subgenres.desc: Harder, festival-oriented offshoot of Wave, combining its "reese" basses and icy synths with Trap [EDM] drum patterns, build-up-drop structures, and fuller sound influenced by Trance and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: House
subgenres.desc: Generally features a four-on-the-floor beat within 110-140 BPM, a groove built on swing and syncopation, synthesized basslines, repetitive melodic elements, and an upbeat mood.

subgenres.name: Acid House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s, characterised by repetitive basslines created with the distinctive modulated "squelching" sound of the Roland TB-303 synthesiser.

subgenres.name: Afro House
subgenres.desc: Emerged by fusing Deep House with Southern African Music, characterized by hypnotizing drum patterns of shakers and congas, often sampled African vocals or soulful original features, and spiritual, organic, melodic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: 3-Step
subgenres.desc: Distinct three-kick-drum rhythm, blends influences from Amapiano and Broken Beat, resulting in relaxed, freeform, playful, Jazz-like feel.

subgenres.name: Amapiano
subgenres.desc: House from South Africa deriving from previous popular genres including Gqom, Kwaito, and Deep House.

subgenres.name: Afropiano
subgenres.desc: Blends the easy-going, poppy, and melodic Afrobeats sound and rhythms with major Amapiano elements, like lush, jazzy, and laid-back atmospheres often featuring light piano chords.

subgenres.name: Ambient House
subgenres.desc: Primarily British genre developed in the 1990s with beats, synthesizers, and vocals in styles similar to House, treated with effects that are often described as "dream-like" or "chilled out".

subgenres.name: Ballroom
subgenres.desc: Emerging from the predominantly Black and LGBT Harlem ballroom culture, it is characterized by hard-hitting rhythms, generally improvised chanting by MCs known as commentators, and a distinctive crash sample.

subgenres.name: Baltimore Club
subgenres.desc: Drew on the "booty bass" syncopation of Miami Bass, combined with Breakbeat rhythms around 130 BPM and chopped up vocal samples as found in Ghetto House.

subgenres.name: Bass House
subgenres.desc: Busy, punchy percussion, prominent basslines and dirty, distorted synths resembling other bass music genres, with influences including Brostep, Fidget House, Bassline, Speed Garage, and Tech House.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: Bassline
subgenres.desc: Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.

subgenres.name: Big Room House
subgenres.desc: Energetic, festival-oriented style characterized by heavy reverb, intense build-ups, strong kicks, minimalistic drop melodies, and sparse, raw breakdowns.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Bass
subgenres.desc: Originated in the 2010s in Brazil, taking influences from Deep House and Tech House, characterized by deep, punchy basslines making use of detuning and filtering effects.

subgenres.name: Mega funk
subgenres.desc: Blends funk vocal performances with production derived from mainstage 2010s House genres like Brazilian Bass and Slap House.

subgenres.name: Slap House
subgenres.desc: Taking influences from Brazilian Bass and Future House, characterized by prominent, "bouncy" bassline and simple, upbeat melodies.

subgenres.name: Bubbling House
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Netherlands in the 2000s, combining the older style of Bubbling with more modern House, especially Dutch House.

subgenres.name: Changa tuki
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Chicago Hard House
subgenres.desc: Originated from Chicago around the mid-1990s as a development of Ghetto House, emphasizing hard-hitting, off-beat drum patterns, fast tempos, and lack of melodies.

subgenres.name: LA Hard House
subgenres.desc: Distorted, minimalistic TR-909 derived rhythms, basic climaxing structures and heavy reliance on high-pitched synthesizer / hoover sounds.

subgenres.name: Chicago House
subgenres.desc: Umbrella term for a broad variety of House that originated from Chicago in the (mostly mid-to-late) 1980s and early 90s.

subgenres.name: Deep House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United States during the mid-1980s, featuring a relaxed tempo and influences from Jazz, Funk, and Soul.

subgenres.name: Lo-Fi House
subgenres.desc: Primarily distinguished from earlier styles of outsider house by its stricter reliance on deep house elements, cranky, nocturnal, and nostalgic atmospheres, and a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Diva House
subgenres.desc: Dominant, anthemic female vocals, common use of piano stabs, and energetic, driving four-on-the-floor rhythms.

subgenres.name: Hardbag
subgenres.desc: Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.

subgenres.name: Electro House
subgenres.desc: Warm analog basslines, punchy percussion, crisp high-pitched synthesizer leads, and clipped vocal samples.

subgenres.name: Complextro
subgenres.desc: Features densely-layered sound design, fast-paced cut-up sections, aggressive stabs, and common crossover with Brostep and Fidget House.

subgenres.name: Dutch House
subgenres.desc: High-pitched wonky synth melodies and heavy influence from Fidget House which developed in the Netherlands around 2007-08.

subgenres.name: Noiadance
subgenres.desc: Blends Dutch House production with Funk brasileiro vocals and drumming on top of Moombahton rhythms.

subgenres.name: Fidget House
subgenres.desc: Makes heavy use of Breakbeat Hardcore-esque synth stabs, pitch bending of basslines, and cut-up vocal samples, as well as glitchy, or "choppy", 4/4 rhythms.

subgenres.name: French Electro
subgenres.desc: Mixes Electro House with major elements of genres such as Electroclash, Nu-Disco, Synth Funk, and even Electro-Industrial, resulting in a harsh, punchy, and funky midtempo sound.

subgenres.name: Melbourne Bounce
subgenres.desc: Offbeat basslines giving it a "bouncy" groove, and minimalistic, side-chained melodies often making use of Dutch House-influenced synths, horns or vocal chops, resulting in a flippant, party-oriented atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Eletrofunk
subgenres.desc: Blends Funk brasileiro vocals with production from popular late 2000s and early 2010s House.

subgenres.name: Euro House
subgenres.desc: Vocal-focused style emerging in the late 1980s in Europe, developing in parallel with Eurodance.

subgenres.name: Hardbag
subgenres.desc: Development of handbag / Diva House characterized by heavier, hard hitting percussion, more pronounced rave and early Hard Dance elements, and fewer vocals.

subgenres.name: Festival Progressive House
subgenres.desc: Uplifting, melodic, energetic but clean drops, featuring modern supersaws and pianos, taking influences from Progressive House, Uplifting Trance, but applying them to a form structurally closer to Big Room House and Electro House.

subgenres.name: French House
subgenres.desc: Originated in France in the mid-1990s, characterized by the use of filtered (low-pass, phaser, etc.) samples of Funk and Disco.

subgenres.name: Funky House
subgenres.desc: Funky, warm, catchy basslines on top of looped Funk or Disco samples, resulting in an upbeat, bouncy, and pacy groove.

subgenres.name: Future Funk
subgenres.desc: Sample-based style influenced by French House and Synth Funk that utilizes Vaporwave editing techniques.

subgenres.name: Future House
subgenres.desc: Features distinctive metallic-sounding drops and frequency-modulated basslines at around 120-130 BPM.

subgenres.name: Future Bounce
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Melbourne Bounce and Future House that combines the former's basslines and bouncy, upbeat drops with the latter's metallic, pronounced synth leads.

subgenres.name: Slap House
subgenres.desc: Taking influences from Brazilian Bass and Future House, characterized by prominent, "bouncy" bassline and simple, upbeat melodies.

subgenres.name: Garage House
subgenres.desc: Disco-influenced style of House that developed in the 1980s, incorporating elements of Gospel, Soul, and Dub, before evolving into a more upbeat style that prominently features crisp syncopated hi-hats and synth stabs.

subgenres.name: Gospel House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates heavy Gospel elements and singing borrowed from classic and contemporary gospel, usually in the form of choir vocals and call-and-response chants.

subgenres.name: Jersey Sound
subgenres.desc: Soulful, melodic, Gospel-infused House music developed in Newark, NJ in the late 1980s and early 1990s with an emphasis on songcraft.

subgenres.name: Ghetto House
subgenres.desc: Rough sound based around minimal drum machine-driven tracks and heavy usage of vocal samples.

subgenres.name: Juke
subgenres.desc: Faster than Ghetto House, playing at 160bpm, and makes striking use of unconventional drum patterns which differ wildly from other House styles.

subgenres.name: G-House
subgenres.desc: Deep, dark form of House music that primarily incorporates rap samples or original rapping on top of minimal, bassy beats.

subgenres.name: Hip House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates production elements of early Hip Hop and usually rapping into 1980s House.

subgenres.name: Italo House
subgenres.desc: Originated in Italy during the late 1980s, making use of anthemic pianos, diva vocals, and Dance-Pop song structures.

subgenres.name: Jackin' House
subgenres.desc: Punchy, 'shuffly' percussion, strong grooves, funky basslines, and chopped-up samples.

subgenres.name: Kwaito
subgenres.desc: Emerged from South Africa in the early 1990s, taking influence from Disco and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Bacardi
subgenres.desc: Bacardi is a type of House music from South Africa derived from Kwaito, delivering upbeat, danceable rhythms with lively snares and hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Latin House
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Latin music (various Hispanic American Music and Brazilian Music genres), including their melodies, vocals, and instruments, as well as additional Latin percussion.

subgenres.name: Melodic House
subgenres.desc: Arpeggiated synth lines, focus on a chilled and laid-back atmosphere, and influence from genres such as Progressive House and Deep House.

subgenres.name: Microhouse
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down, minimal form of House, originating in the late 90s, which takes influence from Minimal Techno, Glitch and IDM.

subgenres.name: Organic House
subgenres.desc: Subtle drums and grooves, slow tempos, and acoustic, traditional instrumentation, resulting in an organic, warm sound and spiritual atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Outsider House
subgenres.desc: Mostly derived from Deep House; intentional use of rough, lo-fi production, often utilizing a mix of analog/analog-like and digital instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Lo-Fi House
subgenres.desc: Primarily distinguished from earlier styles of outsider house by its stricter reliance on deep house elements, cranky, nocturnal, and nostalgic atmospheres, and a distinct dreamy, lo-fi aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Phonk House
subgenres.desc: Merges Drift Phonk's nocturnal atmospheres, cowbell melodies, vocal samples, and energetic production, with House rhythms and tempos, characterized by a banging and upbeat sound.

subgenres.name: Progressive House
subgenres.desc: Trance-influenced strain of House that grew to prominence in the early 1990s, using polished production and gradual progressions.

subgenres.name: Romanian Popcorn
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the second half of the 2000s in Romania, often featuring brass melodies and "staccato" pluck grooves.

subgenres.name: Speed Garage
subgenres.desc: Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.

subgenres.name: Stutter House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2020s taking influences from Melodic House, Trance, and Future Garage; features distinctive chopping of vocal samples and pads.

subgenres.name: Tech House
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1990s taking influences from Techno, broadly characterized by minimalistic and repetitive melodies, focus on the bassline, and constant groove recognizable by prominent off-beat hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Deep Tech
subgenres.desc: Incorporates UK Garage rhythms and synths stabs, influences from British rave music, UK Bass and UK Deep House, resulting in an urban, subdued, but danceable sound with deep, muted basslines.

subgenres.name: Rominimal
subgenres.desc: Hypnotic, minimal, and "dubby" loops, featuring subtle and intricate synth pads, cranky, clicky percussion, and bouncy, pulsing basslines.

subgenres.name: Tribal House
subgenres.desc: Prominent, syncopated rhythms of tribal drums such as toms and bongos on top of a House beat, usually resulting in a percussive, energetic sound, while ranging in mood.

subgenres.name: Guaracha [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Originated in Colombia, featuring "fluttering" trumpets, accordion, and tambora drums.

subgenres.name: Tropical House
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Deep House featuring slow tempos around 100-115 BPM, light percussion and acoustic instrumentation, setting out to create a relaxed, summery, beach-like atmosphere.

subgenres.name: UK Hard House
subgenres.desc: Defined by offbeat bass patterns, compressed 909-style drums, buildup-drop structures, hoover sounds, and tempos between 120 and 155 BPM.

subgenres.name: Scouse House
subgenres.desc: Features an upbeat and energetic sound often described as being "bouncy", influenced somewhat by Happy Hardcore.

subgenres.name: Hardbass
subgenres.desc: Bouncy hard bass beats, fast tempo, usually 150-175 BPM, and occasional lyrics or rapping.

subgenres.name: Speed House
subgenres.desc: Mixes busy, dirty sound design and intense drums derived from Bass House with fast tempos from 140-160 BPM, pumping basslines, and other UK Hard House influences.

subgenres.name: UK Jackin'
subgenres.desc: Successor to British Bassline, characterized by strong basslines, dark atmospheres, and dominant grooves.

subgenres.name: Vinahouse
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced House popular in Vietnam, remixing Vietnamese melodies.

subgenres.name: Hypertechno
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 2020s by mixing fast tempos, prominent basslines, and hard-hitting drums derived from popular Techno with simplistic, catchy melodies and vocals, often influenced by 2000s Hard Dance, Eurodance and Electropop.

subgenres.name: Hyper Techno
subgenres.desc: Exaggerated fast form of Belgian Techno for the Japanese market, focusing mainly on synth sounds and samples typical of 1990s dance music.

subgenres.name: Jungle Terror
subgenres.desc: Emerging mostly from Dutch House and Big Room House, incorporates Tribal House-influenced percussion, hard kicks, and animal sounds resulting in a wild, jungle-resembling atmosphere in a festival EDM-oriented context.

subgenres.name: Krushclub
subgenres.desc: Bitcrushed synths and occasionally bitcrushed vocals, energetic Jersey Club-derived beats, and elements of Sigilkore's dark production style.

subgenres.name: Kuduro
subgenres.desc: Angolan music combining traditional Kilapanga and Semba with Techno and House.

subgenres.name: Batida
subgenres.desc: Initially developed in the late '80s in Luanda, Angola, as a mixture of Soca- and Zouk-based percussion samples.

subgenres.name: Makina
subgenres.desc: Spanish Techno developed in the early 1990s; strongly influenced by New Beat and EBM, but aiming for a lighter sound.

subgenres.name: Manyao
subgenres.desc: Asian Electronic Dance Music that mixes vocals and melodies from Mandopop with fairly hard, melodic EDM.

subgenres.name: Melodic Bass
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of Melodic Dubstep with euphoric sound design taking influences from Future Bass, guitar melodies and pop-driven structures

subgenres.name: Midtempo Bass
subgenres.desc: Harsh synth leads and a usual tempo of around 90-110 BPM.

subgenres.name: Moombahcore
subgenres.desc: High-pitched synth leads, gritty percussion, a kick-snare pattern, aggressive bass drops, and around 110 BPM while often paralleling Complextro or Brostep.

subgenres.name: Moombahton
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of Dutch House characterized by tempos in the 100-110 BPM range, Reggaetón-influenced rhythms, bass-heavy kicks and high-pitched synths.

subgenres.name: Nerdcore Techno
subgenres.desc: Stylistically diverse form of underground Japanese Electronic Dance Music utilizing energetic beats built around samples from pop and/or nerd culture.

subgenres.name: Nu-Disco
subgenres.desc: 21st-century trend mixing modern, polished Electronic production with the aesthetics, structures, and lively, organic beats of 1970s and 1980s Disco.

subgenres.name: Ori deck
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Moombahton and Dubstep to create a style characterized by sluggish, kick-heavy dembow rhythms.

subgenres.name: Post-Dubstep
subgenres.desc: Minimalistic, atmospheric sound design and eclectic drum patterns, derived from but not fitting Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Shangaan Electro
subgenres.desc: South African genre with very fast BPM (around 180) featuring MIDI keyboard sounds and marimba.

subgenres.name: Singeli
subgenres.desc: Developed in Tanzania in the mid-2000s; fuses incredibly rapid beats, usually between 180-300BPM, with MCing and musical influences from older Tanzanian genres.

subgenres.name: Skweee
subgenres.desc: Mid-2000s offshoot of the Nordic Electro scene which uses simple, analogue or Chiptune-inspired synthesizer leads and basslines to create stripped-down, midtempo grooves drawing on Synth Funk and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Slimepunk
subgenres.desc: Loud synth leads with a distorted, gritty, and "slimy" sound design, usually laid on top of production inspired by or taken directly from genres such as Halftime, Trap [EDM], Brostep, and other forms of 2010s EDM.

subgenres.name: Techno
subgenres.desc: Highly beat-driven, repetitive, and mechanical, typically featuring minimal chord variation and melodies, focuses on rhythms and timbral variety; generally produced for club environments.

subgenres.name: Acid Techno
subgenres.desc: Incorporates "squelching" synths from Acid House into a mechanical and usually more energetic Techno context.

subgenres.name: Ambient Techno
subgenres.desc: Blends the mechanical, repetitive beats of Techno with atmospheres and textures inspired by Ambient music, resulting in slower tempos and more understated rhythms.

subgenres.name: Belgian Techno
subgenres.desc: Early form of Hardcore [EDM], resulting from the further evolution of New Beat due to the strong influence of Techno and EBM.

subgenres.name: Bleep Techno
subgenres.desc: Established in the late 1980s in the breakdancing and early rave scene of Yorkshire in the North of England, notable for its "bleepy" synth lines and heavy sub-bass.

subgenres.name: Detroit Techno
subgenres.desc: Features a signature mechanical, detached sound that echoed the atmosphere of Detroit's nightlife and incorporated influences from Electro and Chicago House as well as Synthpop and Electro-Disco.

subgenres.name: Freetekno
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 1990s, commonly played at free parties in Europe, and features a repetitive pounding kick drum at tempos of 170 BPM or above.

subgenres.name: Hardgroove Techno
subgenres.desc: Features shuffling grooves with heavy emphasis on layered percussive elements; often includes a mix of samples and drum machines played at a range of 135-140 BPM.

subgenres.name: Hard Techno
subgenres.desc: Typically rave-oriented form characterized by hard, prominent kick drums, pounding rhythms, fast tempos around 140-160 BPM, and aggressive, often distorted sounds.

subgenres.name: Schranz
subgenres.desc: Characterised by fast tempos, aggressive "whooshing" beat patterns, heavy compression and straightforward song structures.

subgenres.name: Industrial Techno
subgenres.desc: Harder, darker style of Techno which draws parallels with factories and the rhythm of machinery.

subgenres.name: Birmingham Sound
subgenres.desc: Cold, mechanical, and hypnotic tracks, typically lacking the harsher and noisier elements of later Industrial Techno.

subgenres.name: Melodic Techno
subgenres.desc: Trance-influenced subgenre that was established in the mid-to-late 2010s, characterized by gradually progressing structure, and hypnotizing, atmospheric sound with arpeggiated, minor melodies, playing at around 120-125 BPM.

subgenres.name: Minimal Techno
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down and sparse, often featuring a dark sound and a slow, steady development through the track.

subgenres.name: Dub Techno
subgenres.desc: Fuses elements of Minimal Techno with characteristics of Dub.

subgenres.name: Peak Time Techno
subgenres.desc: Hard, dynamic, energetic and accessible subgenre featuring strong kicks, massive dirty synths, tempos around 130 BPM, more suspenseful structures with breaks and build-ups, and big, modern, festival-oriented sound; rose to high popularity in the late 2010s.

subgenres.name: Wonky Techno
subgenres.desc: Strays from the standard beat of Techno, opting for a more fractured sound.

subgenres.name: Techno Bass
subgenres.desc: Minimal, stripped-down with an emphasis on low-frequency bass partitions.

subgenres.name: Car Audio Bass
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimalistic extreme form, focused on ultra-low frequency sine wave notes and mainly intended for stress testing subwoofer sound systems.

subgenres.name: Tecnorumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.

subgenres.name: Trance
subgenres.desc: Evolving, tension-building structures with rapid, minor arpeggios on top of a hypnotic, four-on-the-floor drum patterns at fast tempo around 130-150 BPM.

subgenres.name: Acid Trance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates "squelching" acid basslines into Trance's evolving structure.

subgenres.name: Big Room Trance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates production features associated with Big Room House and dirty, distorted leads influenced by Electro House, Dutch House and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Dream Trance
subgenres.desc: Slow tempo (about 130 BPM) with strong roots in Progressive House, using beats typical of Eurodance and Dance-Pop; emphasizes a laid-back, carefree, and dreamlike sound.

subgenres.name: Euro Trance
subgenres.desc: Emerged as a fusion with Eurodance, features fast tempos, more accessible grooves and structures, and simple, catchy melodies with vocals and saw synth leads.

subgenres.name: Hands Up
subgenres.desc: Prominent, melodic supersaw leads, Dance-Pop derived hooks, and a strong reliance on sidechained basslines and hard, powerful drums.

subgenres.name: Buchiage Trance
subgenres.desc: Japanese style that emerged in Shibuya's club scene in the 2000s and was primarily marketed to gyaru, infused with melodic and rhythmic influence from Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: Hard Trance
subgenres.desc: Rave-oriented form of Trance infusing its atmospheres with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melodic / bassline sections, initially spawning out of the first wave in early-1990s Western Europe.

subgenres.name: Hi-Tech Full-On
subgenres.desc: Largely Japanese genre with an energetic and glitchy sound derived from Full-On Psytrance and Complextro.

subgenres.name: Ibiza Trance
subgenres.desc: Builds on the relaxing island atmosphere of Balearic Beat, though with a slightly faster tempo of around 130 BPM.

subgenres.name: NRG
subgenres.desc: Derived from UK Hard House; featuring darker, more anthemic Trance beats and a tempo of 155-165 BPM.

subgenres.name: Progressive Trance
subgenres.desc: Combination of Trance and Progressive House which emerged in Western Europe in the early to mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a psychedelic feel and an energetic sound; based around influences from Goa Trance and Acid Trance.

subgenres.name: Dark Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Uses more complex sound design based on dark atmospheres and fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Hi-Tech Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Glitchy sound design, morphing synth lines, strange sounds typically evoking futuristic or alien-like atmospheres, and faster tempos than most other forms of Psytrance.

subgenres.name: Psycore
subgenres.desc: Pushes the dark atmospheres of Dark Psytrance to the extreme through the usage of exceptionally high tempos and experimental soundscapes influenced by Dark Ambient and Glitch.

subgenres.name: Forest Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Mimicks the ambience of a forest by using swarming and teeming effects as well as natural samples; features straightforward song structures.

subgenres.name: Full-On Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Faster and more intense, usually set around 145-150 BPM and featuring harder rolling basslines, vocal samples and "spacey" effects.

subgenres.name: Goa Trance
subgenres.desc: Forerunner of Psytrance styles that emerged in the early 1990s, distinguished by old-school, organic sound with rapid, oriental-inspired melodies.

subgenres.name: Nitzhonot
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced, featuring rapid melodic lines and usually hard and high-pitched kicks.

subgenres.name: Progressive Psytrance
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2000s, featuring a slow tempo range and clean production.

subgenres.name: Zenonesque
subgenres.desc: Experimental and leftfield approach to Progressive Psytrance, mixing the atmospheric and clean Psytrance production typical of it with funky and jazzy elements.

subgenres.name: Suomisaundi
subgenres.desc: Finnish-based deviation of Psytrance with an emphasis on free-form experimentation and humor.

subgenres.name: Tech Trance
subgenres.desc: Late 1990s-emerging subgenre characterized by energetic percussion with loud kicks, filtered hi-hats and tribal drums; side-chained, detuned and repetitive leads, as well as other raw, distorted, and complex sounds influenced by Techno, Hard Trance and Electro House.

subgenres.name: Uplifting Trance
subgenres.desc: Euphoric melodies, buildup-breakdown-anthem structures, common usage of supersaws, and a BPM range of usually around 135-142.

subgenres.name: Vocal Trance
subgenres.desc: Melodic, polished, Pop-like, and vocal-focused with around 120-145 BPM and frequent overlap with Progressive Trance, Uplifting Trance, and Euro Trance.

subgenres.name: Trap [EDM]
subgenres.desc: Trap-influenced syncopated percussion with 808 samples and fast-paced hi-hats.

subgenres.name: Festival Trap
subgenres.desc: Massive, sub-bass-heavy drops with simple melodies, synth leads and production influenced by Big Room House; highly popular from 2013 to 2015.

subgenres.name: Hard Trap
subgenres.desc: Often abrasive subgenre of Trap [EDM] with heavy influence from Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Heaven Trap
subgenres.desc: Blends Trap [EDM]’s signature percussion and sub-basses with euphoric, uplifting, melodious drops prominently derived from Festival Progressive House, contrary to the gritty, "dirty" nature of other EDM trap styles.

subgenres.name: Hybrid Trap
subgenres.desc: Blending Trap [EDM]'s typical percussion and sub-basses with major influences from heavy bass music genres, and in particular, metallic, gritty, and off-kilter sound design, originally derived from Brostep.

subgenres.name: Twerk
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced; draws influence from Bounce and Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Tribal Guarachero
subgenres.desc: Features percussion from Cumbia and Mexican Folk Music with upbeat Electro House-derived production and fast, triplet-oriented rhythmic patterns.

subgenres.name: UK Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent bass/sub-basses, a deep, dark, airy, and mechanical sound derived from Dubstep, and eclectic production influenced by UK Funky, Juke/Footwork, Techno, and Breakbeat.

subgenres.name: UK Funky
subgenres.desc: Influenced by UK Garage-related styles and the regional styles of British immigrants, including Soca and West African-inspired Tribal House.

subgenres.name: UK Garage
subgenres.desc: Shuffling rhythms and influences from sources including Contemporary R&B and Hip Hop, as well as many forms of Electronic.

subgenres.name: 2-Step
subgenres.desc: Originating in London and popular in the late 1990s; jittery, shuffling rhythms rarely following a four-on-the-floor pattern.

subgenres.name: Bassline
subgenres.desc: Strong emphasis on intricate basslines as well as four-on-the-floor beat patterns.

subgenres.name: Breakstep
subgenres.desc: Hard-hitting Breakbeat rhythms and heavy, rolling basslines.

subgenres.name: Future Garage
subgenres.desc: Combines the rhythms of late 1990s and early 2000s 2-Step with novel moods and production approaches, commonly featuring jittery, broken rhythms, vocal chops, and warm synth pads and plucks.

subgenres.name: Speed Garage
subgenres.desc: Primarily British style that paved the way for UK Garage, combining cut-up vocal samples and sped up four-on-the-floor Garage House rhythms with Jungle-esque basslines.

subgenres.name: Wonky
subgenres.desc: Off-kilter fusion of Dubstep and Hip Hop which first developed in the mid-to-late 2000s.

subgenres.name: Aquacrunk
subgenres.desc: Syncopated, half-time rhythms inspired by Dubstep and Grime, funky, sludgy, "aquatic"-sounding synths and sound design.

subgenres.name: Electropop
subgenres.desc: Dense, layered, and compressed production, usually coupled with a distinct fuzzy and "warm" low-frequency synthesizer style.

subgenres.name: Epic Collage
subgenres.desc: Cinematic, dense digital collage; frequently utilizes a Deconstructed Club sonic palette and decontextualized novel samples.

subgenres.name: Flashcore
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced short sounds, complex structures with erratic progression, and often dense and atmospheric abstract sound design, featuring recontextualized elements from IDM, Speedcore, Industrial Hardcore, and Breakcore.

subgenres.name: Folktronica
subgenres.desc: Combines sound design techniques from IDM and Glitch with acoustic instrumentation inspired by Contemporary Folk.

subgenres.name: Funktronica
subgenres.desc: Originated in eastern North America around the turn of the 21st century, combining trends of Synth Funk and Italo-Disco.

subgenres.name: Glitch
subgenres.desc: Uses abstract sound design and malfunctioning electronics—CD skips, data corruption, and hardware noise—as main compositional elements.

subgenres.name: Glitch Hop
subgenres.desc: Incorporation of IDM-derived production into drum patterns inspired by Hip Hop beats.

subgenres.name: Graphical Sound
subgenres.desc: Compositional technique in which markings are manually applied to a medium, then processed by a machine to produce synthetic sound from the markings in real time.

subgenres.name: HexD
subgenres.desc: Heavily bit-crushed, sometimes sped-up and pitched-up vocals, and highly compressed, distorted production, typically using preexisting material from other genres.

subgenres.name: Krushclub
subgenres.desc: Bitcrushed synths and occasionally bitcrushed vocals, energetic Jersey Club-derived beats, and elements of Sigilkore's dark production style.

subgenres.name: Horror Synth
subgenres.desc: Combines eerie and haunting synth pads and sharp, abrasive sounds to create atmospheres that accentuated the dark, unnerving, violent, or ghostly themes of horror films.

subgenres.name: Hyperpop
subgenres.desc: Developed and took inspiration from Bubblegum Bass and popular 2000s-2010s Electropop, characterized by eclectic, unconventional, mechanical-sounding and dense production; and by manipulated, usually auto-tuned vocals.

subgenres.name: IDM
subgenres.desc: Emerged through the development of Electronic Dance Music idioms into a less club-oriented and more experimental direction, often incorporating unconventional sound design and complex rhythms.

subgenres.name: Drill and Bass
subgenres.desc: Frenzied, intricate beat programming inspired by Drum and Bass.

subgenres.name: Illbient
subgenres.desc: Combines Ambient soundscapes with Hip Hop drum patterns, breaks, and samples through the busy effect layering of Dub.

subgenres.name: Indietronica
subgenres.desc: Leftfield or DIY approach characterised by simpler Pop-informed melodies, often incorporating vocals or live instrumentation alongside Electronic production.

subgenres.name: Chillwave
subgenres.desc: Emulates vintage aesthetics and popular musical styles of the 1980s/1990s altered by modern recording technology to create a hazy dreamlike atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Chillsynth
subgenres.desc: Mixes Synthwave with major Chillwave elements, characterized by a dreamy and relaxed sound.

subgenres.name: Glitch Pop
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of more experimental Electronic styles like IDM and Glitch.

subgenres.name: Picopop
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2000s as an offshoot of the Japanese Shibuya-kei movement when artists introduced more prominent "bleepy" electronic elements and faster tempos.

subgenres.name: Latin Electronic
subgenres.desc: Combines Electronic with Latin American influences; started at the end of the 1990s.

subgenres.name: Changa tuki
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Digital Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Electro latino
subgenres.desc: Mixes elements of Merengue and Reggaetón with polished production from mainstream House subgenres; often shares traits with Latin Pop, having anthemic melodies and verse-chorus structures.

subgenres.name: Electrotango
subgenres.desc: Combines Tango rhythms and melodies with Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Nortec
subgenres.desc: Samples and synthesizes Mexican styles like Banda sinaloense and Norteño into a sound related to IDM and House.

subgenres.name: Tribal Guarachero
subgenres.desc: Features percussion from Cumbia and Mexican Folk Music with upbeat Electro House-derived production and fast, triplet-oriented rhythmic patterns.

subgenres.name: Livetronica
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Electronic instrumentation into live Rock jamming, drawing on a wide variety of Electronic Dance Music and Downtempo styles.

subgenres.name: Maloya électronique
subgenres.desc: Combines the 6/8 ternary rhythm with Electronic production, using computer music, synthesizers and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Micromontage
subgenres.desc: Arrangement of microsounds on an incredibly small time scale.

subgenres.name: Minimal Wave
subgenres.desc: Retrospective term for more Electronic and minimal forms of New Wave, Post-Punk, Synthpop, and related styles, tending towards a more sparse and lo-fi sound.

subgenres.name: Minimal Synth
subgenres.desc: Minimal and distinctly DIY take on Synthpop with a bleak and naive aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Moogsploitation
subgenres.desc: Moog synthesizer-led music often associated with a wave of Novelty records in the 1960s and 1970s.

subgenres.name: Nightcore
subgenres.desc: Based around the technique of speeding and pitching up pre-existing songs.

subgenres.name: Nu Jazz
subgenres.desc: Electronic styles which feature aesthetics and occasionally instrumentation inspired by Jazz.

subgenres.name: Power Electronics
subgenres.desc: Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.

subgenres.name: Death Industrial
subgenres.desc: Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Power Noise
subgenres.desc: Combines looped samples of Noise with Electronic rhythms.

subgenres.name: Progressive Electronic
subgenres.desc: Synthesizer-driven genre focusing on developing, often longform compositions and drawing inspiration from various sources such as Progressive Rock, Western Classical Music, and Ambient.

subgenres.name: Berlin School
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric, multi-layered synthesizer textures; pioneered in Berlin in the 1970s as an offshoot to the Krautrock movement.

subgenres.name: Space Ambient
subgenres.desc: Flowing and relaxing synthesizer-based music derived from Progressive Electronic, often oriented around imagery of outer space.

subgenres.name: Synthpop
subgenres.desc: Led by melodic synthesizer sounds, often with reverberating drum machine patterns; commonly associated with the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Futurepop
subgenres.desc: Derivative of EBM, retaining its apocalyptic worldview but incorporating heavy influence from the melodic style of Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Pon-chak disco
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by Electro-Disco, featuring cheap "electronic organ" synth leads and minimalistic, repetitive rhythms.

subgenres.name: Techno kayō
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of 1980s Kayōkyoku and Idol kayō incorporating characteristics from Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Synth Punk
subgenres.desc: Appropriates the harsh elements of Punk Rock but replaces the predominance of guitars with synthesizers and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Synthwave
subgenres.desc: Rooted in 1980s synth music, characterized by large, throbbing "retro" synths and visual elements, often features upbeat percussion and/or epic, cinematic atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Chillsynth
subgenres.desc: Mixes Synthwave with major Chillwave elements, characterized by a dreamy and relaxed sound.

subgenres.name: Darksynth
subgenres.desc: Incorporates atmospheric Horror Synth and faster tempos into a much heavier and darker sound.

subgenres.name: Sovietwave
subgenres.desc: Scene of Synthwave that emerged in the early 2010s, taking its inspiration from Soviet Electronic electronic music and Soviet pop.

subgenres.name: Tecnobrega
subgenres.desc: Fast and electronic-based style that evolved from Brega calypso, particularly associated with peripheral areas of the city of Belém.

subgenres.name: Tecnofunk
subgenres.desc: Raw and vulgar Tecnobrega and Funk brasileiro fusion developed in the late 2010s by DJs in Belém do Pará.

subgenres.name: Vapor
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre beginning with the rise of Vaporwave and the aesthetics that it spawned.

subgenres.name: Barber Beats
subgenres.desc: Borrows elements from Downtempo, Trip Hop, and Instrumental Hip Hop; emulates 1990s and 2000s Chillout music.

subgenres.name: Dreampunk
subgenres.desc: Accentuates ambiance and a dreamy, futuristic atmosphere, taking influence from Progressive Electronic, as well as Cyberpunk and Dystopian movies.

subgenres.name: Future Funk
subgenres.desc: Sample-based style influenced by French House and Synth Funk that utilizes Vaporwave editing techniques.

subgenres.name: Hardvapour
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Hardcore [EDM] and Techno and made in response to the Vaporwave movement.

subgenres.name: Utopian Virtual
subgenres.desc: Emulates late 20th century futuristic and corporate aesthetics, often using "tacky"-sounding instruments likened to MIDI Music, in contrast to Vaporwave's sample-based approach.

subgenres.name: Vapornoise
subgenres.desc: Uses Noise and other avant-garde techniques not typically found in Vaporwave.

subgenres.name: Vaportrap
subgenres.desc: Incorporates a blend of Trap percussion set to the re-utilization of old samples, such as 1990s pop culture or old computer library sounds.

subgenres.name: Vaporwave
subgenres.desc: Sample-based, involving heavily synthesized and processed manipulation of corporate mood and background (elevator) music, though source material can also include Pop, Contemporary R&B, and Synth Funk.

subgenres.name: Broken Transmission
subgenres.desc: Manipulates samples from TV broadcasts, advertisements, film, radio, and other sources.

subgenres.name: Eccojams
subgenres.desc: Simple, prototypical Vaporwave style, heavily influenced by Chopped and Screwed and Glitch, that features short, slowed-down, lyric focused, sampled loops smothered in reverb and continuously repeated, usually taken from late 20th century music.

subgenres.name: Mallsoft
subgenres.desc: Blends the main characteristics of Vaporwave with what can be described as background/elevator music.

subgenres.name: Slushwave
subgenres.desc: Utilizes a distinct form of sample manipulation to create a “slushy” sound, usually sequenced in soft Ambient-based soundscapes.

subgenres.name: Wave
subgenres.desc: Melancholic, atmospheric, melodic beats, defined by its Trap and Cloud Rap influence, ethereal and cold production style, and abundant use of sub bass.

subgenres.name: Hardwave
subgenres.desc: Harder, festival-oriented offshoot of Wave, combining its "reese" basses and icy synths with Trap [EDM] drum patterns, build-up-drop structures, and fuller sound influenced by Trance and Hardstyle.

subgenres.name: Neo-Grime
subgenres.desc: Mixes Wave with Grime and other forms of UK Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Witch House
subgenres.desc: Nocturnal, occult-themed/horror-inspired, and murky beats with altered, slowed down and heavily processed samples laid on top of slow Hip Hop-derived drum rhythms and droning, dense synthesizers.

name: Experimental
desc: Most radical approaches throughout history, featuring non-traditional production methods resulting in sounds and styles that go largely beyond traditional boundaries.

subgenres.name: Conducted Improvisation
subgenres.desc: Collective improvisation directed by a conductor.

subgenres.name: Data Sonification
subgenres.desc: Usage of data to create sound, soundscapes and music mostly as a way to illustrate its information.

subgenres.name: Drone
subgenres.desc: Focuses on long, sustained tones and tone clusters, or repetition of single notes.

subgenres.name: Electroacoustic
subgenres.desc: Manipulation and processing of sound sources to create atmospheric pieces.

subgenres.name: Acousmatic Music
subgenres.desc: Fixed-media Electroacoustic music designed to be reproduced by multiple loudspeakers without the presence of instrumentalists and visual cues.

subgenres.name: EAI
subgenres.desc: Slow paced, physical, textured aesthetic - often created using unconventional instruments processed through a computer.

subgenres.name: Musique concrète
subgenres.desc: Manipulation of recorded sounds, mostly Field Recordings, natural sounds, and real-world noises, as a process of abstracting "concrete" sounds, or "sound objects", from their acoustic origins.

subgenres.name: Free Improvisation
subgenres.desc: Improvised music which, in descending from Free Jazz and classical Indeterminacy, further abandons the prescriptions of harmonic or rhythmic structures which characterized those genres.

subgenres.name: EAI
subgenres.desc: Slow paced, physical, textured aesthetic - often created using unconventional instruments processed through a computer.

subgenres.name: Futurism
subgenres.desc: Radical and militant attitude, rejection of Western Classical Music and traditional criteria of craft, non-conformity, and a fascination with machines.

subgenres.name: Glitch
subgenres.desc: Uses abstract sound design and malfunctioning electronics—CD skips, data corruption, and hardware noise—as main compositional elements.

subgenres.name: Graphical Sound
subgenres.desc: Compositional technique in which markings are manually applied to a medium, then processed by a machine to produce synthetic sound from the markings in real time.

subgenres.name: Indeterminacy
subgenres.desc: Leaves elements of composition, performance, or both up to chance.

subgenres.name: Industrial
subgenres.desc: Emerged out of Punk and avant-garde art movements in the mid-1970s, often characterized by a bleak, mechanical atmosphere, the use of metallic percussion as well as other unconventional instruments, and extensive use of sampling influenced by Musique concrète.

subgenres.name: Power Electronics
subgenres.desc: Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.

subgenres.name: Death Industrial
subgenres.desc: Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Micromontage
subgenres.desc: Arrangement of microsounds on an incredibly small time scale.

subgenres.name: Modern Creative
subgenres.desc: Style of semi-improvisation that derives heavily from both the composition of Modern Classical and the techniques of Avant-Garde Jazz.

subgenres.name: Musique concrète instrumentale
subgenres.desc: Acoustic, through-composed Classical Music that relies heavily on unconventional instrumental techniques.

subgenres.name: Noise
subgenres.desc: Strays away from conventional structure, tonality, and composition and consists predominantly of noise.

subgenres.name: Ambient Noise Wall
subgenres.desc: Soft, sparse textures inspired by the static composition of Harsh Noise Wall.

subgenres.name: Black Noise
subgenres.desc: Incorporates unconventional sounds with overpowering or constant Noise and Black Metal elements, often being heavily texture-oriented, abrasive, dissonant, atonal, or repetitive.

subgenres.name: Gorenoise
subgenres.desc: Combines and subverts Goregrind and Grindcore with brash Noise and even faster drum tempos.

subgenres.name: Harsh Noise
subgenres.desc: Highly aggressive walls of sound that assault the listener.

subgenres.name: Harsh Noise Wall
subgenres.desc: Harsh, distorted walls of sound that feature few dynamic variations and often take the form of long compositions with little to no change or progression over time.

subgenres.name: Power Electronics
subgenres.desc: Waves of feedback, screeching analog synthesizers, and harsh, screamed vocals.

subgenres.name: Death Industrial
subgenres.desc: Combines the abrasive textures of Noise and Industrial music with dark, brooding drones and atmospheres.

subgenres.name: Power Noise
subgenres.desc: Combines looped samples of Noise with Electronic rhythms.

subgenres.name: Plunderphonics
subgenres.desc: Compositional technique of utilizing and manipulating one or more recognizable recordings to create a new composition.

subgenres.name: Reductionism
subgenres.desc: Experimental music that centers around quiet dynamics and use of silence.

subgenres.name: Lowercase
subgenres.desc: Centered around the digital amplification and processing of quiet sounds.

subgenres.name: Onkyo
subgenres.desc: Exploration of the physical traits of sound rather than music as expression.

subgenres.name: Sound Art
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements from Experimental music and visual arts, with sound utilized as its primary medium and subject.

subgenres.name: Sound Collage
subgenres.desc: Compositional method emphasizing the rough layering of sampled elements, presenting an impression similar to a visual collage.

subgenres.name: Epic Collage
subgenres.desc: Cinematic, dense digital collage; frequently utilizes a Deconstructed Club sonic palette and decontextualized novel samples.

subgenres.name: Sound Poetry
subgenres.desc: Emphasis is placed upon phonetics and the sounds of syllables rather than the meaning of the words themselves.

subgenres.name: Tape Music
subgenres.desc: Explores the nature of audio recorded to magnetic tape and the act of playing sound from it.

subgenres.name: Turntable Music
subgenres.desc: Has its roots in the early half of the twentieth century, with experimental artists using the turntable (as well as the vinyl records it plays) as a distinct instrument in the creation of compositions.

name: Folk
desc: Rooted in mostly oral traditions of the peoples of the world, encompassing international Traditional Folk Music as well as Western Contemporary Folk which arose in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Contemporary Folk
subgenres.desc: Generally acoustic and rooted in modernized Traditional Folk Music; originated with the 20th-century American folk revival.

subgenres.name: American Primitivism
subgenres.desc: Blends avant-garde and neo-classical compositions with traditional Country Blues fingerpicking techniques.

subgenres.name: Anti-Folk
subgenres.desc: Rawer approach to folk, with an often self-mocking and sarcastic tone.

subgenres.name: Avant-Folk
subgenres.desc: Experimental-influenced and playing with instrumentation, rhythm, and other factors not commonly found in folk.

subgenres.name: Free Folk
subgenres.desc: Incorporates improvisation, repetition and extended song lengths.

subgenres.name: Campus Folk
subgenres.desc: Born in Taiwan in the mid-1970s, this movement originated with university students creating their own modern-style songs in the wake of international tensions like Taiwan's isolation from the United Nations and the United States' embrace of the PRC as a diplomatic partner.

subgenres.name: Chamber Folk
subgenres.desc: Gentle fingerpicked acoustic guitar or harp-led music that commonly includes a backing ensemble of harpsichords, strings, horns, or other orchestral instruments.

subgenres.name: Country Folk
subgenres.desc: Emphasises Traditional Country instrumentation as well as influences from contemporary Singer-Songwriter traditions, such as a gentler disposition and prominent lyrical storytelling focus.

subgenres.name: Folk Baroque
subgenres.desc: Originated in England in the early 1960s, featuring a distinctive guitar fingerpicking style of the same name and the DADGAD guitar tuning.

subgenres.name: Folk Pop
subgenres.desc: Blends Contemporary Folk with a Pop sensibility, most popular in the late 1960s and early 1970s and featuring influence from the contemporary Folk Rock style.

subgenres.name: Stomp and Holler
subgenres.desc: Highlights driving "stomping" rhythms and shouted group vocal harmonies, often drawing influences from Pop Rock, Indie Folk, and other genres, while maintaining a characteristically mellow and commercial sound.

subgenres.name: Indie Folk
subgenres.desc: Combines the melodic sensibilities and production style of Indie Rock and Indie Pop with acoustic instrumentation and influences from Folk, Singer-Songwriter, and sometimes Country.

subgenres.name: Stomp and Holler
subgenres.desc: Highlights driving "stomping" rhythms and shouted group vocal harmonies, often drawing influences from Pop Rock, Indie Folk, and other genres, while maintaining a characteristically mellow and commercial sound.

subgenres.name: Loner Folk
subgenres.desc: Lo-fi, downbeat, and frequently depressive atmosphere with psychedelic undertones that emerged among independent creators following the collapse of the counterculture in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Neofolk
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s from the Post-Industrial scene, with a dark, often martial atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Dark Folk
subgenres.desc: Minimalistic and melancholic sound with influence from Nordic Folk Music and even Ambient.

subgenres.name: Neofolklore
subgenres.desc: Short-lived movement that reincorporated traditional Chilean folklore into modern production and styling inspired by foreign musicians.

subgenres.name: Progressive Folk
subgenres.desc: Draws from a variety of sources to subvert traditional acoustic song forms, with diversity ranging from Jazz to Medieval music to various Regional Music traditions.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Folk
subgenres.desc: Acoustic forms that capture an atmosphere that is at turns dream-like, 'spaced-out', whimsical, haunting, mystical, and melancholic.

subgenres.name: Freak Folk
subgenres.desc: Loosely defined 2000s Psychedelic Folk revival closely associated with the New Weird America movement, sometimes also a shorthand for certain leftfield styles of psychedelic and Indie Folk.

subgenres.name: Free Folk
subgenres.desc: Incorporates improvisation, repetition and extended song lengths.

subgenres.name: Udigrudi
subgenres.desc: Movement that emerged in the Brazilian city of Recife during the 1970s that combines psychedelic elements with music of Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Wyrd Folk
subgenres.desc: Closely tied to mysticism, old folk beliefs, and Folk Horror; often described as 'witchy' or 'pagan.'

subgenres.name: Skiffle
subgenres.desc: Grew out of British Trad Jazz, drawing influence from 1920s Jug Bands and the strong rhythms of 1950s Honky Tonk and Rock & Roll.

subgenres.name: Xinyao
subgenres.desc: Singaporean Mandarin-language style, generally featuring harmonised group vocals and backed mainly by acoustic guitar.

subgenres.name: Traditional Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Informed by a long history of tradition in a specific culture or region, mostly associated with the peasantry and non-aristocratic public.

subgenres.name: African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Indigenous music of Africa that is passed down orally from generation to generation, the authors of the songs are usually unknown.

subgenres.name: Ambasse bey
subgenres.desc: African Folk Music developed by the Yabassi people of Cameroon.

subgenres.name: Apala
subgenres.desc: Yoruba Music developed by Muslims during the late 1930s and early 1940s in the Ijebu region of Yorubaland, the current Ogun state.

subgenres.name: Batuque
subgenres.desc: Tradition from Cape Verde, unusual among the islands' music due to its lack of polyphonic singing and its usage of polyrhythms.

subgenres.name: Dagomba Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Dagomba people of northern Ghana.

subgenres.name: Gnawa
subgenres.desc: A mystical musical tradition centred around the qraqab castanets and guembri bass lute, named after its originators, the Afro-Maghrebi Gnawa people.

subgenres.name: Kabye Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kabye people of northern Togo, including some of the most singular styles that can be found in West Africa.

subgenres.name: Kilapanga
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Bakongo people from Angola and Congo that has influenced contemporary styles such as Kuduro.

subgenres.name: Malagasy Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Melodic, chordophone-dominated sound; based on the Austronesian Music of the first settlers that arrived on the island from Borneo.

subgenres.name: Mbenga-Mbuti Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Mbenga and Mbuti people, Pygmy ethnic groups in Central Africa.

subgenres.name: Moutya
subgenres.desc: Tradition that originated in Seychelles among Creole slaves, similar to Séga, although rawer and played only on large flat drums made from goatskin.

subgenres.name: Ngoma
subgenres.desc: Played in Swahili-speaking African countries; primarily focused on rhythm.

subgenres.name: Unyago
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Zanzibar, traditionally played at women's initiation rituals and weddings.

subgenres.name: Southern African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Afrikaner Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Musical traditions developed by the Afrikaner community in southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Khoisan Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses traditions of the Khoisan ethnic family groups.

subgenres.name: Nguni Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Nguni ethnic family groups, a southern Bantu ethnicity.

subgenres.name: Sotho-Tswana Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Sotho-Tswana ethnic family groups from southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Tchinkoumé
subgenres.desc: Tradition from the central region of Benin around Savalou, played with water percussion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Maloya
subgenres.desc: Derived from Traditional Séga, this is the original dance music of La Réunion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Séga
subgenres.desc: Séga dance music born in the 18th century, before its later adoption of Western pop elements.

subgenres.name: Zinli
subgenres.desc: Traditional rhythmic chanting and percussion adapted to multiple West African contexts in the 20th century.

subgenres.name: American Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traces back through the history of European and West African settlement and migration to North America, including parts of northern Mexico and Canada in addition to the United States.

subgenres.name: Appalachian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Appalachian Mountains in the Eastern United States.

subgenres.name: Old-Time
subgenres.desc: Pre-Bluegrass North American string band styles, particularly those rooted in Appalachian Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Various styles of Blues originating in the rural US South, typically relying on expressive vocal delivery and featuring simple, usually acoustic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Delta Blues
subgenres.desc: One of the earliest forms of Blues, named for the Mississippi Delta region of the United States where it developed, with a highly rhythmic style and a typical 12-bar structure.

subgenres.name: Bentonia School
subgenres.desc: Brooding, hypnotic minor-key open-tuning guitar style with a looser structure, often featuring high, "haunting" vocals.

subgenres.name: Hill Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a steady hypnotic groove, sparse percussive and highly energetic guitar riffs, and often features meandering structures with unconventional and usually fewer chord changes compared to Delta Blues.

subgenres.name: Piedmont Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.

subgenres.name: Field Hollers
subgenres.desc: Created by African-American slaves working on cotton plantations, featuring expressive vocals to no strict rhythm.

subgenres.name: Fife and Drum Blues
subgenres.desc: Rooted in martial Fife and Drum Corps music, originated among Afro-American communities in Mississippi.

subgenres.name: Jug Band
subgenres.desc: Usually features a jug as the bass instrument as well as other homemade (or easily affordable) instruments, such as kazoos and washboards.

subgenres.name: Pennsylvania Dutch Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Pennsylvania Dutch.

subgenres.name: Ring Shout
subgenres.desc: Ritual practiced by African-Americans in the US South, characterized by shouting, chanting and people dancing in a circle while praying and clapping.

subgenres.name: Sacred Harp Singing
subgenres.desc: Predominantly 19th-century English hymns with tunes derived from old folk melodies.

subgenres.name: Spiritual
subgenres.desc: African American folk song based around Christian themes, originating during enslavement and emphasizing solidarity and freedom; musical features include call-and-response, "blue" notes, and expressive vocal timbres.

subgenres.name: Talking Blues
subgenres.desc: American Folk Music with spoken or nearly spoken vocals; often features dry humor and social commentary.

subgenres.name: Traditional Black Gospel
subgenres.desc: Born out of Spiritual in the early 20th century with influence from Southern Gospel and Blues, often featuring passionate or energetic vocal performances, motifs of salvation, and testaments of hardship.

subgenres.name: Traditional Cajun Music
subgenres.desc: Earliest and most "pure" form of Cajun Music, employing basic rhythms and frequent fiddle double stops.

subgenres.name: Traditional Country
subgenres.desc: Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Close Harmony
subgenres.desc: Traditional two-part harmony singing performed mostly by brothers.

subgenres.name: Country Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Arabic Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Arabic people.

subgenres.name: Aita
subgenres.desc: Arabic Folk Music from rural Morocco with piercing singing, scratchy viola, and rollicking hand drums.

subgenres.name: Arabic Bellydance Music
subgenres.desc: Accompaniment to traditional belly dances.

subgenres.name: Raqs baladi
subgenres.desc: Egyptian folk dance and its associated musical accompaniment, appearing in the 20th century.

subgenres.name: Ayyalah
subgenres.desc: Traditional Khaliji-Bedouin weapon performance, commonly found across the United Arab Emirates and Northwestern Oman.

subgenres.name: Fijiri
subgenres.desc: Deeply rooted in the Persian Gulf pearl diving culture, and sung during weekly gatherings combining solo and choral sections with minimal percussion.

subgenres.name: Liwa
subgenres.desc: Traditional Khaliji performance with East African Music roots centered around the mizmar and traditional drums, typically sung in Khaliji Arabic and Swahili.

subgenres.name: Nuban
subgenres.desc: Traditional Afro-Emirati Folk performance of Nuban origin most commonly performed in the emirate of Dubai.

subgenres.name: Sa'idi
subgenres.desc: Traditional folkloric performance and form of Arabic Folk Music originating from Upper Egypt.

subgenres.name: Australian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of the European colonists and convicts in Australia.

subgenres.name: Bayawan
subgenres.desc: Distinct muqam tradition of the Dolan subgroup of the Uyghur people, often considered the wildest of the regional muqam variations.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Comprises the various traditions of folk music found in Brazil, often resulting from the interplay of Indigenous, African and European music.

subgenres.name: Aboio
subgenres.desc: Cattle-herding songs originating in rural Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Aboio cantado
subgenres.desc: Aboio that features rhyming verses.

subgenres.name: Banda de pífano
subgenres.desc: Lively music played by bands consisting of two fifes and percussion.

subgenres.name: Candomblé Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religion that influenced the secular Afoxé.

subgenres.name: Cantoria
subgenres.desc: Sung poetry of itinerant cantadores from Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Repente
subgenres.desc: Contest of fully improvised poetry sung in different stanza formats.

subgenres.name: Capoeira Music
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian style that accompanies and sets the rhythm and energy of the capoeira martial art, originating in the 19th century with the relocation of African slaves to the states of Bahia and Rio de Janeiro.

subgenres.name: Fandango caiçara
subgenres.desc: Style of fandango born in coastal Southern Brazil amidst the Caiçara people.

subgenres.name: Jongo
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian cultural manifestation involving music and dance; composed of percussion instruments and chants.

subgenres.name: Ponto de umbanda
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian religious ritualistic praise sung by priests to evoke entities; typically accompanied by claps and traditional drums known as atabaque.

subgenres.name: Lundu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian music and dance that emerged in the 18th century with influences from African drumming with European fandango.

subgenres.name: Maracatu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian genre which accompanies the cultural manifestation of the same name, hailing from the northeastern state of Pernambuco.

subgenres.name: Modinha
subgenres.desc: Popular during the 18th and 19th centuries in Brazil; characterized by sentimental works with amorous themes, poetic lyrics, acoustic instrumentation and operatic vocals.

subgenres.name: Rasqueado
subgenres.desc: Regional dance and its accompanying music from the Brazilian midwest, predominantly the state of Mato Grosso.

subgenres.name: Samba de roda
subgenres.desc: Mixed Portuguese culture with African slave traditions, as well as sharing roots and similarities with Batuque and Jongo.

subgenres.name: Sertanejo de raiz
subgenres.desc: Earliest form of Sertanejo, emerging in pre-World War II rural Brazil during the late 1920s; quickly strummed acoustic guitars, most commonly the 10-string viola caipira and classical guitar, and a highly emotive vocal style.

subgenres.name: Moda de viola
subgenres.desc: Style of Sertanejo de raiz predominant in southeast, south, and west-central Brazil.

subgenres.name: Toada de Boi
subgenres.desc: Slow, heavy-percussed tunes celebrating the folkloric Ox, originally from Bumba-meu-boi June parties in Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Xaxado
subgenres.desc: Features a strong rhythmic beat, sliding tap dances, and stories of backland bandits.

subgenres.name: Canadian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the European settlers who arrived in Canada.

subgenres.name: Canadian Maritime Folk
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of Canada's Maritimes (Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick).

subgenres.name: Cape Breton Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Celtic Folk Music that emerged in Cape Breton, an island at the eastern shore of Nova Scotia, through immigrants from Scotland and Ireland.

subgenres.name: Cape Breton Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Distinctive Celtic fiddling originating from the Scottish immigrants who settled in Canada on Cape Breton Island.

subgenres.name: French-Canadian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Brought by French colonists to their Nouvelle-France settlements, primarily based around French Folk Music with influences from English Folk Music and Celtic Folk Music, typically played during gatherings and holidays.

subgenres.name: Métis Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Canadian style blending First Nations and European musical influences into an up-tempo style of fiddling characterized by the use of syncopation and indigenous rhythms.

subgenres.name: Newfoundland Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada's easternmost province.

subgenres.name: Caribbean Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre that covers the different forms of Traditional Folk Music from the Caribbean.

subgenres.name: Bele
subgenres.desc: Drum-based folkdance with a strong Afro-influence, conducted by duos of dancers and accompanied by call-and-response singing, particularly popular in Martinique, Dominica and Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Benna
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of Antigua & Barbuda, using call-and-response and bawdy lyrics.

subgenres.name: Bomba
subgenres.desc: Percussive style from Puerto Rico, generally considered to be derived from West Africa.

subgenres.name: Fungi
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music native to the Virgin Islands, named after a local dish which features a "mixed-up" flavor that can be compared to the style that combines Western instruments with local ones.

subgenres.name: Haitian Vodou Drumming
subgenres.desc: Form of rhythmic performance by Haitian Vodou practitioners, played at associated ceremonies.

subgenres.name: Jibaro
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the mountain-dwelling jibaro people that live primarily in Puerto Rico.

subgenres.name: Kaiso
subgenres.desc: Trinidadian folk considered to be the precursor of Calypso, led by "griot" storytellers who sing derogatory lyrics to the sound of drums and guitars in a call-and-response manner in order to rebel against slaveowners.

subgenres.name: Kitchen Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Cayman Islands music played during kitchen dance parties, centered around fiddle and percussion (handmade or kitchen grater) playing.

subgenres.name: Kumina
subgenres.desc: Folk religious ritual of Jamaica, featuring extensive musical and dance elements, greatly inspired Rastafari religion and music.

subgenres.name: Mento
subgenres.desc: Jamaican folk originating in the late 19th century which brought together African and European elements, going on to influence the rhythm in Reggae.

subgenres.name: Méringue
subgenres.desc: Haitian genre that dates back to the early 19th century; the roots of Compas.

subgenres.name: Plena
subgenres.desc: Folk genre from Puerto Rico played with hand drums called panderetas.

subgenres.name: Ripsaw
subgenres.desc: Indigenous style of the Turks and Caicos Islands, featuring a handsaw as the primary instrument.

subgenres.name: Tumba
subgenres.desc: African-style percussion alongside Latin influences and often explicit lyrics.

subgenres.name: Virgin Islander Cariso
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Virgin Islands, sung exclusively by women to the beat of one or two drums.

subgenres.name: Caucasian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Caucasus region, a mountainous area that connects Eastern Europe to Asia.

subgenres.name: Abkhazian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Republic of Abkhazia, a disputed territory on the Black Sea in northwestern Georgia.

subgenres.name: Chechen Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Chechens, a Northeast Caucasian ethnic group predominantly living in the Republic of Chechnya, a federal subject of Russia.

subgenres.name: Circassian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the native Circassian peoples of Northern Caucasus, residing in the Republics of Adygea, Karachay-Cherkessia, and Kabardino-Balkaria respectively, which are federal subjects of the Russian Federation, as well as the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, with a significant diaspora population in modern Turkey.

subgenres.name: Dagestani Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Dagestani people.

subgenres.name: Avar Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Avar people.

subgenres.name: Georgian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Georgian people, who mostly live in Georgia.

subgenres.name: Batonebi Songs
subgenres.desc: Traditional Georgian Lullabies often meant to soothe sick children.

subgenres.name: Ossetian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk music of Ossetians, an ethnic group that mainly inhabits a region located on both sides of the Greater Caucasus Mountains.

subgenres.name: Chukchi Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Chukchi people.

subgenres.name: Drinking Song
subgenres.desc: Songs meant to be sung locally while consuming alcohol, often in bars, pubs, or taverns.

subgenres.name: East Asian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: All the forms of Traditional Folk Music from East Asia, including Japanese Folk Music, Chinese Folk Music, and Korean Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Amami shimauta
subgenres.desc: Tradition from the Amami Islands, located in southern Japan.

subgenres.name: Chinese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the Chinese people.

subgenres.name: Chaozhou xianshi
subgenres.desc: Traditional and instrumental ensemble music originating from Chaozhou; played mainly on stringed instruments.

subgenres.name: Han Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Chinese folk form often played at weddings and funerals, using the Suona (a form of oboe) and Chuigushou (a specific type of percussive ensemble), together with heterophony.

subgenres.name: Haozi
subgenres.desc: Chinese Work Song that originated from collective manual labor and usually follows a call-and-response structure, aiming to coordinate work.

subgenres.name: Jiangnan sizhu
subgenres.desc: Originating from Jiangnan region and played by a varying ensemble of stringed instruments, flutes, mouth organs and small percussions.

subgenres.name: Shan'ge
subgenres.desc: Folk songs found in upland regions of China, typically sung while working.

subgenres.name: Indigenous Taiwanese Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the various Austronesian people groups that make up the indigenous population of the island of Taiwan.

subgenres.name: Japanese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of Japan.

subgenres.name: Heikyoku
subgenres.desc: Semi-classical bardic tradition in Japan analogous to the troubadour music of medieval Europe.

subgenres.name: Kagura
subgenres.desc: Performed at Shinto shrines for ceremonies and rituals.

subgenres.name: Kouta
subgenres.desc: Kouta, which literally means "little" or "short" song, is one type of the many varieties of Japanese folk songs that is distinguished by its briefness and wittiness.

subgenres.name: Min'yō
subgenres.desc: Form of Japanese Folk Music which literally translates to "folk song".

subgenres.name: Ondō
subgenres.desc: Originally referred to the type of call-and-response form of Gagaku, but later became to be known for and distinguished by a swung 2/2 rhythm and storytelling.

subgenres.name: Rōkyoku
subgenres.desc: Storytelling usually accompanied by a shamisen.

subgenres.name: Taiko
subgenres.desc: Modern style of ensemble drumming, sometimes called kumi-daiko.

subgenres.name: Tsugaru shamisen
subgenres.desc: Shamisen playing originating in the Tsugaru Peninsula of Aomori prefecture, recognizable in its percussive quality and special, slightly larger instrument.

subgenres.name: Korean Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Korean people.

subgenres.name: Muak
subgenres.desc: Korean shamanistic music that accompanies the ritual of gut as performed in all regions of Korea.

subgenres.name: Pansori
subgenres.desc: Korean style of storytelling characterized by over-the-top, passionate singing from a solo vocalist accompanied by minimal drumming.

subgenres.name: Pungmul
subgenres.desc: Consists of drumming, dancing, and singing, and is a tradition deeply ingrained in South Korean culture.

subgenres.name: Sanjo
subgenres.desc: Traditional instrumental Korean Folk Music that focuses on a wide variety of rhythmic changes with many different classical Korean instruments.

subgenres.name: Sinawi
subgenres.desc: Improvisational genre traditionally serving as an accompaniment to Korean shamanic rituals.

subgenres.name: Vietnamese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Vietnamese people, with traditions influenced by both Chinese Music and Austronesian culture through the Cham people.

subgenres.name: Chèo
subgenres.desc: Northern Vietnamese folk musical theatre, characterized by minimal set design and satirical content.

subgenres.name: Quan họ
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Northern Vietnamese provinces of Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang, originally consisting of harmonic, a cappella singing from two competing duos.

subgenres.name: Xẩm
subgenres.desc: Developed in Northern Vietnam, traditionally sung by blind bards accompanied by a đàn bầu or đàn nhị.

subgenres.name: European Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses numerous folk traditions found in Europe.

subgenres.name: Alpine Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Alps, including parts of Germany, Austria, Slovenia, Switzerland, and Italy.

subgenres.name: Canto degli Alpini
subgenres.desc: Created and traditionally sung by choirs formed from the Italian army's Alpine mountain infantry corps, mainly dating back to WWI.

subgenres.name: Ländler
subgenres.desc: Swiss-German dance band music based on the accordion, combining traditional Alpine Folk Music with elements from Schlager and Jazz.

subgenres.name: Narodno zabavna glasba
subgenres.desc: Modernised form of Slovenian Folk Music from the Alpine region of Upper Carniola (Oberkrain).

subgenres.name: Naturjodel
subgenres.desc: Originated in Toggenburg and Appenzell in Switzerland; deep vocal range, relaxed voice, free tempo, polyphony, elongated notes, improvisation, glissando, and use of syllabic sounds.

subgenres.name: Balkan Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Balkan region of Southeastern Europe.

subgenres.name: Albanian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Albania, including the area's traditions as well as influence from Turkish Music.

subgenres.name: Lab Polyphony
subgenres.desc: One of several genres of iso-polyphonic music performed in southern Albania, with "iso" referring to the distinctive drone voice used.

subgenres.name: Musika popullore
subgenres.desc: Tradition in Albania consisting of light, commercial, amplified Albanian Folk Music usually professionally arranged and manufactured in recording studios alongside video clips.

subgenres.name: Tosk Polyphony
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic singing in the Toskëri region of southern Albania.

subgenres.name: Aromanian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Aromanians.

subgenres.name: Balkan Brass Band
subgenres.desc: Balkan Folk Music played by brass bands.

subgenres.name: Bosnian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Bosnians.

subgenres.name: Izvorna bosanska muzika
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic vocal music that developed in Bosnia in the 20th century, bearing connections to traditional Bosnian genres.

subgenres.name: Sevdalinka
subgenres.desc: Melancholic folk song, originating from Bosnia and Herzegovina, typically love-themed and accompanied by instruments like guitar and accordion.

subgenres.name: Bulgarian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Consists of a variety of traditions and styles, with distinct sounds originating from current and historical regions such as Sofia, Dobrudzha, Macedonia and Thrace.

subgenres.name: Croatian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Croats.

subgenres.name: Klapa
subgenres.desc: Traditional form characteristic of the Dalmatia region of Croatia rooted in littoral church singing.

subgenres.name: Csango Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Csango, an ethnic minority group with Hungarian origins living primarily in the Romanian Moldavia region, but who are also found in the Transylvania, Dobruja, Moldova, the Ukrainian Chernivtsi region, and the Tolna region of Hungary.

subgenres.name: Gagauz Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Gagauz people are a Turkic group living mostly in the southern Gagauzia region of Moldova, but also nearby areas like southwestern Ukraine and southeastern Romania.

subgenres.name: Ganga
