subgenres.desc: Back-to-basics Rock approach combining a less mainstream and DIY ethos with melodic, lighthearted and straightforward songwriting.

subgenres.name: Bedroom Pop
subgenres.desc: Named for solo producers and singer-songwriters from the 2010s onward who created intimate, "authentic" music in their own homes, outside of a traditional studio environment.

subgenres.name: C86
subgenres.desc: Distinctly ramshackle, often Twee Pop-infused combination of British Indie Rock and Jangle Pop.

subgenres.name: Chamber Pop
subgenres.desc: Based on the smooth and melodic songwriting of Lounge and other Easy Listening, as well as the orchestration of Baroque Pop and the production styles of other 1960s pop genres.

subgenres.name: Neo-Acoustic
subgenres.desc: Cross-section of Indie Pop and Jangle Pop with more prominent acoustic instrumentation and songwriting/arrangements that draw from Sophisti-Pop.

subgenres.name: Tontipop
subgenres.desc: Spanish scene known for its exuberant, child-like sound drawing directly from British Twee Pop, as well as Yé-yé, Bubblegum, and Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Twee Pop
subgenres.desc: Distinct Post-Punk background and often jangling guitars, defined by a cute aesthetic and lyrics combined with an indie/DIY attitude and a simplicity often indebted to Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Cuddlecore
subgenres.desc: Rawer and more Punk informed, downplaying jangly guitars in favor of heavier yet still light-hearted tones; often features influence from the contemporary Riot Grrrl movement.

subgenres.name: Irish Showband
subgenres.desc: Phenomenon lasting from the mid-1950s until the early 1980s, often performed a mixture of currently popular music and skits.

subgenres.name: Italo Pop
subgenres.desc: Romantic style developed in Italy in the late 1950s including various influences such as Chanson and Schlager.

subgenres.name: Canzone neomelodica
subgenres.desc: Elements are derived from Canzone napoletana.

subgenres.name: Jazz Pop
subgenres.desc: Pop that incorporates elements from Jazz.

subgenres.name: J-Pop
subgenres.desc: Commercial Pop of Japan after the advent of the Heisei era (1989), characterized by modernized production, a more eclectic sound palette, and a more westernized vocal style.

subgenres.name: Akishibu-kei
subgenres.desc: Otaku inclined update of the style pioneered by the Shibuya-kei scene, mixed with J-Pop and often tied to Anime and Video Game Music.

subgenres.name: Denpa
subgenres.desc: Underground style aiming to be bizarre yet catchy, using off-key and high-pitched vocals, strange or nonsensical lyrics, repetitive chants, onomatopoeia, frantic and "off-kilter" production, and "moe" aesthetics.

subgenres.name: Wa Euro
subgenres.desc: Traditional form of J-Pop that emerged in the second half of the 1980s from late Hi-NRG, '80s British Dance-Pop and Italo-Disco/Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: J-Euro
subgenres.desc: Italian-oriented Japanese scene of Eurobeat, which emerged with Japanese-language covers of Italian songs in the early-to-mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Yakousei
subgenres.desc: Eclectic style of J-Pop developed in the late 2010s and influenced by the Vocaloid Scene; incorporates indie sensibilities, danceable rhythms and a focus on introspective lyricism.

subgenres.name: Kayōkyoku
subgenres.desc: Japanese popular music prominent during the later period of the Shōwa era (early 1950s to late 1980s).

subgenres.name: Idol kayō
subgenres.desc: More Westernized and upbeat form of Kayōkyoku popular in the 1970s and 1980s which acted as a precursor to J-Pop.

subgenres.name: Mood kayō
subgenres.desc: Early form of Kayōkyoku dominant in the 1950s and 1960s, prominently influenced by American Jazz, Hispanic American Music, and Hawaiian Music.

subgenres.name: Techno kayō
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of 1980s Kayōkyoku and Idol kayō incorporating characteristics from Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Korean Ballad
subgenres.desc: South Korean Pop from the 1980s to the early 90s taking influence from western Blues, Synthpop, Soul and Contemporary Folk.

subgenres.name: Oriental Ballad
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s in South Korea, taking influence from more traditional forms of Korean Music.

subgenres.name: K-Pop
subgenres.desc: Contemporary style from South Korea, based on multiple mainstream influences such as Contemporary R&B, Dance-Pop, and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Semi-Trot
subgenres.desc: Contemporary form of Trot which takes influences from modern K-Pop and recent Pop substyles.

subgenres.name: Latin Pop
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements and tropes from Hispanic and Latin American forms of music into a commercial Pop context.

subgenres.name: Cumbia pop
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Río de la Plata region in the mid-2010s, featuring Latin Pop influences and lyrics related to romance, youth, and fun.

subgenres.name: Tropipop
subgenres.desc: Subgenre of Colombian origin fusing Vallenato instrumentation into a Latin Pop context.

subgenres.name: Lokal musik
subgenres.desc: Created by local, rural artists from Papua New Guinea that incorporate some elements of Papuan Folk Music into Pop.

subgenres.name: Mulatós
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, danceable Hungarian Pop that takes strong influence from Hungarian Folk Music and Romani Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Nederpop
subgenres.desc: Dutch language Pop which originally arose in the 1970s to describe the style of the 1950s and 1960s, but would also later be used for 1980s artists who incorporated elements of Ska and Reggae.

subgenres.name: Palingsound
subgenres.desc: Originating from Volendam in the Netherlands; harmonizing vocals and orchestrated arrangements.

subgenres.name: New Music
subgenres.desc: Developed when Japanese Singer-Songwriters incorporated elements of Contemporary Folk and Pop Rock with Kayōkyoku songwriting.

subgenres.name: OPM
subgenres.desc: Filipino ballads prominent in the 1970s to early 1980s, combining the sentimentality, lush arrangements and vocal techniques of Kundiman with the instrumentations and rhythms of Manila Sound and Soft Rock.

subgenres.name: Orthodox Pop
subgenres.desc: Combines Orthodox Jewish themes and prayer with Pop songwriting, usually sung in Hebrew.

subgenres.name: Persian Pop
subgenres.desc: Hybrid of Iranian and Persian-language popular music with Western instruments such as the guitar, drum kit, and synthesizer.

subgenres.name: Pop Batak
subgenres.desc: Combines Western genres of music and instrumentation with a typical Batak flair, like lyrics about Batak life and the use of some traditional Batak instruments.

subgenres.name: Pop Ghazal
subgenres.desc: Employs traditional Ghazal's verse, meter, and poetic inclinations in a pop form.

subgenres.name: Pop Minang
subgenres.desc: Combines Minangkabau traditions with Pop structures and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Talempong goyang
subgenres.desc: Blends traditional Talempong elements with contemporary Pop influences, often featuring a female vocalist, and encourages audience participation.

subgenres.name: Pop Raï
subgenres.desc: Fuses melodic sensibilities into the traditional Raï structure, with increased utilization of synthesizers, guitars, and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Pop Reggae
subgenres.desc: Light, commercial form of Reggae designed to crossover and break through to a more mainstream Pop audience.

subgenres.name: Pop Rock
subgenres.desc: Fuses conventional verse-chorus song structure and especially melodic songwriting with usage of guitars, drums, and propulsive rhythms.

subgenres.name: Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1960s in the United Kingdom, drawing on Rock & Roll and the late 1950s Skiffle revival in a simple guitar-band format with strong melodies.

subgenres.name: Freakbeat
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of the Mod movement which combines elements of British Rhythm & Blues and Beat with studio effects common in Psychedelia such as fuzztones, flanging and chorus; often seen as a British relative of the American Garage Psych scene.

subgenres.name: Group Sounds
subgenres.desc: Japanese bands in the mid-to-late 1960s who began performing a style of Beat primarily in English.

subgenres.name: Jovem Guarda
subgenres.desc: 1960s Brazilian youth-oriented Pop Rock, with romantic lyrics and influenced by Merseybeat and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: Merseybeat
subgenres.desc: Light, highly melodic style of Beat popular in the UK during the early 1960s, named due to the abundance of bands from Liverpool beside the River Mersey.

subgenres.name: Nederbeat
subgenres.desc: Dutch answer to the British Beat boom of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Beat Rock
subgenres.desc: Japan-exclusive subgenre which combines Pop melodicism with a punchy, driving sound drawing on Punk Rock and New Wave.

subgenres.name: Big Music
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Post-Punk and popular in the 1980s, with anthemic songwriting and a grandiose, stadium-ready sound.

subgenres.name: Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United Kingdom in the early 1990s, with a style hearkening back to the traditional guitar-driven songs and melodic hooks found in the British Pop Rock of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Jangle Pop
subgenres.desc: Treble-heavy guitars with arpeggiated melodies, distinct basslines, and often propulsive, repetitive strum-rhythms; frequently influenced by Post-Punk.

subgenres.name: C86
subgenres.desc: Distinctly ramshackle, often Twee Pop-infused combination of British Indie Rock and Jangle Pop.

subgenres.name: Dolewave
subgenres.desc: Loose, low-key, and sardonic with erudite lyrics and considerable influence from the Dunedin Sound and Slacker Rock; came to prominence in Melbourne in the early 2010s.

subgenres.name: Neo-Acoustic
subgenres.desc: Cross-section of Indie Pop and Jangle Pop with more prominent acoustic instrumentation and songwriting/arrangements that draw from Sophisti-Pop.

subgenres.name: Paisley Underground
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Los Angeles in the early 1980s, featuring the energy of Power Pop and New Wave adorned with retro Psychedelia.

subgenres.name: Neon Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Scene culture; combines the upbeat tempos and catchy melodies of Pop Punk and Power Pop with synthesizers, auto-tuned vocals, or Dance beats, emphasizing a distinctly polished, hook-oriented sound.

subgenres.name: Piano Rock
subgenres.desc: Primarily based around piano riffs and melodies, rather than having guitar as the focal instrument.

subgenres.name: Pop Yeh-Yeh
subgenres.desc: Blends Western Beat and Psychedelia styles with asli singing and melodies drawn from Malay Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Post-Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s as a Britpop expansion mainly characterized by acoustic-leaning instrumentation, lush string arrangements, and mid-tempo song structures, as well as less apparent lyrical concerns for Britain in favor of introspective, contemplative themes.

subgenres.name: Power Pop
subgenres.desc: Combines 1960s Pop melodies with loud power chords; characterized by prominent, sometimes jangly electric guitars, clear vocals, crisp harmonies, and economical arrangements.

subgenres.name: Soft Rock
subgenres.desc: Clean production and light instrumentation paired with harmonious, radio-friendly songwriting; gained huge commercial success in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Tropical Rock
subgenres.desc: Combines influences from Country Rock and Caribbean Music to create an acoustic and breezy "island" themed sound.

subgenres.name: Yacht Rock
subgenres.desc: Slick Pop Rock influenced by smoother R&B styles, popular in the late 1970s and often associated with California.

subgenres.name: Stereo
subgenres.desc: Burmese Pop Rock genre which emerged in the mid-1960s.

subgenres.name: Twee Pop
subgenres.desc: Distinct Post-Punk background and often jangling guitars, defined by a cute aesthetic and lyrics combined with an indie/DIY attitude and a simplicity often indebted to Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Cuddlecore
subgenres.desc: Rawer and more Punk informed, downplaying jangly guitars in favor of heavier yet still light-hearted tones; often features influence from the contemporary Riot Grrrl movement.

subgenres.name: Vocal Surf
subgenres.desc: Appropriates the sounds of instrumental Surf Rock, combining surfing- and car-themed lyrics with a style that draws primarily from Doo-Wop and Rock & Roll.

subgenres.name: Pop Soul
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Pop and Soul; originated in the 1960s as an attempt to give soul crossover success.

subgenres.name: Motown Sound
subgenres.desc: Succinct, catchy song structures; complex arrangements; Gospel-influenced vocals; highly melodic and rhythmic bass lines; 4-4 drum patterns; often syncopated piano parts; regular use of horn and string sections; and historically a distinctive reverb and treble-heavy production.

subgenres.name: Pop Sunda
subgenres.desc: Mixes Sundanese traditions with Pop structures and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: P-Pop
subgenres.desc: Commercialized style from the Philippines, which served as the successor of Manila Sound and OPM, featuring various contemporary Western influences and primarily sung in Tagalog and English.

subgenres.name: Progressive Pop
subgenres.desc: Milder counterpart to Progressive Rock, emerging in the late 1960s and introducing complex songwriting and arrangements into a Pop context.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Pop
subgenres.desc: Combines unconventional instrumentation with studio effects to create a psychedelic atmosphere within melodic Pop music.

subgenres.name: Rabiz
subgenres.desc: Elements of Armenian folk in its instrumentation, oftentimes incorporating influences from Arabic and other West Asian forms on a background of synthesizer arrangements.

subgenres.name: Rigsar
subgenres.desc: Dominant form of popular music in Bhutan which broke traditions to move towards a more Western and Indian approach.

subgenres.name: Rumba catalana
subgenres.desc: Cheerful Catalan genre that takes influences from Rumba cubana, Andalusian Rumba flamenca, and Pop.

subgenres.name: Russian Chanson
subgenres.desc: Divided into lyrical and criminal chanson, it is best described as narrative-driven popular music inspired by crime and prison.

subgenres.name: Schlager
subgenres.desc: Light, sentimental, melodic pop music common mainly in northern and central Europe.

subgenres.name: Humppa
subgenres.desc: Finnish music related to Jazz and the Foxtrot.

subgenres.name: Levenslied
subgenres.desc: Dutch genre that enjoyed widespread popularity in the pre-Rock & Roll era. with simple melody and rhythm and lyrics composed of couplets and refrains.

subgenres.name: Volkstümliche Musik
subgenres.desc: Light Pop with borrowings from German Folk Music (volksmusik), often misleadingly labeled as being volksmusik.

subgenres.name: Sertanejo romântico
subgenres.desc: Electric instrumentation and romantic lyrics, made popular nationwide during the mid-to-late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Sertanejo universitário
subgenres.desc: Modernized style combining rural themes and acoustic instrumentation with commercial production and Electronic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Agronejo
subgenres.desc: Early 2020s movement characterized by lyrical content with heavy agribusiness imagery, often featuring several Dance genres' sonic elements.

subgenres.name: Arrocha sertanejo
subgenres.desc: Merged the Arrocha style with the younger audience creating a more energetic and more danceable rhythm.

subgenres.name: Funknejo
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the rhythms, production, and idioms of Funk brasileiro into the universitário genre.

subgenres.name: Sophisti-Pop
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from Jazz, classic R&B and Soul along with a slick, polished production style while retaining elements from its New Wave roots.

subgenres.name: Soviet Estrada
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the USSR during the early 1930s, and encompassed the dominating popular music style composed by government-approved songwriters and the primary repertoire of professionally trained performers.

subgenres.name: Sunshine Pop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1960s, characterized by a cheerful or wistful sound, light, lush production, and prominent vocal harmonies.

subgenres.name: Synthpop
subgenres.desc: Led by melodic synthesizer sounds, often with reverberating drum machine patterns; commonly associated with the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Futurepop
subgenres.desc: Derivative of EBM, retaining its apocalyptic worldview but incorporating heavy influence from the melodic style of Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Pon-chak disco
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by Electro-Disco, featuring cheap "electronic organ" synth leads and minimalistic, repetitive rhythms.

subgenres.name: Techno kayō
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of 1980s Kayōkyoku and Idol kayō incorporating characteristics from Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Tarz
subgenres.desc: Popular music from Afghanistan that combines various ethnic and regional traditions with influences from Indian, Persian, and Western popular music.

subgenres.name: Teen Pop
subgenres.desc: Oriented to teen audiences and almost always sung by teens.

subgenres.name: Toytown Pop
subgenres.desc: Niche offshoot of British Psychedelic Pop most popular in the late 1960s and early 70s; typically featuring strong influence from Music Hall and Novelty, as well as the culture of Victorian and Edwardian Britain, and characterised by a whimsical, childlike atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Traditional Pop
subgenres.desc: Predominant form of Western commercial popular music in the pre-Rock & Roll era, particularly in the USA and starting with Tin Pan Alley; typically vocal-oriented with an orchestral arrangement.

subgenres.name: British Dance Band
subgenres.desc: Came from the dancehalls of the 1920s and 1930s, combining a British take on Jazz with the Music Hall tradition.

subgenres.name: Mood kayō
subgenres.desc: Early form of Kayōkyoku dominant in the 1950s and 1960s, prominently influenced by American Jazz, Hispanic American Music, and Hawaiian Music.

subgenres.name: Romanţe
subgenres.desc: Expressive and poetic Romanian style, generally sung similar to a Chanson and composed for piano and guitar orchestral arrangements.

subgenres.name: Standards
subgenres.desc: Traditional compositions originating from the 1910s and onward which have become widely known, performed, and recorded across the world.

subgenres.name: Tin Pan Alley
subgenres.desc: Early era of popular song in the USA, broadly from the 1890s-1930s; influences include Ragtime, Vaudeville, and Parlour Music.

subgenres.name: Turkish Pop
subgenres.desc: Started in the late 1950s, when Turkish artists started to write their own lyrics to Western popular tunes.

subgenres.name: Vocal Trance
subgenres.desc: Melodic, polished, Pop-like, and vocal-focused with around 120-145 BPM and frequent overlap with Progressive Trance, Uplifting Trance, and Euro Trance.

subgenres.name: Yé-yé
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, trendy Pop that emerged in Southern Europe in the early 1960s, focusing on image and risqué lyrics.

name: Psychedelia
desc: Umbrella of styles intended to replicate or enhance the altered state of consciousness brought on by the use of psychedelic drugs, originating in the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Neo-Psychedelia
subgenres.desc: Developments in Psychedelia since the early 1980s, building on the drug-inspired styles developed in the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Baggy
subgenres.desc: Blends Dance and Funk-based grooves with a laid-back, psychedelic atmosphere; features jangly guitars, looping basslines, four-bar drum patterns, and a hypnotic, carefree feel rooted in the Madchester scene of the late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Dream Pop
subgenres.desc: Reverberated guitars, effects-laden vocals, and dense productions, creating a psychedelic, spacious, and dreamlike sound.

subgenres.name: Hypnagogic Pop
subgenres.desc: 21st century style that refracts the pop culture of past decades through surreal, low-fidelity production and emulation of outdated media formats or equipment.

subgenres.name: Paisley Underground
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Los Angeles in the early 1980s, featuring the energy of Power Pop and New Wave adorned with retro Psychedelia.

subgenres.name: Space Rock Revival
subgenres.desc: Draws from the aesthetics and atmospheric soundscapes of Space Rock combined with the more minimal, back-to-basics approach of the Post-Punk era.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Folk
subgenres.desc: Acoustic forms that capture an atmosphere that is at turns dream-like, 'spaced-out', whimsical, haunting, mystical, and melancholic.

subgenres.name: Freak Folk
subgenres.desc: Loosely defined 2000s Psychedelic Folk revival closely associated with the New Weird America movement, sometimes also a shorthand for certain leftfield styles of psychedelic and Indie Folk.

subgenres.name: Free Folk
subgenres.desc: Incorporates improvisation, repetition and extended song lengths.

subgenres.name: Udigrudi
subgenres.desc: Movement that emerged in the Brazilian city of Recife during the 1970s that combines psychedelic elements with music of Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Wyrd Folk
subgenres.desc: Closely tied to mysticism, old folk beliefs, and Folk Horror; often described as 'witchy' or 'pagan.'

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Pop
subgenres.desc: Combines unconventional instrumentation with studio effects to create a psychedelic atmosphere within melodic Pop music.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Rock
subgenres.desc: Often attempts to emulate or enhance the effects of psychedelic drugs, typically through a variety of instrumental and studio effects or eclectic influences.

subgenres.name: Acid Rock
subgenres.desc: Heavier with an emphasis on instrumental jamming and "wah" guitar effects.

subgenres.name: Freakbeat
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of the Mod movement which combines elements of British Rhythm & Blues and Beat with studio effects common in Psychedelia such as fuzztones, flanging and chorus; often seen as a British relative of the American Garage Psych scene.

subgenres.name: Garage Psych
subgenres.desc: Emerged from mid-1960s US Garage Rock; characterised by fuzz guitars, cheap organs, experimentation with psychedelic effects and surreal lyricism, and a retained emphasis on raw energy and the pop song format.

subgenres.name: Heavy Psych
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Blues Rock's heavy dependence on riffs and improvisatory leanings; features thick, fuzzy guitars, usually slow-to-mid tempos, and extended soloing sections.

subgenres.name: Raga Rock
subgenres.desc: Influenced by South Asian Music, featuring a droning compositional quality and commonly incorporating instruments like sitar, tambura, and tablas.

subgenres.name: Space Rock
subgenres.desc: Heavy use of synthesizers and guitar effects to create dense atmospheric soundscapes intended to evoke images of outer space and science fiction scenarios.

subgenres.name: Space Rock Revival
subgenres.desc: Draws from the aesthetics and atmospheric soundscapes of Space Rock combined with the more minimal, back-to-basics approach of the Post-Punk era.

subgenres.name: Xian Psych
subgenres.desc: Portrays Christian and biblical themes through a surreal, transcendent atmosphere, occasionally drawing influence from Christian Liturgical Music.

subgenres.name: Zamrock
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Copperbelt region of Zambia in the 1970s, characterized by its blend of local sounds with influence from Funk, Hard Rock, and Blues Rock.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Soul
subgenres.desc: Soul which incorporates the effects and instrumentation of Psychedelic Rock.

subgenres.name: Psychsploitation
subgenres.desc: Short-lived genre seeking to capitalise on the popularity of Psychedelia in the 1960s, featuring quickly and cheaply recorded material played by session musicians and put out by budget labels.

subgenres.name: Sitarsploitation
subgenres.desc: Variant of Exotica capitalising on the surge of Western interest in Indian music in the late 1960s; featured melodies played on the sitar (or instruments imitating it) atop Easy Listening accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Stoner Metal
subgenres.desc: Combines elements of Doom Metal with elements of Psychedelic Rock and Blues Rock to create a melodic yet heavy sound.

subgenres.name: Stoner Rock
subgenres.desc: Psychedelic timbres, raw production, and stylistic influence from Doom Metal and Heavy Psych.

subgenres.name: Tropicália
subgenres.desc: Blends Brazilian popular styles with the influence of Anglo-American Psychedelia; emerged as part of Brazil's late-1960s counterculture.

name: Punk
desc: Musical and cultural product of Punk Rock known for its simplistic, brash playstyle and anti-establishment themes.

subgenres.name: Art Punk
subgenres.desc: Combines the stripped-down aggression of rudimentary Punk Rock with frequent experimentation ranging from instrumental interplay, noise, dissonance, and/or influences from other genres such as Jazz or Funk.

subgenres.name: Egg Punk
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s; features lo-fi production, eccentric lyrics, quick tempos, nasally vocals, and cheap keyboard sounds.

subgenres.name: Cowpunk
subgenres.desc: Mixes together Country Rock, Rockabilly, and Contemporary Folk with the familiar punk sound.

subgenres.name: Digital Hardcore
subgenres.desc: High-tempo fusion of Hardcore Punk and Electronic, combining harsh vocals and electric guitars of the former with electronic instruments.

subgenres.name: Emo
subgenres.desc: Focuses on emotional lyrics, expressive vocals, melodic songwriting, and dynamic song structures.

subgenres.name: Emocore
subgenres.desc: Emerged primarily in Washington D.C. in 1985 as a reaction to the stagnant Hardcore Punk scene, with a less aggressive style that was more melodic and often featured emotional, introspective lyrics.

subgenres.name: Emo-Pop
subgenres.desc: Mainstream derivative of Emo, puts more emphasis on the poppy sensibilities of Alternative Rock and Pop Punk.

subgenres.name: Mall Screamo
subgenres.desc: Heavy instrumentation, melodic verse-chorus songwriting, and expressive singing contrasted with screaming vocals.

subgenres.name: Midwest Emo
subgenres.desc: Characterized by shifts between loud and soft dynamics, off-key, strained and emotional vocals, sometimes with intricate instrumental arrangements and layered arpeggiated guitar parts.

subgenres.name: Screamo
subgenres.desc: Intense, aggressive and complex approach to Emo featuring higher levels of abrasiveness and dissonance, accompanied by guitar-focused melodicism and harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Emoviolence
subgenres.desc: Shorter length and volatile song structures, while borrowing techniques from Powerviolence such as blast beats, unconventional screaming and noisier sounds.

subgenres.name: Folk Punk
subgenres.desc: Influenced by various forms of Folk, including Traditional Folk Music as well as Contemporary Folk and Folk Rock.

subgenres.name: Celtic Punk
subgenres.desc: Infuses the sounds of Celtic Folk Music into Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Gypsy Punk
subgenres.desc: Strong Eastern European influences, especially various kinds of Romani Folk Music and Balkan Folk Music as well as Klezmer.

subgenres.name: Hardcore [Punk]
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the first wave of Hardcore Punk beginning in the 1970s, as well as its derivative styles that incorporate diverse musical influences and stray away from the core Punk Rock sound.

subgenres.name: Beatdown Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Heavy, urban-inspired and breakdown-oriented with strong relations to Metalcore.

subgenres.name: Electronicore
subgenres.desc: Hybrid of Metalcore and/or Post-Hardcore with various Electronic Dance Music styles, utilizing Electronic instrumentation and occasional Dance beats.

subgenres.name: Grindcore
subgenres.desc: Brief and intense song structures featuring a plethora of blast beats, down-tuned and tremolo-picked guitars, and abrasive, usually raw production.

subgenres.name: Cybergrind
subgenres.desc: Standard conventions of Grindcore taken to an even more discordant and rapid-fire extreme, with added Electronic dimensions of computer-generated noises and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Deathgrind
subgenres.desc: Combines the intensity and high-pitched screams of Grindcore with the technicality and low guttural vocals of Death Metal.

subgenres.name: Goregrind
subgenres.desc: Death Metal-influenced riffs with rhythms ranging from very fast to slower mid-tempos correlated with pitch-shifted vocals, sloppy playing and production, and gore-themed aesthetics.

subgenres.name: Gorenoise
subgenres.desc: Combines and subverts Goregrind and Grindcore with brash Noise and even faster drum tempos.

subgenres.name: Pornogrind
subgenres.desc: Groovy, mid-tempo style known for its exaggerated bouncy rhythm and common pornographic themes.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Noisegrind
subgenres.desc: Noise-driven, defined by its rawness, feedback usage, and very brief song structures.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s, often featuring extensive use of yelling or screaming, a stripped-down production style, and very short songs.

subgenres.name: Burning Spirits
subgenres.desc: Emphasis on delivering a very energetic and triumphant sound with flashy and soaring Metal solos, "melodramatic" or "uplifting" chord progressions, and singalong, over the top, harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Crossover Thrash
subgenres.desc: Mixes the metallic instrumentation of Thrash Metal with the ethos and approach of Hardcore Punk.

subgenres.name: Crust Punk
subgenres.desc: Metallic outgrowth of Anarcho-Punk featuring a down-tuned, high-gain guitar sound, frequent D-Beat drum patterns, guttural vocals, and politically-charged lyrics often featuring apocalyptic imagery.

subgenres.name: Blackened Crust
subgenres.desc: Borrows heavily from Black Metal production, blast beats, tremolo guitar, and vocals, while retaining the core Crust Punk sound, lyrical themes, and aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Neocrust
subgenres.desc: Melodic, dark, and atmospheric style that often incorporates influences from Sludge Metal, Post-Metal, Black Metal, and Screamo.

subgenres.name: Stenchcore
subgenres.desc: Heavier, more metallic form of Crust Punk drawing influence from Thrash Metal as well as Death Metal and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: D-Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1980s, features Metal influences, shouted vocals, and a distinct drum style known as the D-beat.

subgenres.name: Melodic Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the USA in the early to mid-1980s, placing emphasis on melodic vocals and technical guitar riffs rather than raw aggression.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

subgenres.name: Street Punk
subgenres.desc: Driven by Oi! style group vocals, catchy melodies, and aggressive songwriting akin to Punk Rock of the 1970s fused with Hardcore Punk of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Thrashcore
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, brief song structures, and the occasional use of blast beats.

subgenres.name: Powerviolence
subgenres.desc: Originated from the West Coast California Hardcore Punk scene in the late 1980s, utilizing strong elements of Noise Rock and abrupt tempo changes.

subgenres.name: Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Drop-tuned guitar riffs, constant double kick drumming with varying tempos and techniques, breakdown sections, and screaming or shouting vocals.

subgenres.name: Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Integrates brutal palm-muted and tremolo-picked riffing, blast beat-focused drumming, and guttural vocals of Death Metal with groovy breakdown sections.

subgenres.name: Downtempo Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimal songs emphasizing breakdowns, atmosphere, and dissonance with downtuned guitars.

subgenres.name: Mathcore
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically complex, featuring unconventional time signatures, syncopated and dissonant riffs and erratic metric shifts.

subgenres.name: Melodic Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Originated in the late 1990s when some metalcore bands infused elements of Melodic Death Metal into their sound to create a more metallic and melodic style.

subgenres.name: Thall
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rapid release bends and a precise playstyle while contrasting pitch-shifted high and low notes, with ambient sections for atmosphere and buildup.

subgenres.name: Nintendocore
subgenres.desc: Fuses Post-Hardcore and Metalcore influences with Chiptune instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Noisecore
subgenres.desc: Short blasts of riff-less, Noise-driven music accompanied with chaotic drums and screamed vocals.

subgenres.name: Post-Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s from Hardcore Punk that expanded on its aggression and dynamics through longer and more complex arrangements.

subgenres.name: Emocore
subgenres.desc: Emerged primarily in Washington D.C. in 1985 as a reaction to the stagnant Hardcore Punk scene, with a less aggressive style that was more melodic and often featured emotional, introspective lyrics.

subgenres.name: Mall Screamo
subgenres.desc: Heavy instrumentation, melodic verse-chorus songwriting, and expressive singing contrasted with screaming vocals.

subgenres.name: Screamo
subgenres.desc: Intense, aggressive and complex approach to Emo featuring higher levels of abrasiveness and dissonance, accompanied by guitar-focused melodicism and harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Emoviolence
subgenres.desc: Shorter length and volatile song structures, while borrowing techniques from Powerviolence such as blast beats, unconventional screaming and noisier sounds.

subgenres.name: Swancore
subgenres.desc: High-register clean vocals and technical instrumentation drawn from Math Rock and Progressive Rock.

subgenres.name: Sass
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Post-Hardcore in the early 2000s; characterized by sassy vocal styles and chaotic, erratic instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Mod Revival
subgenres.desc: Late 1970s and early 1980s revival of Mod fashion and music, featuring influence from the nascent Punk Rock scene.

subgenres.name: Pigfuck
subgenres.desc: Sloppy, abrasive and feedback-laden riffing with vulgar and edgy lyricism, informed by Post-Hardcore's aggression and Post-Punk's rhythm section.

subgenres.name: Post-Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged alongside the initial Punk Rock explosion in the mid-to-late 1970s, putting a greater emphasis on experimentation and atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Coldwave
subgenres.desc: Originated in Europe in the late 1970s and early 1980s and is known for its generally dark, gloomy atmosphere and heavy reliance on synthesizers.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk
subgenres.desc: Mixes the energy of Punk Rock with the danceable rhythms of Funk and Disco.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Punchy and danceable variant of Post-Punk Revival that features Electronic instrumentation and influence from Alternative Dance.

subgenres.name: Gothic Rock
subgenres.desc: Combines drama and a dark atmosphere with effects-laden guitars, prominent basslines, propulsive drums, and occasional keyboards and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Deathrock
subgenres.desc: More Punk-oriented offshoot of Gothic Rock that emphasizes energy and an effect-laden sound over pure atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Positive Punk
subgenres.desc: Early goth scene in London that grew out of the Anarcho-Punk movement and promoted themes of virtue and mysticism; commonly features wailing vocals, screeching guitars, prominent basslines, and eclectic drum patterns.

subgenres.name: Post-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Incorporating the sounds and aesthetics of Post-Punk into Indie Rock, with jagged guitarwork, a dominant and danceable rhythm section, clean production, and poppy song structures.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Punchy and danceable variant of Post-Punk Revival that features Electronic instrumentation and influence from Alternative Dance.

subgenres.name: Proto-Punk
subgenres.desc: Used to describe what influenced or in some way resembled Punk Rock before that genre's commercial breakthrough in 1976.

subgenres.name: Punk Blues
subgenres.desc: Fusion of the instrumentation and scales of Blues Rock with Punk.

subgenres.name: Punk Poetry
subgenres.desc: Fast and rhythmic vocal delivery of political or satirical themes; frequently backed by Post-Punk or Minimal Wave instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Punk Rock
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, loud and distorted riffs, simple songs, frequent use of power chords, and shouted vocals, originating in the mid-1970s in response to commercial, sentimental, and complex Rock.

subgenres.name: Anarcho-Punk
subgenres.desc: Intentionally rougher and sloppier sound, with lyrics pertaining to anarchist ideology and sociopolitical injustices.

subgenres.name: Celtic Punk
subgenres.desc: Infuses the sounds of Celtic Folk Music into Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Deathrock
subgenres.desc: More Punk-oriented offshoot of Gothic Rock that emphasizes energy and an effect-laden sound over pure atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Deutschpunk
subgenres.desc: Partly a reaction to the commercialization of the German movement Neue Deutsche Welle; characterized by extreme speed, consciously basic songwriting, crude musicianship, and radical leftism.

subgenres.name: Egg Punk
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s; features lo-fi production, eccentric lyrics, quick tempos, nasally vocals, and cheap keyboard sounds.

subgenres.name: Garage Punk
subgenres.desc: Combination of the raw fuzztones of the original Garage Rock bands of the 1960s with the tempo and attitude of Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Glam Punk
subgenres.desc: Contrasts a snotty, nihilistic, and combative attitude of punk with theatrics and flamboyance.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Punk

subgenres.desc: Mixes the metallic instrumentation of Thrash Metal with the ethos and approach of Hardcore Punk.

subgenres.name: Stenchcore
subgenres.desc: Heavier, more metallic form of Crust Punk drawing influence from Thrash Metal as well as Death Metal and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: D-Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1980s, features Metal influences, shouted vocals, and a distinct drum style known as the D-beat.

subgenres.name: Melodic Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the USA in the early to mid-1980s, placing emphasis on melodic vocals and technical guitar riffs rather than raw aggression.

subgenres.name: Powerviolence
subgenres.desc: Originated from the West Coast California Hardcore Punk scene in the late 1980s, utilizing strong elements of Noise Rock and abrupt tempo changes.

subgenres.name: Horror Punk
subgenres.desc: Thematically and lyrically derived from Horror movies, typically with a nostalgic and campy attitude.

subgenres.name: Könsrock
subgenres.desc: Inspired by Post-Punk but with a more bizarre atmosphere with unusual or comic vocal techniques and a lyrical focus on the offensive and scatological.

subgenres.name: Oi!
subgenres.desc: Rejection of perceived intellectualism and elitism in Post-Punk and Art Punk, characterized by a return to a straightforward, melodic Punk Rock sound, sing-along choruses, and a lyrical focus on working class youth culture.

subgenres.name: Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Blends the loud, fast-paced sound of Punk Rock with the melodic hooks of Pop.

subgenres.name: Easycore
subgenres.desc: Combines the radio-friendly stylings of second-wave Pop Punk with Metalcore-inspired breakdowns, lower guitar tunings, and occasional unclean vocals.

subgenres.name: Neon Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Scene culture; combines the upbeat tempos and catchy melodies of Pop Punk and Power Pop with synthesizers, auto-tuned vocals, or Dance beats, emphasizing a distinctly polished, hook-oriented sound.

subgenres.name: Seishun Punk
subgenres.desc: Short-lived Japanese style popular in the early 2000s, characterized by a raw and abrasive style, Folk-inspired songwriting, and youth-oriented straightforward lyrics.

subgenres.name: Positive Punk
subgenres.desc: Early goth scene in London that grew out of the Anarcho-Punk movement and promoted themes of virtue and mysticism; commonly features wailing vocals, screeching guitars, prominent basslines, and eclectic drum patterns.

subgenres.name: Psychobilly
subgenres.desc: Cross-pollination of Punk Rock and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: Ska Punk
subgenres.desc: Utilizes skank rhythms, walking basslines, and often horn instrumentation in combination with a fast-paced Punk Rock playstyle.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

subgenres.name: Skate Punk
subgenres.desc: Combines the speed of Melodic Hardcore with the catchiness of Pop Punk, finding a middle ground between the two.

subgenres.name: Surf Punk
subgenres.desc: Punk Rock that incorporates elements of Surf Rock.

subgenres.name: Vikingarock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from Nordic Folk Music and the imagery of Viking romanticism and Norse mythology.

subgenres.name: Synth Punk
subgenres.desc: Appropriates the harsh elements of Punk Rock but replaces the predominance of guitars with synthesizers and drum machines.

name: R&B
desc: Umbrella of styles covering the most popular forms of Black American music from the late 1940s, when the term Rhythm & Blues first appeared; includes the developments of Soul and Funk in the '60s and '70s, and the Contemporary R&B of the 1980s onward.

subgenres.name: Acid Jazz
subgenres.desc: Eclectic scene consisting of influences from Jazz, Funk, Hip Hop, Soul, and various styles of Dance that gained popularity during the 1990s.

subgenres.name: Beach Music
subgenres.desc: Danceable 4/4 "blues shuffle" rhythmic structure, vocal harmonies, and moderate tempos.

subgenres.name: Blue-Eyed Soul
subgenres.desc: Usually refers to a Pop or Pop Rock song that contains strong Gospel-like elements, primarily popularized by white American and British singers in the 1960s through the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Boogie
subgenres.desc: Continuation of the Disco sound with increased influence from Funk, Synth Funk, and R&B and a slower tempo, often featuring drum machines and filter modulated synthesizers.

subgenres.name: Contemporary R&B
subgenres.desc: Soulful, passionate and melismatic vocals originally derived from popular Soul and Disco, as well as smooth, lush and often synthesized production variously influenced by Hip Hop, Funk, and related strands of Pop.

subgenres.name: Alternative R&B
subgenres.desc: Deviating from the traditional styles of Contemporary R&B and featuring smooth, reverberated, Electronic-influenced production with heavy bass and often reverberated vocals.

subgenres.name: Hip Hop Soul
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop-oriented style that evolved out of New Jack Swing in the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: New Jack Swing
subgenres.desc: Mixes light Hip Hop & Funk production techniques with Contemporary R&B vocals and melodies as well as swinging and danceable drum grooves.

subgenres.name: Trap Soul
subgenres.desc: Mixes passionate vocals derived from Contemporary R&B with laid-back, nocturnal and atmospheric Trap production.

subgenres.name: UK Street Soul
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1980s and early 1990s; combines raw basslines and breakbeats with Contemporary R&B/Soul vocals.

subgenres.name: Doo-Wop
subgenres.desc: Heavy emphasis on male four-part harmonies and light instrumentation; peaked in popularity in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Funk
subgenres.desc: Danceable, syncopated grooves carried by bass and drums alongside percussive guitar, keyboard, and/or horn parts, with rhythmic emphasis on the downbeat.

subgenres.name: Afro-Funk
subgenres.desc: Strongly mixed with traditional and more modern genres in sub-Saharan West Africa.

subgenres.name: Britfunk
subgenres.desc: Energetic, up-tempo style born out of late-1970s British Jazz-Funk nightclubs.

subgenres.name: Deep Funk
subgenres.desc: Focuses more on grooves and rhythm than songwriting.

subgenres.name: Go-Go
subgenres.desc: Dominated by drums and percussion (primarily congas) with heavily syncopated rhythms, bursts of horns, and call-and-response vocals.

subgenres.name: Bounce Beat
subgenres.desc: Modernized, youth oriented form heavily utilizing rototoms, timbale and keyboards for grooves.

subgenres.name: Jazz-Funk
subgenres.desc: Jazz highly influenced by Funk.

subgenres.name: Latin Funk
subgenres.desc: Funk combined with Hispanic American Music styles.

subgenres.name: P-Funk
subgenres.desc: Features a "fat", monotonic drum sound, spaced-out synthesizers, "squelchy" basslines, tight, syncopated horns, and sometimes heavy guitars.

subgenres.name: Porn Groove
subgenres.desc: Primarily found in the soundtracks to Pornographic films of the 1970s; characterized by a wah-wah electric guitar sound, slapped basslines, and minimal drums.

subgenres.name: Synth Funk
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down and futuristic, driven by synthesizer melodies and often incorporating drum machines.

subgenres.name: Minneapolis Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in late 1970s Minneapolis, characterized by glossy Contemporary R&B-influenced production techniques, angular New Wave-inspired rhythms, and a larger emphasis on electric guitar layers.

subgenres.name: New Orleans R&B
subgenres.desc: Increased rhythmic complexity with added focus on piano and horns.

subgenres.name: Rhythm & Blues
subgenres.desc: Predominantly African American style that retains the defined backbeats, Blues chord progressions/melodies and passionate singing/shouting of Jump Blues, while appealing more to an urban audience with smaller bands and reduced Jazz influence.

subgenres.name: British Rhythm & Blues
subgenres.desc: A style infusing Rock and R&B that was hugely popular in the United Kingdom between 1963 and 1966.

subgenres.name: Swamp Pop
subgenres.desc: Uniquely Cajun style of Rhythm & Blues distinguished by tripleted pianos and a slow Blues structure.

subgenres.name: Twist
subgenres.desc: Simple, fast, and energetic dance popular in the early 1960s.

subgenres.name: West Side Sound
subgenres.desc: Created in the 1950s by working-class Mexican-American teenagers in San Antonio, Texas, as a result of significant stylistic cross-pollination and an accommodating racial climate; features prominent tenor sax sections and Hammond organs.

subgenres.name: Soul
subgenres.desc: Originated in the African American culture of the 20th century, resulting from the combination of the ecstatic vocals of Gospel with the upbeat instrumentation of Rhythm & Blues, consisting of guitar, bass and percussion.

subgenres.name: Chicago Soul
subgenres.desc: Combination of the hard, groove-oriented rhythms of Southern Soul and the sophisticated gloss of the Motown Sound which was developed in Chicago.

subgenres.name: Country Soul
subgenres.desc: Combining the gritty horn-driven sound of Southern Soul with the textures and aesthetics of Country.

subgenres.name: Deep Soul
subgenres.desc: Draws on the typical Southern Soul groove and accentuates the Gospel and Blues influence, particularly Chicago Blues.

subgenres.name: Latin Soul
subgenres.desc: Soul combined with Hispanic American Music, such as Salsa and Mambo.

subgenres.name: Neo-Soul
subgenres.desc: Emerged during the mid-to-late 1990s; defined by a combination of Soul with the rhythmic percussion and groove of Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Philly Soul
subgenres.desc: Defined by lush arrangements, often borrowing upon the orchestral instrumentation seen on productions from the 1960s, with the commercial atmosphere exemplified by Pop Soul and the Motown Sound.

subgenres.name: Pop Soul
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Pop and Soul; originated in the 1960s as an attempt to give soul crossover success.

subgenres.name: Motown Sound
subgenres.desc: Succinct, catchy song structures; complex arrangements; Gospel-influenced vocals; highly melodic and rhythmic bass lines; 4-4 drum patterns; often syncopated piano parts; regular use of horn and string sections; and historically a distinctive reverb and treble-heavy production.

subgenres.name: Progressive Soul
subgenres.desc: Greater harmonic complexity, less conventional song structures, and conceptual, socially conscious or introspective lyrical themes, incorporating diverse influences and instrumentation from Jazz, Funk, Rock, and beyond.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Soul
subgenres.desc: Soul which incorporates the effects and instrumentation of Psychedelic Rock.

subgenres.name: Smooth Soul
subgenres.desc: Slow tempo ballads with silky, often sensual, vocals and light, polished arrangements, creating an intimate, romantic atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Southern Soul
subgenres.desc: Soul primarily from the American South that was popular in the 1960s and 1970s, with a gritty and raw sound that places an emphasis on the groove, making it highly danceable.

subgenres.name: Soul Blues
subgenres.desc: Shares similarities with Soul and incorporates the eponymous soulful inflections of Gospel, Jump Blues and soul into the vocals.

name: Reggae / Ska / Dancehall
desc: Umbrella for related forms of Jamaican Music which have grown beyond their regional roots to become global phenomena.

subgenres.name: Dancehall
subgenres.desc: Developed from Reggae in the late 1970s, when Roots Reggae became more stripped-down, with an increased emphasis on pure rhythm.

subgenres.name: Bubbling
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Netherlands in the late 1980s, fusing sped-up Dancehall with Dutch Antillean music and contemporary Dutch rave.

subgenres.name: Digital Dancehall
subgenres.desc: First, pre-Ragga style of Dancehall to popularize Electronic rhythms that arose in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Flex Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Largely instrumental; infused with Electronic Dance Music elements.

subgenres.name: Gommance
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Réunion, mixing Caribbean, African and Afro-Dutch influences.

subgenres.name: Ragga
subgenres.desc: Hardcore style with a deejay (equivalent to an MC in Hip Hop) rapping over predominantly Electronic rhythms.

subgenres.name: Shatta
subgenres.desc: French Caribbean Dancehall subgenre with a focus on sparse percussion, heavy basslines and lyrics revolving around partying and sensuality, often in Creole.

subgenres.name: Trap Dancehall
subgenres.desc: Combines midtempo Dancehall rhythms and tempos with major elements borrowed from Trap, namely in percussion and drum rhythms.

subgenres.name: Zess
subgenres.desc: Trinidadian style that originated in the country's slums in the late 2010s, defined by its sexual, violent, and occasionally gang-related lyrics and its influence from Soca, as well as occasional influences from Hip Hop and Funk brasileiro.

subgenres.name: Reggae
subgenres.desc: Developed in the 1960s; shuffling "bubble" and offbeat rhythms played on an organ, and staccato guitar and piano chords known as "skank."

subgenres.name: Deejay
subgenres.desc: Reggae in which a deejay (similar to an MC in Hip Hop) talks or chants lyrics over a pre-recorded reggae rhythm.

subgenres.name: Digital Dancehall
subgenres.desc: First, pre-Ragga style of Dancehall to popularize Electronic rhythms that arose in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Dub
subgenres.desc: Primarily instrumental Reggae which developed from the extensive use of studio techniques and effects like reverb and delay.

subgenres.name: Lovers Rock
subgenres.desc: Smooth, quiet Reggae beats with lyrics focusing on romance and love.

subgenres.name: Pacific Reggae
subgenres.desc: Developed in Pacific island communities, incorporating elements from local Oceanian Music styles.

subgenres.name: Jawaiian
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian branch of Reggae, typically blends local traditional melodies, harmonies, incorporating specialty instruments such as ukulele and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Pop Reggae
subgenres.desc: Light, commercial form of Reggae designed to crossover and break through to a more mainstream Pop audience.

subgenres.name: Roots Reggae
subgenres.desc: Primarily defined through the political, spiritual, and socially conscious messages of its lyrics.

subgenres.name: Dub Poetry
subgenres.desc: Poetry with Dub and Reggae backing rhythms, originating in Jamaica in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Seggae
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Séga and Reggae, popular on Mauritius and other Mascarene Islands.

subgenres.name: Skinhead Reggae
subgenres.desc: Early subgenre prominent from 1968 to 1971; known for its high tempos and driving rhythms compared with the more languid pace of most later styles.

subgenres.name: Rocksteady
subgenres.desc: Jamaican popular music that blossomed briefly between 1966 and 1968 as an evolution of Ska, being slower, more relaxed, and soulful.

subgenres.name: Ska
subgenres.desc: Originated in Jamaica in the late 1950s, characterized by a signature off-beat rhythm (referred to as the ‘skank’ rhythm), chop-style guitar work, busy bass lines and a use of horn sections.

subgenres.name: 2 Tone
subgenres.desc: Combines 1960s Jamaican Ska with Punk Rock and New Wave to create tracks played at faster tempos and with a harder edge than the original Jamaican records.

subgenres.name: Jamaican Ska
subgenres.desc: Originated in Jamaica with groups who combined Jazz and Rhythm & Blues with rhythms of traditional Caribbean Music like Mento and Calypso.

subgenres.name: New Tone
subgenres.desc: Musically and socio-politically progressive movement noted for combatting prejudices and mixing together different styles of music, such as Electronic, Hip Hop, or Emo.

subgenres.name: Spouge
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Calypso and Ska originating in Barbados during the 1960s and 70s.

subgenres.name: Third Wave Ska
subgenres.desc: Expanded on the 2 Tone period, adding further Rock elements resulting in a heavier sound.

subgenres.name: Ska Punk
subgenres.desc: Utilizes skank rhythms, walking basslines, and often horn instrumentation in combination with a fast-paced Punk Rock playstyle.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

name: Regional Music
desc: Music of regional cultural traditions, that is or was predominantly played and produced in these regions.

subgenres.name: African Music
subgenres.desc: All forms with roots in Africa.

subgenres.name: African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Indigenous music of Africa that is passed down orally from generation to generation, the authors of the songs are usually unknown.

subgenres.name: Ambasse bey
subgenres.desc: African Folk Music developed by the Yabassi people of Cameroon.

subgenres.name: Apala
subgenres.desc: Yoruba Music developed by Muslims during the late 1930s and early 1940s in the Ijebu region of Yorubaland, the current Ogun state.

subgenres.name: Batuque
subgenres.desc: Tradition from Cape Verde, unusual among the islands' music due to its lack of polyphonic singing and its usage of polyrhythms.

subgenres.name: Dagomba Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Dagomba people of northern Ghana.

subgenres.name: Gnawa
subgenres.desc: A mystical musical tradition centred around the qraqab castanets and guembri bass lute, named after its originators, the Afro-Maghrebi Gnawa people.

subgenres.name: Kabye Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kabye people of northern Togo, including some of the most singular styles that can be found in West Africa.

subgenres.name: Kilapanga
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Bakongo people from Angola and Congo that has influenced contemporary styles such as Kuduro.

subgenres.name: Malagasy Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Melodic, chordophone-dominated sound; based on the Austronesian Music of the first settlers that arrived on the island from Borneo.

subgenres.name: Mbenga-Mbuti Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Mbenga and Mbuti people, Pygmy ethnic groups in Central Africa.

subgenres.name: Moutya
subgenres.desc: Tradition that originated in Seychelles among Creole slaves, similar to Séga, although rawer and played only on large flat drums made from goatskin.

subgenres.name: Ngoma
subgenres.desc: Played in Swahili-speaking African countries; primarily focused on rhythm.

subgenres.name: Unyago
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Zanzibar, traditionally played at women's initiation rituals and weddings.

subgenres.name: Southern African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Afrikaner Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Musical traditions developed by the Afrikaner community in southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Khoisan Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses traditions of the Khoisan ethnic family groups.

subgenres.name: Nguni Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Nguni ethnic family groups, a southern Bantu ethnicity.

subgenres.name: Sotho-Tswana Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Sotho-Tswana ethnic family groups from southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Tchinkoumé
subgenres.desc: Tradition from the central region of Benin around Savalou, played with water percussion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Maloya
subgenres.desc: Derived from Traditional Séga, this is the original dance music of La Réunion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Séga
subgenres.desc: Séga dance music born in the 18th century, before its later adoption of Western pop elements.

subgenres.name: Zinli
subgenres.desc: Traditional rhythmic chanting and percussion adapted to multiple West African contexts in the 20th century.

subgenres.name: Afro-Jazz
subgenres.desc: African-styled percussion and rhythms.

subgenres.name: Cape Verdean Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed in the archipelago of Cape Verde.

subgenres.name: Batuque
subgenres.desc: Tradition from Cape Verde, unusual among the islands' music due to its lack of polyphonic singing and its usage of polyrhythms.

subgenres.name: Coladeira
subgenres.desc: Originated as a more uptempo and lively form of Morna before bringing in outside influences.

subgenres.name: Funaná
subgenres.desc: Upbeat Cape Verdean style which developed on the island of Santiago, based around the diatonic accordion and rhythm provided by the ferrinho.

subgenres.name: Morna
subgenres.desc: Slow tempo, monotonality, and the use of the violão, the Cape Verdean classical guitar, as the main instrumental accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Central African Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the areas speaking Adamawa-Eastern languages and many Bantu languages, through most of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, all of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, the islands of São Tomé and Príncipe, Republic of the Congo, most of the Central African Republic, and large parts of Cameroon, Angola, and the northern parts of Zambia.

subgenres.name: Ambasse bey
subgenres.desc: African Folk Music developed by the Yabassi people of Cameroon.

subgenres.name: Assiko
subgenres.desc: Music and dance of the Bassa people of southern Cameroon, which features a singer accompanied by a guitarist and improvised percussion.

subgenres.name: Banda Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Banda people, a Central African ethnic group mostly residing in the Central African Republic and its neighboring countries.

subgenres.name: Bend-skin
subgenres.desc: Most closely linked to the Bamileke people of the Western Province of Cameroon; drums and improvised maracas are the sole instrumentation backing up a vocalist who alternates between rapping and singing.

subgenres.name: Bikutsi
subgenres.desc: Developed from the Traditional Folk Music of the Ewondo people in Cameroon, with a name translating as "let's beat the earth" that comes from the stomping dance style that often accompanies it.

subgenres.name: Congolese Rumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of Congolese musical elements with Cuban Music (specifically Son cubano and  Rumba cubana) popular between the 1940s and early 1970s.

subgenres.name: Kalindula
subgenres.desc: Features multiple rumba-like lead guitars and quick steady basslines, while mixing together elements of other percussion-heavy Zambian styles.

subgenres.name: Kilapanga
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Bakongo people from Angola and Congo that has influenced contemporary styles such as Kuduro.

subgenres.name: Kizomba
subgenres.desc: Combines elements of Angolan Semba and French Caribbean Zouk.

subgenres.name: Tarraxinha
subgenres.desc: Heavy-hitting beats and electronic bass, putting less emphasis on melodies and vocals.

subgenres.name: Kuduro
subgenres.desc: Angolan music combining traditional Kilapanga and Semba with Techno and House.

subgenres.name: Batida
subgenres.desc: Initially developed in the late '80s in Luanda, Angola, as a mixture of Soca- and Zouk-based percussion samples.

subgenres.name: Makossa
subgenres.desc: Similar to Soukous, but makes more use of a horn section and bass rhythm.

subgenres.name: Mangambeu
subgenres.desc: Celebratory style featuring mbira-like instruments and polyrhythms, from western Cameroon.

subgenres.name: Mbenga-Mbuti Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Mbenga and Mbuti people, Pygmy ethnic groups in Central Africa.

subgenres.name: Mbolé
subgenres.desc: Festive, energetic and urban, influenced by Bikutsi, Bend-skin and Makossa; mainly based on hand-clapping and drumming accompanied by rhythmic singing.

subgenres.name: Puxa
subgenres.desc: Energetic dance style that combines solid bass lines with subtle melodies and harmonies of São Toméan music.

subgenres.name: Semba
subgenres.desc: Style from Angola featuring danceable percussion, lyrics often taking the form of a story, and sometimes accompaniment from a guitar.

subgenres.name: Soukous
subgenres.desc: Danceable, guitar-based style from the Congo area.

subgenres.name: Kwassa kwassa
subgenres.desc: Faster form of Soukous that was pioneered in the late 1980s and early 1990s, named after a popular dance.

subgenres.name: Tradi-moderne congolais
subgenres.desc: Updates traditional Congolese music with electric instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Twa Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Great Lakes Twa people.

subgenres.name: Zamrock
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Copperbelt region of Zambia in the 1970s, characterized by its blend of local sounds with influence from Funk, Hard Rock, and Blues Rock.

subgenres.name: East African Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions which originate from the eastern subregion of the African continent, encompassing a wide variety of cultures and styles.

subgenres.name: Acholi Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Acholi people, who inhabit a region known as “Acholiland,” spanning parts of northern Uganda and southern South Sudan.

subgenres.name: Acholitronix
subgenres.desc: Fusion of traditional Acholi rhythms and melodies with Electronic production, originating in the city of Gulu.

subgenres.name: Baganda Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Baganda people, a Bantu ethnic group indigenous to Uganda.

subgenres.name: Buganda Royal Court Music
subgenres.desc: Highest traditional and refined musical forms of Buganda, reserved for the Kabaka (the king of Buganda).

subgenres.name: Kadongo kamu
subgenres.desc: Oldest form of mainstream music in Uganda, dating back to the early 1950s, translating to “one little guitar” from the Luganda language.

subgenres.name: Mataali
subgenres.desc: Islamic praise genre of the Muslim community of Buganda, named after the frame drum on which the rhythm is played.

subgenres.name: Benga
subgenres.desc: Kenyan popular music based around the Traditional Folk Music of the Luo people from the area.

subgenres.name: Beni
subgenres.desc: Festive Zanzibari Marching Band music that emerged in the late 19th century.

subgenres.name: Bongo Flava
subgenres.desc: Tanzanian genre originating in the mid-1990s in the Dar es Salaam area, combining the influence of Rhythm & Blues, Afrobeat, and Dancehall with native Tanzanian styles like Taarab and Muziki wa dansi.

subgenres.name: Comorian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Comoros Islands and Mayotte off the eastern coast of Africa, combining influences from other East African Music and Malagasy Music.

subgenres.name: Dinka Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Dinka people, the most populous ethnic group of South Sudan.

subgenres.name: Genge
subgenres.desc: Combines elements of Dancehall with various traditions of Kenya.

subgenres.name: Gengetone
subgenres.desc: Takes strong influence from Reggaetón and modern Dancehall, featuring more explicit lyrics and harder beats.

subgenres.name: Gogo Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Gogo People (Wagogo), who inhabit Central Tanzania.

subgenres.name: Inkiranya
subgenres.desc: Influential drumming style originating in Burundi carried out by a percussion ensemble.

subgenres.name: Kapuka
subgenres.desc: Includes elements from Hip Hop and Reggae, as well as Kenyan traditions.

subgenres.name: Kidandali
subgenres.desc: Popular form of Ugandan music, originally derived from Kadongo kamu and Soukous.

subgenres.name: Kidumbak
subgenres.desc: Centered on two small kidumbak drums, fiddle, and singer; closely related to Taarab.

subgenres.name: Marrabenta
subgenres.desc: Fast, guitar driven, urban dance music from Mozambique that originated in Maputo in the 1950s, taking cues from Mozambican folk and a variety of foreign sounds.

subgenres.name: Mchiriku
subgenres.desc: Pairs amplified keyboards with hectic, intricate percussion and vocals drawn from earlier Tanzanian styles.

subgenres.name: Muziki wa dansi
subgenres.desc: Popular in Tanzania with strong connections to Soukous and often associated with Jazz, whose name means "dance music" in Swahili.

subgenres.name: Ngoma
subgenres.desc: Played in Swahili-speaking African countries; primarily focused on rhythm.

subgenres.name: Unyago
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Zanzibar, traditionally played at women's initiation rituals and weddings.

subgenres.name: Omutibo
subgenres.desc: Mid-20th century Kenyan popular music which centres around a fingerpicked acoustic guitar.

subgenres.name: Shilluk Music
subgenres.desc: All musical forms of the Shilluk people of the Upper Nile region of South Sudan.

subgenres.name: Singeli
subgenres.desc: Developed in Tanzania in the mid-2000s; fuses incredibly rapid beats, usually between 180-300BPM, with MCing and musical influences from older Tanzanian genres.

subgenres.name: Soga Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Soga people, a Bantu ethnic group residing in Eastern Uganda.

subgenres.name: Taarab
subgenres.desc: Prominent violin, qanun (an Egyptian zither-like instrument), and sung Swahili poetry, often accompanied by African drums and other percussion.

subgenres.name: Timbila
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Chopi people of the Inhambane province of Mozambique, named for the mbila, the wooden xylophone-like instrument on which it is played.

subgenres.name: Twa Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Great Lakes Twa people.

subgenres.name: Malagasy Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Malagasy peoples.

subgenres.name: Kalon'ny fahiny
subgenres.desc: Fusion of music from the highlands of Madagascar and western Operetta.

subgenres.name: Malagasy Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Melodic, chordophone-dominated sound; based on the Austronesian Music of the first settlers that arrived on the island from Borneo.

subgenres.name: Salegy
subgenres.desc: Features rich, harmonized vocals and chiming guitar lines.

subgenres.name: Tsapiky
subgenres.desc: Very fast and jerky rhythms, guitar duets, and polyharmonic chants.

subgenres.name: North African Music
subgenres.desc: Music of North Africa.

subgenres.name: Amazigh Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Amazigh people, the indigenous people of Northwest Africa (with main hubs in Morocco and Algeria) and certain parts of West Africa.

subgenres.name: Ahwash
subgenres.desc: Associated with the Tashelhit-speaking peoples of southern and central Morocco, and performed in large groups, combining singing, poetry and drumming.
