subgenres.name: Malay Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Malay people, who are native to Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, northern Indonesia, and southern Thailand.

subgenres.name: Pop Yeh-Yeh
subgenres.desc: Blends Western Beat and Psychedelia styles with asli singing and melodies drawn from Malay Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Minangkabau Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Minangkabau people.

subgenres.name: Pop Minang
subgenres.desc: Combines Minangkabau traditions with Pop structures and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Talempong goyang
subgenres.desc: Blends traditional Talempong elements with contemporary Pop influences, often featuring a female vocalist, and encourages audience participation.

subgenres.name: Saluang klasik
subgenres.desc: Played by a duo or a trio of musicians, including a saluang (a kind of end-blown bamboo flute) player and a traditional singer.

subgenres.name: Talempong
subgenres.desc: Gong-chime ensemble focused around the talempong kettle gong.

subgenres.name: Pakacaping Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional genres of music found among the ethnicities of Indonesian archipelago, particularly on South Sulawesi, Borneo and North Sumatra.

subgenres.name: Polynesian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of Polynesia.

subgenres.name: Fijian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Fijian people.

subgenres.name: Vude
subgenres.desc: Blends traditional local music with elements of Disco, Country and Rock.

subgenres.name: Hawaiian Music
subgenres.desc: Includes a variety of syncopated rhythms, percussion and vocal styles, including chanting (mele) and falsetto.

subgenres.name: Hapa haole
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian musical traditions adapted to popular American Jazz and Pop styles.

subgenres.name: Jawaiian
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian branch of Reggae, typically blends local traditional melodies, harmonies, incorporating specialty instruments such as ukulele and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Slack-Key Guitar
subgenres.desc: Originated in Hawaii and typically played with one's thumb in an alternating-bass pattern on the lower two or three strings.

subgenres.name: Himene tarava
subgenres.desc: Protestant choral songs in Tahiti and other southern Polynesian islands.

subgenres.name: Māori Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the indigenous Māori people of New Zealand.

subgenres.name: Samoan Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Samoan people.

subgenres.name: Tahitian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Tahitian people.

subgenres.name: Sundanese Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Sundanese people.

subgenres.name: Gamelan degung
subgenres.desc: Sundanese Gamelan performed by a small orchestra of bronze gongs and metallophones.

subgenres.name: Jaipongan
subgenres.desc: Sundanese performance music; uses instruments typical for Gamelan ensembles, but expands the drum section.

subgenres.name: Kacapi suling
subgenres.desc: Sundanese music played by an ensemble consisting of one or two kacapis (zithers), one suling (flute), and occasionally a set of kendangs (drums).

subgenres.name: Ketuk tilu
subgenres.desc: Traditional village dance and its accompanying music, which is played by a small gong-chime ensemble and accompanied by a Sundanese singer.

subgenres.name: Kliningan
subgenres.desc: Sundanese vocal music accompanied by Gamelan instrumentation, typically of the gamelan saléndro variety.

subgenres.name: Pop Sunda
subgenres.desc: Mixes Sundanese traditions with Pop structures and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Tarawangsa
subgenres.desc: Sacred ceremonial music originating in the Rancakalong district, played with the jentreng harp and the tarawangsa bowed lute.

subgenres.name: Tembang Sunda Cianjuran
subgenres.desc: Sung free-verse poetry in Sundanese language, usually by a solo vocalist, accompanied by a mellow-sounding Kacapi suling ensemble.

subgenres.name: Caribbean Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre covering all forms with roots in the Caribbean region.

subgenres.name: Aleke
subgenres.desc: Derived from traditional Surinamese Maroon music, especially aukansi, features distinct faster rhythms.

subgenres.name: Bachata
subgenres.desc: Romantic dance and accompanying music originating in the Dominican Republic, featuring arpeggiated chords in the melody.

subgenres.name: Brukdown
subgenres.desc: Belizean Creole genre typified by the use of accordion, banjo, and a distinctive percussion section.

subgenres.name: Bullerengue
subgenres.desc: Afro-Colombian popular genre which features a strong emphasis on rhythm and improvisation and a call-and-response format.

subgenres.name: Calypso
subgenres.desc: Genre from Trinidad and Tobago featuring a brass section and percussion.

subgenres.name: Calipso venezolano
subgenres.desc: Derived from Trinidadian Calypso, popular in the eastern region of Venezuela and associated with Carnival.

subgenres.name: Spouge
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Calypso and Ska originating in Barbados during the 1960s and 70s.

subgenres.name: Caribbean Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre that covers the different forms of Traditional Folk Music from the Caribbean.

subgenres.name: Bele
subgenres.desc: Drum-based folkdance with a strong Afro-influence, conducted by duos of dancers and accompanied by call-and-response singing, particularly popular in Martinique, Dominica and Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Benna
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of Antigua & Barbuda, using call-and-response and bawdy lyrics.

subgenres.name: Bomba
subgenres.desc: Percussive style from Puerto Rico, generally considered to be derived from West Africa.

subgenres.name: Fungi
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music native to the Virgin Islands, named after a local dish which features a "mixed-up" flavor that can be compared to the style that combines Western instruments with local ones.

subgenres.name: Haitian Vodou Drumming
subgenres.desc: Form of rhythmic performance by Haitian Vodou practitioners, played at associated ceremonies.

subgenres.name: Jibaro
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the mountain-dwelling jibaro people that live primarily in Puerto Rico.

subgenres.name: Kaiso
subgenres.desc: Trinidadian folk considered to be the precursor of Calypso, led by "griot" storytellers who sing derogatory lyrics to the sound of drums and guitars in a call-and-response manner in order to rebel against slaveowners.

subgenres.name: Kitchen Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Cayman Islands music played during kitchen dance parties, centered around fiddle and percussion (handmade or kitchen grater) playing.

subgenres.name: Kumina
subgenres.desc: Folk religious ritual of Jamaica, featuring extensive musical and dance elements, greatly inspired Rastafari religion and music.

subgenres.name: Mento
subgenres.desc: Jamaican folk originating in the late 19th century which brought together African and European elements, going on to influence the rhythm in Reggae.

subgenres.name: Méringue
subgenres.desc: Haitian genre that dates back to the early 19th century; the roots of Compas.

subgenres.name: Plena
subgenres.desc: Folk genre from Puerto Rico played with hand drums called panderetas.

subgenres.name: Ripsaw
subgenres.desc: Indigenous style of the Turks and Caicos Islands, featuring a handsaw as the primary instrument.

subgenres.name: Tumba
subgenres.desc: African-style percussion alongside Latin influences and often explicit lyrics.

subgenres.name: Virgin Islander Cariso
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Virgin Islands, sung exclusively by women to the beat of one or two drums.

subgenres.name: Champeta
subgenres.desc: Colombian genre heavily influenced by the traditional music of San Basilio de Palenque as well as modern Caribbean and African sensibilities.

subgenres.name: Cuban Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the wide variety of traditions from the island of Cuba.

subgenres.name: Abakuá Music
subgenres.desc: Ritual music associated with the Abakuá religious fraternity of Cuba, descending from the Ékpè tradition of West Africa.

subgenres.name: Chachachá
subgenres.desc: Ballroom dance music derived from Danzón.

subgenres.name: Changüí
subgenres.desc: One of the oldest popular Cuban styles, originating in the 19th century with slaves that worked in sugar refineries near Baracoa who combined elements of Spanish popular songs with Bantu traditions.

subgenres.name: Conga
subgenres.desc: Evolved alongside Rumba cubana in the late 19th century, featuring large and heterogenous percussion sections performing simple and syncopated rhythms alongside a small wind section.

subgenres.name: Cuban Charanga
subgenres.desc: Played by traditional Cuban ensembles, influenced by Son cubano but performed on European instruments such as piano, bass, violins, and flutes.

subgenres.name: Cubaton
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically and vocally inspired by major elements of Cuban Music.

subgenres.name: Reparto
subgenres.desc: Incorporating Cuban Music elements, resulting in dynamic rhythms and a sound palette that typically features  Salsa-like guitar picking.

subgenres.name: Danzón
subgenres.desc: Development on Habanera in 2/4 time, featuring African influence through complex cross-rhythms, that would become the most popular style of dance music in Cuba during the late 19th century and early 20th century.

subgenres.name: Descarga
subgenres.desc: Cuban genre consisting of improvised jam sessions incorporating elements of Jazz and Afro-Cuban music.

subgenres.name: Filin
subgenres.desc: Emotional style that appeared in La Habana during the late 1940s, deeply influenced by the melodic and expressive style of Vocal Jazz.

subgenres.name: Guajira
subgenres.desc: Originally developed in Cuba between the 18th and 19th Century as a narrative style influenced by Tonada chilena.

subgenres.name: Guaracha
subgenres.desc: Humorous song with short notes and a fast tempo that commonly alternates a short fourth line verse with a repeated fourth line chorus.

subgenres.name: Habanera
subgenres.desc: Based around the Habanera rhythm, where the most typical instruments used are guitars, lutes, and bandurrias.

subgenres.name: Mambo
subgenres.desc: Dance-oriented evolution from Danzón during the late 1930s.

subgenres.name: Mozambique
subgenres.desc: Cuban genre featuring energetic, African-influenced percussion.

subgenres.name: Pachanga
subgenres.desc: Combination of Merengue, Conga, Rumba cubana, and Cumbia; fast, festive, and playful.

subgenres.name: Pilón
subgenres.desc: Featuring rhythms described as mimicking those created while pounding sugarcane with African baton-like tools.

subgenres.name: Rumba cubana
subgenres.desc: Folkloric manifestation of Afro-Cuban music that encompasses dance, voice, and drums.

subgenres.name: Guaguancó
subgenres.desc: Emerged after the abolition of slavery in Cuba in 1886; usually features a lead singer, accompanied by three large drums, known as tumbadoras or congas, and a call-and-response chorus.

subgenres.name: Santería Music
subgenres.desc: Afro-Cuban genre played in religious rituals, combining traditions from both the Cuban and the Yorùbá people.

subgenres.name: Son cubano
subgenres.desc: Cuban style popular from the 1920s to the 1950s that combines the structure of Spanish song-oriented styles with African rhythms and percussion.

subgenres.name: Bolero son
subgenres.desc: Blend of Bolero and Son cubano that appeared during the 1920s.

subgenres.name: Son montuno
subgenres.desc: Developed in the 1940s, characterized by more elaborate instrumental arrangements and larger ensembles typically adding a horn section, conga drums, and piano.

subgenres.name: Songo
subgenres.desc: Cuban style originating in the late 1960s, combining elements from Rumba cubana and Son cubano with Jazz and Funk.

subgenres.name: Timba
subgenres.desc: Combines Salsa with other genres such as Hip Hop, Disco, Funk, Jazz and Rock.

subgenres.name: Trova
subgenres.desc: One of the most ancient expressions of Cuban Music, based around lone Singer-Songwriters who use nothing but a guitar as their preferred accompaniment and place emphasis on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Tumba francesa
subgenres.desc: Combination of traditional music from Benin with French ballroom dancing that originates in the Oriente province (formerly Santiago de Cuba Province) in Cuba.

subgenres.name: Cumbia colombiana
subgenres.desc: Style that incorporates elements of Colombian traditional music, which includes and keeps influences from Spanish, African, and Indigenous cultures.

subgenres.name: Dembow
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Dominican Republic during the early 1990s, featuring rapping indebted to Hip Hop and a style drawing on Dancehall, particularly the "Dem Bow" riddim.

subgenres.name: French Caribbean Music
subgenres.desc: Music from the French Antilles (Martinique, Guadeloupe, Dominica, Saint Lucia) and from Haiti.

subgenres.name: Bele
subgenres.desc: Drum-based folkdance with a strong Afro-influence, conducted by duos of dancers and accompanied by call-and-response singing, particularly popular in Martinique, Dominica and Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Biguine
subgenres.desc: Dating back to the 19th century; originating as a fusion of traditional Bele music with Polka.

subgenres.name: Bouyon
subgenres.desc: With a name translating to "broth", this fast-paced genre from Dominica originated as a blend of various traditional and modern Caribbean styles.

subgenres.name: Cadence lypso
subgenres.desc: Caribbean genre originating in the 1970s, combining elements of Haiti's Cadence rampa and Compas with Trinidad's Calypso.

subgenres.name: Dennery Segment
subgenres.desc: Developed in Saint Lucia in the early 2010s; heavily influenced by Angolan Kuduro, as well as incorporating elements of Zouk and Lucian drums alongside suggestive lyrics usually sung in Kwéyòl (Saint Lucian Creole).

subgenres.name: Gwo ka
subgenres.desc: Developed in the island of Guadeloupe; driven by a group of gwo ka drums.

subgenres.name: Haitian Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the styles of music developed by the Haitian people.

subgenres.name: Cadence rampa
subgenres.desc: Developed in parallel with Compas, based on Méringue with a stronger Cuban influence.

subgenres.name: Compas
subgenres.desc: Popular genre from Haiti, updating the older Méringue style with influences from Mambo and Jazz.

subgenres.name: Haitian Vodou Drumming
subgenres.desc: Form of rhythmic performance by Haitian Vodou practitioners, played at associated ceremonies.

subgenres.name: Méringue
subgenres.desc: Haitian genre that dates back to the early 19th century; the roots of Compas.

subgenres.name: Rabòday
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced rhythm inspired by Rara, with Electronic instrumentation and humorous sexual and political lyrics.

subgenres.name: Rara
subgenres.desc: Derived from the Haitian Vodou Drumming tradition, often played at street festivals and carnivals and usually having celebratory or political lyrics.

subgenres.name: Rasin
subgenres.desc: Blends the highly rhythmic drumming of traditional Haitian Vodou music with Rock-influenced electric instrumentation such as guitar, keyboard, and bass.

subgenres.name: Twoubadou
subgenres.desc: Pastoral, often satirical Haitian style usually performed by small groups centered around the acoustic guitar.

subgenres.name: Kréyol djaz
subgenres.desc: Combines Jazz with various styles of French Caribbean Music.

subgenres.name: Tumbélé
subgenres.desc: Combines Haitian Compas, Soukous and Cuban Guaguancó with the local style of Biguine.

subgenres.name: Zouk
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced danceable pop that began in early 1980s French Antilles, merging and updating more traditional local genres.

subgenres.name: Cabo-Zouk
subgenres.desc: Popular in Cape Verde and the Cape Verdean diaspora in Europe and North America, with a slow and sensuous tempo, and favoring more sophisticated studio productions.

subgenres.name: Zouk Love
subgenres.desc: More sentimental form of Zouk which emerged in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Gaita zuliana
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the state of Zulia in the 1950s, merging Spanish Folk Music and Venezuelan Christmas carols.

subgenres.name: Garifuna Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Garifuna, an Afro-Indigenous people from Central America and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

subgenres.name: Punta
subgenres.desc: Garifuna Music with influences from other Caribbean genres such as Reggae, Soca, and Zouk, as well as Hispanic American Music.

subgenres.name: Goombay
subgenres.desc: Bahamian music centered around the drum known as the goombay, a sort of membranophone.

subgenres.name: Indo-Caribbean Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Indo-Caribbean diaspora.

subgenres.name: Baithak gana
subgenres.desc: Indo-Caribbean genre from Suriname, consisting of Bhojpuri Folk Music with local Caribbean influence.

subgenres.name: Chutney
subgenres.desc: Indo-Caribbean genre developing as a fusion of Bhojpuri Folk Music with traditional Caribbean songs; later influenced by Calypso, Soca and Filmi.

subgenres.name: Chutney Soca
subgenres.desc: Mixture of Soca rhythms with Chutney's Indo-Caribbean traits and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Tassa
subgenres.desc: Drum ensemble descended from a mixture of northern Indian drumming traditions.

subgenres.name: Jamaican Music
subgenres.desc: Regional music of Jamaica ranges from its cultural origins in traditional and religious folk of the late 19th and early 20th centuries to the international popularity of Reggae from the 1970s onwards.

subgenres.name: Dancehall
subgenres.desc: Developed from Reggae in the late 1970s, when Roots Reggae became more stripped-down, with an increased emphasis on pure rhythm.

subgenres.name: Bubbling
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Netherlands in the late 1980s, fusing sped-up Dancehall with Dutch Antillean music and contemporary Dutch rave.

subgenres.name: Digital Dancehall
subgenres.desc: First, pre-Ragga style of Dancehall to popularize Electronic rhythms that arose in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Flex Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Largely instrumental; infused with Electronic Dance Music elements.

subgenres.name: Gommance
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Réunion, mixing Caribbean, African and Afro-Dutch influences.

subgenres.name: Ragga
subgenres.desc: Hardcore style with a deejay (equivalent to an MC in Hip Hop) rapping over predominantly Electronic rhythms.

subgenres.name: Shatta
subgenres.desc: French Caribbean Dancehall subgenre with a focus on sparse percussion, heavy basslines and lyrics revolving around partying and sensuality, often in Creole.

subgenres.name: Trap Dancehall
subgenres.desc: Combines midtempo Dancehall rhythms and tempos with major elements borrowed from Trap, namely in percussion and drum rhythms.

subgenres.name: Zess
subgenres.desc: Trinidadian style that originated in the country's slums in the late 2010s, defined by its sexual, violent, and occasionally gang-related lyrics and its influence from Soca, as well as occasional influences from Hip Hop and Funk brasileiro.

subgenres.name: Jamaican Ska
subgenres.desc: Originated in Jamaica with groups who combined Jazz and Rhythm & Blues with rhythms of traditional Caribbean Music like Mento and Calypso.

subgenres.name: Kumina
subgenres.desc: Folk religious ritual of Jamaica, featuring extensive musical and dance elements, greatly inspired Rastafari religion and music.

subgenres.name: Mento
subgenres.desc: Jamaican folk originating in the late 19th century which brought together African and European elements, going on to influence the rhythm in Reggae.

subgenres.name: Nyahbinghi
subgenres.desc: Performed at Rastafari religious ceremonies, consisting of tripartite hand-drumming and often accompanied by vocal chants.

subgenres.name: Reggae
subgenres.desc: Developed in the 1960s; shuffling "bubble" and offbeat rhythms played on an organ, and staccato guitar and piano chords known as "skank."

subgenres.name: Deejay
subgenres.desc: Reggae in which a deejay (similar to an MC in Hip Hop) talks or chants lyrics over a pre-recorded reggae rhythm.

subgenres.name: Digital Dancehall
subgenres.desc: First, pre-Ragga style of Dancehall to popularize Electronic rhythms that arose in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Dub
subgenres.desc: Primarily instrumental Reggae which developed from the extensive use of studio techniques and effects like reverb and delay.

subgenres.name: Lovers Rock
subgenres.desc: Smooth, quiet Reggae beats with lyrics focusing on romance and love.

subgenres.name: Pacific Reggae
subgenres.desc: Developed in Pacific island communities, incorporating elements from local Oceanian Music styles.

subgenres.name: Jawaiian
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian branch of Reggae, typically blends local traditional melodies, harmonies, incorporating specialty instruments such as ukulele and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Pop Reggae
subgenres.desc: Light, commercial form of Reggae designed to crossover and break through to a more mainstream Pop audience.

subgenres.name: Roots Reggae
subgenres.desc: Primarily defined through the political, spiritual, and socially conscious messages of its lyrics.

subgenres.name: Dub Poetry
subgenres.desc: Poetry with Dub and Reggae backing rhythms, originating in Jamaica in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Seggae
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Séga and Reggae, popular on Mauritius and other Mascarene Islands.

subgenres.name: Skinhead Reggae
subgenres.desc: Early subgenre prominent from 1968 to 1971; known for its high tempos and driving rhythms compared with the more languid pace of most later styles.

subgenres.name: Rocksteady
subgenres.desc: Jamaican popular music that blossomed briefly between 1966 and 1968 as an evolution of Ska, being slower, more relaxed, and soulful.

subgenres.name: Junkanoo
subgenres.desc: Highly rhythmic Bahamian style which traditionally accompanies the arts festival and street parade of the same name.

subgenres.name: Kaseko
subgenres.desc: Surinamese popular music with roots in Surinamese Creole music, which was influenced by folk traditions of Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

subgenres.name: Merengue
subgenres.desc: Dominican Republic dance genre that had a commercial boom at the end of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Mambo urbano
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically simpler and more eclectic style, absorbing influences from Hip Hop, Reggaetón, and other modern genres, particularly in regards to vocals.

subgenres.name: Merecumbé
subgenres.desc: Colombian genre which combines Cumbia with Merengue.

subgenres.name: Merengue típico
subgenres.desc: Earliest, most stripped-down form of Merengue.

subgenres.name: Merenhouse
subgenres.desc: Popularized by Dominican-American artists of the 1990s, blending modern Merengue with electronic instrumentation and the combination of rapping/singing vocals.

subgenres.name: Tecnomerengue
subgenres.desc: Fuses basic Merengue rhythms with influences from Cumbia and Lambada, being largely synthesized, with live instruments usually limited to percussion and brass.

subgenres.name: Palo de mayo
subgenres.desc: Upbeat music accompanying maypole dancing from the Caribbean coast of Central America.

subgenres.name: Parang
subgenres.desc: Latin-Caribbean genre central to Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela traditionally used for nighttime celebrations in Trinidadian towns.

subgenres.name: Porro
subgenres.desc: Lively Hispanic American Music and dance style native to Colombia which gained popularity in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Soca
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, poppy and danceable style rooted in Calypso and Indo-Caribbean Music; developed in the late 1960s and early 1970s in Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Bashment Soca
subgenres.desc: Highly energetic, Dancehall-influenced form of Soca developed in Barbados featuring dancefloor-oriented lyrics delivered in an aggressive chanting style.

subgenres.name: Chutney Soca
subgenres.desc: Mixture of Soca rhythms with Chutney's Indo-Caribbean traits and instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Dennery Segment
subgenres.desc: Developed in Saint Lucia in the early 2010s; heavily influenced by Angolan Kuduro, as well as incorporating elements of Zouk and Lucian drums alongside suggestive lyrics usually sung in Kwéyòl (Saint Lucian Creole).

subgenres.name: Power Soca
subgenres.desc: Often at a tempo of 160 BPM and incorporating hard, frantic rhythms, highly synthesized production, and call-and-response vocals.

subgenres.name: Rapso
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Soca and Hip Hop unique to Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Steel Band
subgenres.desc: Ensembles made out of steel drums that often perform Standards, Calypso, and Western Classical Music with densely rhythmic and colorful arrangements.

subgenres.name: Tropicanibalismo
subgenres.desc: Colombian scene born in the early 2000s with the intention of reinventing Colombian coastal music, from a more current and experimental approach.

subgenres.name: Vallenato
subgenres.desc: Accordion-led style of folk and popular music originating in Colombia's Caribbean region.

subgenres.name: Central American Music
subgenres.desc: Music from the Central American region (including Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama).

subgenres.name: Brukdown
subgenres.desc: Belizean Creole genre typified by the use of accordion, banjo, and a distinctive percussion section.

subgenres.name: Cumbia salvadoreña
subgenres.desc: Takes influence from local Salvadoran music and traditionally features a distinctive ensemble.

subgenres.name: Garifuna Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Garifuna, an Afro-Indigenous people from Central America and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

subgenres.name: Punta
subgenres.desc: Garifuna Music with influences from other Caribbean genres such as Reggae, Soca, and Zouk, as well as Hispanic American Music.

subgenres.name: Palo de mayo
subgenres.desc: Upbeat music accompanying maypole dancing from the Caribbean coast of Central America.

subgenres.name: Purísima
subgenres.desc: Nicaraguan Hymn to the Immaculate Conception of Mary, sung during holiday celebrations and in liturgical or parochial services.

subgenres.name: Son de pascua
subgenres.desc: Lively instrumental Christmas songs from Central America composed in 6/8 or triple meter.

subgenres.name: Son nica
subgenres.desc: Nicaraguan popular rhythm in distinctive guitar strums, with lyrics relating to the countryside and peasant life.

subgenres.name: Tamborera
subgenres.desc: Panamanian popular genre which mixes local Tamborito with Cuban Music rhythms featuring the tambora as the main percussion instrument.

subgenres.name: Tamborito
subgenres.desc: Folk music and dance from Panama dating back to the 17th century.

subgenres.name: Xuc
subgenres.desc: Danceable style from El Salvador developed in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Christian Liturgical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditionally accompanies church services, as well as extra-liturgical functions such as processionals and sermons.

subgenres.name: Anglican Chant
subgenres.desc: Simple, harmonized, English-language setting of the Christian liturgy, principally devised by the Anglican Church.

subgenres.name: Armenian Church Music
subgenres.desc: One of the oldest branches of Christian culture, this is the predominantly vocal music of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

subgenres.name: Byzantine Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical chant of Christian churches following the Orthodox rite.

subgenres.name: Coptic Music
subgenres.desc: Church music specifically made for worship in the Coptic (Egyptian) Orthodox Church.

subgenres.name: Ethiopian Church Music
subgenres.desc: Sacred tradition of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, sung in an ancient Semitic language called Ge'ez and credited with assembling the current Ethiopian notation system.

subgenres.name: Kyivan Chant
subgenres.desc: Chant form inspired by Znamenny Chant that's characterized by simplified melodic and rhythmic structures.

subgenres.name: Mass
subgenres.desc: Composition that sets to music text from the liturgy of the Eucharist, principally from the Latin rites of the Roman Catholic Church.

subgenres.name: Requiem
subgenres.desc: Musical setting commemorating the deceased with text usually derived from the Roman Catholic mass of the dead.

subgenres.name: Passion
subgenres.desc: Musical re-enactment of the suffering and crucifixion of Christ, typically based on one of the four canonical Gospels.

subgenres.name: Plainsong
subgenres.desc: Monophonic chanting in the context of Roman Catholic and modern Anglican liturgy.

subgenres.name: Ambrosian Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical chant practiced in parts of Italy and Switzerland, characterized by stepped melodic progression.

subgenres.name: Canto beneventano
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition of Southern Italy characterized by lengthy melodies, extensive use of repetition, and a steady, undulating progression.

subgenres.name: Canto mozárabe
subgenres.desc: Iberian form of plainchant that flourished roughly 550-1085 AD.

subgenres.name: Celtic Chant

subgenres.desc: Flamenco of Andalusia in southern Spain, rooted in traditional music and dances and developed mostly after the 18th century by the Romani people of Andalusia (known locally as gitanos).

subgenres.name: Saeta
subgenres.desc: Traditional religious praise song that originated in Andalusia, Spain towards the end of the late Middle Ages.

subgenres.name: Sevillanas
subgenres.desc: Named after the city of Seville in Spain, typically rhythmic with a 3/4 beat and guitar accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Aragonese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Aragonese people.

subgenres.name: Asturian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Asturian people.

subgenres.name: Canarian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the Canary Islands.

subgenres.name: Chotis madrileño
subgenres.desc: Spanish variant which developed through the incorporation of regional folk influences and an association with the local castizo culture in Madrid, the capital of Spain.

subgenres.name: Copla
subgenres.desc: Evolved from Spanish theatrical styles like Cuplé and has strong links to Flamenco.

subgenres.name: Cuplé
subgenres.desc: Originally developed in the 19th century as a blend of old theatre Spanish styles based in short monologues (jácara and tonadilla) and French Couplet.

subgenres.name: Galician Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Galician people.

subgenres.name: Pasodoble
subgenres.desc: Mainly instrumental Spanish style primarily associated with bullfighting and popular celebrations, believed to originate from a double-time military march from France in the 18th century.

subgenres.name: Valencian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Valencian Country.

subgenres.name: Tecnorumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.

subgenres.name: Villancico
subgenres.desc: Style of polyphonic lyric poetry popular between the 14th and 18th centuries that developed in Spain, Portugal, and their associated colonies.

subgenres.name: Irish Showband
subgenres.desc: Phenomenon lasting from the mid-1950s until the early 1980s, often performed a mixture of currently popular music and skits.

subgenres.name: Italian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Italian people.

subgenres.name: Canto beneventano
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition of Southern Italy characterized by lengthy melodies, extensive use of repetition, and a steady, undulating progression.

subgenres.name: Canzone d'autore
subgenres.desc: Music of the Italian Singer-Songwriters that emerged in the 1960s and early 1970s, initially influenced by French Chanson with the addition of uniquely Italian sensibilities.

subgenres.name: Italian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of Italy.

subgenres.name: Canto degli Alpini
subgenres.desc: Created and traditionally sung by choirs formed from the Italian army's Alpine mountain infantry corps, mainly dating back to WWI.

subgenres.name: Canzone napoletana
subgenres.desc: Sung in the Neapolitan language by a male voice with instrumental accompaniment, originating in the Italian city of Naples and the surrounding regions.

subgenres.name: Liscio
subgenres.desc: Italian popular genre characterized by the fast execution of solo instruments such as clarinet, saxophone, or the accordion.

subgenres.name: Sardinian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Sardinia, an island in the Mediterranean Sea.

subgenres.name: Cantu a chiterra
subgenres.desc: Traditional monophonic singing accompanied by a chittera sarda from the Mediterranean island of Sardinia.

subgenres.name: Cantu a tenore
subgenres.desc: Secular Polyphonic Chant from the Mediterranean island of Sardinia.

subgenres.name: Stornello
subgenres.desc: Italian folk poetry, generally improvised and handed down by street singers, carters or sellers.

subgenres.name: Tarantella
subgenres.desc: Fast upbeat tempo, switching between major and minor modes while gradually increasing in speed.

subgenres.name: Pizzica
subgenres.desc: Italian Folk dance and music from Apulia, belonging to the family of Tarantella.

subgenres.name: Tammurriata
subgenres.desc: Italian folk from Campania, belonging to the family of Tarantella.

subgenres.name: Trallalero
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic Traditional Folk Music originating in the Ligurian region of Genoa, in northern Italy.

subgenres.name: Lauda
subgenres.desc: Vernacular, devotional sung poetry, composed in Italy in the late Medieval and Renaissance periods.

subgenres.name: Old Roman Chant
subgenres.desc: Plainchant tradition of Medieval Rome that was closely related to Gregorian Chant, though often more musically ornate.

subgenres.name: Opera buffa
subgenres.desc: Lighthearted and amusing counterpart to Opera seria; developed in Naples in the first half of the 18th century.

subgenres.name: Opera semiseria
subgenres.desc: Popular in the early and middle 19th century, containing appeals to emotion of Opera seria as well as some comedy elements present in Opera buffa.

subgenres.name: Opera seria
subgenres.desc: Italian Opera popular among European nobility and royalty throughout most of the 18th century, typified by its exaggerated dramatic flair and interspersed with dry recitative.

subgenres.name: Kabarett
subgenres.desc: Theatrical entertainment consisting of mixed elements of music, sketches, monologues, dialogues, lyric poetry and/or ballads.

subgenres.name: Kalmyk Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Kalmyks, a Mongol Buddhist ethnic group inhabiting the Republic of Kalmykia, a federal subject of the Russian Federation.

subgenres.name: Kleinkunst
subgenres.desc: Dutch-language genre from the Netherlands and Flanders with influences from Cabaret, protest songs, Chanson, and folk.

subgenres.name: Kyivan Chant
subgenres.desc: Chant form inspired by Znamenny Chant that's characterized by simplified melodic and rhythmic structures.

subgenres.name: Madrigal
subgenres.desc: Secular polyphonic music based around poetry and generally performed by unaccompanied vocal ensembles of two to eight persons.

subgenres.name: Medieval Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Composed during the Medieval period lasted approximately from the 5th to the late 15th centuries.

subgenres.name: Ars antiqua
subgenres.desc: Mainly sacred European medieval music from the period of 1170 to 1310, featuring the birth of measuring time in music and the use of polyphonies for four voices.

subgenres.name: Ars nova
subgenres.desc: Period (around 1310-1380) that succeeded Ars antiqua, mixing the sacred with the secular.

subgenres.name: Ars subtilior
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the final period of late medieval music (around 1380-1420) and continued to use the technique of isorhythms but with added complexity.

subgenres.name: Contenance angloise
subgenres.desc: Distinct style of Polyphonic Chant developed in fifteenth-century England.

subgenres.name: Medieval Lyric Poetry
subgenres.desc: Lyric poetry from Medieval Europe, roughly from the 11th to the 14th century, most prominently the troubadours of southern France.

subgenres.name: Plainsong
subgenres.desc: Monophonic chanting in the context of Roman Catholic and modern Anglican liturgy.

subgenres.name: Ambrosian Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical chant practiced in parts of Italy and Switzerland, characterized by stepped melodic progression.

subgenres.name: Canto beneventano
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition of Southern Italy characterized by lengthy melodies, extensive use of repetition, and a steady, undulating progression.

subgenres.name: Canto mozárabe
subgenres.desc: Iberian form of plainchant that flourished roughly 550-1085 AD.

subgenres.name: Celtic Chant
subgenres.desc: Extinct tradition of Catholic liturgical chant developed by the Celtic Christians of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany.

subgenres.name: Gallican Chant
subgenres.desc: Extinct plainchant tradition originating from the region of Gaul (now modern-day France).

subgenres.name: Gregorian Chant
subgenres.desc: Liturgical, monophonic chant that accompanied Mass and other rituals in Western Christianity.

subgenres.name: Sarum Chant
subgenres.desc: Latin Plainsong tradition of Salisbury, England, characterized by its unadorned simplicity.

subgenres.name: Old Roman Chant
subgenres.desc: Plainchant tradition of Medieval Rome that was closely related to Gregorian Chant, though often more musically ornate.

subgenres.name: Mélodie
subgenres.desc: French form typically with a greater emphasis on emotional restraint, refinement, subtlety, and concision.

subgenres.name: Mittelalter-Metal
subgenres.desc: Emerged as a metallic style in the mid-to-late 1990s from the German Neo-Medieval movement.

subgenres.name: Mittelalter-Rock
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1990s from the German Neo-Medieval movement, incorporating medieval instruments with Rock music.

subgenres.name: Mulatós
subgenres.desc: Upbeat, danceable Hungarian Pop that takes strong influence from Hungarian Folk Music and Romani Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Nordic Music
subgenres.desc: Music from the Nordic countries, including Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and Finland.

subgenres.name: Dansbandsmusik
subgenres.desc: Nordic Pop style originating from 1960s Pop Rock, incorporating Swing, Schlager, Nordic Old Time Dance Music and Country influences.

subgenres.name: Dansktop
subgenres.desc: Danish equivalent to Dansbandsmusik with Schlager and Country influences and Contemporary Folk and Pop elements.

subgenres.name: Greenlandic Music
subgenres.desc: Majorly from Inuit ethnic groups in Greenland, a large island between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans.

subgenres.name: Kalattut
subgenres.desc: Distinctive Folk tradition shaped by European cultural exchanges and indigenous Greenlandic heritage.

subgenres.name: Tivaner inngernerlu
subgenres.desc: Pre-colonial Inuit Folk tradition centered around the qilaat (drum).

subgenres.name: Uaajeerneq
subgenres.desc: Ancient Greenlandic-Inuit dramatic performance characterized by percussion and idiosyncratic expression.

subgenres.name: Vaigat
subgenres.desc: Contemporary popular music shaped by American cultural exchanges and indigenous Greenlandic heritage.

subgenres.name: Nordic Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of Nordic countries of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden.

subgenres.name: Danish Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Danish people.

subgenres.name: Faroese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Faroe Islands.

subgenres.name: Finnish Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Finnish people.

subgenres.name: Icelandic Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Iceland, including a variety of styles like the rímur, the kvædaskapur and langspil instrumental music.

subgenres.name: Joik
subgenres.desc: Traditional Sami singing style found in northern Finland, Sweden, Norway and Russia.

subgenres.name: Nordic Old Time Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre strongly related to Nordic Folk Music having less complex structures, easy rhythms, and melodic lines.

subgenres.name: Polska
subgenres.desc: Traditional Nordic dance with a 3/4 rhythm.

subgenres.name: Hambo
subgenres.desc: Traditional Swedish dance with a 3/4 rhythm and an emphasis on the first beat.

subgenres.name: Norwegian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Norway, primarily intended as accompaniment for dancing and coming in two main varieties, instrumental and vocal music.

subgenres.name: Swedish Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Swedish people, commonly incorporating fiddle, accordion, flute, nyckelharpa, and/or voice.

subgenres.name: Hambo
subgenres.desc: Traditional Swedish dance with a 3/4 rhythm and an emphasis on the first beat.

subgenres.name: Nordic Folk Rock
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Nordic Folk Music and Rock.

subgenres.name: Rautalanka
subgenres.desc: Nordic guitar style mainly influenced by Rock & Roll, and traditional European Schlager.

subgenres.name: Visa
subgenres.desc: Nordic balladry focusing on lyrical content and simple vocal melodies.

subgenres.name: Nòva cançon
subgenres.desc: Arose in the Occitania region of southern France, sung in the Occitan language as a way to preserve their culture and resist forced usage of French.

subgenres.name: Opéra-comique
subgenres.desc: French style of Opera characterized by the use of some spoken dialogues to connect major arias and sung parts, as well as a more restrained approach to recitatives.

subgenres.name: Polish Music
subgenres.desc: Music rooted in the traditions of the Poles.

subgenres.name: Chicago Polka
subgenres.desc: Polish-American style known for slower tempo, improvisation and the ensemble typically including the clarinet, trumpet, and concertina.

subgenres.name: Disco polo
subgenres.desc: Polish Dance-Pop, originally established from contemporary wedding / feast songs and Italo-Disco.

subgenres.name: Eastern-Style Polka
subgenres.desc: Fast, urban Polish-American style performed by a Big Band-like ensemble.

subgenres.name: Mazur
subgenres.desc: Lively triple-time national dance with folk origins, popular with the nobility and in the 19th century ballrooms.

subgenres.name: Mazurka
subgenres.desc: Folk or folk-inspired form based on the triple-time rhythm of Mazur, Kujawiak and Oberek.

subgenres.name: Miejski folk
subgenres.desc: Alternative and Punk music influenced by Folklor miejski and Contemporary Folk.

subgenres.name: Poezja śpiewana
subgenres.desc: Polish sung poetry; the poem is the centerpiece of a song, often with sparse instrumental accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Polish Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Poles.

subgenres.name: Folklor miejski
subgenres.desc: Urban folk street band traditions of Polish cities.

subgenres.name: Warsaw City Folk
subgenres.desc: Traditional urban poetry sung in the Warsaw dialect by buskers, and accompanied by street bands.

subgenres.name: Kashubian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kashubian people of northwestern Poland.

subgenres.name: Krakowiak
subgenres.desc: Fast, syncopated, duple-time national dance of Poland.

subgenres.name: Kujawiak
subgenres.desc: Calm, triple-time national dance of Poland.

subgenres.name: Kujon
subgenres.desc: Melancholic triple-time folk dance from Łowicz and Łęczyca regions, related to Kujawiak and Oberek.

subgenres.name: Kurpian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kurpian people of eastern Poland.

subgenres.name: Oberek
subgenres.desc: Fastest triple-time national dance of Poland.

subgenres.name: Polish Goral Music
subgenres.desc: Music of indigenous highlanders native to the Western Beskids and the Podhale regions in Southern Poland.

subgenres.name: Polonaise
subgenres.desc: Stately national dance with music in triple meter and moderate tempo.

subgenres.name: Renaissance Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses Western Classical Music from the 15th to 16th centuries.

subgenres.name: Contenance angloise
subgenres.desc: Distinct style of Polyphonic Chant developed in fifteenth-century England.

subgenres.name: Elizabethan Song
subgenres.desc: Monophonic style developed in Renaissance England that is typically composed in strophic form for one to several vocalists with instrumental accompaniment ranging from solo lute to chamber ensemble.

subgenres.name: Franco-Flemish School
subgenres.desc: Musical movement centered in the Low Countries, known for its intricate polyphony, emotional expression, and influence on European sacred and secular music from the 1440s to 1550.

subgenres.name: Romanian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Romanian people.

subgenres.name: Manele
subgenres.desc: Mixture of Romanian Music with Turkish, Middle Eastern, Balkan, and Romani influences, usually electronic in production.

subgenres.name: Muzică de mahala
subgenres.desc: Appeared in the 1980s, incorporating modern instruments and based on the model of Balkan Pop-Folk in neighboring countries.

subgenres.name: Romanian Etno Music
subgenres.desc: Romanian style which emerged in the early 1990s as a revival of Romanian Folk Music, blending traditional music with dance-pop rhythms.

subgenres.name: Romanian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Romanians.

subgenres.name: Bocet
subgenres.desc: Traditional Romanian music sung by women mourning at a funeral.

subgenres.name: Colinde
subgenres.desc: Christmas music from Romanian folklore with ritualistic and pagan roots.

subgenres.name: Doină
subgenres.desc: Melancholic, lyrical folk song characterised by its free rhythm.

subgenres.name: Muzică lăutărească
subgenres.desc: Strongly influenced by folk from Turkey, Russia, and Western Europe, and even by Byzantine Church music.

subgenres.name: Romanţe
subgenres.desc: Expressive and poetic Romanian style, generally sung similar to a Chanson and composed for piano and guitar orchestral arrangements.

subgenres.name: Russian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Russian people.

subgenres.name: Avtorskaya pesnya
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Soviet Union taking cues from forms of Russian Romance and Russian poetry with the main focus on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Bard Rock
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock music and styles with Avtorskaya pesnya.

subgenres.name: Russian Chanson
subgenres.desc: Divided into lyrical and criminal chanson, it is best described as narrative-driven popular music inspired by crime and prison.

subgenres.name: Russian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Eastern Slavic Folk Music native to the Russian people.

subgenres.name: Russian Orthodox Liturgical Music
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Russian Orthodox Church, implemented with the Christianization of Kievan Rus' in 988.

subgenres.name: Choral Concerto
subgenres.desc: Composition for unaccompanied choir, set to sacred texts of Eastern Orthodox tradition.

subgenres.name: Znamenny Chant
subgenres.desc: Prototypical liturgical chant of the Russian Orthodox Church.

subgenres.name: Russian Romance
subgenres.desc: Popular Russian genre of melancholy balladry.

subgenres.name: Schlager
subgenres.desc: Light, sentimental, melodic pop music common mainly in northern and central Europe.

subgenres.name: Humppa
subgenres.desc: Finnish music related to Jazz and the Foxtrot.

subgenres.name: Levenslied
subgenres.desc: Dutch genre that enjoyed widespread popularity in the pre-Rock & Roll era. with simple melody and rhythm and lyrics composed of couplets and refrains.

subgenres.name: Volkstümliche Musik
subgenres.desc: Light Pop with borrowings from German Folk Music (volksmusik), often misleadingly labeled as being volksmusik.

subgenres.name: Schottische
subgenres.desc: Social dance with a simple, bouncy rhythm in 2/4 or 4/4 which originated from central Europe by the late 18th century, developing into a wide number of regional variations around the world.

subgenres.name: Chotis madrileño
subgenres.desc: Spanish variant which developed through the incorporation of regional folk influences and an association with the local castizo culture in Madrid, the capital of Spain.

subgenres.name: Singspiel
subgenres.desc: German form of Opera distinguished by the prominent usage of spoken dialogues mixed with lyrical or folklore arias/ballads.

subgenres.name: Tragédie en musique
subgenres.desc: French Opera genre developed by Jean-Baptiste Lully and Philippe Quinault in the second half of the 17th century, consisting of alterations made to the coeval Italian format to better fit the French language and please an audience more accustomed to the ballet de cour.

subgenres.name: Trampská hudba
subgenres.desc: Associated with the tramping lifestyle, typically mixing acoustic guitar driven Contemporary Folk with strong Country influences and vocal harmonies in peaceful, simple and relatively short songs.

subgenres.name: Verismo
subgenres.desc: Developed in Italy around the turn of the 20th century and favored melodramatic realism, a rejection of bel canto standards, and declamatory singing.

subgenres.name: Waltz
subgenres.desc: Typically in a 3/4 time signature and popular in the 18th century in central Europe, as it accompanied the ballroom dance of the same name.

subgenres.name: Valsa brasileira
subgenres.desc: Brazillian Waltz characterized by its slow rhythms and romantic sound.

subgenres.name: Vals venezolano
subgenres.desc: Venezuelan dance music that employs heavy use of syncopation, complex rhythms, and regional instruments.

subgenres.name: Hispanic Music
subgenres.desc: Music of Hispanic America and Spain, and the genres shared between them.

subgenres.name: Canción melódica
subgenres.desc: Sentimental vocal music sung in Spanish with a focus on the chorus, originally developed in the first half of the 20th century from a variety of traditional Hispanic genres.

subgenres.name: Bolero-Beat
subgenres.desc: Latin American style stemming from both Canción melódica and the British Beat.

subgenres.name: Música cebolla
subgenres.desc: Chilean offshoot of Canción melódica that expresses a much more melancholic or nostalgic side.

subgenres.name: Hispanic American Music
subgenres.desc: Includes all genres created by Hispanic Americans.

subgenres.name: Afro-Cuban Jazz
subgenres.desc: Combines Jazz with the rhythms of Afro-Cuban music.

subgenres.name: Argentine Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the Argentine people.

subgenres.name: Cuarteto
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Argentinian province of Córdoba, usually with an upbeat rhythm and originally performed with a four-piece band.

subgenres.name: Cumbia argentina
subgenres.desc: Almost always features synthesizer keyboards and electronic percussion with an upbeat rhythm.

subgenres.name: Cumbia santafesina
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Argentinian province of Santa Fe, particularly in its capital city Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz, with lyrics that tend to be romantic and relatively clean compared to later Cumbia argentina.

subgenres.name: Cumbia turra
subgenres.desc: Cumbia argentina heavily influenced by Reggaetón and characterized by hard-hitting bass and heavy use of samples and Auto-Tune.

subgenres.name: Cumbia villera
subgenres.desc: Developed in the villa miserias (shanty towns) by the lower classes of Argentina in the early 2000s, featuring basic rhythms and low budget productions combined with lyrics that can be openly sexual or touch on sociopolitical issues.

subgenres.name: Guaracha santiagueña
subgenres.desc: Fast, upbeat and danceable rhythm originated in the province of Santiago del Estero, Argentina as a fusion of Chacarera and Chamamé.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: RKT
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2010s, characterized by minimalistic, rhythm-centric production heavily influenced by Cumbia villera and other Cumbia argentina styles.

subgenres.name: Avanzada
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Polka paraguaya and Guarania with elements of Bossa nova and MPB.

subgenres.name: Bachata
subgenres.desc: Romantic dance and accompanying music originating in the Dominican Republic, featuring arpeggiated chords in the melody.

subgenres.name: Bailecito
subgenres.desc: Agile and lively dance derived from Zamacueca, typical of the western and central region of Bolivia.

subgenres.name: Bolero
subgenres.desc: Ballad with a 2/4 time signature that appeared in eastern Cuba towards the end of the 19th century.

subgenres.name: Bolero son
subgenres.desc: Blend of Bolero and Son cubano that appeared during the 1920s.

subgenres.name: Filin
subgenres.desc: Emotional style that appeared in La Habana during the late 1940s, deeply influenced by the melodic and expressive style of Vocal Jazz.

subgenres.name: Boogaloo
subgenres.desc: Upbeat fusion of American Rhythm & Blues and Jazz with Son cubano which originated in the early 1960s in New York City and became popular with both its Black and Latino communities.

subgenres.name: Bullerengue
subgenres.desc: Afro-Colombian popular genre which features a strong emphasis on rhythm and improvisation and a call-and-response format.

subgenres.name: Caporal
subgenres.desc: Bolivian neofolkloric dance music characterized by a double beat bass drum pattern that emerged in the latter half of the twentieth century.

subgenres.name: Carnaval cruceño
subgenres.desc: Danceable genre, similar to the Polka, from the city of Santa Cruz, Bolivia, characteristic of the area’s Carnival celebrations and generally composed for brass band musicians.

subgenres.name: Champeta
subgenres.desc: Colombian genre heavily influenced by the traditional music of San Basilio de Palenque as well as modern Caribbean and African sensibilities.

subgenres.name: Chilean Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the Chilean people.

subgenres.name: Canto a lo poeta
subgenres.desc: Sung poetry traditional to Chile and transmitted orally from one generation to another.

subgenres.name: Chilote Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Chiloé Archipelago.

subgenres.name: Cumbia chilena
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Chilean Music into the traditional sound of Cumbia.

subgenres.name: Nueva cumbia chilena
subgenres.desc: Rock-infused instrumentation, incorporating an eclectic repertoire of influences, such as Ska, Salsa, Indigenous Andean Music, Reggae, and Bolero.

subgenres.name: Jazz guachaca
subgenres.desc: Encompasses Jazz influences with Hispanic American Music styles such as Cueca, Bolero, Tango and Corrido.

subgenres.name: Mambo chileno
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2010s in Chile, characterized by upbeat rhythms and rapping, usually on topics of parties, dancing, and urban life.

subgenres.name: Música cebolla
subgenres.desc: Chilean offshoot of Canción melódica that expresses a much more melancholic or nostalgic side.

subgenres.name: Música típica chilena
subgenres.desc: Incorporation of rural folklore music to urban fields, adding vocal groups accompanied mainly by guitar and a "huaso" symbolism.

subgenres.name: Neofolklore
subgenres.desc: Short-lived movement that reincorporated traditional Chilean folklore into modern production and styling inspired by foreign musicians.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción chilena
subgenres.desc: Socially conscious style that sought to recover traditional Chilean folk music and fuse it with the broader musical trends of Latin America.

subgenres.name: Tonada chilena
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk from the Chilean countryside distinguished by its prominent melody.

subgenres.name: Chuntunqui romántico
subgenres.desc: Vibrant Bolivian genre set in 6/8 meter featuring choral refrains, harmonic progressions, and lyrics exploring the subject of romantic love.

subgenres.name: Conjunto andino
subgenres.desc: Urban folk ensembles using musical instruments of Andean Indigenous origin or association; despite frequent association with Indigenous villages, they bear little resemblance to the Indigenous expressions of the Southern Andes.

subgenres.name: Cuban Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the wide variety of traditions from the island of Cuba.

subgenres.name: Abakuá Music
subgenres.desc: Ritual music associated with the Abakuá religious fraternity of Cuba, descending from the Ékpè tradition of West Africa.

subgenres.name: Chachachá
subgenres.desc: Ballroom dance music derived from Danzón.

subgenres.name: Changüí
subgenres.desc: One of the oldest popular Cuban styles, originating in the 19th century with slaves that worked in sugar refineries near Baracoa who combined elements of Spanish popular songs with Bantu traditions.

subgenres.name: Conga
subgenres.desc: Evolved alongside Rumba cubana in the late 19th century, featuring large and heterogenous percussion sections performing simple and syncopated rhythms alongside a small wind section.

subgenres.name: Cuban Charanga
subgenres.desc: Played by traditional Cuban ensembles, influenced by Son cubano but performed on European instruments such as piano, bass, violins, and flutes.

subgenres.name: Cubaton
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically and vocally inspired by major elements of Cuban Music.

subgenres.name: Reparto
subgenres.desc: Incorporating Cuban Music elements, resulting in dynamic rhythms and a sound palette that typically features  Salsa-like guitar picking.

subgenres.name: Danzón
subgenres.desc: Development on Habanera in 2/4 time, featuring African influence through complex cross-rhythms, that would become the most popular style of dance music in Cuba during the late 19th century and early 20th century.

subgenres.name: Descarga
subgenres.desc: Cuban genre consisting of improvised jam sessions incorporating elements of Jazz and Afro-Cuban music.

subgenres.name: Filin
subgenres.desc: Emotional style that appeared in La Habana during the late 1940s, deeply influenced by the melodic and expressive style of Vocal Jazz.

subgenres.name: Guajira
subgenres.desc: Originally developed in Cuba between the 18th and 19th Century as a narrative style influenced by Tonada chilena.

subgenres.name: Guaracha
subgenres.desc: Humorous song with short notes and a fast tempo that commonly alternates a short fourth line verse with a repeated fourth line chorus.

subgenres.name: Habanera
subgenres.desc: Based around the Habanera rhythm, where the most typical instruments used are guitars, lutes, and bandurrias.

subgenres.name: Mambo
subgenres.desc: Dance-oriented evolution from Danzón during the late 1930s.

subgenres.name: Mozambique
subgenres.desc: Cuban genre featuring energetic, African-influenced percussion.

subgenres.name: Pachanga
subgenres.desc: Combination of Merengue, Conga, Rumba cubana, and Cumbia; fast, festive, and playful.

subgenres.name: Pilón
subgenres.desc: Featuring rhythms described as mimicking those created while pounding sugarcane with African baton-like tools.

subgenres.name: Rumba cubana
subgenres.desc: Folkloric manifestation of Afro-Cuban music that encompasses dance, voice, and drums.

subgenres.name: Guaguancó
subgenres.desc: Emerged after the abolition of slavery in Cuba in 1886; usually features a lead singer, accompanied by three large drums, known as tumbadoras or congas, and a call-and-response chorus.

subgenres.name: Santería Music
subgenres.desc: Afro-Cuban genre played in religious rituals, combining traditions from both the Cuban and the Yorùbá people.

subgenres.name: Son cubano
subgenres.desc: Cuban style popular from the 1920s to the 1950s that combines the structure of Spanish song-oriented styles with African rhythms and percussion.

subgenres.name: Bolero son
subgenres.desc: Blend of Bolero and Son cubano that appeared during the 1920s.

subgenres.name: Son montuno
subgenres.desc: Developed in the 1940s, characterized by more elaborate instrumental arrangements and larger ensembles typically adding a horn section, conga drums, and piano.

subgenres.name: Songo
subgenres.desc: Cuban style originating in the late 1960s, combining elements from Rumba cubana and Son cubano with Jazz and Funk.

subgenres.name: Timba
subgenres.desc: Combines Salsa with other genres such as Hip Hop, Disco, Funk, Jazz and Rock.

subgenres.name: Trova
subgenres.desc: One of the most ancient expressions of Cuban Music, based around lone Singer-Songwriters who use nothing but a guitar as their preferred accompaniment and place emphasis on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Tumba francesa
subgenres.desc: Combination of traditional music from Benin with French ballroom dancing that originates in the Oriente province (formerly Santiago de Cuba Province) in Cuba.

subgenres.name: Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Danceable folk genre formed during the 19th century in Colombia and eastern Panama.

subgenres.name: Cumbia argentina
subgenres.desc: Almost always features synthesizer keyboards and electronic percussion with an upbeat rhythm.

subgenres.name: Cumbia santafesina
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Argentinian province of Santa Fe, particularly in its capital city Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz, with lyrics that tend to be romantic and relatively clean compared to later Cumbia argentina.

subgenres.name: Cumbia turra
subgenres.desc: Cumbia argentina heavily influenced by Reggaetón and characterized by hard-hitting bass and heavy use of samples and Auto-Tune.

subgenres.name: Cumbia villera
subgenres.desc: Developed in the villa miserias (shanty towns) by the lower classes of Argentina in the early 2000s, featuring basic rhythms and low budget productions combined with lyrics that can be openly sexual or touch on sociopolitical issues.

subgenres.name: Cumbia chilena
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Chilean Music into the traditional sound of Cumbia.

subgenres.name: Nueva cumbia chilena
subgenres.desc: Rock-infused instrumentation, incorporating an eclectic repertoire of influences, such as Ska, Salsa, Indigenous Andean Music, Reggae, and Bolero.

subgenres.name: Cumbia colombiana
subgenres.desc: Style that incorporates elements of Colombian traditional music, which includes and keeps influences from Spanish, African, and Indigenous cultures.

subgenres.name: Cumbia mexicana
subgenres.desc: Incorporation of Rock & Roll, Mexican popular music, and Cuban influences, often adopting electric instruments, brass ensembles, accordion, and Cuban timbales, while retaining a beat-driven sound and traditional Colombian features.

subgenres.name: Cumbia sonidera
subgenres.desc: Cumbia mexicana from Mexico City that developed in the 1990s as discomóviles (analogous to DJs) experimented with slowing down original cumbia to fit the popular dance tempos.

subgenres.name: Cumbia rebajada
subgenres.desc: Based on Cumbia colombiana slowed down to around 76 bpm, with a lower timbre and less joyful sound.

subgenres.name: Cumbia peruana
subgenres.desc: Developed in Peru and diversified into various subgenres, each with its own regional influences.

subgenres.name: Chicha
subgenres.desc: Emerged during the Andean migration to the Peruvian coast between the 1960s and 1980s; largely influenced by Huayno and occasionally Psychedelic Rock

subgenres.name: Cumbia amazónica
subgenres.desc: Mixes Cumbia peruana with selvatic dances, Afro-Latin rhythms, Surf Rock, and Psychedelic Rock between the 1960s and 1980s.

subgenres.name: Cumbia norteña peruana
subgenres.desc: Developed on the Peruvian coast, with influences from Cumbia colombiana and cumbia ecuatoriana and lyrics mostly about love and heartbreak.

subgenres.name: Cumbia pop
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Río de la Plata region in the mid-2010s, featuring Latin Pop influences and lyrics related to romance, youth, and fun.

subgenres.name: Cumbia salvadoreña
subgenres.desc: Takes influence from local Salvadoran music and traditionally features a distinctive ensemble.

subgenres.name: Digital Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Merecumbé
subgenres.desc: Colombian genre which combines Cumbia with Merengue.

subgenres.name: Currulao
subgenres.desc: Pacific coast Afro-Colombian music and folk dance performed by a marimba/percussion ensemble with heavy use of call-and-response vocals.

subgenres.name: Dembow
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Dominican Republic during the early 1990s, featuring rapping indebted to Hip Hop and a style drawing on Dancehall, particularly the "Dem Bow" riddim.

subgenres.name: Gaita zuliana
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the state of Zulia in the 1950s, merging Spanish Folk Music and Venezuelan Christmas carols.

subgenres.name: Guarania
subgenres.desc: Slow and melancholic rhythms, primarily performed on the Paraguayan harp.

subgenres.name: Hispanic American Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses many varieties of folk traditions from Hispanic America.

subgenres.name: Bambuco
subgenres.desc: Follows a 6/8 or 3/4 time signature with non-percussive instrumentation, often melancholic in sound with bright guitars and a rich melodic base.

subgenres.name: Bomba
subgenres.desc: Percussive style from Puerto Rico, generally considered to be derived from West Africa.

subgenres.name: Candombe
subgenres.desc: Uruguayan popular music originating among Montevideo's Afro-Uruguayan population, based on three differently-sized drums.

subgenres.name: Canto a lo poeta
subgenres.desc: Sung poetry traditional to Chile and transmitted orally from one generation to another.

subgenres.name: Carranga
subgenres.desc: Colombian folk music that originated in Boyacá province, best known for its wordplay and humorous lyrics.

subgenres.name: Chacarera
subgenres.desc: Originated in northwest Argentina and southern Bolivia around 1850, typically in 6/8 and traditionally performed with instruments like the guitar, bombo legüero (traditional drum), and violin.

subgenres.name: Chamamé
subgenres.desc: Mixes native Guaraní music with Polka paraguaya and European Schottische music.

subgenres.name: Chamamé tropical
subgenres.desc: Takes heavy influence from the energy and instrumentation of Cumbia, popular in the late 1970s and 1980s.

subgenres.name: Chamarrita rioplatense
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance featuring similar rhythms to Milonga and typically performed with the guitar and accordion.

subgenres.name: Cueca
subgenres.desc: Popular in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia, accompanied by a 6/8 or 3/4 time signature and usually structured into 14 verses.

subgenres.name: Jibaro
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the mountain-dwelling jibaro people that live primarily in Puerto Rico.

subgenres.name: Joropo
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Creole music and the Venezuelan waltz.

subgenres.name: Malagueña venezolana
subgenres.desc: Traditional musical accompaniment to the Venezuelan 'velorios de cruz de mayo' celebrations, played with the mandolin (as lead instrument), cuatro and guitar.

subgenres.name: Mexican Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Mexican people.

subgenres.name: Canto cardenche
subgenres.desc: Overtly dramatic, and melancholic A cappella performed in the Comarca Lagunera region in northeast Mexico.

subgenres.name: Pirekua
subgenres.desc: Traditional style of the P’urhépecha people, typically slow and in 3/8 or 6/8 time.

subgenres.name: Son calentano
subgenres.desc: Usually dominated by violin with accompaniment mainly provided by guitars and tamboras, occasionally dancers will stomp over a platform.

subgenres.name: Son huasteco
subgenres.desc: Bold rhythmic structure, lively violin playing, and extensive use of falsetto.

subgenres.name: Son istmeño
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, traditionally played by guitar, requinto, marimba, and bajoquinto, usually played in 3/4 time.

subgenres.name: Son jarocho
subgenres.desc: Mexican Folk Music from the Gulf Coast Mexican state of Veracruz, with both Spanish and indigenous influences.

subgenres.name: Trova yucateca
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by Cuban Music, freely embracing Bolero, clave and Bambuco.

subgenres.name: Milonga
subgenres.desc: Characterized by a slow rhythm usually performed on a guitar; generally considered a precursor to Tango.

subgenres.name: Muliza
subgenres.desc: Mestizo folk genre popular in the central Peruvian Andes, characterized by a pronounced, though sedate, rhythm; traces of Andean melody; and octosyllabic verses.

subgenres.name: Música llanera
subgenres.desc: Traditional music originating from the Llanos region of Colombia and Venezuela.

subgenres.name: Plena
subgenres.desc: Folk genre from Puerto Rico played with hand drums called panderetas.

subgenres.name: Saya
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced, percussive traditional genre created by the Afro-Bolivian people.

subgenres.name: Tamborito
subgenres.desc: Folk music and dance from Panama dating back to the 17th century.

subgenres.name: Taquirari
subgenres.desc: Developed by the indigenous peoples of eastern Bolivia, bringing in some elements of Hispanic Music, and featuring a syncopated rhythm.

subgenres.name: Tonada chilena
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk from the Chilean countryside distinguished by its prominent melody.

subgenres.name: Yaraví
subgenres.desc: Peruvian criollo-mestizo songs with recurring themes of sadness and unrequited love, usually in 6/8 meter.

subgenres.name: Zamacueca
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance of 19th century Peru, sung in the minor mode and accompanied by a varying combination of guitar, vihuela, harp and cajón.

subgenres.name: Zamba
subgenres.desc: Folk dance that evolved out of Peruvian Zamacueca during the 19th century.

subgenres.name: Huayno
subgenres.desc: Andean dance music that incorporates both pre-Hispanic and Western musical elements.

subgenres.name: Bolivian Huayño
subgenres.desc: One of the most popular genres of Andean music in Bolivia, particularly present in the departments of Cochabamba, Chuquisaca, La Paz, Oruro and Potosí.

subgenres.name: Carnavalito
subgenres.desc: Fast and lively; mostly played in northwestern Argentina in the provinces of Jujuy, Salta, and Tucumán.

subgenres.name: Chimaychi
subgenres.desc: Slower variant, traditionally lacking guitar or mandolin, found in the eastern provinces of Áncash department.

subgenres.name: Latin Alternative
subgenres.desc: Incorporates common elements from Hispanic American Music like Cumbia, Tango or Mexican Music into Rock.

subgenres.name: Nueva cumbia chilena
subgenres.desc: Rock-infused instrumentation, incorporating an eclectic repertoire of influences, such as Ska, Salsa, Indigenous Andean Music, Reggae, and Bolero.

subgenres.name: Latin American Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Western Classical Music with influences from Hispanic American Music.

subgenres.name: Latin Disco
subgenres.desc: Disco that incorporates elements from Hispanic American Music styles.

subgenres.name: Latin Electronic
subgenres.desc: Combines Electronic with Latin American influences; started at the end of the 1990s.

subgenres.name: Changa tuki
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Caracas; highly influenced by 1990s Techno and Tribal House, featuring fast tempos, strident synthesizers, hard-thumping percussion lines, and plenty of breakbeats.

subgenres.name: Digital Cumbia
subgenres.desc: Mixes an Electronic sound into traditional Cumbia through influences from House, Dancehall, Hyphy, and Dubstep.

subgenres.name: Electro latino
subgenres.desc: Mixes elements of Merengue and Reggaetón with polished production from mainstream House subgenres; often shares traits with Latin Pop, having anthemic melodies and verse-chorus structures.

subgenres.name: Electrotango
subgenres.desc: Combines Tango rhythms and melodies with Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Nortec

subgenres.name: Tribal Guarachero

subgenres.name: Latin Funk

subgenres.name: Latin Pop
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements and tropes from Hispanic and Latin American forms of music into a commercial Pop context.

subgenres.name: Cumbia pop
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Río de la Plata region in the mid-2010s, featuring Latin Pop influences and lyrics related to romance, youth, and fun.

subgenres.name: Tropipop
subgenres.desc: Subgenre of Colombian origin fusing Vallenato instrumentation into a Latin Pop context.

subgenres.name: Latin Rock

subgenres.name: Latin Soul

subgenres.name: Merengue
subgenres.desc: Dominican Republic dance genre that had a commercial boom at the end of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Mambo urbano
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically simpler and more eclectic style, absorbing influences from Hip Hop, Reggaetón, and other modern genres, particularly in regards to vocals.

subgenres.name: Merecumbé
subgenres.desc: Colombian genre which combines Cumbia with Merengue.

subgenres.name: Merengue típico
subgenres.desc: Earliest, most stripped-down form of Merengue.

subgenres.name: Merenhouse
subgenres.desc: Popularized by Dominican-American artists of the 1990s, blending modern Merengue with electronic instrumentation and the combination of rapping/singing vocals.

subgenres.name: Tecnomerengue
subgenres.desc: Fuses basic Merengue rhythms with influences from Cumbia and Lambada, being largely synthesized, with live instruments usually limited to percussion and brass.

subgenres.name: Mexican Music
subgenres.desc: Music of Mexico and those deeply rooted in Mexican traditions.

subgenres.name: Bandas de viento de México
subgenres.desc: Mexican ensemble with many regional variations dating back to the 1860s and 1870s, when locals attempted to imitate the military bands that were present in the country.

subgenres.name: Banda sinaloense
subgenres.desc: Performed with militaristic-type arrangements of traditional Bandas de viento de México, with prominence on the tuba/sousaphone backing and tenor tuned horns.

subgenres.name: Movimiento alterado
subgenres.desc: Arose from Sinaloa in the late 2000s; radicalizes some of the characteristics of Banda sinaloense and Norteño.

subgenres.name: Tecnobanda
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s from the Banda sinaloense tradition, replacing certain instruments with synthesizers and electric instruments, allowing for faster tempos.

subgenres.name: Chilena
subgenres.desc: Developed when music from the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca in Mexico mixed with Cueca brought by Chilean sailors to the region in the 19th century.

subgenres.name: Corrido
subgenres.desc: Narrative ballad which arose in the late 18th century and flourished after the Mexican Independence War, originally meant for folk singers to spread news throughout Mexico accompanied by a guitar.

subgenres.name: Cumbia mexicana
subgenres.desc: Incorporation of Rock & Roll, Mexican popular music, and Cuban influences, often adopting electric instruments, brass ensembles, accordion, and Cuban timbales, while retaining a beat-driven sound and traditional Colombian features.

subgenres.name: Cumbia sonidera

subgenres.name: Cumbia rebajada
subgenres.desc: Based on Cumbia colombiana slowed down to around 76 bpm, with a lower timbre and less joyful sound.

subgenres.name: Cumbiatón
subgenres.desc: Combining Reggaetón  with Cumbia mexicana, and less frequently with other forms of traditional Mexican Music.

subgenres.name: Mariachi
subgenres.desc: Mexican style performed in unique costumes by ensembles known as mariachi bands, with a distinctive sound combining high, bright tones with low and rich voicings.

subgenres.name: Mexican Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Mexican people.

subgenres.name: Canto cardenche

subgenres.name: Trova yucateca
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by Cuban Music, freely embracing Bolero, clave and Bambuco.

subgenres.name: Norteño
subgenres.desc: More traditional, rural version of Tejano Music whose name translates to "northern".

subgenres.name: Cumbia norteña mexicana
subgenres.desc: Norteño heavily influenced by Cumbia.

subgenres.name: Duranguense
subgenres.desc: Features aspects of banda music, sped up, with the addition of synthesizers.

subgenres.name: Movimiento alterado
subgenres.desc: Arose from Sinaloa in the late 2000s; radicalizes some of the characteristics of Banda sinaloense and Norteño.

subgenres.name: Sierreño
subgenres.desc: Norteño that is mainly played with guitars, as opposed to the traditional bajo sexto used in norteño.

subgenres.name: Corrido tumbado
subgenres.desc: Modern take of regional Mexican music derived from Sierreño with heavy influence from the atmosphere of Trap music, while not engaging in that genre's characteristic sound.

subgenres.name: Ranchera
subgenres.desc: Originating in rural Mexico in the 19th century and popularized in the 1930s; emphasizes passionate and emotional performances and love-focused lyrics, often performed with a Mariachi ensemble.

subgenres.name: Tejano Music
subgenres.desc: Mexican-American style infusing the conjunto Norteño ensemble with European dances and American popular music.

subgenres.name: New Mexico Music
subgenres.desc: Derived from the Traditional Folk Music of New Mexico mixed with influences from Western, Country and Norteño, particularly associated with Spanish-speaking Nuevomexicanos.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción latinoamericana
subgenres.desc: Politically-charged messages associated with the rise of leftist social movements; striving for a renewal of traditional Latin and Hispanic American Folk Music expressions.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción chilena
subgenres.desc: Socially conscious style that sought to recover traditional Chilean folk music and fuse it with the broader musical trends of Latin America.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: Onda nueva
subgenres.desc: Based on Joropo, it incorporates elements of Bossa nova and Jazz.

subgenres.name: Pasillo
subgenres.desc: Traditional dance popular in Ecuador and Colombia; based on European Waltz and often performed with guitar and mandolin.

subgenres.name: Peruvian Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the Peruvian people.

subgenres.name: Chimaychi
subgenres.desc: Slower variant, traditionally lacking guitar or mandolin, found in the eastern provinces of Áncash department.

subgenres.name: Cumbia peruana
subgenres.desc: Developed in Peru and diversified into various subgenres, each with its own regional influences.

subgenres.name: Chicha
subgenres.desc: Emerged during the Andean migration to the Peruvian coast between the 1960s and 1980s; largely influenced by Huayno and occasionally Psychedelic Rock

subgenres.name: Cumbia amazónica
