subgenres.name: Cumbia norteña peruana
subgenres.desc: Developed on the Peruvian coast, with influences from Cumbia colombiana and cumbia ecuatoriana and lyrics mostly about love and heartbreak.

subgenres.name: Huaylarsh
subgenres.desc: Festive Andean music with vibrant rhythm featuring saxophones and violins, typical of the central Peruvian region.

subgenres.name: Música criolla peruana
subgenres.desc: Coastal Peruvian music tradition blending Spanish, African, and local influences, developed in urban contexts through creolized European dance forms.

subgenres.name: Festejo
subgenres.desc: Happy and danceable Afro-Peruvian rhythm originating in the 17th century.

subgenres.name: Landó
subgenres.desc: 16th-century Afro-Peruvian dance and music style, played primarily on the cajón and the creole guitar in a 12/8 rhythm.

subgenres.name: Marinera
subgenres.desc: Component of the coastal dance of the same name, often considered the national dance of Peru.

subgenres.name: Polka peruana
subgenres.desc: Peruvian adaptation of European Polka, blending Afro-Peruvian rhythms and criollo melodies.

subgenres.name: Tondero
subgenres.desc: Backing to the fast-paced dance that originated in northern Peru in the region of Piura of the same name; bands consist of a singer, a small chorus, two guitarists, along with the cajón and sometimes a spoon player.

subgenres.name: Vals criollo
subgenres.desc: Originally characterized by its 3/4 time, heavy reliance on strongly plucked phrase on upper strings, and its guitar solo; often accompanied by a duet or a solo singer, normally singing about patriotic themes or social dilemmas.

subgenres.name: Tunantada
subgenres.desc: Originating in the central Peruvian region, characterized by cheerful and festive rhythm, with indigenous and mestizo influences.

subgenres.name: Polka paraguaya
subgenres.desc: Popular music originating in Paraguay and the Province of Corrientes (Argentina), derived from the Bohemian polka and traditional music of Hispanic-Jesuit origin.

subgenres.name: Porro
subgenres.desc: Lively Hispanic American Music and dance style native to Colombia which gained popularity in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Purísima
subgenres.desc: Nicaraguan Hymn to the Immaculate Conception of Mary, sung during holiday celebrations and in liturgical or parochial services.

subgenres.name: Reggaetón
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Dancehall and mainly characterized by its heavy emphasis on the "dembow" rhythm; developed in Puerto Rico in the early 1990s under heavy influence from Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Bachatón
subgenres.desc: Mixes Bachata melodies and instrumentation with Reggaetón rhythms, rapping, and DJing.

subgenres.name: Cubaton
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically and vocally inspired by major elements of Cuban Music.

subgenres.name: Reparto
subgenres.desc: Incorporating Cuban Music elements, resulting in dynamic rhythms and a sound palette that typically features  Salsa-like guitar picking.

subgenres.name: Cumbiatón
subgenres.desc: Combining Reggaetón  with Cumbia mexicana, and less frequently with other forms of traditional Mexican Music.

subgenres.name: Doble paso
subgenres.desc: Frenetic and intense high tempo variant in comparison to the standard drum patterns, often used to accompany the dance of the same name.

subgenres.name: Neoperreo
subgenres.desc: Heavy emphasis on rhythm, influence from global trends in club music, and generally progressive lyrics.

subgenres.name: RKT
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2010s, characterized by minimalistic, rhythm-centric production heavily influenced by Cumbia villera and other Cumbia argentina styles.

subgenres.name: Romantic Style
subgenres.desc: Melodic and sentimental style characterized by emotive vocals and mellow sound with a less explicit tone, emphasizing romantic love themes, blending Contemporary R&B, Latin Pop and romantic ballad influences, popularized during early 2000s to 2010s.

subgenres.name: Rhumba
subgenres.desc: Commercial adaptation of various Latin American genres; developed during the 1930s as the so-called "rhumba craze" unfolded in the United States.

subgenres.name: Rioplatense Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the people of the Rio de la Plata region.

subgenres.name: Candombe
subgenres.desc: Uruguayan popular music originating among Montevideo's Afro-Uruguayan population, based on three differently-sized drums.

subgenres.name: Candombe beat
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Uruguayan Candombe with elements of Rock music.

subgenres.name: Chamarrita rioplatense
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance featuring similar rhythms to Milonga and typically performed with the guitar and accordion.

subgenres.name: Cumbia pop
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Río de la Plata region in the mid-2010s, featuring Latin Pop influences and lyrics related to romance, youth, and fun.

subgenres.name: Electrotango
subgenres.desc: Combines Tango rhythms and melodies with Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Milonga
subgenres.desc: Characterized by a slow rhythm usually performed on a guitar; generally considered a precursor to Tango.

subgenres.name: Murga uruguaya
subgenres.desc: Variant originated in Montevideo that stands out for its rhythms, nasal vocals and choral arrangements.

subgenres.name: Tango
subgenres.desc: Melancholic sound generally led by a guitar or bandoneon, originating in Buenos Aires by the late 19th century and gaining worldwide popularity from the 1920s to the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Finnish Tango
subgenres.desc: Melancholic style developed in Finland in the 1930s and 1940s, influenced by traditional minor-key Finnish Folk Music melodies and the rhythms of German marches.

subgenres.name: Tango nuevo
subgenres.desc: Adds new elements into traditional Argentine Tango, most importantly the incorporation of Jazz and Western Classical Music.

subgenres.name: Rock andino
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the Andean countries in the late 1960s and early 1970s, incorporating traditional instruments and harmonies from Indigenous Andean Music within a Rock format.

subgenres.name: Salsa
subgenres.desc: Often incorporating congas, timbales and bongos as well as smaller instruments, such as maracas, clave and güiro.

subgenres.name: Salsa choke
subgenres.desc: Colombian style that takes heavy influence from Reggaetón, House, Hip Hop, and various Afro-Colombian and Colombian Pacific styles.

subgenres.name: Salsa dura

subgenres.name: Salsa romántica

subgenres.name: Timba

subgenres.name: Son de pascua

subgenres.name: Son nica
subgenres.desc: Nicaraguan popular rhythm in distinctive guitar strums, with lyrics relating to the countryside and peasant life.

subgenres.name: Tamborera

subgenres.name: Tropicanibalismo
subgenres.desc: Colombian scene born in the early 2000s with the intention of reinventing Colombian coastal music, from a more current and experimental approach.

subgenres.name: Vallenato
subgenres.desc: Accordion-led style of folk and popular music originating in Colombia's Caribbean region.

subgenres.name: Vals venezolano
subgenres.desc: Venezuelan dance music that employs heavy use of syncopation, complex rhythms, and regional instruments.

subgenres.name: Xuc
subgenres.desc: Danceable style from El Salvador developed in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Murga
subgenres.desc: Popular carnival music traditional in some cities of Spain and Hispanic America.

subgenres.name: Murga uruguaya
subgenres.desc: Variant originated in Montevideo that stands out for its rhythms, nasal vocals and choral arrangements.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción
subgenres.desc: Latin American (Nueva canción latinoamericana) and Spanish (Nueva canción española) movement during the 1960s and 1970s.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción española
subgenres.desc: Arose in Spain in the 1960s, inspired in part by Nova cançó's reclaiming of Catalan regional identity, that spread across the country in regional variations.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción latinoamericana
subgenres.desc: Politically-charged messages associated with the rise of leftist social movements; striving for a renewal of traditional Latin and Hispanic American Folk Music expressions.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción chilena
subgenres.desc: Socially conscious style that sought to recover traditional Chilean folk music and fuse it with the broader musical trends of Latin America.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: Philippine Rondalla
subgenres.desc: Ensemble of plucked string instruments typically performed for traditional Filipino folk dances; known for its distinct sparkling and tinkling tremolo sound.

subgenres.name: Romance
subgenres.desc: Form of narrative sung Poetry rooted in medieval Spanish oral tradition, characterized by octosyllabic verses and assonant rhyme. Evolving from epic Medieval Lyric Poetry, and later spread across Hispanic America.

subgenres.name: Spanish Music
subgenres.desc: Music of Spain.

subgenres.name: Bolero español
subgenres.desc: Spanish genre originating in the 18th century, based around moderate tempos in a 3/4 time signature accompanied by a dance of the same name.

subgenres.name: Flamenco
subgenres.desc: Traditional Spanish style based around fiery acoustic guitar rhythms, emotional vocals, and accompaniment from traditional percussion and dance.

subgenres.name: Bulería
subgenres.desc: Fast flamenco made up of a 12 beat cycle characterized by its vibrant, spontaneous and festive style.

subgenres.name: Flamenco nuevo
subgenres.desc: Contemporary style of Flamenco which departs from tradition by incorporating influences from other genres like Jazz, Blues, and Rock.

subgenres.name: Flamenco Jazz
subgenres.desc: Combination of Jazz with Flamenco nuevo, the contemporary style of Flamenco, which was pioneered in the late 1960s.

subgenres.name: Rumba flamenca
subgenres.desc: Flamenco subgenre, derived from the exchange of influences between Spain and Latin America.

subgenres.name: Flamenco Pop
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Flamenco sub-styles into a more commercial Pop form; particularly through the vocal style and rhythms.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción española
subgenres.desc: Arose in Spain in the 1960s, inspired in part by Nova cançó's reclaiming of Catalan regional identity, that spread across the country in regional variations.

subgenres.name: Rock andaluz
subgenres.desc: Emerged during the mid-1970s in Spain; primarily utilizes Flamenco and often Symphonic Prog elements.

subgenres.name: Rumba catalana
subgenres.desc: Cheerful Catalan genre that takes influences from Rumba cubana, Andalusian Rumba flamenca, and Pop.

subgenres.name: Spanish Classical Music

subgenres.name: Canto mozárabe

subgenres.name: Zarzuela

subgenres.name: Género chico

subgenres.name: Zarzuela barroca

subgenres.name: Zarzuela grande
subgenres.desc: Romantic musical comedy akin to Operetta developed during the mid-19th century.

subgenres.name: Spanish Folk Music

subgenres.name: Andalusian Folk Music

subgenres.name: Saeta

subgenres.name: Sevillanas

subgenres.name: Aragonese Folk Music

subgenres.name: Asturian Folk Music

subgenres.name: Canarian Folk Music

subgenres.name: Copla

subgenres.name: Cuplé
subgenres.desc: Originally developed in the 19th century as a blend of old theatre Spanish styles based in short monologues (jácara and tonadilla) and French Couplet.

subgenres.name: Galician Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Galician people.

subgenres.name: Pasodoble
subgenres.desc: Mainly instrumental Spanish style primarily associated with bullfighting and popular celebrations, believed to originate from a double-time military march from France in the 18th century.

subgenres.name: Valencian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Valencian Country.

subgenres.name: Tecnorumba
subgenres.desc: Blend of the themes and singing style of Rumba flamenca with the most commercial forms of House, Techno, and Makina.

subgenres.name: Tonada potosina

subgenres.name: Harawi

subgenres.name: Huaylarsh

subgenres.name: Huayno

subgenres.name: Bolivian Huayño

subgenres.name: Chimaychi

subgenres.name: Morenada

subgenres.name: Tonada potosina
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk sung in Quechua, played on charangos and guitarillas, with a catchy, lively rhythm.

subgenres.name: Inuit Vocal Games

subgenres.name: Mesoamerican Music

subgenres.name: Ancient Levitical Music

subgenres.name: Chazzanut

subgenres.name: Ashkenazi Cantorial Music
subgenres.desc: Artistic, refined form of Chazzanut that greatly borrows from and implements elements of Western Classical Music and Christian Liturgical Music into the context of liturgical singing and chanting.

subgenres.name: Kriyat haTorah
subgenres.desc: Practice of ritual liturgical chanting of the Masoretic text of the Tanakh, often done during synagogue services.

subgenres.name: Piyyut

subgenres.name: Muzikat dika'on

subgenres.name: Muzika yehudit mekorit
subgenres.desc: Rooted in traditional Jewish Music, especially Hasidic Music; incorporates modern influences, typically written on subjects of devotion and religion.

subgenres.name: Oriental Jewish Music
subgenres.desc: Comprises the many traditions and styles of the various groups of Jews from the cultural East, loosely covering the Jewish groups of the Middle East, North Africa, and Central Asia.

subgenres.name: Baqashot
subgenres.desc: Collection of prayers, songs, supplications, and poems traditionally sung by Sephardic Jewish communities on Saturdays mornings.

subgenres.name: Orthodox Pop

subgenres.name: Sephardic Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the various musical traditions of Sephardi Jews.

subgenres.name: Baqashot
subgenres.desc: Collection of prayers, songs, supplications, and poems traditionally sung by Sephardic Jewish communities on Saturdays mornings.

subgenres.name: Ladino Folksong
subgenres.desc: Ladino-language Traditional Folk Music tunes that were written and preserved by Sephardic Jews.

subgenres.name: Maftirim

subgenres.name: Maqāmic Music

subgenres.name: Arabic Classical Music

subgenres.name: Andalusian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Arabic Classical Music tradition that had its beginnings in Al-Andalus, the medieval Islamic Iberian peninsula, which later spread and developed in the Maghreb.

subgenres.name: Iraqi Maqam
subgenres.desc: Highly structured but semi-improvised and rhythmically complex compositions built around set structures which consist of specific maqam modes.

subgenres.name: Sawt

subgenres.name: Azerbaijani Mugham
subgenres.desc: Highly improvisational form of modal music characterized by the singing style and the themes of Azerbaijan’s history.

subgenres.name: Persian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional art music of the Persian civilization.

subgenres.name: Shashmaqam
subgenres.desc: Modal suite that brings together lyrical and instrumental songs, poetry, and dance shared by Tajik Music and Uzbek Music.

subgenres.name: Sufiana kalam
subgenres.desc: Classical music from Kashmir, the northernmost part of the Indian subcontinent.

subgenres.name: Turkish Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Classical music of Turkey, which uses the makam modal system, with the primary emphasis often being on the singers, who are accompanied by small ensembles.

subgenres.name: Turkish Mevlevi Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music performed among Turkish practitioners of the Mevlevi order of Sufism.

subgenres.name: Twelve Muqam
subgenres.desc: Uyghur muqam suite of 12 different muqam performances, originating in Southern Xinjiang.

subgenres.name: Northern American Music

subgenres.name: Ambient Americana

subgenres.name: Americana

subgenres.name: American Folk Music

subgenres.name: Appalachian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Appalachian Mountains in the Eastern United States.

subgenres.name: Old-Time
subgenres.desc: Pre-Bluegrass North American string band styles, particularly those rooted in Appalachian Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Various styles of Blues originating in the rural US South, typically relying on expressive vocal delivery and featuring simple, usually acoustic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Delta Blues
subgenres.desc: One of the earliest forms of Blues, named for the Mississippi Delta region of the United States where it developed, with a highly rhythmic style and a typical 12-bar structure.

subgenres.name: Bentonia School
subgenres.desc: Brooding, hypnotic minor-key open-tuning guitar style with a looser structure, often featuring high, "haunting" vocals.

subgenres.name: Hill Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a steady hypnotic groove, sparse percussive and highly energetic guitar riffs, and often features meandering structures with unconventional and usually fewer chord changes compared to Delta Blues.

subgenres.name: Piedmont Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.

subgenres.name: Field Hollers
subgenres.desc: Created by African-American slaves working on cotton plantations, featuring expressive vocals to no strict rhythm.

subgenres.name: Fife and Drum Blues
subgenres.desc: Rooted in martial Fife and Drum Corps music, originated among Afro-American communities in Mississippi.

subgenres.name: Jug Band
subgenres.desc: Usually features a jug as the bass instrument as well as other homemade (or easily affordable) instruments, such as kazoos and washboards.

subgenres.name: Pennsylvania Dutch Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Pennsylvania Dutch.

subgenres.name: Ring Shout
subgenres.desc: Ritual practiced by African-Americans in the US South, characterized by shouting, chanting and people dancing in a circle while praying and clapping.

subgenres.name: Sacred Harp Singing
subgenres.desc: Predominantly 19th-century English hymns with tunes derived from old folk melodies.

subgenres.name: Spiritual
subgenres.desc: African American folk song based around Christian themes, originating during enslavement and emphasizing solidarity and freedom; musical features include call-and-response, "blue" notes, and expressive vocal timbres.

subgenres.name: Talking Blues
subgenres.desc: American Folk Music with spoken or nearly spoken vocals; often features dry humor and social commentary.

subgenres.name: Traditional Black Gospel
subgenres.desc: Born out of Spiritual in the early 20th century with influence from Southern Gospel and Blues, often featuring passionate or energetic vocal performances, motifs of salvation, and testaments of hardship.

subgenres.name: Traditional Cajun Music
subgenres.desc: Earliest and most "pure" form of Cajun Music, employing basic rhythms and frequent fiddle double stops.

subgenres.name: Traditional Country
subgenres.desc: Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Close Harmony

subgenres.name: Country Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: American Primitivism
subgenres.desc: Blends avant-garde and neo-classical compositions with traditional Country Blues fingerpicking techniques.

subgenres.name: Barbershop

subgenres.name: Jubilee

subgenres.name: Boogie Woogie

subgenres.name: Canadian Folk Music

subgenres.name: Canadian Maritime Folk

subgenres.name: Cape Breton Fiddling

subgenres.name: French-Canadian Folk Music

subgenres.name: Métis Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Canadian style blending First Nations and European musical influences into an up-tempo style of fiddling characterized by the use of syncopation and indigenous rhythms.

subgenres.name: Newfoundland Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada's easternmost province.

subgenres.name: Chanson québécoise
subgenres.desc: French-language music of the Québécois singer-songwriters.

subgenres.name: Chicago Polka
subgenres.desc: Polish-American style known for slower tempo, improvisation and the ensemble typically including the clarinet, trumpet, and concertina.

subgenres.name: Coon Song
subgenres.desc: Lyrical trend popular in the United States from around 1880 to 1920 that presents a racist and highly stereotyped image of African Americans connected with the subject matter and style of minstrel shows.

subgenres.name: Country
subgenres.desc: American genre derived from Southern and Appalachian forms of American Folk Music and later Rock and Pop influences, with a focus on the life and culture of rural America.

subgenres.name: Alt-Country
subgenres.desc: Arose in the 1980s and 1990s, performed by artists with roots in Alternative Rock and Indie Rock who were disconnected from the mainstream Country industry.

subgenres.name: Gothic Country
subgenres.desc: Evokes the Southern Gothic literary genre through morbid lyrical themes and melancholic sounds that emphasize its American Folk Music and Post-Punk influences.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Born in the Appalachian region of the United States during the late 1930s, characterized by fingerpicked banjo along with other traditional instruments.

subgenres.name: Progressive Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Modernization with varied influences including Jazz, Folk, Rock, and other forms of Country.

subgenres.name: Jamgrass
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes instrumental jamming and extended performances with many outside influences.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Contemporary Country
subgenres.desc: Incorporates both heavily Pop-influenced styles, and the more pop-averse movement of Neo-Traditionalist Country.

subgenres.name: Boyfriend Country
subgenres.desc: Soft, sentimental, and acoustic-leaning style featuring romantic lyrics, slick Contemporary R&B stylings, and light percussion.

subgenres.name: Bro-Country
subgenres.desc: 21st century style with an often party-oriented sound and lyrical content, taking strong influence from Hard Rock, Hip Hop and Pop.

subgenres.name: Neo-Traditionalist Country
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1980s as a reaction to the increased dominance of Country Pop, moving instead towards a Honky Tonk-rooted sound that centered the Singer-Songwriter.

subgenres.name: Country & Irish
subgenres.desc: Developed in Ireland; combines North American Country with Irish Folk Music influences, often in the form of traditional Irish songs that have been adapted into country numbers.

subgenres.name: Country Boogie
subgenres.desc: Uptempo style built around the Boogie Woogie rhythm, with strong beats and prominent electric guitar leads, made popular in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Country Folk
subgenres.desc: Emphasises Traditional Country instrumentation as well as influences from contemporary Singer-Songwriter traditions, such as a gentler disposition and prominent lyrical storytelling focus.

subgenres.name: Country Pop
subgenres.desc: Combination of Country with Pop to appeal to a larger audience.

subgenres.name: Boyfriend Country
subgenres.desc: Soft, sentimental, and acoustic-leaning style featuring romantic lyrics, slick Contemporary R&B stylings, and light percussion.

subgenres.name: Bro-Country
subgenres.desc: 21st century style with an often party-oriented sound and lyrical content, taking strong influence from Hard Rock, Hip Hop and Pop.

subgenres.name: Countrypolitan
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Pop-oriented orchestration and songwriting while reducing the role of Country instrumentation and rhythms; often featuring lush string arrangements and group backing vocals.

subgenres.name: Urban Cowboy
subgenres.desc: Melds Country and 1970s L.A. soft Pop, sometimes leaning towards Disco.

subgenres.name: Honky Tonk
subgenres.desc: Upbeat style that retains much of the common instrumentation of Traditional Country, as well as featuring prominent guitars (especially the steel guitar), strong backbeats and lyrics commonly about the working-class life.

subgenres.name: Bakersfield Sound
subgenres.desc: Heavily based on electric instrumentation and a defined backbeat.

subgenres.name: Truck Driving Country
subgenres.desc: Concerns the lifestyle of professional truck drivers, often drawing from Country Rock and Bakersfield Sound musically.

subgenres.name: Nashville Sound
subgenres.desc: Production style characterized by smooth vocals over a relaxed ensemble of guitars and rhythm section, and variously incorporating elements from other styles of Country and Pop.

subgenres.name: Countrypolitan
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Pop-oriented orchestration and songwriting while reducing the role of Country instrumentation and rhythms; often featuring lush string arrangements and group backing vocals.

subgenres.name: Progressive Country
subgenres.desc: Blend of traditionalist Country styles with elements of Rock, Contemporary Folk, and other countercultural genres; characterized by realistic, self-reflective lyrics and non-traditional songwriting and production elements.

subgenres.name: Outlaw Country
subgenres.desc: Rock-influenced reaction to mainstream Country Pop trends, featuring rebellious personas, darker lyrics, and Western-inspired outlaw imagery.

subgenres.name: Traditional Country
subgenres.desc: Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Close Harmony
subgenres.desc: Traditional two-part harmony singing performed mostly by brothers.

subgenres.name: Country Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Western
subgenres.desc: Reflects and portrays the lifestyles of cowboys and other settlers of the Western United States through both Traditional Folk Music and popular song.

subgenres.name: Western Swing
subgenres.desc: Blend of Traditional Country string instrumentation with the driving rhythms of Jazz and regional dance traditions, often prominently featuring fiddle and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Country Rock
subgenres.desc: Combination of contemporary Rock with more traditional American Country.

subgenres.name: Cosmic Country
subgenres.desc: Synthesizes various American musical influences and the exploratory ethoses of Psychedelia and Progressive Country to create an ethereal and more experimental sound still rooted in traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Cowboy Poetry
subgenres.desc: Descended from the oral traditions of cowboys and ranchers, written with traditional use of rhyme and meter, using humor and slang, and primarily concerning the cowboy profession, lifestyle, and legacy.

subgenres.name: Eastern-Style Polka
subgenres.desc: Fast, urban Polish-American style performed by a Big Band-like ensemble.

subgenres.name: Foxtrot
subgenres.desc: Lightly syncopated ballroom dance form in 4/4, most popular in the 1930s and closely associated with early Big Band Jazz.

subgenres.name: Greenlandic Music
subgenres.desc: Majorly from Inuit ethnic groups in Greenland, a large island between the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans.

subgenres.name: Kalattut
subgenres.desc: Distinctive Folk tradition shaped by European cultural exchanges and indigenous Greenlandic heritage.

subgenres.name: Tivaner inngernerlu
subgenres.desc: Pre-colonial Inuit Folk tradition centered around the qilaat (drum).

subgenres.name: Uaajeerneq
subgenres.desc: Ancient Greenlandic-Inuit dramatic performance characterized by percussion and idiosyncratic expression.

subgenres.name: Vaigat
subgenres.desc: Contemporary popular music shaped by American cultural exchanges and indigenous Greenlandic heritage.

subgenres.name: Hapa haole
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian musical traditions adapted to popular American Jazz and Pop styles.

subgenres.name: Indigenous North American Music
subgenres.desc: Diverse styles and genres developed by the indigenous peoples of present-day Canada, the United States and northwestern Mexico.

subgenres.name: Athabaskan Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Fiddle playing of the Northern Athabaskan Dene people of modern-day Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories.

subgenres.name: Ghost Dance Song
subgenres.desc: Songs accompanying the Ghost Dance, a 19th century religious movement.

subgenres.name: Inuit Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Inuit people, the aboriginal peoples inhabiting the Arctic regions of Canada, Alaska, and Greenland.

subgenres.name: Inuit Vocal Games
subgenres.desc: Practiced by the Inuit of Canada, two vocalists face each other decimeters away and try to outlast each other with intense and unusual vocal techniques.

subgenres.name: Tivaner inngernerlu
subgenres.desc: Pre-colonial Inuit Folk tradition centered around the qilaat (drum).

subgenres.name: Uaajeerneq
subgenres.desc: Ancient Greenlandic-Inuit dramatic performance characterized by percussion and idiosyncratic expression.

subgenres.name: James Bay Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Fiddle playing of the James Bay Cree people, characterised by a fusion of Scottish style with Cree rhythms.

subgenres.name: Métis Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the indigenous Métis people of Canada and the United States.

subgenres.name: Métis Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Canadian style blending First Nations and European musical influences into an up-tempo style of fiddling characterized by the use of syncopation and indigenous rhythms.

subgenres.name: Powwow Music
subgenres.desc: Drum-based traditional music of Plains region Native American tribes, traditionally played at Pow-wows.

subgenres.name: Pueblo Music
subgenres.desc: Rooted in the traditions of the Pueblo peoples, who are indigenous to the southwest United States.

subgenres.name: Rabbit Song
subgenres.desc: Indigenous North American ceremonial song cycles most associated with Southern Paiute, Ute, Mojave, and Chemehuevi traditions which feature short, repetitive, vocable-heavy melodies performed in long sequences that accompany trickster (rabbit) narratives and encode social knowledge.

subgenres.name: Louisiana Music
subgenres.desc: Regional Music from the US state of Louisiana.

subgenres.name: Cajun Music
subgenres.desc: Associated with the Cajun people of Louisiana where the genre was born, commonly regarded as an uptempo, accordion-driven style with a harsh, infectious beat.

subgenres.name: Traditional Cajun Music
subgenres.desc: Earliest and most "pure" form of Cajun Music, employing basic rhythms and frequent fiddle double stops.

subgenres.name: New Orleans Brass Band
subgenres.desc: New Orleans' unique combination of European-styled military bands with African folklore.

subgenres.name: New Orleans R&B
subgenres.desc: Increased rhythmic complexity with added focus on piano and horns.

subgenres.name: Swamp Blues
subgenres.desc: Originated in Baton Rouge, Louisiana in the 1950s, with a laid-back and relaxed sound that takes influence from Zydeco and Cajun Music.

subgenres.name: Swamp Pop
subgenres.desc: Uniquely Cajun style of Rhythm & Blues distinguished by tripleted pianos and a slow Blues structure.

subgenres.name: Zydeco
subgenres.desc: Uptempo accordion-led dance style mixing Creole and Cajun folk with African American popular music influences.

subgenres.name: Nouveau zydeco
subgenres.desc: Adds new elements into contemporary Zydeco, most importantly the incorporation of Funk, Contemporary R&B and Hip Hop characteristics.

subgenres.name: Minstrelsy
subgenres.desc: Popular song and entertainment tradition from the U.S. engendered in variety shows employing racist caricature and blackface.

subgenres.name: New Mexico Music
subgenres.desc: Derived from the Traditional Folk Music of New Mexico mixed with influences from Western, Country and Norteño, particularly associated with Spanish-speaking Nuevomexicanos.

subgenres.name: Pep Band
subgenres.desc: Performs at athletic events, and typically performs modified versions of Pop songs.

subgenres.name: Ragtime
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1890s; piano-led and characterized by a heavily syncopated rhythm.

subgenres.name: Cakewalk
subgenres.desc: Typically in 2/4 time with a distinctive "oompah" rhythm, named for a dance created by enslaved Black Americans as a mockery of the social dances of white slaveholders.

subgenres.name: Classic Ragtime
subgenres.desc: Draws on the complexity and formal structures of Western Classical Music, cycling through multiple strains (themes); emerged from Missouri's Sedalia school.

subgenres.name: Honky-Tonk Piano
subgenres.desc: Nostalgic revival popularised in the 1950s which is more upbeat and whimsical, with a bright and detuned piano sound.

subgenres.name: Novelty Piano
subgenres.desc: Popular in the 1920s; originated in Chicago and took influence from Jazz.

subgenres.name: Ragtime Song
subgenres.desc: Incorporates syncopated, "ragged" rhythms into popular song forms.

subgenres.name: Stride
subgenres.desc: Early form of Ragtime-derived Jazz with improvisational tendencies; named for the performers' left hand "striding" across the piano keyboard.

subgenres.name: Roots Rock
subgenres.desc: Consciously and predominantly incorporates elements of its predecessors and original roots such as Country, Blues, Rhythm & Blues, Rock & Roll, and American Folk Music, but also many other American traditions.

subgenres.name: Swamp Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from the musical styles and traditions of Louisiana.

subgenres.name: Tex-Mex
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock & Roll, Blues, Country, and several types of Hispanic American Music, particularly Tejano Music.

subgenres.name: Sacred Steel
subgenres.desc: Focused on instrumentals and played on the steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Shaker Music
subgenres.desc: Created by the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing, better known as Shakers, for worship.

subgenres.name: Southern Gospel
subgenres.desc: Initially sung A cappella by a Vocal Group quartet, sometimes with a pianist or guitar as accompaniment, with lyrics and messages primarily revolving around the teachings found within Christianity.

subgenres.name: Texan Music
subgenres.desc: Regional Music from the US state of Texas.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Electric Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Originating in (but not limited to) Texas; includes Jazz influences like Swing rhythms and sometimes the addition of a horn section.

subgenres.name: Tejano Music
subgenres.desc: Mexican-American style infusing the conjunto Norteño ensemble with European dances and American popular music.

subgenres.name: Tex-Mex
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock & Roll, Blues, Country, and several types of Hispanic American Music, particularly Tejano Music.

subgenres.name: Tin Pan Alley
subgenres.desc: Early era of popular song in the USA, broadly from the 1890s-1930s; influences include Ragtime, Vaudeville, and Parlour Music.

subgenres.name: Vaudeville
subgenres.desc: Performed in American musical theaters typically as part of a lowbrow, often comedic variety performance.

subgenres.name: Vaudeville Blues
subgenres.desc: Vaudeville incorporating heavy Blues elements.

subgenres.name: Oceanian Music
subgenres.desc: Rooted in the traditions of the geographic region of Oceania.

subgenres.name: Australian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of the European colonists and convicts in Australia.

subgenres.name: Indigenous Australian Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Aboriginal Australians and Torres Strait Islanders, collectively known as Indigenous Australians.

subgenres.name: Djanba
subgenres.desc: Sung and composed in the Murrinh-Patha language and consisting of a mixed group of men and women accompanied by bilma and handclaps, typically without didgeridoo.

subgenres.name: Wangga
subgenres.desc: Originated from the Daly region, consists of performances featuring wood sticks, didgeridoo and voice.

subgenres.name: Melanesian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Oceanian region of Melanesia.

subgenres.name: Fijian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Fijian people.

subgenres.name: Vude
subgenres.desc: Blends traditional local music with elements of Disco, Country and Rock.

subgenres.name: Kaneka
subgenres.desc: New Caledonian style of popular music that draws influence from traditional Melanesian music.

subgenres.name: Lokal musik
subgenres.desc: Created by local, rural artists from Papua New Guinea that incorporate some elements of Papuan Folk Music into Pop.

subgenres.name: Papuan Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Papuan people of New Guinea.

subgenres.name: Tolai Rock
subgenres.desc: Fuses the music of the Tolai people of Papua New Guinea with Rock.

subgenres.name: Micronesian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Micronesian peoples.

subgenres.name: Kantan Chamorrita
subgenres.desc: Improvised verse singing performed in the Chamorro language, traditional of the Marianas islands.

subgenres.name: Pacific Reggae
subgenres.desc: Developed in Pacific island communities, incorporating elements from local Oceanian Music styles.

subgenres.name: Jawaiian
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian branch of Reggae, typically blends local traditional melodies, harmonies, incorporating specialty instruments such as ukulele and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Polynesian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of Polynesia.

subgenres.name: Fijian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Fijian people.

subgenres.name: Vude
subgenres.desc: Blends traditional local music with elements of Disco, Country and Rock.

subgenres.name: Hawaiian Music
subgenres.desc: Includes a variety of syncopated rhythms, percussion and vocal styles, including chanting (mele) and falsetto.

subgenres.name: Hapa haole
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian musical traditions adapted to popular American Jazz and Pop styles.

subgenres.name: Jawaiian
subgenres.desc: Hawaiian branch of Reggae, typically blends local traditional melodies, harmonies, incorporating specialty instruments such as ukulele and steel guitar.

subgenres.name: Slack-Key Guitar
subgenres.desc: Originated in Hawaii and typically played with one's thumb in an alternating-bass pattern on the lower two or three strings.

subgenres.name: Himene tarava
subgenres.desc: Protestant choral songs in Tahiti and other southern Polynesian islands.

subgenres.name: Māori Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the indigenous Māori people of New Zealand.

subgenres.name: Samoan Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Samoan people.

subgenres.name: Tahitian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Tahitian people.

subgenres.name: Polyphonic Chant
subgenres.desc: Chanting that combines two or more melodic lines that are harmonically cohesive but differ in rhythm and utilize non-parallel motion.

subgenres.name: Ars nova
subgenres.desc: Period (around 1310-1380) that succeeded Ars antiqua, mixing the sacred with the secular.

subgenres.name: Ars subtilior
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the final period of late medieval music (around 1380-1420) and continued to use the technique of isorhythms but with added complexity.

subgenres.name: Cante alentejano
subgenres.desc: Traditional Portuguese Music based on vocal music from the Alentejo region.

subgenres.name: Cantu a tenore
subgenres.desc: Secular Polyphonic Chant from the Mediterranean island of Sardinia.

subgenres.name: Contenance angloise
subgenres.desc: Distinct style of Polyphonic Chant developed in fifteenth-century England.

subgenres.name: Ganga
subgenres.desc: Dissonant form of polyphonic singing from the regions of Herzegovina and Dalmatia.

subgenres.name: Himene tarava
subgenres.desc: Protestant choral songs in Tahiti and other southern Polynesian islands.

subgenres.name: Izvorna bosanska muzika
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic vocal music that developed in Bosnia in the 20th century, bearing connections to traditional Bosnian genres.

subgenres.name: Lab Polyphony
subgenres.desc: One of several genres of iso-polyphonic music performed in southern Albania, with "iso" referring to the distinctive drone voice used.

subgenres.name: Madrigal
subgenres.desc: Secular polyphonic music based around poetry and generally performed by unaccompanied vocal ensembles of two to eight persons.

subgenres.name: Paghjella
subgenres.desc: Traditional Polyphonic Chant from Corsica consisting of three registers of vocalists singing in a semicircle.

subgenres.name: Polifonia occitana
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic chant from the Occitan region.

subgenres.name: Seto leelo
subgenres.desc: Style of polyphonic singing of the Seto people.

subgenres.name: Sutartinės
subgenres.desc: Unique form of polyphonic vocal music originating from a small area of Northeastern Lithuania.

subgenres.name: Tosk Polyphony
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic singing in the Toskëri region of southern Albania.

subgenres.name: Trallalero
subgenres.desc: Polyphonic Traditional Folk Music originating in the Ligurian region of Genoa, in northern Italy.

subgenres.name: Prehistoric Music
subgenres.desc: Styles from the first cultural periods of the human species (Homo sapiens, as well as certain Homo neanderthalensis). From its birth in the Paleolithic and Neolithic eras to the Ancient Music era beginning around 2000–3000 BC.

subgenres.name: South American Music
subgenres.desc: Rooted in the traditions of South America.

subgenres.name: Aleke
subgenres.desc: Derived from traditional Surinamese Maroon music, especially aukansi, features distinct faster rhythms.

subgenres.name: Argentine Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the Argentine people.

subgenres.name: Cuarteto
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Argentinian province of Córdoba, usually with an upbeat rhythm and originally performed with a four-piece band.

subgenres.name: Cumbia argentina
subgenres.desc: Almost always features synthesizer keyboards and electronic percussion with an upbeat rhythm.

subgenres.name: Cumbia santafesina
subgenres.desc: Originated in the Argentinian province of Santa Fe, particularly in its capital city Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz, with lyrics that tend to be romantic and relatively clean compared to later Cumbia argentina.

subgenres.name: Cumbia turra
subgenres.desc: Cumbia argentina heavily influenced by Reggaetón and characterized by hard-hitting bass and heavy use of samples and Auto-Tune.

subgenres.name: Cumbia villera
subgenres.desc: Developed in the villa miserias (shanty towns) by the lower classes of Argentina in the early 2000s, featuring basic rhythms and low budget productions combined with lyrics that can be openly sexual or touch on sociopolitical issues.

subgenres.name: Guaracha santiagueña
subgenres.desc: Fast, upbeat and danceable rhythm originated in the province of Santiago del Estero, Argentina as a fusion of Chacarera and Chamamé.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: RKT
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 2010s, characterized by minimalistic, rhythm-centric production heavily influenced by Cumbia villera and other Cumbia argentina styles.

subgenres.name: Avanzada
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Polka paraguaya and Guarania with elements of Bossa nova and MPB.

subgenres.name: Bailecito
subgenres.desc: Agile and lively dance derived from Zamacueca, typical of the western and central region of Bolivia.

subgenres.name: Baithak gana
subgenres.desc: Indo-Caribbean genre from Suriname, consisting of Bhojpuri Folk Music with local Caribbean influence.

subgenres.name: Bambuco
subgenres.desc: Follows a 6/8 or 3/4 time signature with non-percussive instrumentation, often melancholic in sound with bright guitars and a rich melodic base.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Music
subgenres.desc: All forms of music with roots in Brazil.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Classical Music
subgenres.desc: Originated in the late 19th century, taking the European music that had been brought to the country by colonists and brought in parts of Brazilian Music.

subgenres.name: Valsa brasileira
subgenres.desc: Brazillian Waltz characterized by its slow rhythms and romantic sound.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Comprises the various traditions of folk music found in Brazil, often resulting from the interplay of Indigenous, African and European music.

subgenres.name: Aboio
subgenres.desc: Cattle-herding songs originating in rural Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Aboio cantado
subgenres.desc: Aboio that features rhyming verses.

subgenres.name: Banda de pífano
subgenres.desc: Lively music played by bands consisting of two fifes and percussion.

subgenres.name: Candomblé Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religion that influenced the secular Afoxé.

subgenres.name: Cantoria
subgenres.desc: Sung poetry of itinerant cantadores from Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Repente
subgenres.desc: Contest of fully improvised poetry sung in different stanza formats.

subgenres.name: Capoeira Music
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian style that accompanies and sets the rhythm and energy of the capoeira martial art, originating in the 19th century with the relocation of African slaves to the states of Bahia and Rio de Janeiro.

subgenres.name: Fandango caiçara
subgenres.desc: Style of fandango born in coastal Southern Brazil amidst the Caiçara people.

subgenres.name: Jongo
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian cultural manifestation involving music and dance; composed of percussion instruments and chants.

subgenres.name: Ponto de umbanda
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian religious ritualistic praise sung by priests to evoke entities; typically accompanied by claps and traditional drums known as atabaque.

subgenres.name: Lundu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian music and dance that emerged in the 18th century with influences from African drumming with European fandango.

subgenres.name: Maracatu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian genre which accompanies the cultural manifestation of the same name, hailing from the northeastern state of Pernambuco.

subgenres.name: Modinha
subgenres.desc: Popular during the 18th and 19th centuries in Brazil; characterized by sentimental works with amorous themes, poetic lyrics, acoustic instrumentation and operatic vocals.

subgenres.name: Rasqueado
subgenres.desc: Regional dance and its accompanying music from the Brazilian midwest, predominantly the state of Mato Grosso.

subgenres.name: Samba de roda
subgenres.desc: Mixed Portuguese culture with African slave traditions, as well as sharing roots and similarities with Batuque and Jongo.

subgenres.name: Sertanejo de raiz
subgenres.desc: Earliest form of Sertanejo, emerging in pre-World War II rural Brazil during the late 1920s; quickly strummed acoustic guitars, most commonly the 10-string viola caipira and classical guitar, and a highly emotive vocal style.

subgenres.name: Moda de viola
subgenres.desc: Style of Sertanejo de raiz predominant in southeast, south, and west-central Brazil.

subgenres.name: Toada de Boi
subgenres.desc: Slow, heavy-percussed tunes celebrating the folkloric Ox, originally from Bumba-meu-boi June parties in Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Xaxado
subgenres.desc: Features a strong rhythmic beat, sliding tap dances, and stories of backland bandits.

subgenres.name: Brega
subgenres.desc: Overstated, dramatic music with a romantic singing style.

subgenres.name: Arrocha
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Brega's romantic style, with further influence from Axé and Forró, giving it a more sensual and euphoric feel.

subgenres.name: Arrochadeira
subgenres.desc: Developed in the mid-2000s in Bahia by Dan Ventura, merges the electronic keyboards of Arrocha with Pagodão rhythms.

subgenres.name: Bregadeira
subgenres.desc: Fuses contemporary rhythms from the Brazilian Northeast such as Arrocha, Pagodão and Piseiro, with the electronic beats of Funk brasileiro and its subgenres.

subgenres.name: Brega calypso
subgenres.desc: Romantic vocals and lyrics, bubbly and sensual melodies and rhythms, horn sections and lush Caribbean-like guitar riffs over fast tempos.

subgenres.name: Brega funk
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Tecnobrega, features glossy syncopated MIDI pianos and synths, distinct pitched metallic snares and vocal chops over a wonky kick rhythm.

subgenres.name: Batidão romântico
subgenres.desc: Slower and romantic Kizomba-fused beats.

subgenres.name: Tecnobrega
subgenres.desc: Fast and electronic-based style that evolved from Brega calypso, particularly associated with peripheral areas of the city of Belém.

subgenres.name: Tecnofunk
subgenres.desc: Raw and vulgar Tecnobrega and Funk brasileiro fusion developed in the late 2010s by DJs in Belém do Pará.

subgenres.name: Dobrado
subgenres.desc: Brazilian musical genre, played by military bands with wooden, brass and also percussive instruments.

subgenres.name: Funk brasileiro
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop-influenced dance style originating from the favelas of Rio de Janeiro and known primarily as "funk" in Brazil.

subgenres.name: Arrocha funk
subgenres.desc: Slow and gritty Reggaetón-like drums with an emphasis on brass sections influenced by Arrocha.

subgenres.name: Beat bolha

subgenres.name: Beat fino

subgenres.name: Brega funk

subgenres.name: Batidão romântico
subgenres.desc: Slower and romantic Kizomba-fused beats.

subgenres.name: Eletrofunk

subgenres.name: Funk 150 bpm
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, typically reaching 150 bpm and sometimes beyond it, heightened energy and typically faster flows as well.

subgenres.name: Funk carioca
subgenres.desc: Early scene of Funk brasileiro that began in Rio de Janeiro, developed from a local take on American Miami Bass.

subgenres.name: Funk proibidão

subgenres.name: Tamborzão
subgenres.desc: Adds Afro-Brazilian percussive elements such as the atabaque sound into the Miami Bass kick drums.

subgenres.name: Funk consciente
subgenres.desc: Emphasis on conscious lyrics.

subgenres.name: Funk de BH
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric, mellow and minimalistic production with sparse percussion, often featuring sound effects or filtered samples.

subgenres.name: Funk mandelão
subgenres.desc: Simple lyricism, raw and minimalistic production, and distinct drops with bursting bass.

subgenres.name: Beat bruxaria

subgenres.name: Brazilian Phonk

subgenres.name: Funk automotivo

subgenres.name: Ritmada
subgenres.desc: Short, repetitive and resonant beats with more danceable, immersive grooves drawn out of Afro-Brazilian instrumentation, a cleaner, more radio-friendly sound and greater focus on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Funk melody
subgenres.desc: Light and melodic take on Funk brasileiro, developed alongside Funk carioca.

subgenres.name: Funknejo
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the rhythms, production, and idioms of Funk brasileiro into the universitário genre.

subgenres.name: Funk ostentação
subgenres.desc: Late 2000s take on Funk brasileiro from São Paulo state, featuring Pop Rap influences, having a more accessible sound.

subgenres.name: Mega funk

subgenres.name: Noiadance

subgenres.name: Rasteirinha
subgenres.desc: Slow-paced, highly rhythmic with instrumentation derived from Samba and Axé, and Dancehall-inspired grooves.

subgenres.name: Tecnofunk
subgenres.desc: Raw and vulgar Tecnobrega and Funk brasileiro fusion developed in the late 2010s by DJs in Belém do Pará.

subgenres.name: Trapfunk

subgenres.name: MPB

subgenres.name: Tropicália

subgenres.name: Northeastern Brazilian Music
subgenres.desc: Regional styles that combines elements of indigenous, African and European traditions, historically with a focus on life of the northeastern people, such as drought, migration, the struggle for survival, love and nostalgia, and often danced in intense and accelerated movements.

subgenres.name: Aboio

subgenres.name: Aboio cantado
subgenres.desc: Aboio that features rhyming verses.

subgenres.name: Afoxé

subgenres.name: Arrocha

subgenres.name: Arrochadeira
subgenres.desc: Developed in the mid-2000s in Bahia by Dan Ventura, merges the electronic keyboards of Arrocha with Pagodão rhythms.

subgenres.name: Bregadeira
subgenres.desc: Fuses contemporary rhythms from the Brazilian Northeast such as Arrocha, Pagodão and Piseiro, with the electronic beats of Funk brasileiro and its subgenres.

subgenres.name: Axé
subgenres.desc: Developed from a fusion of Frevo, Maracatu, Forró, Reggae and Calypso with roots in the Salvador de Bahia carnival.

subgenres.name: Pagodão
subgenres.desc: Predominance of guitar riffs, atabaques, pandeiros and drums.

subgenres.name: Arrochadeira
subgenres.desc: Developed in the mid-2000s in Bahia by Dan Ventura, merges the electronic keyboards of Arrocha with Pagodão rhythms.

subgenres.name: Samba-reggae
subgenres.desc: Percussion-focused style from Bahia, Brazil, originating in the 1980s and 1990s in the Bahian carnival's afro-blocos.

subgenres.name: Baião

subgenres.name: Banda de pífano

subgenres.name: Brega funk
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Tecnobrega, features glossy syncopated MIDI pianos and synths, distinct pitched metallic snares and vocal chops over a wonky kick rhythm.

subgenres.name: Batidão romântico
subgenres.desc: Slower and romantic Kizomba-fused beats.

subgenres.name: Cantoria

subgenres.name: Repente

subgenres.name: Coco

subgenres.name: Ciranda
subgenres.desc: Employs a metrical scheme of quatrains, long verses, and slow pace, with lyrical themes generally limited to love.

subgenres.name: Embolada

subgenres.name: Forró

subgenres.name: Forró eletrônico

subgenres.name: Forró de favela

subgenres.name: Piseiro

subgenres.name: Forró universitário
subgenres.desc: Originated in the 1990s from university students in the state of São Paulo with influences from genres like Rock, Reggae, and Funk.

subgenres.name: Frevo

subgenres.name: Frevo-canção

subgenres.name: Frevo de bloco

subgenres.name: Frevo de rua

subgenres.name: Frevo elétrico

subgenres.name: Manguebeat

subgenres.name: Maracatu

subgenres.name: Samba de roda

subgenres.name: Udigrudi

subgenres.name: Unakesa

subgenres.name: Xaxado
