subgenres.desc: Festive Andean music with vibrant rhythm featuring saxophones and violins, typical of the central Peruvian region.

subgenres.name: Música criolla peruana
subgenres.desc: Coastal Peruvian music tradition blending Spanish, African, and local influences, developed in urban contexts through creolized European dance forms.

subgenres.name: Festejo
subgenres.desc: Happy and danceable Afro-Peruvian rhythm originating in the 17th century.

subgenres.name: Landó
subgenres.desc: 16th-century Afro-Peruvian dance and music style, played primarily on the cajón and the creole guitar in a 12/8 rhythm.

subgenres.name: Marinera
subgenres.desc: Component of the coastal dance of the same name, often considered the national dance of Peru.

subgenres.name: Polka peruana
subgenres.desc: Peruvian adaptation of European Polka, blending Afro-Peruvian rhythms and criollo melodies.

subgenres.name: Tondero
subgenres.desc: Backing to the fast-paced dance that originated in northern Peru in the region of Piura of the same name; bands consist of a singer, a small chorus, two guitarists, along with the cajón and sometimes a spoon player.

subgenres.name: Vals criollo
subgenres.desc: Originally characterized by its 3/4 time, heavy reliance on strongly plucked phrase on upper strings, and its guitar solo; often accompanied by a duet or a solo singer, normally singing about patriotic themes or social dilemmas.

subgenres.name: Tunantada
subgenres.desc: Originating in the central Peruvian region, characterized by cheerful and festive rhythm, with indigenous and mestizo influences.

subgenres.name: Polka paraguaya
subgenres.desc: Popular music originating in Paraguay and the Province of Corrientes (Argentina), derived from the Bohemian polka and traditional music of Hispanic-Jesuit origin.

subgenres.name: Porro
subgenres.desc: Lively Hispanic American Music and dance style native to Colombia which gained popularity in the 1940s.

subgenres.name: Rioplatense Music
subgenres.desc: Music developed by the people of the Rio de la Plata region.

subgenres.name: Candombe
subgenres.desc: Uruguayan popular music originating among Montevideo's Afro-Uruguayan population, based on three differently-sized drums.

subgenres.name: Candombe beat
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Uruguayan Candombe with elements of Rock music.

subgenres.name: Chamarrita rioplatense
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance featuring similar rhythms to Milonga and typically performed with the guitar and accordion.

subgenres.name: Cumbia pop
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Río de la Plata region in the mid-2010s, featuring Latin Pop influences and lyrics related to romance, youth, and fun.

subgenres.name: Electrotango
subgenres.desc: Combines Tango rhythms and melodies with Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Milonga
subgenres.desc: Characterized by a slow rhythm usually performed on a guitar; generally considered a precursor to Tango.

subgenres.name: Murga uruguaya
subgenres.desc: Variant originated in Montevideo that stands out for its rhythms, nasal vocals and choral arrangements.

subgenres.name: Tango
subgenres.desc: Melancholic sound generally led by a guitar or bandoneon, originating in Buenos Aires by the late 19th century and gaining worldwide popularity from the 1920s to the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Finnish Tango
subgenres.desc: Melancholic style developed in Finland in the 1930s and 1940s, influenced by traditional minor-key Finnish Folk Music melodies and the rhythms of German marches.

subgenres.name: Tango nuevo
subgenres.desc: Adds new elements into traditional Argentine Tango, most importantly the incorporation of Jazz and Western Classical Music.

subgenres.name: Rock andino
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the Andean countries in the late 1960s and early 1970s, incorporating traditional instruments and harmonies from Indigenous Andean Music within a Rock format.

subgenres.name: Salsa choke
subgenres.desc: Colombian style that takes heavy influence from Reggaetón, House, Hip Hop, and various Afro-Colombian and Colombian Pacific styles.

subgenres.name: Saya
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced, percussive traditional genre created by the Afro-Bolivian people.

subgenres.name: Taquirari
subgenres.desc: Developed by the indigenous peoples of eastern Bolivia, bringing in some elements of Hispanic Music, and featuring a syncopated rhythm.

subgenres.name: Tecnomerengue
subgenres.desc: Fuses basic Merengue rhythms with influences from Cumbia and Lambada, being largely synthesized, with live instruments usually limited to percussion and brass.

subgenres.name: Vallenato
subgenres.desc: Accordion-led style of folk and popular music originating in Colombia's Caribbean region.

subgenres.name: Vals venezolano
subgenres.desc: Venezuelan dance music that employs heavy use of syncopation, complex rhythms, and regional instruments.

subgenres.name: Yaraví
subgenres.desc: Peruvian criollo-mestizo songs with recurring themes of sadness and unrequited love, usually in 6/8 meter.

subgenres.name: Zamacueca
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance of 19th century Peru, sung in the minor mode and accompanied by a varying combination of guitar, vihuela, harp and cajón.

subgenres.name: Zamba
subgenres.desc: Folk dance that evolved out of Peruvian Zamacueca during the 19th century.

subgenres.name: Sufi Music
subgenres.desc: Covering the various musical traditions of Sufis.

subgenres.name: Banga
subgenres.desc: Sufi ritual trance music of southern Tunisia performed by Black communities.

subgenres.name: Jilala Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Jilala Sufi order, most notably used in healing trance rituals.

subgenres.name: Kafi
subgenres.desc: Sufi vocal style popular in Pakistan, differentiated from Qawwali by its small ensemble size and simple arrangements.

subgenres.name: Manzuma
subgenres.desc: Melodic, devotional music performed by Sufi Islami communities in Ethiopia and neighboring countries

subgenres.name: Qawwali
subgenres.desc: Sufi Music in India and Pakistan using the raga and tala templates of Hindustani Classical Music, with an emphasis on ecstatic performance and devotional lyricism.

subgenres.name: Rapai dabõih
subgenres.desc: Religious music meant to accompany the dabõih ceremony of the Acehnese people.

subgenres.name: Sufiana kalam
subgenres.desc: Classical music from Kashmir, the northernmost part of the Indian subcontinent.

subgenres.name: Sufi Rock
subgenres.desc: Pakistani subgenre rooted in Sufi tradition, featuring South Asian instruments like the dhol, tabla, and sitar within a Rock band format with lyrics and imagery inspired by traditional Sufi poets.

subgenres.name: Turkish Mevlevi Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music performed among Turkish practitioners of the Mevlevi order of Sufism.

subgenres.name: Traditional Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Informed by a long history of tradition in a specific culture or region, mostly associated with the peasantry and non-aristocratic public.

subgenres.name: African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Indigenous music of Africa that is passed down orally from generation to generation, the authors of the songs are usually unknown.

subgenres.name: Ambasse bey
subgenres.desc: African Folk Music developed by the Yabassi people of Cameroon.

subgenres.name: Apala
subgenres.desc: Yoruba Music developed by Muslims during the late 1930s and early 1940s in the Ijebu region of Yorubaland, the current Ogun state.

subgenres.name: Batuque
subgenres.desc: Tradition from Cape Verde, unusual among the islands' music due to its lack of polyphonic singing and its usage of polyrhythms.

subgenres.name: Dagomba Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Dagomba people of northern Ghana.

subgenres.name: Gnawa
subgenres.desc: A mystical musical tradition centred around the qraqab castanets and guembri bass lute, named after its originators, the Afro-Maghrebi Gnawa people.

subgenres.name: Kabye Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kabye people of northern Togo, including some of the most singular styles that can be found in West Africa.

subgenres.name: Kilapanga
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Bakongo people from Angola and Congo that has influenced contemporary styles such as Kuduro.

subgenres.name: Malagasy Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Melodic, chordophone-dominated sound; based on the Austronesian Music of the first settlers that arrived on the island from Borneo.

subgenres.name: Mbenga-Mbuti Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Mbenga and Mbuti people, Pygmy ethnic groups in Central Africa.

subgenres.name: Moutya
subgenres.desc: Tradition that originated in Seychelles among Creole slaves, similar to Séga, although rawer and played only on large flat drums made from goatskin.

subgenres.name: Ngoma
subgenres.desc: Played in Swahili-speaking African countries; primarily focused on rhythm.

subgenres.name: Unyago
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Zanzibar, traditionally played at women's initiation rituals and weddings.

subgenres.name: Southern African Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Afrikaner Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Musical traditions developed by the Afrikaner community in southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Khoisan Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses traditions of the Khoisan ethnic family groups.

subgenres.name: Nguni Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Nguni ethnic family groups, a southern Bantu ethnicity.

subgenres.name: Sotho-Tswana Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Sotho-Tswana ethnic family groups from southern Africa.

subgenres.name: Tchinkoumé
subgenres.desc: Tradition from the central region of Benin around Savalou, played with water percussion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Maloya
subgenres.desc: Derived from Traditional Séga, this is the original dance music of La Réunion.

subgenres.name: Traditional Séga
subgenres.desc: Séga dance music born in the 18th century, before its later adoption of Western pop elements.

subgenres.name: Zinli
subgenres.desc: Traditional rhythmic chanting and percussion adapted to multiple West African contexts in the 20th century.

subgenres.name: American Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traces back through the history of European and West African settlement and migration to North America, including parts of northern Mexico and Canada in addition to the United States.

subgenres.name: Appalachian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Appalachian Mountains in the Eastern United States.

subgenres.name: Old-Time
subgenres.desc: Pre-Bluegrass North American string band styles, particularly those rooted in Appalachian Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Various styles of Blues originating in the rural US South, typically relying on expressive vocal delivery and featuring simple, usually acoustic instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Texas Blues
subgenres.desc: Laid-back swing rhythms and guitar ornamentation, including solos.

subgenres.name: Delta Blues
subgenres.desc: One of the earliest forms of Blues, named for the Mississippi Delta region of the United States where it developed, with a highly rhythmic style and a typical 12-bar structure.

subgenres.name: Bentonia School
subgenres.desc: Brooding, hypnotic minor-key open-tuning guitar style with a looser structure, often featuring high, "haunting" vocals.

subgenres.name: Hill Country Blues
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a steady hypnotic groove, sparse percussive and highly energetic guitar riffs, and often features meandering structures with unconventional and usually fewer chord changes compared to Delta Blues.

subgenres.name: Piedmont Blues
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 20th century in the southern Appalachian foothills and characterized by a syncopated but melodic Ragtime-based finger-picking acoustic guitar style.

subgenres.name: Field Hollers
subgenres.desc: Created by African-American slaves working on cotton plantations, featuring expressive vocals to no strict rhythm.

subgenres.name: Fife and Drum Blues
subgenres.desc: Rooted in martial Fife and Drum Corps music, originated among Afro-American communities in Mississippi.

subgenres.name: Jug Band
subgenres.desc: Usually features a jug as the bass instrument as well as other homemade (or easily affordable) instruments, such as kazoos and washboards.

subgenres.name: Pennsylvania Dutch Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of the Pennsylvania Dutch.

subgenres.name: Ring Shout
subgenres.desc: Ritual practiced by African-Americans in the US South, characterized by shouting, chanting and people dancing in a circle while praying and clapping.

subgenres.name: Sacred Harp Singing
subgenres.desc: Predominantly 19th-century English hymns with tunes derived from old folk melodies.

subgenres.name: Spiritual
subgenres.desc: African American folk song based around Christian themes, originating during enslavement and emphasizing solidarity and freedom; musical features include call-and-response, "blue" notes, and expressive vocal timbres.

subgenres.name: Talking Blues
subgenres.desc: American Folk Music with spoken or nearly spoken vocals; often features dry humor and social commentary.

subgenres.name: Traditional Black Gospel
subgenres.desc: Born out of Spiritual in the early 20th century with influence from Southern Gospel and Blues, often featuring passionate or energetic vocal performances, motifs of salvation, and testaments of hardship.

subgenres.name: Traditional Cajun Music
subgenres.desc: Earliest and most "pure" form of Cajun Music, employing basic rhythms and frequent fiddle double stops.

subgenres.name: Traditional Country
subgenres.desc: Closely aligned with American Folk Music and Blues roots, from country's inception in Appalachia and the American South until the popularity of Honky Tonk and Country Pop in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Close Harmony
subgenres.desc: Traditional two-part harmony singing performed mostly by brothers.

subgenres.name: Country Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the harmonies and Christian themes of Gospel.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Traditional Bluegrass
subgenres.desc: Driving tempos, acoustic stringed instrumentation, and high vocal harmonies, adhering to the stylistic roots of the Bluegrass genre.

subgenres.name: Bluegrass Gospel
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the religious topics and harmony vocals found in Country Gospel.

subgenres.name: Arabic Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Arabic people.

subgenres.name: Aita
subgenres.desc: Arabic Folk Music from rural Morocco with piercing singing, scratchy viola, and rollicking hand drums.

subgenres.name: Arabic Bellydance Music
subgenres.desc: Accompaniment to traditional belly dances.

subgenres.name: Raqs baladi
subgenres.desc: Egyptian folk dance and its associated musical accompaniment, appearing in the 20th century.

subgenres.name: Ayyalah
subgenres.desc: Traditional Khaliji-Bedouin weapon performance, commonly found across the United Arab Emirates and Northwestern Oman.

subgenres.name: Fijiri
subgenres.desc: Deeply rooted in the Persian Gulf pearl diving culture, and sung during weekly gatherings combining solo and choral sections with minimal percussion.

subgenres.name: Liwa
subgenres.desc: Traditional Khaliji performance with East African Music roots centered around the mizmar and traditional drums, typically sung in Khaliji Arabic and Swahili.

subgenres.name: Nuban
subgenres.desc: Traditional Afro-Emirati Folk performance of Nuban origin most commonly performed in the emirate of Dubai.

subgenres.name: Sa'idi
subgenres.desc: Traditional folkloric performance and form of Arabic Folk Music originating from Upper Egypt.

subgenres.name: Australian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of the European colonists and convicts in Australia.

subgenres.name: Bayawan
subgenres.desc: Distinct muqam tradition of the Dolan subgroup of the Uyghur people, often considered the wildest of the regional muqam variations.

subgenres.name: Brazilian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Comprises the various traditions of folk music found in Brazil, often resulting from the interplay of Indigenous, African and European music.

subgenres.name: Aboio
subgenres.desc: Cattle-herding songs originating in rural Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Aboio cantado
subgenres.desc: Aboio that features rhyming verses.

subgenres.name: Banda de pífano
subgenres.desc: Lively music played by bands consisting of two fifes and percussion.

subgenres.name: Candomblé Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religion that influenced the secular Afoxé.

subgenres.name: Cantoria
subgenres.desc: Sung poetry of itinerant cantadores from Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Repente
subgenres.desc: Contest of fully improvised poetry sung in different stanza formats.

subgenres.name: Capoeira Music
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian style that accompanies and sets the rhythm and energy of the capoeira martial art, originating in the 19th century with the relocation of African slaves to the states of Bahia and Rio de Janeiro.

subgenres.name: Fandango caiçara
subgenres.desc: Style of fandango born in coastal Southern Brazil amidst the Caiçara people.

subgenres.name: Jongo
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian cultural manifestation involving music and dance; composed of percussion instruments and chants.

subgenres.name: Ponto de umbanda
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian religious ritualistic praise sung by priests to evoke entities; typically accompanied by claps and traditional drums known as atabaque.

subgenres.name: Lundu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian music and dance that emerged in the 18th century with influences from African drumming with European fandango.

subgenres.name: Maracatu
subgenres.desc: Afro-Brazilian genre which accompanies the cultural manifestation of the same name, hailing from the northeastern state of Pernambuco.

subgenres.name: Modinha
subgenres.desc: Popular during the 18th and 19th centuries in Brazil; characterized by sentimental works with amorous themes, poetic lyrics, acoustic instrumentation and operatic vocals.

subgenres.name: Rasqueado
subgenres.desc: Regional dance and its accompanying music from the Brazilian midwest, predominantly the state of Mato Grosso.

subgenres.name: Samba de roda
subgenres.desc: Mixed Portuguese culture with African slave traditions, as well as sharing roots and similarities with Batuque and Jongo.

subgenres.name: Sertanejo de raiz
subgenres.desc: Earliest form of Sertanejo, emerging in pre-World War II rural Brazil during the late 1920s; quickly strummed acoustic guitars, most commonly the 10-string viola caipira and classical guitar, and a highly emotive vocal style.

subgenres.name: Moda de viola
subgenres.desc: Style of Sertanejo de raiz predominant in southeast, south, and west-central Brazil.

subgenres.name: Toada de Boi
subgenres.desc: Slow, heavy-percussed tunes celebrating the folkloric Ox, originally from Bumba-meu-boi June parties in Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Xaxado
subgenres.desc: Features a strong rhythmic beat, sliding tap dances, and stories of backland bandits.

subgenres.name: Canadian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the European settlers who arrived in Canada.

subgenres.name: Canadian Maritime Folk
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of Canada's Maritimes (Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick).

subgenres.name: Cape Breton Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Celtic Folk Music that emerged in Cape Breton, an island at the eastern shore of Nova Scotia, through immigrants from Scotland and Ireland.

subgenres.name: Cape Breton Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Distinctive Celtic fiddling originating from the Scottish immigrants who settled in Canada on Cape Breton Island.

subgenres.name: French-Canadian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Brought by French colonists to their Nouvelle-France settlements, primarily based around French Folk Music with influences from English Folk Music and Celtic Folk Music, typically played during gatherings and holidays.

subgenres.name: Métis Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Canadian style blending First Nations and European musical influences into an up-tempo style of fiddling characterized by the use of syncopation and indigenous rhythms.

subgenres.name: Newfoundland Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada's easternmost province.

subgenres.name: Caribbean Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre that covers the different forms of Traditional Folk Music from the Caribbean.

subgenres.name: Bele
subgenres.desc: Drum-based folkdance with a strong Afro-influence, conducted by duos of dancers and accompanied by call-and-response singing, particularly popular in Martinique, Dominica and Trinidad and Tobago.

subgenres.name: Benna
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of Antigua & Barbuda, using call-and-response and bawdy lyrics.

subgenres.name: Bomba
subgenres.desc: Percussive style from Puerto Rico, generally considered to be derived from West Africa.

subgenres.name: Fungi
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music native to the Virgin Islands, named after a local dish which features a "mixed-up" flavor that can be compared to the style that combines Western instruments with local ones.

subgenres.name: Haitian Vodou Drumming
subgenres.desc: Form of rhythmic performance by Haitian Vodou practitioners, played at associated ceremonies.

subgenres.name: Jibaro
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the mountain-dwelling jibaro people that live primarily in Puerto Rico.

subgenres.name: Kaiso
subgenres.desc: Trinidadian folk considered to be the precursor of Calypso, led by "griot" storytellers who sing derogatory lyrics to the sound of drums and guitars in a call-and-response manner in order to rebel against slaveowners.

subgenres.name: Kitchen Dance Music
subgenres.desc: Cayman Islands music played during kitchen dance parties, centered around fiddle and percussion (handmade or kitchen grater) playing.

subgenres.name: Kumina
subgenres.desc: Folk religious ritual of Jamaica, featuring extensive musical and dance elements, greatly inspired Rastafari religion and music.

subgenres.name: Mento
subgenres.desc: Jamaican folk originating in the late 19th century which brought together African and European elements, going on to influence the rhythm in Reggae.

subgenres.name: Méringue
subgenres.desc: Haitian genre that dates back to the early 19th century; the roots of Compas.

subgenres.name: Plena
subgenres.desc: Folk genre from Puerto Rico played with hand drums called panderetas.

subgenres.name: Ripsaw
subgenres.desc: Indigenous style of the Turks and Caicos Islands, featuring a handsaw as the primary instrument.

subgenres.name: Tumba
subgenres.desc: African-style percussion alongside Latin influences and often explicit lyrics.

subgenres.name: Virgin Islander Cariso
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Virgin Islands, sung exclusively by women to the beat of one or two drums.

subgenres.name: Caucasian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Caucasus region, a mountainous area that connects Eastern Europe to Asia.

subgenres.name: Abkhazian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Republic of Abkhazia, a disputed territory on the Black Sea in northwestern Georgia.

subgenres.name: Chechen Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Chechens, a Northeast Caucasian ethnic group predominantly living in the Republic of Chechnya, a federal subject of Russia.

subgenres.name: Circassian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the native Circassian peoples of Northern Caucasus, residing in the Republics of Adygea, Karachay-Cherkessia, and Kabardino-Balkaria respectively, which are federal subjects of the Russian Federation, as well as the territories of the former Ottoman Empire, with a significant diaspora population in modern Turkey.

subgenres.name: Dagestani Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Dagestani people.

subgenres.name: Avar Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Avar people.

subgenres.name: Georgian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Georgian people, who mostly live in Georgia.

subgenres.name: Batonebi Songs
subgenres.desc: Traditional Georgian Lullabies often meant to soothe sick children.

subgenres.name: Ossetian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk music of Ossetians, an ethnic group that mainly inhabits a region located on both sides of the Greater Caucasus Mountains.

subgenres.name: Chukchi Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Chukchi people.

subgenres.name: Drinking Song
subgenres.desc: Songs meant to be sung locally while consuming alcohol, often in bars, pubs, or taverns.

subgenres.name: East Asian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: All the forms of Traditional Folk Music from East Asia, including Japanese Folk Music, Chinese Folk Music, and Korean Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Amami shimauta
subgenres.desc: Tradition from the Amami Islands, located in southern Japan.

subgenres.name: Chinese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the Chinese people.

subgenres.name: Chaozhou xianshi
subgenres.desc: Traditional and instrumental ensemble music originating from Chaozhou; played mainly on stringed instruments.

subgenres.name: Han Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Chinese folk form often played at weddings and funerals, using the Suona (a form of oboe) and Chuigushou (a specific type of percussive ensemble), together with heterophony.

subgenres.name: Haozi
subgenres.desc: Chinese Work Song that originated from collective manual labor and usually follows a call-and-response structure, aiming to coordinate work.

subgenres.name: Jiangnan sizhu
subgenres.desc: Originating from Jiangnan region and played by a varying ensemble of stringed instruments, flutes, mouth organs and small percussions.

subgenres.name: Shan'ge
subgenres.desc: Folk songs found in upland regions of China, typically sung while working.

subgenres.name: Indigenous Taiwanese Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the various Austronesian people groups that make up the indigenous population of the island of Taiwan.

subgenres.name: Japanese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of Japan.

subgenres.name: Heikyoku
subgenres.desc: Semi-classical bardic tradition in Japan analogous to the troubadour music of medieval Europe.

subgenres.name: Kagura
subgenres.desc: Performed at Shinto shrines for ceremonies and rituals.

subgenres.name: Kouta
subgenres.desc: Kouta, which literally means "little" or "short" song, is one type of the many varieties of Japanese folk songs that is distinguished by its briefness and wittiness.

subgenres.name: Min'yō
subgenres.desc: Form of Japanese Folk Music which literally translates to "folk song".

subgenres.name: Ondō
subgenres.desc: Originally referred to the type of call-and-response form of Gagaku, but later became to be known for and distinguished by a swung 2/2 rhythm and storytelling.

subgenres.name: Rōkyoku
subgenres.desc: Storytelling usually accompanied by a shamisen.

subgenres.name: Taiko
subgenres.desc: Modern style of ensemble drumming, sometimes called kumi-daiko.

subgenres.name: Tsugaru shamisen
subgenres.desc: Shamisen playing originating in the Tsugaru Peninsula of Aomori prefecture, recognizable in its percussive quality and special, slightly larger instrument.

subgenres.name: Korean Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Korean people.

subgenres.name: Muak
subgenres.desc: Korean shamanistic music that accompanies the ritual of gut as performed in all regions of Korea.

subgenres.name: Pansori
subgenres.desc: Korean style of storytelling characterized by over-the-top, passionate singing from a solo vocalist accompanied by minimal drumming.

subgenres.name: Pungmul
subgenres.desc: Consists of drumming, dancing, and singing, and is a tradition deeply ingrained in South Korean culture.

subgenres.name: Sanjo
subgenres.desc: Traditional instrumental Korean Folk Music that focuses on a wide variety of rhythmic changes with many different classical Korean instruments.

subgenres.name: Sinawi
subgenres.desc: Improvisational genre traditionally serving as an accompaniment to Korean shamanic rituals.

subgenres.name: Vietnamese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Vietnamese people, with traditions influenced by both Chinese Music and Austronesian culture through the Cham people.

subgenres.name: Chèo
subgenres.desc: Northern Vietnamese folk musical theatre, characterized by minimal set design and satirical content.

subgenres.name: Quan họ
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Northern Vietnamese provinces of Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang, originally consisting of harmonic, a cappella singing from two competing duos.

subgenres.name: Xẩm
subgenres.desc: Developed in Northern Vietnam, traditionally sung by blind bards accompanied by a đàn bầu or đàn nhị.

subgenres.name: European Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Encompasses numerous folk traditions found in Europe.

subgenres.name: Alpine Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Alps, including parts of Germany, Austria, Slovenia, Switzerland, and Italy.

subgenres.name: Canto degli Alpini
subgenres.desc: Created and traditionally sung by choirs formed from the Italian army's Alpine mountain infantry corps, mainly dating back to WWI.

subgenres.name: Ländler
subgenres.desc: Swiss-German dance band music based on the accordion, combining traditional Alpine Folk Music with elements from Schlager and Jazz.

subgenres.name: Narodno zabavna glasba
subgenres.desc: Modernised form of Slovenian Folk Music from the Alpine region of Upper Carniola (Oberkrain).

subgenres.name: Naturjodel

subgenres.name: Chamarrita rioplatense
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance featuring similar rhythms to Milonga and typically performed with the guitar and accordion.

subgenres.name: Cueca
subgenres.desc: Popular in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia, accompanied by a 6/8 or 3/4 time signature and usually structured into 14 verses.

subgenres.name: Jibaro
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the mountain-dwelling jibaro people that live primarily in Puerto Rico.

subgenres.name: Joropo
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Creole music and the Venezuelan waltz.

subgenres.name: Malagueña venezolana
subgenres.desc: Traditional musical accompaniment to the Venezuelan 'velorios de cruz de mayo' celebrations, played with the mandolin (as lead instrument), cuatro and guitar.

subgenres.name: Mexican Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Mexican people.

subgenres.name: Canto cardenche
subgenres.desc: Overtly dramatic, and melancholic A cappella performed in the Comarca Lagunera region in northeast Mexico.

subgenres.name: Pirekua
subgenres.desc: Traditional style of the P’urhépecha people, typically slow and in 3/8 or 6/8 time.

subgenres.name: Son calentano
subgenres.desc: Usually dominated by violin with accompaniment mainly provided by guitars and tamboras, occasionally dancers will stomp over a platform.

subgenres.name: Son huasteco
subgenres.desc: Bold rhythmic structure, lively violin playing, and extensive use of falsetto.

subgenres.name: Son istmeño
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, traditionally played by guitar, requinto, marimba, and bajoquinto, usually played in 3/4 time.

subgenres.name: Son jarocho
subgenres.desc: Mexican Folk Music from the Gulf Coast Mexican state of Veracruz, with both Spanish and indigenous influences.

subgenres.name: Trova yucateca
subgenres.desc: Heavily influenced by Cuban Music, freely embracing Bolero, clave and Bambuco.

subgenres.name: Milonga
subgenres.desc: Characterized by a slow rhythm usually performed on a guitar; generally considered a precursor to Tango.

subgenres.name: Muliza
subgenres.desc: Mestizo folk genre popular in the central Peruvian Andes, characterized by a pronounced, though sedate, rhythm; traces of Andean melody; and octosyllabic verses.

subgenres.name: Música llanera
subgenres.desc: Traditional music originating from the Llanos region of Colombia and Venezuela.

subgenres.name: Plena
subgenres.desc: Folk genre from Puerto Rico played with hand drums called panderetas.

subgenres.name: Saya
subgenres.desc: Fast-paced, percussive traditional genre created by the Afro-Bolivian people.

subgenres.name: Tamborito
subgenres.desc: Folk music and dance from Panama dating back to the 17th century.

subgenres.name: Taquirari
subgenres.desc: Developed by the indigenous peoples of eastern Bolivia, bringing in some elements of Hispanic Music, and featuring a syncopated rhythm.

subgenres.name: Tonada chilena
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk from the Chilean countryside distinguished by its prominent melody.

subgenres.name: Yaraví
subgenres.desc: Peruvian criollo-mestizo songs with recurring themes of sadness and unrequited love, usually in 6/8 meter.

subgenres.name: Zamacueca
subgenres.desc: Traditional genre and dance of 19th century Peru, sung in the minor mode and accompanied by a varying combination of guitar, vihuela, harp and cajón.

subgenres.name: Zamba
subgenres.desc: Folk dance that evolved out of Peruvian Zamacueca during the 19th century.

subgenres.name: Indigenous American Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre encompassing traditions attributed to the indigenous peoples of the Americas.

subgenres.name: Athabaskan Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Fiddle playing of the Northern Athabaskan Dene people of modern-day Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories.

subgenres.name: Ghost Dance Song
subgenres.desc: Songs accompanying the Ghost Dance, a 19th century religious movement.

subgenres.name: Inuit Vocal Games
subgenres.desc: Practiced by the Inuit of Canada, two vocalists face each other decimeters away and try to outlast each other with intense and unusual vocal techniques.

subgenres.name: James Bay Fiddling
subgenres.desc: Fiddle playing of the James Bay Cree people, characterised by a fusion of Scottish style with Cree rhythms.

subgenres.name: Mapuche Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Mapuche people of Chile and Argentina.

subgenres.name: Powwow Music
subgenres.desc: Drum-based traditional music of Plains region Native American tribes, traditionally played at Pow-wows.

subgenres.name: Rabbit Song
subgenres.desc: Indigenous North American ceremonial song cycles most associated with Southern Paiute, Ute, Mojave, and Chemehuevi traditions which feature short, repetitive, vocable-heavy melodies performed in long sequences that accompany trickster (rabbit) narratives and encode social knowledge.

subgenres.name: Tonada potosina
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk sung in Quechua, played on charangos and guitarillas, with a catchy, lively rhythm.

subgenres.name: Unakesa
subgenres.desc: Lay song and dance of the Fulni-ô people.

subgenres.name: Indigenous Australian Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Aboriginal Australians and Torres Strait Islanders, collectively known as Indigenous Australians.

subgenres.name: Djanba
subgenres.desc: Sung and composed in the Murrinh-Patha language and consisting of a mixed group of men and women accompanied by bilma and handclaps, typically without didgeridoo.

subgenres.name: Wangga
subgenres.desc: Originated from the Daly region, consists of performances featuring wood sticks, didgeridoo and voice.

subgenres.name: Industrial Folk Song
subgenres.desc: Details the experiences and aspirations of industrial laborers and their working conditions; frequently rooted in labor causes and often used for protest and organizational purposes.

subgenres.name: Ladino Folksong
subgenres.desc: Ladino-language Traditional Folk Music tunes that were written and preserved by Sephardic Jews.

subgenres.name: Ob-Ugric Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Ob-Ugric people of West Siberia Plain.

subgenres.name: Payada
subgenres.desc: Improvised poetry accompanied by a guitar that is tied to gaucho culture, usually performed in duo as a verse duel.

subgenres.name: Romani Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Romani people, an ethnic group with origins in Northern India, but who have since the Middle Ages settled around Europe, principally Romania, Bulgaria, and Spain, and many other places.

subgenres.name: Samoyedic Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Samoyedic peoples.

subgenres.name: South Asian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre which covers all the Traditional Folk Music forms from South Asia.

subgenres.name: Assamese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Assamese people, a people group mostly from the Northeastern Indian state of Assam.

subgenres.name: Bengali Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Bengali people found mainly in the Indian state of West Bengal and the country of Bangladesh.

subgenres.name: Baul gaan
subgenres.desc: Songs performed by the Bauls, a movement of mystic entertainers influenced by diverse spiritual traditions.

subgenres.name: Bhojpuri Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Bhojpuri people of India, originally from the states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

subgenres.name: Biraha
subgenres.desc: Call-and-response style of folk music developed from the Ahir and neighboring castes of the Bhojpuri people.

subgenres.name: Boduberu
subgenres.desc: Traditional, percussion-based form of music popular in the Maldives, usually following a crescendo structure.

subgenres.name: Burushaski Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Burusho people of northern Pakistan.

subgenres.name: Gujarati Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Gujarati people, who primarily live in the western Indian state of Gujarat.

subgenres.name: Kannada Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Kannada people, a large ethnolinguistic group who mainly inhabit the state of Karnataka in southwestern India.

subgenres.name: Kirtan
subgenres.desc: Call-and-response chanting that involves the singing of devotional mantras and hymns in a bhakti devotional style, occasionally accompanied with traditional folk instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Shabad kirtan
subgenres.desc: Religious Sikh Hymn backed by specially selected ragas and taal.

subgenres.name: Malayali Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Kerala, India primarily sung in the Malayalam language and known for its drumming and percussion.

subgenres.name: Mappila
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk music from Kerala's Malabar region, sung in Arabic inflected Malayalam (Arabi Malayalam), blending Islamic devotional themes with local poetic forms.

subgenres.name: Marathi Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Marathi people, a large ethnic group who mainly inhabit the state of Maharashtra in western India.

subgenres.name: Newa Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Newa people, who live in Nepal, performed with mostly percussive instruments and some wind instruments.

subgenres.name: Odia Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Odia, a large ethnic group who mainly inhabit the state of Odisha in eastern India.

subgenres.name: Pashto Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Pashtun people of southern Afghanistan and north-western Pakistan.

subgenres.name: Punjabi Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Punjabi people, mostly from the Punjab regions of India and Pakistan, covering diverse styles often played with traditional instruments.

subgenres.name: Rajasthani Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Rajasthani people of Western India - who now mostly live in the eponymous Rajasthan state - originated across the various castes that inhabit the region.

subgenres.name: Sinhalese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Sinhalese people, the majority ethnic group of Sri Lanka.

subgenres.name: Sarala gee
subgenres.desc: Blend of Hindustani Classical Music with Sinhalese Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Tamil Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Tamil people.

subgenres.name: Urumi melam
subgenres.desc: Percussive ensemble native to the Tamil Nadu region, taking its name from the urumi drum.

subgenres.name: Telugu Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Telugu people, one of the largest ethnolinguistic groups of India, mainly living in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

subgenres.name: Burrakatha
subgenres.desc: Traditional form of narrative music, featuring a tambura player paired with two drummers who interrupt the main storyteller to provide additional remarks.

subgenres.name: Southeast Asian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Meta-genre covering all folk forms from Southeast Asia, like Gondang, Hmong, Iban, Karen, Keroncong, Khmer, Lao, Lun Bawang, Molam, and Orang Ulu.

subgenres.name: Balitaw
subgenres.desc: Folk originating in the Visayas islands of the Philippines; dialogue or debate in which a man and a woman compete at improvising romantic verses.

subgenres.name: Bamar Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the majority ethnic group of Myanmar.

subgenres.name: Gondang
subgenres.desc: Traditional ensemble in Bataknese traditional music of North Sumatra, taking its name from its leading instrument - a unique set of toned drums.

subgenres.name: Harana
subgenres.desc: Hispanic-influenced lyrical courtship music traditionally sung by men, accompanied by guitar based on the danza rhythm.

subgenres.name: Hmong Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk traditions of the Hmong people, an ethnic group localized in Laos, Vietnam, China, and Thailand.

subgenres.name: Khmer Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Khmer people, who mainly reside in Cambodia.

subgenres.name: Kuda kepang
subgenres.desc: Accompanies a traditional Javanese dance of the same name, featuring a stripped-back version of a Gamelan ensemble that removes softer instruments.

subgenres.name: Lao Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Lao people.

subgenres.name: Malay Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Malay people, who are native to Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, northern Indonesia, and southern Thailand.

subgenres.name: Philippine Rondalla
subgenres.desc: Ensemble of plucked string instruments typically performed for traditional Filipino folk dances; known for its distinct sparkling and tinkling tremolo sound.

subgenres.name: Tarawangsa
subgenres.desc: Sacred ceremonial music originating in the Rancakalong district, played with the jentreng harp and the tarawangsa bowed lute.

subgenres.name: Thai Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Thai people.

subgenres.name: Fon leb
subgenres.desc: Traditional performance music originating in northern Thailand consist of an ensemble with Piphat instruments and a pair of female choreographers.

subgenres.name: Vietnamese Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Vietnamese people, with traditions influenced by both Chinese Music and Austronesian culture through the Cham people.

subgenres.name: Chèo
subgenres.desc: Northern Vietnamese folk musical theatre, characterized by minimal set design and satirical content.

subgenres.name: Quan họ
subgenres.desc: Tradition of the Northern Vietnamese provinces of Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang, originally consisting of harmonic, a cappella singing from two competing duos.

subgenres.name: Xẩm
subgenres.desc: Developed in Northern Vietnam, traditionally sung by blind bards accompanied by a đàn bầu or đàn nhị.

subgenres.name: West Asian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of West Asia, a region that covers much of what is commonly known in English as the Middle East (alternatively Southwestern Asia), includes the distinct but interconnected traditions of numerous ethnic groups.

subgenres.name: Alevi Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Anatolian folk pioneered by Turkish poets and bards, connected to the Alevist heterodox Islamic tradition.

subgenres.name: Armenian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Armenians, which is attested in historic Armenia since antiquity, with unique regional dialects unified by general melodic structure.

subgenres.name: Kef Music
subgenres.desc: Dance-oriented Armenian American music with prominent presence of Anatolian instruments and folkloric melodies (often in the 10/8 meter) paired with novel lyrics relating to a variety of topics.

subgenres.name: Assyrian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Assyrian or Syriac people, who are indigenous to the Upper Mesopotamian region roughly corresponding to ancient Assyria (which includes modern-day northern Iraq, northwestern Iran, northeastern Syria, and southeastern Turkey).

subgenres.name: Ayyalah
subgenres.desc: Traditional Khaliji-Bedouin weapon performance, commonly found across the United Arab Emirates and Northwestern Oman.

subgenres.name: Fijiri
subgenres.desc: Deeply rooted in the Persian Gulf pearl diving culture, and sung during weekly gatherings combining solo and choral sections with minimal percussion.

subgenres.name: Israeli Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Jewish settlers of Eretz Yisra'el.

subgenres.name: Luri Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Luri people of southwestern Iran.

subgenres.name: Meyxana
subgenres.desc: Azerbaijani folk recitative genre.

subgenres.name: Persian Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of the Persian people.

subgenres.name: Turkish Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional Folk Music of Turkish people combines the distinct cultural heritages and traditions of Anatolian civilisations and former Ottoman territories.

subgenres.name: Turkish Black Sea Region Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Folk of the Turkish people who inhabit the northern region by the Black Sea.

subgenres.name: Uzun Hava
subgenres.desc: Semi-improvisational melodic structure in Turkish Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Zeybek
subgenres.desc: Turkish Folk Music music and dance that originated with the Zeybek people during the Ottoman Empire period, with slow and asymmetrical rhythms.

subgenres.name: Work Song
subgenres.desc: Sung by laborers and prisoners while working in factories and fields.

subgenres.name: Aboio
subgenres.desc: Cattle-herding songs originating in rural Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: Aboio cantado
subgenres.desc: Aboio that features rhyming verses.

subgenres.name: Field Hollers
subgenres.desc: Created by African-American slaves working on cotton plantations, featuring expressive vocals to no strict rhythm.

subgenres.name: Haozi
subgenres.desc: Chinese Work Song that originated from collective manual labor and usually follows a call-and-response structure, aiming to coordinate work.

subgenres.name: Military Cadence
subgenres.desc: Call-and-response work song performed by military personnel.

subgenres.name: Òrain luaidh
subgenres.desc: Rhythmic call-and-response style song form that traditionally accompanied the production of tweed cloth through beating the material by hand to soften it after it came off the loom.

subgenres.name: Sea Shanty
subgenres.desc: Songs originally sung by sailors to coordinate work on ships.

subgenres.name: Shan'ge
subgenres.desc: Folk songs found in upland regions of China, typically sung while working.

subgenres.name: Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique that arose in many cultures around the world as a form of calling and communication.

subgenres.name: Country Yodeling
subgenres.desc: Vocal technique of Yodeling, brought to the United States by German settlers, sung over the instrumentation of Traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Naturjodel
subgenres.desc: Originated in Toggenburg and Appenzell in Switzerland; deep vocal range, relaxed voice, free tempo, polyphony, elongated notes, improvisation, glissando, and use of syllabic sounds.

subgenres.name: Turkic-Mongolic Music
subgenres.desc: Group of related traditions which originated among nomadic people of the Central Asian steppes (speakers of Altaic, i.e. Turkic, Mongolic, and Tungusic languages).

subgenres.name: Altai Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Altai people, an ethnic group who live in central Russia near the border of Mongolia and Kazakhstan.

subgenres.name: Bashkir Folk Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional folk of the Bashkir people, a Turkic ethnic group inhabiting the Republic of Bashkortostan (Bashkiria), a federal subject of the Russian Federation, and its neighboring areas on both sides of the Ural mountains.

subgenres.name: Central Asian Throat Singing
subgenres.desc: Shared polyphonic vocal tradition of Mongolia and southern Siberia characterised by complex manipulation of harmonics.

subgenres.name: Kai
subgenres.desc: Prevalent in the Altai-Sayan region and rooted in Shamanic traditions, it is renowned for its emphasis on the low vocal register and is revered as a sacred medium for communicating with all nature and the spirits.

subgenres.name: Mongolian Throat Singing
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Mongolia characterized by many throat singing techniques.

subgenres.name: Tuvan Throat Singing
subgenres.desc: Traditional style of singing found in Tuva, an autonomous region of the Russian Federation situated in southern Siberia.

subgenres.name: Karakalpak Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Karakalpak people, located in northwestern Uzbekistan.

subgenres.name: Khakas Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of the Khakas Republic (part of the Russian Federation), a form of Turkic music related to the musics of neighboring Tuva, Altai and Mongolia.

subgenres.name: Kyrgyz Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditions of Kyrgyzstan, a mountainous nation in Central Asia.

subgenres.name: Mongolian Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Mongols.

subgenres.name: Bogino duu
subgenres.desc: Mongolian Music with tuneful composition and simple structure.

subgenres.name: Buryat Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Buryat people, an ethnic group native to the Republic of Buryatia in Russian Far East.

subgenres.name: Kalmyk Music
subgenres.desc: Music of the Kalmyks, a Mongol Buddhist ethnic group inhabiting the Republic of Kalmykia, a federal subject of the Russian Federation.

subgenres.name: Mongolian Throat Singing
subgenres.desc: Traditional music from Mongolia characterized by many throat singing techniques.

subgenres.name: Urtiin duu
subgenres.desc: Mongolian tradition in which sung syllables are extended into long, meditational, vibrato notes called shuranhai; accompanied by traditional Mongolian instruments such as the morin khuur and limbe.

subgenres.name: Zohioliin duu
subgenres.desc: Mixes modern Pop with Mongolian Music, using local and western instruments.

subgenres.name: Sakha Traditional Music
subgenres.desc: Traditional music of Sakha (a.k.a. Yakut) people, mostly living in their homeland - Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) (part of Russian Federation).

name: Rock
desc: Typically uses a verse-chorus structure with a backbeat rhythm and the electric guitar at the forefront; generally heavier and/or faster than its predecessors.

subgenres.name: Acoustic Rock
subgenres.desc: Rock with acoustic instrumentation, as opposed to the typical electric instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Afro-Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates West African influences; initially emerged in the early 1970s.

subgenres.name: Alternative Rock
subgenres.desc: Performed with a less commercial sensibility, utilizing more eccentric, Punk-influenced sounds, moodier or quirkier lyricism, and sometimes ample amounts of distortion, often paired with Pop-influenced songwriting.

subgenres.name: Alternative Dance
subgenres.desc: Incorporates rhythms and synthesizers from Electronic Dance Music within the context of Alternative Rock and related styles; predominantly popular in the 1990s.

subgenres.name: Grebo
subgenres.desc: Short-lived English subculture and associated music; raw, futuristic, sample-heavy form of Alternative Dance with a dirty guitar sound.

subgenres.name: New Rave
subgenres.desc: High energy mid-2000s style combining the tight and punchy grooves of Dance-Punk Revival with synths and four-on-the-floor rhythms from genres like Electroclash and Electro House.

subgenres.name: Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United Kingdom in the early 1990s, with a style hearkening back to the traditional guitar-driven songs and melodic hooks found in the British Pop Rock of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Dream Pop
subgenres.desc: Reverberated guitars, effects-laden vocals, and dense productions, creating a psychedelic, spacious, and dreamlike sound.

subgenres.name: Emo-Pop
subgenres.desc: Mainstream derivative of Emo, puts more emphasis on the poppy sensibilities of Alternative Rock and Pop Punk.

subgenres.name: Geek Rock
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes a nerdy aesthetic, incorporating synthesizers and other instrumentation less common in Alternative Rock alongside quirky Pop-oriented songwriting and dense, witty lyricism on unconventional topics.

subgenres.name: Grunge
subgenres.desc: Mixes Punk and Metal sensibilities into a mid-tempo approach featuring a heavy, "sludgy" guitar sound, "raspy" vocals and angsty lyricism.

subgenres.name: Indie Rock
subgenres.desc: Associated with a less mainstream-oriented and a DIY approach while often dabbling in Pop-informed melodic songwriting, eclecticism, and adopting an "authentic" or raw style.

subgenres.name: Baggy
subgenres.desc: Blends Dance and Funk-based grooves with a laid-back, psychedelic atmosphere; features jangly guitars, looping basslines, four-bar drum patterns, and a hypnotic, carefree feel rooted in the Madchester scene of the late 1980s.

subgenres.name: C86
subgenres.desc: Distinctly ramshackle, often Twee Pop-infused combination of British Indie Rock and Jangle Pop.

subgenres.name: Dolewave
subgenres.desc: Loose, low-key, and sardonic with erudite lyrics and considerable influence from the Dunedin Sound and Slacker Rock; came to prominence in Melbourne in the early 2010s.

subgenres.name: Dunedin Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Dunedin, New Zealand in the early 1980s, featuring a murky, lo-fi sound that overlaps with contemporaneous Jangle Pop and Slacker Rock styles.

subgenres.name: Garage Rock Revival
subgenres.desc: Incorporated the raucous spirit of '60s Garage Rock into the sensibilities of Alternative Rock and Indie Rock; predominant in the '00s.

subgenres.name: Indie Surf
subgenres.desc: Reverb-drenched, nostalgic, and often lo-fi, with influences from Surf Rock and Vocal Surf; rose to popularity around 2009.

subgenres.name: Math Pop
subgenres.desc: Indie Rock that incorporates clean, melodic vocals and Pop-informed songwriting into the progressive and polyrhythmic instrumentation of Math Rock.

subgenres.name: Midwest Emo
subgenres.desc: Characterized by shifts between loud and soft dynamics, off-key, strained and emotional vocals, sometimes with intricate instrumental arrangements and layered arpeggiated guitar parts.

subgenres.name: New Rave
subgenres.desc: High energy mid-2000s style combining the tight and punchy grooves of Dance-Punk Revival with synths and four-on-the-floor rhythms from genres like Electroclash and Electro House.

subgenres.name: Noise Pop
subgenres.desc: Arose in the mid-1980s; blend of poppier Rock songwriting and melodies with the dissonant, noisy timbres of distorted guitars and frequent use of guitar feedback.

subgenres.name: Post-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Incorporating the sounds and aesthetics of Post-Punk into Indie Rock, with jagged guitarwork, a dominant and danceable rhythm section, clean production, and poppy song structures.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Punchy and danceable variant of Post-Punk Revival that features Electronic instrumentation and influence from Alternative Dance.

subgenres.name: Slacker Rock
subgenres.desc: Raw, noisy, and melodic, with a loose, blasé approach to performances and typically low-fidelity production.

subgenres.name: Shitgaze
subgenres.desc: Blends extremely raw and lo-fi aesthetics, abrasive guitar tones, and typically, the ethos of raucous Garage Rock, to create a sonic wall of deafening distortion evocative of Shoegaze.

subgenres.name: Slowcore
subgenres.desc: Characterized by its subdued, often sombre songwriting and slow tempos, while taking primarily from genres like Dream Pop and Folk Rock.

subgenres.name: Twee Pop
subgenres.desc: Distinct Post-Punk background and often jangling guitars, defined by a cute aesthetic and lyrics combined with an indie/DIY attitude and a simplicity often indebted to Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Cuddlecore
subgenres.desc: Rawer and more Punk informed, downplaying jangly guitars in favor of heavier yet still light-hearted tones; often features influence from the contemporary Riot Grrrl movement.

subgenres.name: Jangle Pop
subgenres.desc: Treble-heavy guitars with arpeggiated melodies, distinct basslines, and often propulsive, repetitive strum-rhythms; frequently influenced by Post-Punk.

subgenres.name: C86
subgenres.desc: Distinctly ramshackle, often Twee Pop-infused combination of British Indie Rock and Jangle Pop.

subgenres.name: Dolewave
subgenres.desc: Loose, low-key, and sardonic with erudite lyrics and considerable influence from the Dunedin Sound and Slacker Rock; came to prominence in Melbourne in the early 2010s.

subgenres.name: Neo-Acoustic
subgenres.desc: Cross-section of Indie Pop and Jangle Pop with more prominent acoustic instrumentation and songwriting/arrangements that draw from Sophisti-Pop.

subgenres.name: Paisley Underground
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Los Angeles in the early 1980s, featuring the energy of Power Pop and New Wave adorned with retro Psychedelia.

subgenres.name: Mall Screamo
subgenres.desc: Heavy instrumentation, melodic verse-chorus songwriting, and expressive singing contrasted with screaming vocals.

subgenres.name: Post-Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s as a Britpop expansion mainly characterized by acoustic-leaning instrumentation, lush string arrangements, and mid-tempo song structures, as well as less apparent lyrical concerns for Britain in favor of introspective, contemplative themes.

subgenres.name: Post-Grunge
subgenres.desc: Combines melodic, radio-friendly songwriting with Grunge characteristics such as heavy guitar tones, Hard Rock-infused riffing, and soft-loud song structures.

subgenres.name: Shimokita-kei
subgenres.desc: Japanese style closely related to the Shimokitazawa indie scene, featuring Pop-informed songwriting, melodic guitar leads, expressive vocals, and often loud, prominent overdriven guitars.

subgenres.name: Shoegaze
subgenres.desc: Dense, noisy, and ethereal washes of sound primarily created with electric guitars and heavy use of effects pedals, such as fuzz, reverb, chorus, and delay, with vocals serving as a dreamy, usually unintelligible melodic layer.

subgenres.name: Anatolian Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Turkish Folk Music, particularly traditional instruments such as the bağlama and saz alongside traditional scales and melodies.

subgenres.name: AOR
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s as an amalgamation of Hard Rock, Pop Rock, and Progressive Rock; characterized by a rich, layered sound, slick production and a heavy reliance on commercial melodic hooks.

subgenres.name: Art Punk
subgenres.desc: Combines the stripped-down aggression of rudimentary Punk Rock with frequent experimentation ranging from instrumental interplay, noise, dissonance, and/or influences from other genres such as Jazz or Funk.

subgenres.name: Egg Punk
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s; features lo-fi production, eccentric lyrics, quick tempos, nasally vocals, and cheap keyboard sounds.

subgenres.name: Art Rock
subgenres.desc: Attempts to expand the bounds of Rock within conventional structures, often using outside influences or experimentation for conceptual or thematic purpose.

subgenres.name: Bard Rock
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock music and styles with Avtorskaya pesnya.

subgenres.name: Blues Rock
subgenres.desc: Relies on the chords/scales and instrumental improvisation of Blues.

subgenres.name: Boogie Rock
subgenres.desc: Straightforward groove-oriented style influenced by Rock & Roll and Boogie Woogie.

subgenres.name: British Rhythm & Blues
subgenres.desc: A style infusing Rock and R&B that was hugely popular in the United Kingdom between 1963 and 1966.

subgenres.name: Candombe beat
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Uruguayan Candombe with elements of Rock music.

subgenres.name: Christian Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Christian lyrics, with topics such as faith, metaphysics, or biblical characters.

subgenres.name: Xian Psych
subgenres.desc: Portrays Christian and biblical themes through a surreal, transcendent atmosphere, occasionally drawing influence from Christian Liturgical Music.

subgenres.name: Comedy Rock
subgenres.desc: Roughly defined as a mix of Rock or any of its subgenres with elements of Comedy such as Satire and Musical Parody, as well as concepts of Novelty.

subgenres.name: Country Rock
subgenres.desc: Combination of contemporary Rock with more traditional American Country.

subgenres.name: Cosmic Country
subgenres.desc: Synthesizes various American musical influences and the exploratory ethoses of Psychedelia and Progressive Country to create an ethereal and more experimental sound still rooted in traditional Country.

subgenres.name: Cowpunk
subgenres.desc: Mixes together Country Rock, Rockabilly, and Contemporary Folk with the familiar punk sound.

subgenres.name: Deutschrock
subgenres.desc: Lyrics address German life, culture, and identity wrapped in upbeat songs, anthemic ballads, and a strong focus on the personality of the lead singer.

subgenres.name: Emo
subgenres.desc: Focuses on emotional lyrics, expressive vocals, melodic songwriting, and dynamic song structures.

subgenres.name: Emocore
subgenres.desc: Emerged primarily in Washington D.C. in 1985 as a reaction to the stagnant Hardcore Punk scene, with a less aggressive style that was more melodic and often featured emotional, introspective lyrics.

subgenres.name: Emo-Pop
subgenres.desc: Mainstream derivative of Emo, puts more emphasis on the poppy sensibilities of Alternative Rock and Pop Punk.

subgenres.name: Mall Screamo
subgenres.desc: Heavy instrumentation, melodic verse-chorus songwriting, and expressive singing contrasted with screaming vocals.

subgenres.name: Midwest Emo
subgenres.desc: Characterized by shifts between loud and soft dynamics, off-key, strained and emotional vocals, sometimes with intricate instrumental arrangements and layered arpeggiated guitar parts.

subgenres.name: Screamo
subgenres.desc: Intense, aggressive and complex approach to Emo featuring higher levels of abrasiveness and dissonance, accompanied by guitar-focused melodicism and harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Emoviolence
subgenres.desc: Shorter length and volatile song structures, while borrowing techniques from Powerviolence such as blast beats, unconventional screaming and noisier sounds.

subgenres.name: Experimental Rock
subgenres.desc: Eschews accessibility and convention, experimenting with song structures, time signatures, rhythm, dissonance, instrumentation, noise, electronics, studio manipulation, and other techniques not traditionally associated with Rock.

subgenres.name: Avant-Prog
subgenres.desc: Focuses on highly complex, dense arrangements often featuring high amounts of dissonance and uncommon time signatures, sometimes extending towards atonality, free time, improvisation, and other avant-garde techniques.

subgenres.name: Brutal Prog
subgenres.desc: Highly intense and visceral songwriting, usually featuring substantial reliance on dissonance, odd time signatures, blistering tempos, angular and mercurial rhythms, and Punk's DIY attitude.

subgenres.name: Zeuhl
subgenres.desc: Epic, operatic sound fusing Jazz, Progressive Rock and Modern Classical music.

subgenres.name: Krautrock
subgenres.desc: Brings together elements of Psychedelic Rock with avant-garde influences, often incorporating hypnotic rhythms, extended improvisation, and Electronic textures.

subgenres.name: Folk Rock
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Folk, particularly in the use of acoustic instrumentation and relatively simple arrangements; has its origins in the American Contemporary Folk movement of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Alpenrock
subgenres.desc: Mixes Hard Rock and Blues Rock with traditional Alpine Folk Music elements such as Yodeling and use of the accordion.

subgenres.name: British Folk Rock
subgenres.desc: Developed in the late 1960s; influenced by traditional British folk music, particularly English Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Celtic Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from Celtic Folk Music and its regional variants.

subgenres.name: Mittelalter-Rock
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1990s from the German Neo-Medieval movement, incorporating medieval instruments with Rock music.

subgenres.name: Nordic Folk Rock
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Nordic Folk Music and Rock.

subgenres.name: Phleng phuea chiwit
subgenres.desc: Political Thai Folk Rock born out of the 1973 student uprising, with a name translating to "songs for life".

subgenres.name: Pinoy Folk Rock
subgenres.desc: Typically sung in Tagalog and pioneered in the 1970s, incorporating elements of indigenous music such as Kulintang gong music and the kubing bamboo jaw harp.

subgenres.name: Rock rural
subgenres.desc: Brazilian Folk Rock that emerged in the 1970s, incorporating elements of Sertanejo, Country Rock, and MPB.

subgenres.name: Funk Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates prominent Funk grooves.

subgenres.name: Funk Metal
subgenres.desc: Melds Funk Rock grooves with slap basslines and metallic guitarwork.

subgenres.name: Garage Rock
subgenres.desc: Raw and energetic, generally employing simple, sloppy, and fuzzbox-distorted guitar melodies in addition to frequent shouting or screaming.

subgenres.name: Frat Rock
subgenres.desc: Early form of Garage Rock with hard Rhythm & Blues grooves, catchy melodies, and a "fratty" focus on partying and girls.

subgenres.name: Freakbeat
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of the Mod movement which combines elements of British Rhythm & Blues and Beat with studio effects common in Psychedelia such as fuzztones, flanging and chorus; often seen as a British relative of the American Garage Psych scene.

subgenres.name: Garage Psych
subgenres.desc: Emerged from mid-1960s US Garage Rock; characterised by fuzz guitars, cheap organs, experimentation with psychedelic effects and surreal lyricism, and a retained emphasis on raw energy and the pop song format.

subgenres.name: Garage Punk
subgenres.desc: Combination of the raw fuzztones of the original Garage Rock bands of the 1960s with the tempo and attitude of Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Garage Rock Revival
subgenres.desc: Incorporated the raucous spirit of '60s Garage Rock into the sensibilities of Alternative Rock and Indie Rock; predominant in the '00s.

subgenres.name: Glam Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Rock & Roll and Blues Rock into catchy Pop Rock melodies, usually accompanied with a strong sense of theatricality.

subgenres.name: Glam Punk
subgenres.desc: Contrasts a snotty, nihilistic, and combative attitude of punk with theatrics and flamboyance.

subgenres.name: Hardcore [Punk]
subgenres.desc: Encompasses the first wave of Hardcore Punk beginning in the 1970s, as well as its derivative styles that incorporate diverse musical influences and stray away from the core Punk Rock sound.

subgenres.name: Beatdown Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Heavy, urban-inspired and breakdown-oriented with strong relations to Metalcore.

subgenres.name: Electronicore
subgenres.desc: Hybrid of Metalcore and/or Post-Hardcore with various Electronic Dance Music styles, utilizing Electronic instrumentation and occasional Dance beats.

subgenres.name: Grindcore
subgenres.desc: Brief and intense song structures featuring a plethora of blast beats, down-tuned and tremolo-picked guitars, and abrasive, usually raw production.

subgenres.name: Cybergrind
subgenres.desc: Standard conventions of Grindcore taken to an even more discordant and rapid-fire extreme, with added Electronic dimensions of computer-generated noises and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Deathgrind
subgenres.desc: Combines the intensity and high-pitched screams of Grindcore with the technicality and low guttural vocals of Death Metal.

subgenres.name: Goregrind
subgenres.desc: Death Metal-influenced riffs with rhythms ranging from very fast to slower mid-tempos correlated with pitch-shifted vocals, sloppy playing and production, and gore-themed aesthetics.

subgenres.name: Gorenoise
subgenres.desc: Combines and subverts Goregrind and Grindcore with brash Noise and even faster drum tempos.

subgenres.name: Pornogrind
subgenres.desc: Groovy, mid-tempo style known for its exaggerated bouncy rhythm and common pornographic themes.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Noisegrind
subgenres.desc: Noise-driven, defined by its rawness, feedback usage, and very brief song structures.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s, often featuring extensive use of yelling or screaming, a stripped-down production style, and very short songs.

subgenres.name: Burning Spirits
subgenres.desc: Emphasis on delivering a very energetic and triumphant sound with flashy and soaring Metal solos, "melodramatic" or "uplifting" chord progressions, and singalong, over the top, harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Crossover Thrash
subgenres.desc: Mixes the metallic instrumentation of Thrash Metal with the ethos and approach of Hardcore Punk.

subgenres.name: Crust Punk
subgenres.desc: Metallic outgrowth of Anarcho-Punk featuring a down-tuned, high-gain guitar sound, frequent D-Beat drum patterns, guttural vocals, and politically-charged lyrics often featuring apocalyptic imagery.

subgenres.name: Blackened Crust
subgenres.desc: Borrows heavily from Black Metal production, blast beats, tremolo guitar, and vocals, while retaining the core Crust Punk sound, lyrical themes, and aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Neocrust
subgenres.desc: Melodic, dark, and atmospheric style that often incorporates influences from Sludge Metal, Post-Metal, Black Metal, and Screamo.

subgenres.name: Stenchcore
subgenres.desc: Heavier, more metallic form of Crust Punk drawing influence from Thrash Metal as well as Death Metal and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: D-Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1980s, features Metal influences, shouted vocals, and a distinct drum style known as the D-beat.

subgenres.name: Melodic Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the USA in the early to mid-1980s, placing emphasis on melodic vocals and technical guitar riffs rather than raw aggression.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

subgenres.name: Street Punk
subgenres.desc: Driven by Oi! style group vocals, catchy melodies, and aggressive songwriting akin to Punk Rock of the 1970s fused with Hardcore Punk of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Thrashcore
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, brief song structures, and the occasional use of blast beats.

subgenres.name: Powerviolence
subgenres.desc: Originated from the West Coast California Hardcore Punk scene in the late 1980s, utilizing strong elements of Noise Rock and abrupt tempo changes.

subgenres.name: Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Drop-tuned guitar riffs, constant double kick drumming with varying tempos and techniques, breakdown sections, and screaming or shouting vocals.

subgenres.name: Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Integrates brutal palm-muted and tremolo-picked riffing, blast beat-focused drumming, and guttural vocals of Death Metal with groovy breakdown sections.

subgenres.name: Downtempo Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimal songs emphasizing breakdowns, atmosphere, and dissonance with downtuned guitars.

subgenres.name: Mathcore
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically complex, featuring unconventional time signatures, syncopated and dissonant riffs and erratic metric shifts.

subgenres.name: Melodic Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Originated in the late 1990s when some metalcore bands infused elements of Melodic Death Metal into their sound to create a more metallic and melodic style.

subgenres.name: Thall
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rapid release bends and a precise playstyle while contrasting pitch-shifted high and low notes, with ambient sections for atmosphere and buildup.

subgenres.name: Nintendocore
subgenres.desc: Fuses Post-Hardcore and Metalcore influences with Chiptune instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Noisecore
subgenres.desc: Short blasts of riff-less, Noise-driven music accompanied with chaotic drums and screamed vocals.

subgenres.name: Post-Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid-1980s from Hardcore Punk that expanded on its aggression and dynamics through longer and more complex arrangements.

subgenres.name: Emocore
subgenres.desc: Emerged primarily in Washington D.C. in 1985 as a reaction to the stagnant Hardcore Punk scene, with a less aggressive style that was more melodic and often featured emotional, introspective lyrics.

subgenres.name: Mall Screamo
subgenres.desc: Heavy instrumentation, melodic verse-chorus songwriting, and expressive singing contrasted with screaming vocals.

subgenres.name: Screamo
subgenres.desc: Intense, aggressive and complex approach to Emo featuring higher levels of abrasiveness and dissonance, accompanied by guitar-focused melodicism and harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Emoviolence
subgenres.desc: Shorter length and volatile song structures, while borrowing techniques from Powerviolence such as blast beats, unconventional screaming and noisier sounds.

subgenres.name: Swancore
subgenres.desc: High-register clean vocals and technical instrumentation drawn from Math Rock and Progressive Rock.

subgenres.name: Sass
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Post-Hardcore in the early 2000s; characterized by sassy vocal styles and chaotic, erratic instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Hard Rock
subgenres.desc: Originated in the mid-to-late 1960s from Psychedelic Rock and Blues Rock with a heavy sound characterized by distorted guitars and power chords.

subgenres.name: Glam Metal
subgenres.desc: Very catchy hooks and guitar riffs, sing-along choruses, and lyrics often glamorizing the "sex, drugs and rock & roll" lifestyle.

subgenres.name: Sleaze Rock
subgenres.desc: Raw and lurid form of Glam Metal with influences from Glam Punk and Blues Rock and back-to-basics songwriting; emerged to counter Pop influences in Hard Rock in the mid-to-late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Heavy Psych
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Blues Rock's heavy dependence on riffs and improvisatory leanings; features thick, fuzzy guitars, usually slow-to-mid tempos, and extended soloing sections.

subgenres.name: Occult Rock
subgenres.desc: Dark and psychedelic atmosphere with lyrical references to esoteric subjects such as occultism, Satanism, fantasy, and horror; closely associated sonically and culturally with Heavy Metal and its offshoots.

subgenres.name: Stoner Rock
subgenres.desc: Psychedelic timbres, raw production, and stylistic influence from Doom Metal and Heavy Psych.

subgenres.name: Heartland Rock
subgenres.desc: Borrows elements from Folk Rock, Roots Rock, and 1950s-60s Rock & Roll; often characterized by its conscious, communal lyrical concerns and working-class appeal.

subgenres.name: Industrial Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates abrasive guitars and synthesizers inspired by Industrial and various Post-Industrial styles.

subgenres.name: Machine Rock
subgenres.desc: Emphasises a mechanical sound that centres heavy, Punk Rock-inspired guitar riffs over Electro-Industrial beats, while incorporating cyberpunk themes and imagery.

subgenres.name: Jam Band
subgenres.desc: Arose in late 1960s America, usually performed in a live setting and combines diverse styles under the Rock umbrella, often influenced by genres such as Funk, Jazz, Country and Blues.

subgenres.name: Jamgrass
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes instrumental jamming and extended performances with many outside influences.

subgenres.name: Livetronica
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Electronic instrumentation into live Rock jamming, drawing on a wide variety of Electronic Dance Music and Downtempo styles.

subgenres.name: Jazz-Rock
subgenres.desc: Strongly influenced by Jazz in structure and/or instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Jersey Shore Sound
subgenres.desc: Stylistically correlated to Heartland Rock, with cultural origins in coastal New Jersey; characterized by its horn-heavy mixture of 1960s Rock & Roll, Rhythm & Blues, and Doo-Wop.

subgenres.name: Latin Rock
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Rock, often Psychedelic Rock, with Latin American rhythms, especially Afro-Latin genres.

subgenres.name: Manguebeat
subgenres.desc: Counterculture fusion of traditional Northeastern Brazilian Music genres with modern Rock and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Math Rock
subgenres.desc: Explores complex and unconventional rhythmic patterns through unusual syncopation, stop-start structures, polyrhythms and complex time signatures, angular melodies, and technical instrumental performances.

subgenres.name: Math Pop
subgenres.desc: Indie Rock that incorporates clean, melodic vocals and Pop-informed songwriting into the progressive and polyrhythmic instrumentation of Math Rock.

subgenres.name: Metal
subgenres.desc: Driving and distorted riffs, aggressive drumming, vigorous vocals, and an all-around show of brute force in its early days, since branching into dozens of subgenres.

subgenres.name: Alternative Metal
subgenres.desc: Mid-tempo style emphasizing melodicism and rhythmic heaviness; branches outside of the stylistic conventions of Metal.

subgenres.name: Funk Metal
subgenres.desc: Melds Funk Rock grooves with slap basslines and metallic guitarwork.

subgenres.name: Neue Deutsche Härte
subgenres.desc: Alternative Metal and Industrial Metal that incorporates various aspects of electronic music, specifically Electronic Dance Music.

subgenres.name: Nu Metal
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes bouncy, drop-tuned riffs, alternating vocal styles, and genre-bending, often incorporating Hip Hop and Funk Metal elements.

subgenres.name: Rap Metal
subgenres.desc: Features rapped vocals, typically formed around heavy, mid-tempo, and groove-oriented playing in addition to elements of Hip Hop beats such as record scratching.

subgenres.name: Avant-Garde Metal
subgenres.desc: Often breaking the bounds of the genre through experimental structures and instrumentation, or by incorporating outside influences.

subgenres.name: Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Highly distorted, treble-heavy guitars, tremolo-picked riffs, blast beats and double bass drumming, shrieked vocals, and raw, lo-fi production; often focuses on occult, dark imagery and atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Atmospheric Black Metal
