subgenres.desc: Repetitive riffs and melodies, slower tempos, synthesized ambient textures, and guitar effects creating atmospheric soundscapes.

subgenres.name: Blackgaze
subgenres.desc: Fuses tremolo-picked riffing, intense drumming and harsh vocal techniques with mellow, dreamy textures, major-key melodies and extended build-ups.

subgenres.name: Black 'n' Roll
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Hard Rock, Glam Rock, and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: Black Noise
subgenres.desc: Incorporates unconventional sounds with overpowering or constant Noise and Black Metal elements, often being heavily texture-oriented, abrasive, dissonant, atonal, or repetitive.

subgenres.name: Dissonant Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Dissonant atonal riffing, cleaner production style, and complex song structures.

subgenres.name: DSBM
subgenres.desc: Lethargic, melancholic, and repetitive sound; depressive and misanthropic themes; vocals ranging from high-pitched wails and screams to strained cleans; often featuring non-distorted sections.

subgenres.name: Hellenic Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Black metal scene in Greece with more mid-tempo songwriting and pronounced Heavy Metal influence.

subgenres.name: Melodic Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Stronger emphasis on melody, generally with cleaner production and more diverse arrangements.

subgenres.name: Pagan Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Folk song-inspired melodies, traditional instruments, acoustic guitar passages, and often cleanly sung vocals, centered on romanticized pagan themes and imagery.

subgenres.name: Symphonic Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Symphonic soundscapes, typically but not always synthesized.

subgenres.name: War Metal
subgenres.desc: Aggressive, chaotic, and heavily Death Metal-influenced, featuring muddy, bass-heavy production and often incorporating war-themed lyrics.

subgenres.name: Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Heavily distorted, down-tuned guitars, palm-muted, tremolo-picked riffs, double-kick and blast beat percussion, chromatic chord progressions, minor keys, abrupt changes in tempo, and guttural vocals.

subgenres.name: Brutal Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes abrasiveness, chunky rhythmic atonal riffs, and low guttural vocals.

subgenres.name: Slam Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Focuses on slow or midtempo (as well as breakdown-style) sections built on chromatic, palm-muted riffs - so-called "slams".

subgenres.name: Death 'n' Roll
subgenres.desc: Incorporates a groove-oriented, Hard Rock-influenced approach while retaining heavily distorted rhythm guitars and gruff or occasionally growled vocals.

subgenres.name: Deathgrind
subgenres.desc: Combines the intensity and high-pitched screams of Grindcore with the technicality and low guttural vocals of Death Metal.

subgenres.name: Melodic Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Utilizes the guitar harmonies and melodic focus of Heavy Metal while generally retaining down-tuned, heavily distorted guitars and a harsh, aggressive sound.

subgenres.name: Gothenburg Sound
subgenres.desc: Pioneering Melodic Death Metal style and scene of Gothenburg, Sweden.

subgenres.name: Technical Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Focuses on challenging, demanding songwriting and instrumental skill.

subgenres.name: Dissonant Death Metal
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes discordant, dense songwriting and utilizes pinch harmonics, scratchy guitar leads, and atonality.

subgenres.name: Djent
subgenres.desc: Groovy polymeters, syncopated power chord chugs, palm-muted, distorted guitars, and significant focus on production and tone.

subgenres.name: Thall
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rapid release bends and a precise playstyle while contrasting pitch-shifted high and low notes, with ambient sections for atmosphere and buildup.

subgenres.name: Doom Metal
subgenres.desc: Plodding tempos, repeated chords, and thick, distorted, down-tuned guitars in a style focused on foreboding, atmosphere, and tension.

subgenres.name: Death Doom Metal
subgenres.desc: Fuses down-tuned guitars, growled vocals, and aggressive, often double-kick drumming with a mournful, somber atmosphere and plodding tempos.

subgenres.name: Funeral Doom Metal
subgenres.desc: Features exceptionally slow, funeral dirge-like tempos; crushing, sluggish guitars; mournful, melancholic atmosphere; and distant, hushed growls and grunts.

subgenres.name: Traditional Doom Metal
subgenres.desc: Monotonous and heavy playing style; repetitive, rough, and sometimes atonal guitar riffs; a "rocking to sleep" bass; and influences from both Blues Rock and Psychedelic Rock.

subgenres.name: Epic Doom Metal
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Heavy Metal influence and theatrical vocals.

subgenres.name: Drone Metal
subgenres.desc: Extremely slow tempos, highly sustained, repetitive guitar notes, and minimalist song structures often omitting a traditional rhythm section and vocals.

subgenres.name: Folk Metal
subgenres.desc: Features influences from various types of Traditional Folk Music expressed through melodies and/or traditional instrumentation, notably having a large scene in Europe.

subgenres.name: Celtic Metal
subgenres.desc: Features Celtic Folk Music elements.

subgenres.name: Mittelalter-Metal
subgenres.desc: Emerged as a metallic style in the mid-to-late 1990s from the German Neo-Medieval movement.

subgenres.name: Gothic Metal
subgenres.desc: Usually low-to-mid-tempo songwriting featuring down-tuned, plodding riffing, a somber atmosphere shaped by ample usage of keyboards and synthesizers, and vocal styles ranging from harsh growls to baritone singing and female operatic vocals.

subgenres.name: Grindcore
subgenres.desc: Brief and intense song structures featuring a plethora of blast beats, down-tuned and tremolo-picked guitars, and abrasive, usually raw production.

subgenres.name: Cybergrind
subgenres.desc: Standard conventions of Grindcore taken to an even more discordant and rapid-fire extreme, with added Electronic dimensions of computer-generated noises and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Deathgrind
subgenres.desc: Combines the intensity and high-pitched screams of Grindcore with the technicality and low guttural vocals of Death Metal.

subgenres.name: Goregrind
subgenres.desc: Death Metal-influenced riffs with rhythms ranging from very fast to slower mid-tempos correlated with pitch-shifted vocals, sloppy playing and production, and gore-themed aesthetics.

subgenres.name: Gorenoise
subgenres.desc: Combines and subverts Goregrind and Grindcore with brash Noise and even faster drum tempos.

subgenres.name: Pornogrind
subgenres.desc: Groovy, mid-tempo style known for its exaggerated bouncy rhythm and common pornographic themes.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Noisegrind
subgenres.desc: Noise-driven, defined by its rawness, feedback usage, and very brief song structures.

subgenres.name: Groove Metal
subgenres.desc: Midtempo riffs influenced by Thrash Metal but with a greater focus on rhythmic syncopation and heaviness over speed.

subgenres.name: Heavy Metal
subgenres.desc: Heavier outgrowth of Hard Rock featuring greater distortion and intensity along with lesser Blues influences.

subgenres.name: Speed Metal
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, double-time feel, aggressive riffs, precise, often virtuosic soloing and expressive vocal styles.

subgenres.name: US Power Metal
subgenres.desc: American style influenced by NWOBHM that features heavily distorted guitars paired with more aggressive riffs, mid-tempo Heavy Metal rhythms, and over-the-top theatrical vocals with fantasy or conceptual themes.

subgenres.name: Industrial Metal
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the abrasive and heavy sound of Industrial into Metal, using elements like synthesizers and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Cyber Metal
subgenres.desc: Originated around 1999, influenced by EBM and Aggrotech with more melodic and less repetitive riffs as well as harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Neue Deutsche Härte
subgenres.desc: Alternative Metal and Industrial Metal that incorporates various aspects of electronic music, specifically Electronic Dance Music.

subgenres.name: Kawaii Metal
subgenres.desc: Fuses various Metal substyles with J-Pop's upbeat melodicism and song structures, utilizing kawaii lyricism and an idol music aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Drop-tuned guitar riffs, constant double kick drumming with varying tempos and techniques, breakdown sections, and screaming or shouting vocals.

subgenres.name: Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Integrates brutal palm-muted and tremolo-picked riffing, blast beat-focused drumming, and guttural vocals of Death Metal with groovy breakdown sections.

subgenres.name: Downtempo Deathcore
subgenres.desc: Slow and minimal songs emphasizing breakdowns, atmosphere, and dissonance with downtuned guitars.

subgenres.name: Mathcore
subgenres.desc: Rhythmically complex, featuring unconventional time signatures, syncopated and dissonant riffs and erratic metric shifts.

subgenres.name: Melodic Metalcore
subgenres.desc: Originated in the late 1990s when some metalcore bands infused elements of Melodic Death Metal into their sound to create a more metallic and melodic style.

subgenres.name: Thall
subgenres.desc: Utilizes rapid release bends and a precise playstyle while contrasting pitch-shifted high and low notes, with ambient sections for atmosphere and buildup.

subgenres.name: Neoclassical Metal
subgenres.desc: Greatly influenced by Western Classical Music in its style of playing and composing.

subgenres.name: Post-Metal
subgenres.desc: Atmospheric and dense metallic riffs, unconventional songwriting, sonic experimentation, and adoption of eclectic influences.

subgenres.name: Atmospheric Sludge Metal
subgenres.desc: Combines slow, churning guitar riffs and thunderous percussion with dark, extensive otherworldly sonic landscapes.

subgenres.name: Blackgaze
subgenres.desc: Fuses tremolo-picked riffing, intense drumming and harsh vocal techniques with mellow, dreamy textures, major-key melodies and extended build-ups.

subgenres.name: Doomgaze
subgenres.desc: Gloomy and sombre atmosphere, amplified by the slow tempo and melancholy of Doom Metal, combined with the effects, washes of sound, and vocals found within Shoegaze.

subgenres.name: Power Metal
subgenres.desc: Developed from Heavy Metal and Speed Metal, emphasizing speed, vocal melody and harmonized lead guitars.

subgenres.name: Progressive Metal
subgenres.desc: Fuses amplified, guitar-driven sound with technical proficiency, virtuosity, complex compositions, innovative arrangements, eclecticism, and additional instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Sludge Metal
subgenres.desc: Mixes Doom Metal's slow pacing, down-tuned riffing style and dark atmosphere with Hardcore Punk's aggression, abrasiveness and harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Atmospheric Sludge Metal
subgenres.desc: Combines slow, churning guitar riffs and thunderous percussion with dark, extensive otherworldly sonic landscapes.

subgenres.name: Southern Metal
subgenres.desc: Blues-influenced style that primarily incorporates Sludge Metal and Stoner Metal with metallic Southern Rock riffs.

subgenres.name: Stenchcore
subgenres.desc: Heavier, more metallic form of Crust Punk drawing influence from Thrash Metal as well as Death Metal and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: Stoner Metal
subgenres.desc: Combines elements of Doom Metal with elements of Psychedelic Rock and Blues Rock to create a melodic yet heavy sound.

subgenres.name: Symphonic Metal
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of symphonic and Orchestral Music.

subgenres.name: Thrash Metal
subgenres.desc: Blistering tempos, palm-muted, technical riffing influenced by Speed Metal, aggressive drumming utilizing double-kick and skank beats, and diverse vocal styles ranging from harsh to clean techniques.

subgenres.name: Crossover Thrash
subgenres.desc: Mixes the metallic instrumentation of Thrash Metal with the ethos and approach of Hardcore Punk.

subgenres.name: Technical Thrash Metal
subgenres.desc: Places great emphasis on complex songwriting and demanding instrumental parts.

subgenres.name: Trance Metal
subgenres.desc: Tempo between 130 and 160 BPM, played with keyboards and metal instrumentation, sung with harsh and aggressive vocals including many clean melodic styles; regularly uses elements of Melodic Death Metal, Symphonic Metal, and Electronic Dance Music.

subgenres.name: Viking Metal
subgenres.desc: Developed out of Black Metal and embodies an epic, Viking-like aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Miejski folk
subgenres.desc: Alternative and Punk music influenced by Folklor miejski and Contemporary Folk.

subgenres.name: New Wave
subgenres.desc: Broad term referring to a variety of styles that saw popularity in the wake of the Punk Rock explosion of 1976-77, initially strongly associated with more accessible and stylish offshoots of punk; developed alongside Post-Punk, similarly emphasising freshness and daring.

subgenres.name: 2 Tone
subgenres.desc: Combines 1960s Jamaican Ska with Punk Rock and New Wave to create tracks played at faster tempos and with a harder edge than the original Jamaican records.

subgenres.name: Beat Rock
subgenres.desc: Japan-exclusive subgenre which combines Pop melodicism with a punchy, driving sound drawing on Punk Rock and New Wave.

subgenres.name: Mod Revival
subgenres.desc: Late 1970s and early 1980s revival of Mod fashion and music, featuring influence from the nascent Punk Rock scene.

subgenres.name: Noise Rock
subgenres.desc: Explores dissonance and distortion through unconventional playing and guitar effects, commonly augmented by lo-fi production and bursts of feedback.

subgenres.name: Pigfuck
subgenres.desc: Sloppy, abrasive and feedback-laden riffing with vulgar and edgy lyricism, informed by Post-Hardcore's aggression and Post-Punk's rhythm section.

subgenres.name: Shitgaze
subgenres.desc: Blends extremely raw and lo-fi aesthetics, abrasive guitar tones, and typically, the ethos of raucous Garage Rock, to create a sonic wall of deafening distortion evocative of Shoegaze.

subgenres.name: Pop Rock
subgenres.desc: Fuses conventional verse-chorus song structure and especially melodic songwriting with usage of guitars, drums, and propulsive rhythms.

subgenres.name: Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1960s in the United Kingdom, drawing on Rock & Roll and the late 1950s Skiffle revival in a simple guitar-band format with strong melodies.

subgenres.name: Freakbeat
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of the Mod movement which combines elements of British Rhythm & Blues and Beat with studio effects common in Psychedelia such as fuzztones, flanging and chorus; often seen as a British relative of the American Garage Psych scene.

subgenres.name: Group Sounds
subgenres.desc: Japanese bands in the mid-to-late 1960s who began performing a style of Beat primarily in English.

subgenres.name: Jovem Guarda
subgenres.desc: 1960s Brazilian youth-oriented Pop Rock, with romantic lyrics and influenced by Merseybeat and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: Merseybeat
subgenres.desc: Light, highly melodic style of Beat popular in the UK during the early 1960s, named due to the abundance of bands from Liverpool beside the River Mersey.

subgenres.name: Nederbeat
subgenres.desc: Dutch answer to the British Beat boom of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Beat Rock
subgenres.desc: Japan-exclusive subgenre which combines Pop melodicism with a punchy, driving sound drawing on Punk Rock and New Wave.

subgenres.name: Big Music
subgenres.desc: Rooted in Post-Punk and popular in the 1980s, with anthemic songwriting and a grandiose, stadium-ready sound.

subgenres.name: Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United Kingdom in the early 1990s, with a style hearkening back to the traditional guitar-driven songs and melodic hooks found in the British Pop Rock of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Jangle Pop
subgenres.desc: Treble-heavy guitars with arpeggiated melodies, distinct basslines, and often propulsive, repetitive strum-rhythms; frequently influenced by Post-Punk.

subgenres.name: C86
subgenres.desc: Distinctly ramshackle, often Twee Pop-infused combination of British Indie Rock and Jangle Pop.

subgenres.name: Dolewave
subgenres.desc: Loose, low-key, and sardonic with erudite lyrics and considerable influence from the Dunedin Sound and Slacker Rock; came to prominence in Melbourne in the early 2010s.

subgenres.name: Neo-Acoustic
subgenres.desc: Cross-section of Indie Pop and Jangle Pop with more prominent acoustic instrumentation and songwriting/arrangements that draw from Sophisti-Pop.

subgenres.name: Paisley Underground
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Los Angeles in the early 1980s, featuring the energy of Power Pop and New Wave adorned with retro Psychedelia.

subgenres.name: Neon Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Scene culture; combines the upbeat tempos and catchy melodies of Pop Punk and Power Pop with synthesizers, auto-tuned vocals, or Dance beats, emphasizing a distinctly polished, hook-oriented sound.

subgenres.name: Piano Rock
subgenres.desc: Primarily based around piano riffs and melodies, rather than having guitar as the focal instrument.

subgenres.name: Pop Yeh-Yeh
subgenres.desc: Blends Western Beat and Psychedelia styles with asli singing and melodies drawn from Malay Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Post-Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1990s as a Britpop expansion mainly characterized by acoustic-leaning instrumentation, lush string arrangements, and mid-tempo song structures, as well as less apparent lyrical concerns for Britain in favor of introspective, contemplative themes.

subgenres.name: Power Pop
subgenres.desc: Combines 1960s Pop melodies with loud power chords; characterized by prominent, sometimes jangly electric guitars, clear vocals, crisp harmonies, and economical arrangements.

subgenres.name: Soft Rock
subgenres.desc: Clean production and light instrumentation paired with harmonious, radio-friendly songwriting; gained huge commercial success in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Tropical Rock
subgenres.desc: Combines influences from Country Rock and Caribbean Music to create an acoustic and breezy "island" themed sound.

subgenres.name: Yacht Rock
subgenres.desc: Slick Pop Rock influenced by smoother R&B styles, popular in the late 1970s and often associated with California.

subgenres.name: Stereo
subgenres.desc: Burmese Pop Rock genre which emerged in the mid-1960s.

subgenres.name: Twee Pop
subgenres.desc: Distinct Post-Punk background and often jangling guitars, defined by a cute aesthetic and lyrics combined with an indie/DIY attitude and a simplicity often indebted to Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Cuddlecore
subgenres.desc: Rawer and more Punk informed, downplaying jangly guitars in favor of heavier yet still light-hearted tones; often features influence from the contemporary Riot Grrrl movement.

subgenres.name: Vocal Surf
subgenres.desc: Appropriates the sounds of instrumental Surf Rock, combining surfing- and car-themed lyrics with a style that draws primarily from Doo-Wop and Rock & Roll.

subgenres.name: Post-Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged alongside the initial Punk Rock explosion in the mid-to-late 1970s, putting a greater emphasis on experimentation and atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Coldwave
subgenres.desc: Originated in Europe in the late 1970s and early 1980s and is known for its generally dark, gloomy atmosphere and heavy reliance on synthesizers.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk
subgenres.desc: Mixes the energy of Punk Rock with the danceable rhythms of Funk and Disco.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Punchy and danceable variant of Post-Punk Revival that features Electronic instrumentation and influence from Alternative Dance.

subgenres.name: Gothic Rock
subgenres.desc: Combines drama and a dark atmosphere with effects-laden guitars, prominent basslines, propulsive drums, and occasional keyboards and drum machines.

subgenres.name: Deathrock
subgenres.desc: More Punk-oriented offshoot of Gothic Rock that emphasizes energy and an effect-laden sound over pure atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Positive Punk
subgenres.desc: Early goth scene in London that grew out of the Anarcho-Punk movement and promoted themes of virtue and mysticism; commonly features wailing vocals, screeching guitars, prominent basslines, and eclectic drum patterns.

subgenres.name: Post-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Incorporating the sounds and aesthetics of Post-Punk into Indie Rock, with jagged guitarwork, a dominant and danceable rhythm section, clean production, and poppy song structures.

subgenres.name: Dance-Punk Revival
subgenres.desc: Punchy and danceable variant of Post-Punk Revival that features Electronic instrumentation and influence from Alternative Dance.

subgenres.name: Post-Rock
subgenres.desc: Emphasis on timbre, texture, and atmosphere over traditional conventions while often embracing influences from genres not usually associated with Rock.

subgenres.name: Progressive Rock
subgenres.desc: Complex harmonies, instrumental virtuosity, and usually multi-section song structures featuring a broad range of instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Avant-Prog
subgenres.desc: Focuses on highly complex, dense arrangements often featuring high amounts of dissonance and uncommon time signatures, sometimes extending towards atonality, free time, improvisation, and other avant-garde techniques.

subgenres.name: Brutal Prog
subgenres.desc: Highly intense and visceral songwriting, usually featuring substantial reliance on dissonance, odd time signatures, blistering tempos, angular and mercurial rhythms, and Punk's DIY attitude.

subgenres.name: Zeuhl
subgenres.desc: Epic, operatic sound fusing Jazz, Progressive Rock and Modern Classical music.

subgenres.name: Canterbury Scene
subgenres.desc: Developed in the counterculture of Canterbury in the late 1960s, emphasizing the influence of Jazz-Rock and Jazz Fusion.

subgenres.name: Neo-Canterbury
subgenres.desc: Movement reviving the signature style of the Canterbury Scene, often updating it with modern influences.

subgenres.name: Neo-Prog
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1980s in the United Kingdom from the influence of Symphonic Prog, utilizing a synth-driven sound that focuses on Pop-informed melodicism while de-emphasizing guitar riffing.

subgenres.name: Symphonic Prog
subgenres.desc: Incorporates Classical Music elements that can manifest in longer form works that deviate from traditional popular song structures, and the use of lush keyboards to replicate Orchestral Music textures.

subgenres.name: Proto-Punk
subgenres.desc: Used to describe what influenced or in some way resembled Punk Rock before that genre's commercial breakthrough in 1976.

subgenres.name: Psychedelic Rock
subgenres.desc: Often attempts to emulate or enhance the effects of psychedelic drugs, typically through a variety of instrumental and studio effects or eclectic influences.

subgenres.name: Acid Rock
subgenres.desc: Heavier with an emphasis on instrumental jamming and "wah" guitar effects.

subgenres.name: Freakbeat
subgenres.desc: Outgrowth of the Mod movement which combines elements of British Rhythm & Blues and Beat with studio effects common in Psychedelia such as fuzztones, flanging and chorus; often seen as a British relative of the American Garage Psych scene.

subgenres.name: Garage Psych
subgenres.desc: Emerged from mid-1960s US Garage Rock; characterised by fuzz guitars, cheap organs, experimentation with psychedelic effects and surreal lyricism, and a retained emphasis on raw energy and the pop song format.

subgenres.name: Heavy Psych
subgenres.desc: Influenced by Blues Rock's heavy dependence on riffs and improvisatory leanings; features thick, fuzzy guitars, usually slow-to-mid tempos, and extended soloing sections.

subgenres.name: Raga Rock
subgenres.desc: Influenced by South Asian Music, featuring a droning compositional quality and commonly incorporating instruments like sitar, tambura, and tablas.

subgenres.name: Space Rock
subgenres.desc: Heavy use of synthesizers and guitar effects to create dense atmospheric soundscapes intended to evoke images of outer space and science fiction scenarios.

subgenres.name: Space Rock Revival
subgenres.desc: Draws from the aesthetics and atmospheric soundscapes of Space Rock combined with the more minimal, back-to-basics approach of the Post-Punk era.

subgenres.name: Xian Psych
subgenres.desc: Portrays Christian and biblical themes through a surreal, transcendent atmosphere, occasionally drawing influence from Christian Liturgical Music.

subgenres.name: Zamrock
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Copperbelt region of Zambia in the 1970s, characterized by its blend of local sounds with influence from Funk, Hard Rock, and Blues Rock.

subgenres.name: Pub Rock
subgenres.desc: Stripped-down style developed in the United Kingdom in the early to mid-1970s, mainly as a reaction to the perceived excess and pretension of Progressive Rock and Glam Rock.

subgenres.name: Punk Blues
subgenres.desc: Fusion of the instrumentation and scales of Blues Rock with Punk.

subgenres.name: Punk Rock
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, loud and distorted riffs, simple songs, frequent use of power chords, and shouted vocals, originating in the mid-1970s in response to commercial, sentimental, and complex Rock.

subgenres.name: Anarcho-Punk
subgenres.desc: Intentionally rougher and sloppier sound, with lyrics pertaining to anarchist ideology and sociopolitical injustices.

subgenres.name: Celtic Punk
subgenres.desc: Infuses the sounds of Celtic Folk Music into Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Deathrock
subgenres.desc: More Punk-oriented offshoot of Gothic Rock that emphasizes energy and an effect-laden sound over pure atmosphere.

subgenres.name: Deutschpunk
subgenres.desc: Partly a reaction to the commercialization of the German movement Neue Deutsche Welle; characterized by extreme speed, consciously basic songwriting, crude musicianship, and radical leftism.

subgenres.name: Egg Punk
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2010s; features lo-fi production, eccentric lyrics, quick tempos, nasally vocals, and cheap keyboard sounds.

subgenres.name: Garage Punk
subgenres.desc: Combination of the raw fuzztones of the original Garage Rock bands of the 1960s with the tempo and attitude of Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Glam Punk
subgenres.desc: Contrasts a snotty, nihilistic, and combative attitude of punk with theatrics and flamboyance.

subgenres.name: Hardcore Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1970s, often featuring extensive use of yelling or screaming, a stripped-down production style, and very short songs.

subgenres.name: Burning Spirits
subgenres.desc: Emphasis on delivering a very energetic and triumphant sound with flashy and soaring Metal solos, "melodramatic" or "uplifting" chord progressions, and singalong, over the top, harsh vocals.

subgenres.name: Crossover Thrash
subgenres.desc: Mixes the metallic instrumentation of Thrash Metal with the ethos and approach of Hardcore Punk.

subgenres.name: Crust Punk
subgenres.desc: Metallic outgrowth of Anarcho-Punk featuring a down-tuned, high-gain guitar sound, frequent D-Beat drum patterns, guttural vocals, and politically-charged lyrics often featuring apocalyptic imagery.

subgenres.name: Blackened Crust
subgenres.desc: Borrows heavily from Black Metal production, blast beats, tremolo guitar, and vocals, while retaining the core Crust Punk sound, lyrical themes, and aesthetic.

subgenres.name: Neocrust
subgenres.desc: Melodic, dark, and atmospheric style that often incorporates influences from Sludge Metal, Post-Metal, Black Metal, and Screamo.

subgenres.name: Stenchcore
subgenres.desc: Heavier, more metallic form of Crust Punk drawing influence from Thrash Metal as well as Death Metal and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: D-Beat
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the early 1980s, features Metal influences, shouted vocals, and a distinct drum style known as the D-beat.

subgenres.name: Melodic Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the USA in the early to mid-1980s, placing emphasis on melodic vocals and technical guitar riffs rather than raw aggression.

subgenres.name: Mincecore
subgenres.desc: Raw and simplistic with heavy reliance on Punk structures while including political and socially aware themes.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

subgenres.name: Street Punk
subgenres.desc: Driven by Oi! style group vocals, catchy melodies, and aggressive songwriting akin to Punk Rock of the 1970s fused with Hardcore Punk of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Thrashcore
subgenres.desc: Fast tempos, brief song structures, and the occasional use of blast beats.

subgenres.name: Powerviolence
subgenres.desc: Originated from the West Coast California Hardcore Punk scene in the late 1980s, utilizing strong elements of Noise Rock and abrupt tempo changes.

subgenres.name: Horror Punk
subgenres.desc: Thematically and lyrically derived from Horror movies, typically with a nostalgic and campy attitude.

subgenres.name: Könsrock
subgenres.desc: Inspired by Post-Punk but with a more bizarre atmosphere with unusual or comic vocal techniques and a lyrical focus on the offensive and scatological.

subgenres.name: Oi!
subgenres.desc: Rejection of perceived intellectualism and elitism in Post-Punk and Art Punk, characterized by a return to a straightforward, melodic Punk Rock sound, sing-along choruses, and a lyrical focus on working class youth culture.

subgenres.name: Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Blends the loud, fast-paced sound of Punk Rock with the melodic hooks of Pop.

subgenres.name: Easycore
subgenres.desc: Combines the radio-friendly stylings of second-wave Pop Punk with Metalcore-inspired breakdowns, lower guitar tunings, and occasional unclean vocals.

subgenres.name: Neon Pop Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged from Scene culture; combines the upbeat tempos and catchy melodies of Pop Punk and Power Pop with synthesizers, auto-tuned vocals, or Dance beats, emphasizing a distinctly polished, hook-oriented sound.

subgenres.name: Seishun Punk
subgenres.desc: Short-lived Japanese style popular in the early 2000s, characterized by a raw and abrasive style, Folk-inspired songwriting, and youth-oriented straightforward lyrics.

subgenres.name: Positive Punk
subgenres.desc: Early goth scene in London that grew out of the Anarcho-Punk movement and promoted themes of virtue and mysticism; commonly features wailing vocals, screeching guitars, prominent basslines, and eclectic drum patterns.

subgenres.name: Psychobilly
subgenres.desc: Cross-pollination of Punk Rock and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: Ska Punk
subgenres.desc: Utilizes skank rhythms, walking basslines, and often horn instrumentation in combination with a fast-paced Punk Rock playstyle.

subgenres.name: Skacore
subgenres.desc: Fuses skank rhythms and frantic blasts of horns with hardcore intensity.

subgenres.name: Crack Rock Steady
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements of Crust Punk and sometimes Metal, coupled with anti-establishment lyrics.

subgenres.name: Skate Punk
subgenres.desc: Combines the speed of Melodic Hardcore with the catchiness of Pop Punk, finding a middle ground between the two.

subgenres.name: Surf Punk
subgenres.desc: Punk Rock that incorporates elements of Surf Rock.

subgenres.name: Vikingarock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from Nordic Folk Music and the imagery of Viking romanticism and Norse mythology.

subgenres.name: Rap Rock
subgenres.desc: Fusion of Hip Hop and Rock, often featuring the former’s rhythmic vocal delivery and the latter’s heavy, distorted instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Rap Metal
subgenres.desc: Features rapped vocals, typically formed around heavy, mid-tempo, and groove-oriented playing in addition to elements of Hip Hop beats such as record scratching.

subgenres.name: Reggae Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates the offbeat rhythms and staccato "skank" guitar of Reggae.

subgenres.name: Rock & Roll
subgenres.desc: Developed in the United States and popularized in the 1950s, featuring prominent Blues scales, poppy structures, and strong rhythms.

subgenres.name: Indorock
subgenres.desc: Predominantly instrumental style influenced by Country, Malay Music, and Hawaiian Music; created in the late 1950s by Indo and Moluccan expatriates from Indonesia to the Netherlands.

subgenres.name: Rockabilly
subgenres.desc: Blends the sound of Country with that of Rhythm & Blues, often accompanied by driving guitars, frantic vocals, and slap-back echo in the bass.

subgenres.name: Psychobilly
subgenres.desc: Cross-pollination of Punk Rock and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: Twist
subgenres.desc: Simple, fast, and energetic dance popular in the early 1960s.

subgenres.name: Rock andaluz
subgenres.desc: Emerged during the mid-1970s in Spain; primarily utilizes Flamenco and often Symphonic Prog elements.

subgenres.name: Rock andino
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the Andean countries in the late 1960s and early 1970s, incorporating traditional instruments and harmonies from Indigenous Andean Music within a Rock format.

subgenres.name: Rock Musical
subgenres.desc: Style of musical theatre inspired by Rock.

subgenres.name: Rock Opera
subgenres.desc: Hybrid of rock and, sometimes, musical theatre stylings with heavily rock-tinged songs combining to tell a coherent story.

subgenres.name: Roots Rock
subgenres.desc: Consciously and predominantly incorporates elements of its predecessors and original roots such as Country, Blues, Rhythm & Blues, Rock & Roll, and American Folk Music, but also many other American traditions.

subgenres.name: Swamp Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates influences from the musical styles and traditions of Louisiana.

subgenres.name: Tex-Mex
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock & Roll, Blues, Country, and several types of Hispanic American Music, particularly Tejano Music.

subgenres.name: Southern Rock
subgenres.desc: Emerged from the American South in the early 1970s, blending Blues Rock, Hard Rock, and Rock & Roll with elements of Country and Contemporary Folk.

subgenres.name: Sufi Rock
subgenres.desc: Pakistani subgenre rooted in Sufi tradition, featuring South Asian instruments like the dhol, tabla, and sitar within a Rock band format with lyrics and imagery inspired by traditional Sufi poets.

subgenres.name: Surf Music
subgenres.desc: Evolved from late 1950s instrumental Rock & Roll in the USA, particularly associated with the surfing culture in Southern California.

subgenres.name: Hot Rod Music
subgenres.desc: Features prominent lyrics about hot rods and car culture and incorporates Sound Effects and guitar textures to mimic sounds made by automobiles.

subgenres.name: Indie Surf
subgenres.desc: Reverb-drenched, nostalgic, and often lo-fi, with influences from Surf Rock and Vocal Surf; rose to popularity around 2009.

subgenres.name: Surf Punk
subgenres.desc: Punk Rock that incorporates elements of Surf Rock.

subgenres.name: Surf Rock
subgenres.desc: Short instrumental songs with Rock & Roll rhythms overlaid with cheerful melodies played on reverb-drenched tremolo guitar.

subgenres.name: Eleki
subgenres.desc: Japanese Surf Rock that emerged during the early to mid-1960s, incorporating elements of Japanese Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Rautalanka
subgenres.desc: Nordic guitar style mainly influenced by Rock & Roll, and traditional European Schlager.

subgenres.name: Wong shadow
subgenres.desc: Small, short-lived guitar Pop movement in Thailand in the 1960s, fusing Surf Rock  with local melodies.

subgenres.name: Vocal Surf
subgenres.desc: Appropriates the sounds of instrumental Surf Rock, combining surfing- and car-themed lyrics with a style that draws primarily from Doo-Wop and Rock & Roll.

subgenres.name: Symphonic Rock
subgenres.desc: Incorporates elements resembling Orchestral Music.

subgenres.name: Tolai Rock
subgenres.desc: Fuses the music of the Tolai people of Papua New Guinea with Rock.

subgenres.name: Zolo
subgenres.desc: Mostly retroactive term grouping disparate artists, characterized by jerky, staccato rhythms, "boingy" guitars, and "wobbly" keyboards.

subgenres.name: Afrofuturism
subgenres.desc: Movement rooted in Jazz and Funk, blending futuristic aesthetics and themes with African and Afrodiasporic culture.

subgenres.name: Akron Sound
subgenres.desc: Early Punk and New Wave scene in Akron, Ohio, and nearby Kent from the mid-1970s to the early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Alté
subgenres.desc: More subdued, atmospheric, minimalist, and eclectic production and vocal styles compared to earlier styles, as well as more socially conscious lyrics.

subgenres.name: Anarcho-Punk
subgenres.desc: Intentionally rougher and sloppier sound, with lyrics pertaining to anarchist ideology and sociopolitical injustices.

subgenres.name: Asian Underground
subgenres.desc: South Asian diasporic movement defined by musical acts, producers and DJs fusing contemporary Electronic music with Bhangra and other traditional styles.

subgenres.name: Aussie Pub Rock
subgenres.desc: Straightforward Rock acts associated with the Australian pub circuit of the 1970s and 1980s.

subgenres.name: Authenticité
subgenres.desc: Post-independence cultural movement born in socialist Guinea aiming to reclaim pre-colonial heritage and forge a shared national identity, largely through government-funded programs, national orchestras, and radical rejection of European influences.

subgenres.name: Bay Area Thrash Metal
subgenres.desc: Highly influential Thrash Metal scene centered around the San Francisco Bay Area.

subgenres.name: Beach Music
subgenres.desc: Danceable 4/4 "blues shuffle" rhythmic structure, vocal harmonies, and moderate tempos.

subgenres.name: Beijing New Sound
subgenres.desc: Pioneering Chinese indie Rock movement in the late '90s that renewed the heavy narratives of early '90s Chinese rock with its stylish sound and personal themes.

subgenres.name: Bérite Club
subgenres.desc: Originated in the underground club scene of Paris in the mid-to-late 2010s, drawing on a variety of international club styles for its combination of prominent and erratic drum programming with freezing and looping chopped-up samples.

subgenres.name: Bernese Dialect Scene
subgenres.desc: Influential scene of artists centered in the Swiss city of Bern, featuring poetic lyrics in Bernese German.

subgenres.name: Bloghouse
subgenres.desc: Internet-based movement from the mid-to-late-2000s which broadly distilled scenes most associated with online music blogging, mp3-sharing and remix culture, intersecting within Dance styles such as Electroclash, Electro House, New Rave and Nu-Disco in a brash and carefree fashion.

subgenres.name: Bosstown Sound
subgenres.desc: Short-lived Psychedelic Rock and Psychedelic Pop scene in Boston, Massachusetts; marketed byMGM Recordsas Boston’s response to the San Francisco Sound.

subgenres.name: Bristol Sound
subgenres.desc: UK-based scene associated with Bristol's soundsystem culture and early Trip Hop within the late 1980s to late 1990s, featuring a bass-heavy, spaced-out sound largely inspired by Dub, Soul and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: British Rhythm & Blues
subgenres.desc: A style infusing Rock and R&B that was hugely popular in the United Kingdom between 1963 and 1966.

subgenres.name: British Trad Jazz
subgenres.desc: Popular mid-1950s to early '60s revival of Dixieland; pushed out commercially by Beat music in 1963.

subgenres.name: Britpop
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the United Kingdom in the early 1990s, with a style hearkening back to the traditional guitar-driven songs and melodic hooks found in the British Pop Rock of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Brno Alternative Scene
subgenres.desc: Semi-official, avant-garde scene active primarily in the the 1980s in the Czech Socialist Republic.

subgenres.name: BRock
subgenres.desc: Brazilian New Wave movement of the 1980s, influenced by radio-friendly Pop Rock and Punk subculture.

subgenres.name: Brony Music
subgenres.desc: Fan works, created by the brony community, relating to the My Little Pony franchise.

subgenres.name: Burger-Highlife
subgenres.desc: Created by Ghanaian immigrants to Germany in the late 1970s, generally employing synthesizers and Western post-production techniques alongside guitar-driven Highlife instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Campus Folk
subgenres.desc: Born in Taiwan in the mid-1970s, this movement originated with university students creating their own modern-style songs in the wake of international tensions like Taiwan's isolation from the United Nations and the United States' embrace of the PRC as a diplomatic partner.

subgenres.name: Canterbury Scene
subgenres.desc: Developed in the counterculture of Canterbury in the late 1960s, emphasizing the influence of Jazz-Rock and Jazz Fusion.

subgenres.name: Neo-Canterbury
subgenres.desc: Movement reviving the signature style of the Canterbury Scene, often updating it with modern influences.

subgenres.name: Cascadian Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Scene hailing from the Pacific Northwest region of the United States and Canada marked by nature-centric imagery, oftentimes incorporating elements of Post-Metal.

subgenres.name: CBGB Scene
subgenres.desc: Early Punk scene built around artists who frequently played at the East Village's CBGB club in the mid-1970s.

subgenres.name: CCM
subgenres.desc: Popular music focused on Christian spirituality and faith.

subgenres.name: Praise & Worship
subgenres.desc: Christian music with lyrics focused on the greatness of God.

subgenres.name: Praise Break
subgenres.desc: High-energy, improvisational "break" for worshiping God in Black churches.

subgenres.name: Urban Contemporary Gospel
subgenres.desc: Inspired by Gospel music, featuring Christian lyrics adapted to contemporary rhythms and styles.

subgenres.name: Česká alternativní scéna
subgenres.desc: Semi-official scene active during the Normalisation era in the Czech Socialist Republic.

subgenres.name: Česká nová vlna
subgenres.desc: Diverse New Wave scene active intermittently in the 1980s in the Czech Socialist Republic.

subgenres.name: Český underground
subgenres.desc: Antiestablishment musical counterculture active primarily in the 1970s and 1980s in the Czech Socialist Republic.

subgenres.name: Chicago No Wave
subgenres.desc: 1990s Experimental Rock scene in Chicago, Illinois; so named due to its deconstructionist approach to Rock music, similar to that of the No Wave scene in late 1970s New York City.

subgenres.name: Chicago School
subgenres.desc: Predominantly 1990s Post-Rock scene which blends influences from Indie Rock and Jazz with an expanded instrumental palette and a diverse approach to sonic exploration.

subgenres.name: Chikipunk
subgenres.desc: Peruvian scene of the late 1990s and early 2000s as a new scene of Pop Punk, Melodic Hardcore, Skate Punk, Emo and Nu Metal bands without influences from Rock subterráneo.

subgenres.name: Christian Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Developed in the 1990s in the United States, incorporating faith-based Christian messages into Hardcore [Punk] music.

subgenres.name: Cleveland Punk
subgenres.desc: Early Punk scene in Cleveland, Ohio during the 1970s and early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Clube da esquina
subgenres.desc: Brazilian movement from the state of Minas Gerais, mostly active in the 1960s and 1970s.

subgenres.name: Cocktail Nation
subgenres.desc: Decidedly ironic take on Lounge that emerged in the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: C-Pop
subgenres.desc: Commercialized style performed by Chinese communities across China and Taiwan, alongside its large diaspora.

subgenres.name: Cantopop
subgenres.desc: Modern commercial Pop music sung in the Cantonese language, usually produced in Hong Kong or adjacent regions.

subgenres.name: Gufeng
subgenres.desc: Emphasizes Chineseness and an "ancient" atmosphere, and often features semi-classical lyrics.

subgenres.name: Hokkien Pop
subgenres.desc: Modern Pop music sung in Hokkien dialects, with its industry largely centered across Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

subgenres.name: Mandopop
subgenres.desc: C-Pop in which songs are performed in Mandarin.

subgenres.name: Zhongguo feng
subgenres.desc: Inspired by traditional elements of Chinese Music with lyrical themes constantly revolving around Chinese culture and tales.

subgenres.name: Crisálida sónica
subgenres.desc: Peruvian scene of the mid-1990s influenced by Shoegaze, Post-Rock, Space Rock Revival, IDM and Ambient.

subgenres.name: Dariacore
subgenres.desc: SoundCloud-based scene developed in the early 2020s, combining prominent vocal samples and distorted, dense production with influences from a wide range of Electronic Dance Music genres, often incorporating musical and visual references to popular media and internet culture.

subgenres.name: Darmstadt School
subgenres.desc: Circle of post-World War II Western European composers of avant-garde Modern Classical, exploring Serialism and other innovations.

subgenres.name: Dek Bass
subgenres.desc: Prominent heavy, sustained bass tones, percussion derived from South Asian Music, and often high-pitched sound effects or samples; commonly played at extreme volumes in DJ/sound system competitions.

subgenres.name: Demoscene
subgenres.desc: Computer art subculture originating in the 1980s based on the creation of demos and overcoming technical limitations.

subgenres.name: Desi Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip hop music created on the Indian subcontinent and the South Asian diaspora, especially India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.

subgenres.name: Deutschrock
subgenres.desc: Lyrics address German life, culture, and identity wrapped in upbeat songs, anthemic ballads, and a strong focus on the personality of the lead singer.

subgenres.name: Dolewave
subgenres.desc: Loose, low-key, and sardonic with erudite lyrics and considerable influence from the Dunedin Sound and Slacker Rock; came to prominence in Melbourne in the early 2010s.

subgenres.name: Donosti Sound
subgenres.desc: Sentimental and melancholic scene, influenced by Twee Pop, that emerged in the late 1980s in Donostia / San Sebastián, Spain.

subgenres.name: Doom WAD Music
subgenres.desc: Typically but not exclusively MIDI Music, associated with mods for the 1993 first-person shooter video game Doom and other games in the Doom engine.

subgenres.name: Doujin Music
subgenres.desc: Independently-released music derived from the wider doujin movement in Japan, largely released at events such as Comiket and M3, and primarily focused on otaku interests.

subgenres.name: Touhou Music
subgenres.desc: Stemming from doujin bullet hell video game franchiseTouhou Project, including original music and derivative fan arrangements of varying styles.

subgenres.name: Dunedin Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Dunedin, New Zealand in the early 1980s, featuring a murky, lo-fi sound that overlaps with contemporaneous Jangle Pop and Slacker Rock styles.

subgenres.name: Düsseldorf School
subgenres.desc: Krautrock scene which developed alongside Berlin School music in the early 1970s; known for its characteristic ‘motorik beat,’ as well as for playing a major role in the evolution of Electronic music.

subgenres.name: East Coast Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Highly influential Hip Hop scene that developed in New York City, particularly in the South Bronx, during the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Bronx Drill
subgenres.desc: Bronx scene that popularized Sample Drill and aggressive New York Drill delivery and production in the early 2020s.

subgenres.name: Brooklyn Drill
subgenres.desc: Brooklyn scene that kickstarted New York Drill in the mid-2010s, primarily through adopted UK Drill production.

subgenres.name: DMV Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop from artists in the Greater Washington metropolitan area, including the District of Columbia, southern Maryland, and northern Virginia.

subgenres.name: Emo Revival
subgenres.desc: Movement beginning in the late 2000s inspired by the styles of 1990s Midwest Emo, often associated with Math Rock-inflected "twinkly" style.

subgenres.name: English Underground
subgenres.desc: Countercultural scene in the United Kingdom, centred around London clubs like UFO and Middle Earth, which peaked in 1966 and 1967.

subgenres.name: Ladbroke Grove Scene
subgenres.desc: English Underground scene which blossomed in Ladbroke Grove, London, soon after the closure of the popular West End psychedelic club Middle Earth in 1968; faded by the mid-'70s, especially following the rise of Pub Rock and Punk.

subgenres.name: Epadunk
subgenres.desc: Swedish party-oriented scene emerging in the early 2020s, featuring Electronic Dance Music-leaning sound and vulgar lyrics.

subgenres.name: Filk
subgenres.desc: Broad fandom movement that emerged from Science Fiction conventions in the 1950s focused on original lyrics about fan interests set to popular melodies and original compositions across an eclectic range of genres.

subgenres.name: First Wave of Detroit Techno
subgenres.desc: Influential 1980s scene that invented Detroit Techno and was active in Electro, House, and Synthpop.

subgenres.name: Florida Fast Music
subgenres.desc: DJing and production technique originally developed in South Florida, that primarily involves speeding up Hip Hop, Contemporary R&B, and East Coast Club records.

subgenres.name: Fort Thunder Scene
subgenres.desc: Late '90s – early 2000s Noise and Noise Rock scene that formed around an art commune in Providence, Rhode Island.

subgenres.name: Franco-Flemish School
subgenres.desc: Musical movement centered in the Low Countries, known for its intricate polyphony, emotional expression, and influence on European sacred and secular music from the 1440s to 1550.

subgenres.name: Frapcore
subgenres.desc: Emerged in France in the mid-2010s, uses French rapping with 4-on-the-floor Hardcore [EDM] and especially Gabber instrumentals.

subgenres.name: Free Noise
subgenres.desc: 1990s New Zealand scene consisting of Rock-based groups with a focus on Free Improvisation, Drone, and Noise music.

subgenres.name: French Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop originating from France, typically performed in the French language.

subgenres.name: Friese bries
subgenres.desc: New Wave and Punk inspired music scene located in the province of Friesland in the Netherlands in the mid-1980s.

subgenres.name: Furry Music
subgenres.desc: Created by and for the furry fandom/subculture, an independent art movement focused on anthropomorphic characters.

subgenres.name: Futurism
subgenres.desc: Radical and militant attitude, rejection of Western Classical Music and traditional criteria of craft, non-conformity, and a fascination with machines.

subgenres.name: Gothenburg Sound
subgenres.desc: Pioneering Melodic Death Metal style and scene of Gothenburg, Sweden.

subgenres.name: Grebo
subgenres.desc: Short-lived English subculture and associated music; raw, futuristic, sample-heavy form of Alternative Dance with a dirty guitar sound.

subgenres.name: Greenwich Village Scene
subgenres.desc: Collective of folk singers who mainly performed in small venues (basements, bars, and coffee houses) throughout Greenwich Village from the late 1950s to mid-1960s.

subgenres.name: Group Sounds
subgenres.desc: Japanese bands in the mid-to-late 1960s who began performing a style of Beat primarily in English.

subgenres.name: Hamburger Schule
subgenres.desc: Combines traditions of the Neue Deutsche Welle based on Grunge with Pop hooks and elements of Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Harlem Renaissance
subgenres.desc: Influential 1920s and '30s cultural movement centered on the African American community in Harlem, New York.

subgenres.name: Hellenic Black Metal
subgenres.desc: Black metal scene in Greece with more mid-tempo songwriting and pronounced Heavy Metal influence.

subgenres.name: High Quality Rip
subgenres.desc: Community based on bait-and-switch remixes of music, localized online.

subgenres.name: Hipco
subgenres.desc: Developed in Liberia, often featuring conscious and political lyrics and influences from local dance styles.

subgenres.name: Hip-hopolo
subgenres.desc: 2000s Polish Hip Hop scene focused on a mainstream approach; received massive popularity and overwhelming criticism from the hip hop community.

subgenres.name: Hoboken Sound
subgenres.desc: Predominantly 1980s New Jersey scene that blended contemporary Post-Punk and New Wave with Power Pop melodicism and Garage Rock directness, becoming heavily influential to early American Jangle Pop and Alternative Rock as a whole.

subgenres.name: Holy Terror
subgenres.desc: Offshoot of the Process Church of Final Judgement and The Abraxas Foundation sects, focused on the occult and demonology, as well as apocalyptic, misanthropic themes.

subgenres.name: Hưng ca
subgenres.desc: Diasporic Vietnamese movement originating in the United States during the 1980s; characterised by nationalistic and socio-political lyrics.

subgenres.name: Japanese Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Bands from Japan, performing styles such as Burning Spirits, Crust Punk, and Thrashcore.

subgenres.name: Japanese Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop which is created by artists who are either based in or from Japan.

subgenres.name: Japanese Idol
subgenres.desc: Contemporary Japanese singer-dancers valued mainly for their personality and charisma, often performing as groups in a cutesy and youthful style.

subgenres.name: Alternative Idol
subgenres.desc: Unconventional approaches characterized by alternative music styles and often unusual public images.

subgenres.name: J-core
subgenres.desc: Eclectic scene of Japanese Hardcore [EDM] heavily associated with Doujin Music.

subgenres.name: Future Core
subgenres.desc: Blends the speed, basslines, and rhythms of UK Hardcore (mostly coming from the J-core sphere) with euphoric, woozy synths, 7th chords and arpeggios, and vocal chops of Future Bass, particularly Kawaii Future Bass.

subgenres.name: Jersey Shore Sound
subgenres.desc: Stylistically correlated to Heartland Rock, with cultural origins in coastal New Jersey; characterized by its horn-heavy mixture of 1960s Rock & Roll, Rhythm & Blues, and Doo-Wop.

subgenres.name: Jovem Guarda
subgenres.desc: 1960s Brazilian youth-oriented Pop Rock, with romantic lyrics and influenced by Merseybeat and Rockabilly.

subgenres.name: J-Pop
subgenres.desc: Commercial Pop of Japan after the advent of the Heisei era (1989), characterized by modernized production, a more eclectic sound palette, and a more westernized vocal style.

subgenres.name: Akishibu-kei
subgenres.desc: Otaku inclined update of the style pioneered by the Shibuya-kei scene, mixed with J-Pop and often tied to Anime and Video Game Music.

subgenres.name: Denpa
subgenres.desc: Underground style aiming to be bizarre yet catchy, using off-key and high-pitched vocals, strange or nonsensical lyrics, repetitive chants, onomatopoeia, frantic and "off-kilter" production, and "moe" aesthetics.

subgenres.name: Wa Euro
subgenres.desc: Traditional form of J-Pop that emerged in the second half of the 1980s from late Hi-NRG, '80s British Dance-Pop and Italo-Disco/Eurobeat.

subgenres.name: J-Euro
subgenres.desc: Italian-oriented Japanese scene of Eurobeat, which emerged with Japanese-language covers of Italian songs in the early-to-mid-1990s.

subgenres.name: Yakousei
subgenres.desc: Eclectic style of J-Pop developed in the late 2010s and influenced by the Vocaloid Scene; incorporates indie sensibilities, danceable rhythms and a focus on introspective lyricism.

subgenres.name: Kansai No Wave
subgenres.desc: Late '70s to early '80s scene from the Kansai region of Japan, sharing the brash oppositional, anti-music attitude of New York City No Wave.

subgenres.name: Kawaii Metal
subgenres.desc: Fuses various Metal substyles with J-Pop's upbeat melodicism and song structures, utilizing kawaii lyricism and an idol music aesthetic.

subgenres.name: K-Pop
subgenres.desc: Contemporary style from South Korea, based on multiple mainstream influences such as Contemporary R&B, Dance-Pop, and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Semi-Trot
subgenres.desc: Contemporary form of Trot which takes influences from modern K-Pop and recent Pop substyles.

subgenres.name: LA Beat Scene
subgenres.desc: Los Angeles scene from the 2000s to mid-2010s where DJs and beatmakers added off-kilter rhythms and textures to Hip Hop and Electronic.

subgenres.name: Laurel Canyon Scene
subgenres.desc: 1960s and 1970s Rock counterculture originating from the Laurel Canyon neighborhood of Los Angeles, highly influential to the development of contemporary Folk Rock and Soft Rock.

subgenres.name: Leningrad Rock Club Scene
subgenres.desc: Community of primarily Post-Punk and New Wave bands in the 1980s USSR that sprung up around the Leningrad Rock Club, the first legal venue of its kind allowed under cautious government oversight.

subgenres.name: Little Band Scene
subgenres.desc: Experimental Post-Punk scene which occurred in Melbourne in 1978-1981, based around intentionally short-lived bands with a small amount of material.

subgenres.name: Loft Jazz
subgenres.desc: New York based independent Jazz scene defined by casual performances in lofts and apartments.

subgenres.name: Louisville Sound
subgenres.desc: Predominantly Punk and indie scene from Kentucky in the 1980s and 1990s, heavily influential in the development of Post-Hardcore, Math Rock, and a distinctly American form of Post-Rock.

subgenres.name: Madchester
subgenres.desc: Manchester-based eclectic, Dance-infused music and cultural phenomenon from the late 1980s to the early 1990s emphasising drug and rave culture.

subgenres.name: Maidcore
subgenres.desc: Eclectic internet music scene mixing elements of Metal, Post-Rock, and Electronic that originated on Russian social media in the mid-2010s; comprised of artists portrayed as 'maid' characters derived from the Japanese Nijiura imageboard.

subgenres.name: Manguebeat
subgenres.desc: Counterculture fusion of traditional Northeastern Brazilian Music genres with modern Rock and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: Manila Sound
subgenres.desc: Mid-to-late 1970s scene that emerged in Manila, Philippines, drawing from Soft Rock, Disco, Hard Rock, as well as Funk, with themes of romance and urban life.

subgenres.name: Mentai Rock
subgenres.desc: Japanese Rock & Roll artists from Fukuoka from the late 1970s to early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Merseybeat
subgenres.desc: Light, highly melodic style of Beat popular in the UK during the early 1960s, named due to the abundance of bands from Liverpool beside the River Mersey.

subgenres.name: Midwest Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop from artists based within the midwestern region of the United States.

subgenres.name: Minneapolis Sound
subgenres.desc: Emerged in late 1970s Minneapolis, characterized by glossy Contemporary R&B-influenced production techniques, angular New Wave-inspired rhythms, and a larger emphasis on electric guitar layers.

subgenres.name: Młoda Polska
subgenres.desc: Neoromantic composers attempting to create a new Polish national style.

subgenres.name: Mod
subgenres.desc: 1960s youth subculture in the United Kingdom, drawing from British Rhythm & Blues, Beat, Garage Rock, and Pop sensibilities alongside a distinctive fashion style.

subgenres.name: Mod Revival
subgenres.desc: Late 1970s and early 1980s revival of Mod fashion and music, featuring influence from the nascent Punk Rock scene.

subgenres.name: Moscow School
subgenres.desc: School of Russian Western Classical Music composers centered on Moscow in the mid-to-late 19th century.

subgenres.name: Motswako
subgenres.desc: Mainly rapped in a mixture of Setswana and English, incorporating additional languages and local South African and Botswanan influences, particularly Kwaito.

subgenres.name: Movida madrileña
subgenres.desc: Countercultural scene developed in Madrid, Spain, in the late 1970s as a reflection of the newfound freedom after the end of the Franco’s dictatorship; mainly playing New Wave, Synthpop and Post-Punk.

subgenres.name: Nardcore
subgenres.desc: Hardcore Punk scene originating in Oxnard, California, in the early 1980s which often emphasizes speed, aggression, and technicality, and is heavily associated with the local southern California skateboarding culture and a D.I.Y. ethos.

subgenres.name: Nederbeat
subgenres.desc: Dutch answer to the British Beat boom of the 1960s.

subgenres.name: Nerdcore Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Themes touch on such nerd mainstays as science, computers, and science fiction.

subgenres.name: Nerdcore Techno
subgenres.desc: Stylistically diverse form of underground Japanese Electronic Dance Music utilizing energetic beats built around samples from pop and/or nerd culture.

subgenres.name: Neue Deutsche Welle
subgenres.desc: Eclectic German scene influenced by Synthpop and various styles of Punk, sometimes associated with Industrial.

subgenres.name: Neue Volksmusik
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the Southern German region from  in the 1980s onwards as a reaction to the conservatism of Alpine Folk Music scenes, combining the genre with outside sources and paired with a strong sense of irony and progressive political views.

subgenres.name: New Brunswick Basement Scene
subgenres.desc: Underground Punk Rock, Emo, and Indie Rock scene centred around Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

subgenres.name: New London Jazz
subgenres.desc: Contemporary and eclectic Jazz scene based in London, UK, that pulls from a variety of styles, including Spiritual Jazz, Afro-Jazz, and Jazz Fusion, and is often influenced by other genres such as Electronic, Dub, and Hip Hop.

subgenres.name: New Music
subgenres.desc: Developed when Japanese Singer-Songwriters incorporated elements of Contemporary Folk and Pop Rock with Kayōkyoku songwriting.

subgenres.name: New Orleans Blues
subgenres.desc: Diverse scene in New Orleans since the beginning of the 20th century, commonly associated with a sound led by rollicking pianos with syncopated beats and backed by horns.

subgenres.name: New Partisans
subgenres.desc: Short-lived movement in the mid-to-late 1980s in Sarajevo which attempted to synthesise Pop Rock with elements of Yugoslav Folk music and the ideals of the 1940s Yugoslav partisan movement.

subgenres.name: New Pop
subgenres.desc: British-centric movement of 1980s acts utilising Post-Punk ideals in a mainstream Pop context, characterised by cross-style experimentation and a strong focus on visual aesthetics.

subgenres.name: New Primitivism
subgenres.desc: Cross-media movement in Sarajevo, active primarily in the 1980s and inspired by Yugoslav New Wave and Yugoslav Punk.

subgenres.name: New Romantic
subgenres.desc: UK cultural movement associated with the early 1980s and defined by a distinct, flamboyant fashion sense.

subgenres.name: New Tone
subgenres.desc: Musically and socio-politically progressive movement noted for combatting prejudices and mixing together different styles of music, such as Electronic, Hip Hop, or Emo.

subgenres.name: New Wave of New Wave
subgenres.desc: Short-lived British New Wave and Punk Rock revival scene, active primarily around 1993-94 before being pushed out by the mass popularity of Britpop; often derided as a media construct.

subgenres.name: New Way of Danish Fuck You
subgenres.desc: Copenhagen underground scene active in the late 2000s and early 2010s, drawing on Post-Punk, Industrial, Noise, Hardcore Punk, and Black Metal and embracing a raw, lo-fi, cassette-based recording style and DIY ethos.

subgenres.name: New Weird America
subgenres.desc: Diverse movement that originated in the Northeastern United States during the late 1990s and 2000s which reshaped mid-20th century Contemporary Folk influences through a psychedelic and avant-garde approach.

subgenres.name: New Weird Finland
subgenres.desc: Rose to prominence in the early 2000s, based around a collective of musicians living primarily in the Finnish cities of Tampere, Turku and Helsinki and with a sound primarily rooted in Psychedelia, particularly Psychedelic Folk and its subgenres Free Folk and Freak Folk.

subgenres.name: New York Hardcore
subgenres.desc: Hardcore Punk bands from New York City from the 1980s and onwards.

subgenres.name: New York School
subgenres.desc: Circle of avant-garde composers based in 1950s New York, most well known for pioneering the use of chance as a method of composition.

subgenres.name: NOLA Sludge
subgenres.desc: New Orleans–based Louisiana Metal scene, commonly cited as the birthplace of Sludge Metal.

subgenres.name: Northern Gothic
subgenres.desc: Modern recontexualisation of Gothic music, influenced by the regional politics, culture and geography of post-industrial 21st-century Northern England.

subgenres.name: Northern Soul
subgenres.desc: Soul popular in northern England in the late 1960s and early 1970s, consisting primarily of lesser-known American artists in the mid-1960s copying the Motown Sound.

subgenres.name: Nova srpska scena
subgenres.desc: Serbian Alternative Rock scene subject to media interest in the '00s and early '10s; influenced by the Yugoslav New Wave and contemporary Indie Rock.

subgenres.name: Nova vanguarda paulistana
subgenres.desc: Southeastern Brazilian scene that emerged in the late 2000s based on experimentation with Samba and MPB styles.

subgenres.name: Novaya scena
subgenres.desc: Diverse Ukrainian avant-garde scene which emerged in the late 1980s.

subgenres.name: Novo Dub
subgenres.desc: Alternative Electronic scene incorporating various influences, predominant in France.

subgenres.name: No Wave
subgenres.desc: Underground, avant-garde, anti-art movement and music scene based in New York City around 1976-1980; commonly incorporates elements like dissonance, atonality, and stream-of-consciousness lyrics into various genres.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción
subgenres.desc: Latin American (Nueva canción latinoamericana) and Spanish (Nueva canción española) movement during the 1960s and 1970s.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción española
subgenres.desc: Arose in Spain in the 1960s, inspired in part by Nova cançó's reclaiming of Catalan regional identity, that spread across the country in regional variations.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción latinoamericana
subgenres.desc: Politically-charged messages associated with the rise of leftist social movements; striving for a renewal of traditional Latin and Hispanic American Folk Music expressions.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción chilena
subgenres.desc: Socially conscious style that sought to recover traditional Chilean folk music and fuse it with the broader musical trends of Latin America.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: Nueva ola
subgenres.desc: Latin American movement in the late 1950s and the 1960s incorporating assorted styles of Western popular music, primarily Rock & Roll and Pop.

subgenres.name: NWOBHM
subgenres.desc: Acronym for new wave of British Heavy Metal, which occurred in the late 1970s, taking some influence from Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Onkyo
subgenres.desc: Exploration of the physical traits of sound rather than music as expression.

subgenres.name: OPM
subgenres.desc: Filipino ballads prominent in the 1970s to early 1980s, combining the sentimentality, lush arrangements and vocal techniques of Kundiman with the instrumentations and rhythms of Manila Sound and Soft Rock.

subgenres.name: Paisley Underground
subgenres.desc: Emerged in Los Angeles in the early 1980s, featuring the energy of Power Pop and New Wave adorned with retro Psychedelia.

subgenres.name: Palm Desert Scene
subgenres.desc: Originated during the 1990s in Palm Desert, California, based in classic Hard Rock, Psychedelic Rock and the Alternative Rock sounds of the era.

subgenres.name: Pansy Craze
subgenres.desc: Period of popularity and visibility of LGBT+ and drag performers in US cities from the late 1920s to mid-1930s.

subgenres.name: Pop Kreatif
subgenres.desc: Scene from Indonesia made popular in the 1970s-80s; commonly features lush melodies and progressive arrangements borrowed from modern styles of Jazz, Pop Rock and R&B.

subgenres.name: Pop Yeh-Yeh
subgenres.desc: Blends Western Beat and Psychedelia styles with asli singing and melodies drawn from Malay Folk Music.

subgenres.name: Positive Punk
subgenres.desc: Early goth scene in London that grew out of the Anarcho-Punk movement and promoted themes of virtue and mysticism; commonly features wailing vocals, screeching guitars, prominent basslines, and eclectic drum patterns.

subgenres.name: P-Pop
subgenres.desc: Commercialized style from the Philippines, which served as the successor of Manila Sound and OPM, featuring various contemporary Western influences and primarily sung in Tagalog and English.

subgenres.name: Progg
subgenres.desc: Swedish movement centred around left-wing politics; emerged in the late 1960s and declined by the late 1970s due to internal divisions and the changing political climate.

subgenres.name: Psichedelia occulta italiana
subgenres.desc: Psychedelic scene from Italy with a distinctly brooding, dark atmosphere indebted to the country's media and a warped approach to Italian cultural memory.

subgenres.name: Psychsploitation
subgenres.desc: Short-lived genre seeking to capitalise on the popularity of Psychedelia in the 1960s, featuring quickly and cheaply recorded material played by session musicians and put out by budget labels.

subgenres.name: Sitarsploitation
subgenres.desc: Variant of Exotica capitalising on the surge of Western interest in Indian music in the late 1960s; featured melodies played on the sitar (or instruments imitating it) atop Easy Listening accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Q-Pop
subgenres.desc: Glamorous, catchy pop scene that emerged in Kazakhstan in the 2010s, inspired by K-Pop.

subgenres.name: Queercore
subgenres.desc: Movement mainly distinguished by its lyrical content expressing the viewpoints of the LGBTQ+ community, as well as promoting queer pride and unity.

subgenres.name: RABM
subgenres.desc: Leftist movement related to Crust Punk that variably espouses Marxist, environmentalist, and anarchist views.

subgenres.name: Red Dirt
subgenres.desc: Oklahoman and Texan acts descended from the Stillwater, Oklahoma independent Country scene of the 1980s.

subgenres.name: Revolution Summer
subgenres.desc: Collection of bands coalesced around the goal of rejuvenating the Washington DC Hardcore Punk scene in the summer of 1985, creating the early foundations for Post-Hardcore and Emo in the process.

subgenres.name: Riot Grrrl
subgenres.desc: Underground feminist Punk movement originating in the United States in the early 1990s.

subgenres.name: Road Rap
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the mid 2000s from Brixton and Peckham featuring abrasive tones, prominent Grime influence, and lyrics depicting circumstances of street gang violence in the UK.

subgenres.name: Rock barrial
subgenres.desc: Argentinian scene that started in the 1990s, inspired by Rock & Roll, Blues Rock, Roots Rock, and sometimes Hard Rock, directed to a national public and dismissing modern international trends, often featuring lyrics describing the life in low-income neighbourhoods.

subgenres.name: Rock in Opposition
subgenres.desc: Short-lived, international movement of ‘uncommercial’ Progressive Rock bands with left-wing politics; began its activity in early 1978 and faded out by the end of 1980, with 'reunion' festivals taking place from 2007 onwards.

subgenres.name: Rock radical vasco
subgenres.desc: Punk music movement developed around 1983 by Basque Country and Navarre bands with a crude and abrasive sound and a 'radical' stance against the system, religion, the police and the 'Spanish State'.

subgenres.name: Rock sónico
subgenres.desc: Argentinian scene emerging in the early 1990s, influenced by Shoegaze, Noise Pop, Neo-Psychedelia, and sometimes Downtempo or Slacker Rock, defined by noisy, reverb-soaked guitars, introspective lyrics and lo-fi production.

subgenres.name: Rock subterráneo
subgenres.desc: Peruvian artistic and countercultural movement that emerged after the return to democracy in 1980, diversifying into various Punk styles between 1983 and 1992.

subgenres.name: Rock triste
subgenres.desc: Brazilian Indie Rock movement popularized via the internet in mid 2010s commonly associated with styles such as Shoegaze, Midwest Emo, Dream Pop and relatives, iconic for its emphasis in melancholic and sad lyrics.

subgenres.name: Rock urbano español
subgenres.desc: Spanish scene originating in the mid-to-late 1970s that gained dominance with the end of the Francoist dictatorship and the end of censorship around lyrical topics like social issues.

subgenres.name: Rock urbano mexicano
subgenres.desc: Scene born in the mid-to-late 1980s mainly in the marginal areas of Mexico City that took elements from Blues Rock, Hard Rock and Folk Rock.

subgenres.name: Roman School
subgenres.desc: Composers of primarily Christian Liturgical Music active in Rome in the 16th and 17th centuries, developing a musically conservative compositional style seen as appropriate for church performance.

subgenres.name: Romanticism
subgenres.desc: Expressive and emotional qualities, especially in terms of melody.

subgenres.name: Grand opéra
subgenres.desc: French style characterized by its enlarged scope and sense of grandeur, with bigger orchestras and casts, and ornate sceneries and costumes.

subgenres.name: New German School
subgenres.desc: Mid-19th-century Romantic movement experimenting in harmonics and form and engaged in social issues.

subgenres.name: Romantische Oper
subgenres.desc: Early 19th century Germanic style of Opera influenced by German Folk Music and legends with a focus on fantasy, emotivity, heroic figures, and nationalism.

subgenres.name: Saint Petersburg School
subgenres.desc: Interrelated circles of 19th century Russian Western Classical Music composers focused on developing a distinctly Russian national style.

subgenres.name: Russemusikk
subgenres.desc: Norwegian music crafted for the country's graduate celebrations known as russefeiring, typically features melodic, danceable, energetic production, and party-oriented, explicit singing and rapping.

subgenres.name: San Diego Sound
subgenres.desc: Artistically diverse Punk and indie scene based around San Diego in the 1990s.

subgenres.name: San Francisco Sound
subgenres.desc: Influential Psychedelic Rock scene that developed out of Folk Rock in the mid 1960s; often emphasized atypical chord progressions and instrumental improvisation in the form of roving basslines and “cross-talking” guitars.

subgenres.name: Haight-Ashbury Scene
subgenres.desc: Influential Psychedelic Rock scene which emerged by summer 1966 in the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco and peaked in terms of notoriety by summer 1967, coinciding with a massive influx of visitors, media interest, and ensuing commercialisation.

subgenres.name: Scene
subgenres.desc: Youth subculture popularized in the 2000s via MySpace, spanning Metalcore, Pop Punk, Post-Hardcore, and related genres; associated with androgynous hairstyles, mall-sourced fashion, the Warped Tour festival circuit, and varied crossover with Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Happy Rock
subgenres.desc: Late 2000s Brazilian movement made as a response against Emo with a bright aesthetic, heavy use of electronic instruments and distorted vocals.

subgenres.name: Scottish Folk Revival
subgenres.desc: Revival of Scottish Folk Music which began around 1950 in Scotland and stagnated in the early 1970s.

subgenres.name: Seapunk
subgenres.desc: Short-lived early 2010s internet movement associated with oceanic imagery and computer graphics, deriving into vivid fashion trends, often incorporating aquatic elements into Electronic styles and visual aesthetics as well as influences by prominent tropes of 1990s rave culture.

subgenres.name: Second British Folk Revival
subgenres.desc: Revival of Folk music in the United Kingdom which began at the end of the Second World War, peaked in the early-to-mid 1970s, and lost wider relevance by the end of the decade.

subgenres.name: Second Viennese School
subgenres.desc: Influential circle of composers of very late Romanticism and Modern Classical who developed Expressionism and Serialism.

subgenres.name: Second Wave of Detroit Techno
subgenres.desc: Transformative 1990s era of the Detroit Techno scene in Detroit, with harsher sounds and often militantly anti-corporate attitude.

subgenres.name: Shibuya-kei
subgenres.desc: Eclectic scene emerging from the Shibuya district of Tokyo near the end of the 1980s; often borrows kitschy, retro-inspired aesthetics alongside diverse musical influences from Indie Pop, 1960s Pop and Easy Listening, Jazz, and Electronic styles.

subgenres.name: Akishibu-kei
subgenres.desc: Otaku inclined update of the style pioneered by the Shibuya-kei scene, mixed with J-Pop and often tied to Anime and Video Game Music.

subgenres.name: Picopop
subgenres.desc: Originated in the early 2000s as an offshoot of the Japanese Shibuya-kei movement when artists introduced more prominent "bleepy" electronic elements and faster tempos.

subgenres.name: Shimokita-kei
subgenres.desc: Japanese style closely related to the Shimokitazawa indie scene, featuring Pop-informed songwriting, melodic guitar leads, expressive vocals, and often loud, prominent overdriven guitars.

subgenres.name: Siberian Punk
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the late 1980s, often blending the noisy, abrasive sound of Garage Punk and Post-Punk with radical anti-totalitarian lyrics drawing from British Punk influences.

subgenres.name: SoundClown
subgenres.desc: Scene focused on comedic, often ironic edits of pre-existing music, popular on SoundCloud in the mid-2010s.

subgenres.name: Southern Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Hip Hop from artists based in the Southern region of the United States.

subgenres.name: South Florida SoundCloud Rap
subgenres.desc: Mid-to-late 2010s Hip Hop scene noted for its use of internet platform SoundCloud to promote and distribute music, as well as lo-fi production and transgressive approaches to rapping.

subgenres.name: Sovietwave
subgenres.desc: Scene of Synthwave that emerged in the early 2010s, taking its inspiration from Soviet Electronic electronic music and Soviet pop.

subgenres.name: Straight Edge
subgenres.desc: Developed in the early 1980s DC Hardcore Punk scene, promoting abstinence from the use of substances such as alcohol, tobacco, and other drugs.

subgenres.name: Krishnacore
subgenres.desc: Straight Edge subculture that spawned from the New York Hardcore scene, promoting the Hare Krishna movement.

subgenres.name: Vegan Straight Edge
subgenres.desc: Espouses veganism, environmentalism, and animal liberation causes.

subgenres.name: H8000
subgenres.desc: Belgian Hardcore [Punk] scene centered in West Flanders, famed for its Vegan Straight Edge Metalcore.

subgenres.name: Hardline
subgenres.desc: Militant outgrowth of Vegan Straight Edge influenced by deep ecology.

subgenres.name: Youth Crew
