subgenres.desc: Hardcore Punk subculture that emerged in the mid-1980s New York Hardcore scene, distinguished by its optimistic and moralistic outlook and close ties to Straight Edge.

subgenres.name: Sunset Strip Glam Metal
subgenres.desc: 1980s Glam Metal scene based in West Hollywood, California, United States.

subgenres.name: Swing Revival
subgenres.desc: Born out of 1990s alternative music; sometimes incorporating elements from newer genres such as Rockabilly, Ska, and Punk Rock.

subgenres.name: Taqwacore
subgenres.desc: Punk subculture that emerged in the United States during the early 2000s, exploring Islam, its culture, and interpretations.

subgenres.name: Teutonic Thrash Metal
subgenres.desc: Influential German Thrash Metal scene originating in the early 1980s.

subgenres.name: Texas Psychedelia
subgenres.desc: Influential, pioneering Psychedelic Rock scene active primarily in the mid- to late 1960s that grew out of the Texas Garage Rock scene.

subgenres.name: The Batcave
subgenres.desc: Foundational Gothic Rock scene in the early to mid-1980s, centered on the Batcave club nights held in Soho, London.

subgenres.name: The Wave
subgenres.desc: Group of American Post-Hardcore bands in the 2010s performing an aggressive style of '90s-inspired music in the wake of Emo-Pop's waning popularity.

subgenres.name: Tontipop
subgenres.desc: Spanish scene known for its exuberant, child-like sound drawing directly from British Twee Pop, as well as Yé-yé, Bubblegum, and Synthpop.

subgenres.name: T-Pop
subgenres.desc: Mainstream Pop from Thailand made popular since the early 1980s, predominantly sung in Central Thai dialect and featuring westernized compositions ranging within various styles.

subgenres.name: Tropicália
subgenres.desc: Blends Brazilian popular styles with the influence of Anglo-American Psychedelia; emerged as part of Brazil's late-1960s counterculture.

subgenres.name: Tropicanibalismo
subgenres.desc: Colombian scene born in the early 2000s with the intention of reinventing Colombian coastal music, from a more current and experimental approach.

subgenres.name: Trova rosarina
subgenres.desc: 1970s Argentine movement of socially conscious Singer-Songwriters from Rosario.

subgenres.name: Udigrudi
subgenres.desc: Movement that emerged in the Brazilian city of Recife during the 1970s that combines psychedelic elements with music of Northeastern Brazil.

subgenres.name: UK82
subgenres.desc: UK scene that occurred during the early 1980s, consisting of developing hardcore styles such as early Street Punk and D-Beat bands.

subgenres.name: UK Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Scene of the United Kingdom, influenced by American rap.

subgenres.name: Ultra
subgenres.desc: Late 1970s and 1980s Dutch DIY scene of musicians influenced by Post-Punk and experimental Electronic music.

subgenres.name: Urban Grooves
subgenres.desc: Scene of Zimbabwean music that emerged in the 2000s, primarily inspired by popular American and European music of the time mixed with local elements.

subgenres.name: Vanguarda paulista
subgenres.desc: Brazilian cultural movement that began in the city of São Paulo and lasted from 1979 to 1985; united a variety of artists who had no access to major labels due to their experimental, avant-garde approach to MPB.

subgenres.name: Vietnamese New Wave
subgenres.desc: Youth culture popularized within the Vietnamese American diaspora in the 1980s, known for its stylish fashion sense and musically led by Euro-Disco and Dance-Pop covers.

subgenres.name: Visual kei
subgenres.desc: Fashion-oriented styles that take influence from Gothic Rock, Glam Rock, and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: Kote kei
subgenres.desc: Beginning in the mid-1990s, featuring goth-inspired, androgynous and over-the-top outfits meant to evoke a sense of otherworldliness, often paired with aggressive instrumentation, decadent and shocking lyrics, as well as harsh and unusual vocals.

subgenres.name: Nagoya kei
subgenres.desc: Nagoya-based scene lasting though the 1990s and early 2000s; characterized by a simpler and gloomier visual presentation along with a darker, heavy sound inspired by Post-Punk, Gothic Rock and Heavy Metal.

subgenres.name: Soft Visual
subgenres.desc: Starting in the 1990s, featuring more toned-down "classy" and "casual"-style outfits with a natural style of makeup, along with more pop-oriented songwriting, contrasting the darkness of contemporary styles of Visual kei.

subgenres.name: Vixa
subgenres.desc: Polish club scene, derived from various House subgenres and focused on bootleg remixes of popular songs

subgenres.name: Vocaloid Scene
subgenres.desc: Associated with the online scene centered around use of character-focused vocal synthesis software such as Vocaloid or UTAU, marketed specifically to fans, and often accompanied by animated music videos featuring the characters.

subgenres.name: Utaite
subgenres.desc: Amateur online singers who primarily perform covers of Vocaloid and Anime music, often under a pseudonymous identity.

subgenres.name: Voëlvry Movement
subgenres.desc: Anti-apartheid songwriting movement in the Afrikaans language.

subgenres.name: V-Pop
subgenres.desc: Western-sounding Pop with Vietnamese lyrics, or pop that borrows sounds from popular Vietnamese genres and re-imagines them with more accessible and/or upbeat structures.

subgenres.name: Warez Scene
subgenres.desc: Underground online subculture of piracy groups specializing in obtaining, cracking, and distributing digital media.

subgenres.name: West Coast Hip Hop
subgenres.desc: Artists who originate from the West Coast region of the United States.

subgenres.name: West Coast Sound of Holland
subgenres.desc: Underground scene of primarily Techno and Electro emphasizing a stripped-down, throwback sound.

subgenres.name: West Side Sound
subgenres.desc: Created in the 1950s by working-class Mexican-American teenagers in San Antonio, Texas, as a result of significant stylistic cross-pollination and an accommodating racial climate; features prominent tenor sax sections and Hammond organs.

subgenres.name: Windmill Scene
subgenres.desc: Eclectic scene built around The Windmill pub in Brixton that emerged in the 2010s; commonly associated with erratic Post-Punk-inspired instrumentation and spoken vocals.

subgenres.name: Wizard Rock
subgenres.desc: Rock-oriented Harry Potter fan music scene.

subgenres.name: Women's Music Movement
subgenres.desc: Movement and network of female artists and music professionals, most active in America in the 1970s, associated with the underground women's separatist (and particularly lesbian separatist) branches of feminism.

subgenres.name: Xibei feng
subgenres.desc: Blends Traditional Folk Music elements from northwestern China with Western Rock, Pop, Contemporary Folk, and other styles, characterized by its rugged and bold style.

subgenres.name: Yass
subgenres.desc: Coined in the early 1990s by a group of Polish Avant-Garde Jazz musicians to describe their cross-genre, often arrhythmic, improvised sound.

subgenres.name: YTPMV
subgenres.desc: Internet-based musical remixes which sequence small samples from audiovisual material as a method of composition, usually with a humorous or memetic approach.

subgenres.name: OtoMAD
subgenres.desc: Music-driven remixes that take heavy inspiration from Japanese internet culture.

subgenres.name: Yugoslav New Wave
subgenres.desc: Punk and New Wave-influenced scene in late-1970s and early '80s Yugoslavia.

subgenres.name: Zamrock
subgenres.desc: Developed in the Copperbelt region of Zambia in the 1970s, characterized by its blend of local sounds with influence from Funk, Hard Rock, and Blues Rock.

subgenres.name: Zimdancehall
subgenres.desc: Zimbabwean form of Dancehall that emerged in the 2000s.

name: Singer-Songwriter
desc: Heavily focused on lyrics and songwriting, with musical accompaniment tending to take lower precedence.

subgenres.name: Avtorskaya pesnya
subgenres.desc: Originating in the Soviet Union taking cues from forms of Russian Romance and Russian poetry with the main focus on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Bard Rock
subgenres.desc: Mixes Rock music and styles with Avtorskaya pesnya.

subgenres.name: Canzone d'autore
subgenres.desc: Music of the Italian Singer-Songwriters that emerged in the 1960s and early 1970s, initially influenced by French Chanson with the addition of uniquely Italian sensibilities.

subgenres.name: Chanson à texte
subgenres.desc: French-language songs emphasising sophisticated and poetic lyricism.

subgenres.name: Euskal kantagintza berria
subgenres.desc: Basque genre born during the 1960s inspired by Nova cançó and Chanson.

subgenres.name: Kleinkunst
subgenres.desc: Dutch-language genre from the Netherlands and Flanders with influences from Cabaret, protest songs, Chanson, and folk.

subgenres.name: Liedermacher
subgenres.desc: German style having its origins in literature and theatre rather than American forms like Blues or Rock.

subgenres.name: Música de intervenção
subgenres.desc: Wave of Portuguese singer-songwriters in the 1960s and 1970s who agitated against the Estado Novo regime and the colonial war waged by Portugal against national liberation fronts.

subgenres.name: Nova cançó
subgenres.desc: Arose in Catalonia during the Franco dictatorship, sung in Catalan as a way to resist restrictions placed on regional languages in Spain and retain a regional identity.

subgenres.name: Nòva cançon
subgenres.desc: Arose in the Occitania region of southern France, sung in the Occitan language as a way to preserve their culture and resist forced usage of French.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción
subgenres.desc: Latin American (Nueva canción latinoamericana) and Spanish (Nueva canción española) movement during the 1960s and 1970s.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción española
subgenres.desc: Arose in Spain in the 1960s, inspired in part by Nova cançó's reclaiming of Catalan regional identity, that spread across the country in regional variations.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción latinoamericana
subgenres.desc: Politically-charged messages associated with the rise of leftist social movements; striving for a renewal of traditional Latin and Hispanic American Folk Music expressions.

subgenres.name: Nueva canción chilena
subgenres.desc: Socially conscious style that sought to recover traditional Chilean folk music and fuse it with the broader musical trends of Latin America.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

subgenres.name: Nuevo Cancionero
subgenres.desc: Musical-literary movement in Argentina that aimed to reevaluate and reinvigorate "la música popular nativa" (native popular music) and to be the voice of poor and marginalized Argentines.

subgenres.name: Poezja śpiewana
subgenres.desc: Polish sung poetry; the poem is the centerpiece of a song, often with sparse instrumental accompaniment.

subgenres.name: Trova
subgenres.desc: One of the most ancient expressions of Cuban Music, based around lone Singer-Songwriters who use nothing but a guitar as their preferred accompaniment and place emphasis on lyrics.

subgenres.name: Nueva trova
subgenres.desc: Found inspiration in the 1950s Cuban Revolution and had the intention of introducing new musical ideas to the original Trova.

name: Spoken Word
desc: Usually unaccompanied vocal readings.

subgenres.name: Fairy Tales
subgenres.desc: Recorded for children with or without background music.

subgenres.name: Folktales
subgenres.desc: Traditional stories passed down throughout many generations.

subgenres.name: Guided Meditation
subgenres.desc: Practice wherein an instructor guides the listener through the process of meditation throughout a session.

subgenres.name: Interview
subgenres.desc: Recording of a specific person/s during a formal conversation arranged for historical archiving or media broadcast, often in a question and answer format in which the interviewee shares their views and personal anecdotes with the audience.

subgenres.name: Lectures
subgenres.desc: Oral presentation with the intention to educate the audience on a specific topic.

subgenres.name: Poetry
subgenres.desc: Encompasses many forms of literature that use style and rhythm to evoke ideas and emotions further than the prosaic meaning of the literature itself.

subgenres.name: Beat Poetry
subgenres.desc: Stream-of-consciousness Poetry originating with the Beats in the 1950s.

subgenres.name: Cowboy Poetry
subgenres.desc: Descended from the oral traditions of cowboys and ranchers, written with traditional use of rhyme and meter, using humor and slang, and primarily concerning the cowboy profession, lifestyle, and legacy.

subgenres.name: Dub Poetry
subgenres.desc: Poetry with Dub and Reggae backing rhythms, originating in Jamaica in the 1970s.

subgenres.name: Jazz Poetry
subgenres.desc: Emerged in the 1920s, incorporating the style and rhythms of Jazz as both art forms spread throughout African-American communities in the United States.

subgenres.name: Punk Poetry
subgenres.desc: Fast and rhythmic vocal delivery of political or satirical themes; frequently backed by Post-Punk or Minimal Wave instrumentation.

subgenres.name: Slam Poetry
subgenres.desc: Developed in the US during the late 1980s and early 1990s with the growing popularity of poetry slams, a form of poetry competition in which competing performers recite poems in front of a crowd.

subgenres.name: Sound Poetry
subgenres.desc: Emphasis is placed upon phonetics and the sounds of syllables rather than the meaning of the words themselves.

subgenres.name: Radio Drama
subgenres.desc: Narrative storytelling performed by voice actors and produced for radio broadcasting or published on audio media such as tapes or CDs.

subgenres.name: Speeches
subgenres.desc: Rhetorical acts performed publicly wherein a speaker typically monologues around a particular topic.

subgenres.name: Sermons
subgenres.desc: Religious oral addresses delivered with the intent to uplift or educate an audience.

subgenres.name: Stand-Up Comedy
subgenres.desc: Comedy where the performer speaks directly to their intended audience, with origins beginning in the late 19th century.
